**Provider error classification.** Retrying a permanent failure spends budget forever on a token that will never work; dead-lettering a transient one loses a notification that would have succeeded on the next attempt. Both mistakes come from treating the response as a boolean.

| Status class | Examples | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **2xx accepted** | 200, 202 | mark Delivered, await webhook for a terminal state where the channel has one |
| **429 throttled** | rate-limited | requeue after the `Retry-After` interval, ignoring your own backoff curve |
| **5xx server error** | provider degraded | jittered exponential backoff, up to the attempt budget |
| **4xx permanent, bad token** | 410 Gone (APNs), `UNREGISTERED` (FCM) | mark Failed and prune the token from the user's device list |
| **4xx permanent, bad payload** | 400, 413 | mark Failed and alert; this is a code bug, not bad data |
| **4xx auth** | 403 | mark Failed and page; a cert has expired and every send on this channel is failing |

**The retry budget, and why it stops.** Four attempts at 30 seconds, 5 minutes and 1 hour, then the dead-letter queue. Jitter every interval (`delay = base × 2^attempt × random(0.5, 1.5)`), because an unjittered curve synchronises: when APNs returns from a 10-minute outage, every message queued during it retries in the same instant and re-throttles the provider you were waiting for. Honour `Retry-After` over your own curve, since the provider knows when its throttle resets and ignoring the hint extends it. The reason the budget ends at roughly an hour is not cost, it is staleness: a notification about a delivery that already arrived is worse than no notification, so past the budget the right action is to record the failure and let a human look at the DLQ, never to keep trying.

**What none of this protects against** is the caller sending two logically different requests for the same event, with different idempotency keys, because two services both decided to notify. No hop above catches that, since to the system they are two notifications. It is caught by attribution in the status store and by looking at per-user send rate, which is one more reason the per-user gate belongs in front of the queues.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Broadcast against the provider ceiling.** A full-base send is 15M messages, 1.5 times a normal day, arriving as one API call. *Mitigation:* broadcasts go through a batch path that writes to the queue at a paced rate, never through the synchronous API, and are smeared over 60 minutes to land at 4,200/s against a ~10k/s push ceiling. On FCM, the batch endpoint takes up to 500 tokens per call with per-token errors in the response body, which collapses the request count by 500x for the same message rate. Note the smear window is set by the ceiling, so if transactional traffic grows the window has to widen with it.
- **Provider outage.** APNs or SES can be unavailable for tens of minutes. *Mitigation:* a circuit breaker per provider on error rate; when it trips the worker stops consuming so the queue backs up safely rather than burning the retry budget. Cross-channel fallback (push fails, so send email) is available for high-priority traffic only, and it interacts with the per-user gate: the fallback must consume the same rate-limit budget, or an outage becomes a way to double every user's notification count.
- **Stale device tokens.** Users uninstall and the token stays in the table until a send returns 410 or `UNREGISTERED`, so every broadcast pays for devices that no longer exist. *Mitigation:* prune on the permanent-failure response as it arrives, and once a week send a silent push to tokens idle for 90 days and prune the ones that error. At 15M tokens a few percent of dead weight is hundreds of thousands of wasted sends per broadcast.
- **Publisher lag between outbox and queue.** A slow or stuck publisher leaves messages in the outbox table while the queue reads empty and the workers idle, which every standard queue-depth alert reports as healthy. *Mitigation:* graph outbox depth and publisher lag as first-class metrics, alert when outbox depth grows while worker utilisation is low, and shard the outbox so publisher instances read disjoint ranges in parallel.
- **Template rendering on the send path.** Rendering localised content per notification adds 10 to 50ms, which is invisible at 120/s and is 4,200 concurrent renders during a broadcast. *Mitigation:* pre-render the static shell per `(template_id, locale)` when the template is published and substitute only the per-user variables at send time. Per-user values cannot be pre-rendered by definition, so the split has to be explicit in the template format rather than assumed.
- **Status store write volume.** Every attempt writes, so 10M sends a day at four possible attempts is a write-heavy workload against a store that is read almost never. *Mitigation:* keep 7 days hot for the status API and archive the rest to columnar files, and batch attempt writes per worker poll rather than one round trip per attempt.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upstream | APNs or FCM outage | sustained 5xx rate from worker calls | circuit breaker per provider; the queue backs up safely at 7-day retention; cross-channel fallback for high-priority traffic only |
| Upstream | SES bounce rate trips an account-level send pause | account-level error on every send | bounce and complaint webhook consumer prunes dead recipients continuously; keep the standby email provider warm so failover does not start cold |
| Crash | Ingestion node lost mid-write | DB committed but nothing enqueued | outbox row commits in the same transaction; the publisher replays unpublished rows after restart |
| Crash | Worker dies after the provider call, before the offset commit | redelivery of an already-sent message | `sent:{notif_id}` check before the provider call narrows the window; `apns-id` lets the provider drop what does slip through |
| Network | Partition between workers and provider | provider call timeouts | jittered backoff, circuit-break after threshold, and a bounded attempt budget so a partitioned provider cannot consume the fleet |
| Correctness | Caller omits `idempotency_key` and retries | duplicate notifications reaching users | the key is a required field and requests without it are rejected at the contract boundary, not defaulted |
| Correctness | Preference change lands after the message is queued | user receives a notification seconds after opting out | worker re-checks preferences at dequeue as a second gate; the cost is one cache read per send |
| Resource | Broadcast accepted synchronously | queue depth jumps to 15M in seconds | broadcasts route to the batch path only; the synchronous API rejects segment-wide targets |
| Resource | Stale device tokens accumulate | rising 410 and `UNREGISTERED` rate per broadcast | prune on permanent failure as it happens; weekly silent push to tokens idle 90 days |

**Unresolved**

**Delivery and display are different things, and we can only measure the first.** A 200 from APNs means Apple accepted the message. The device may be off for two days and the notification silently expires; it may arrive and sit unread in a tray of forty others; the user may have muted the app at the OS level, which is invisible to us because it looks identical to successful delivery. Every SLO in this document is really an acceptance SLO wearing a delivery label. The partial fix is client-side receipts, where the app posts back when a notification is rendered or opened, which we would do and which biases hard: it only reports from users engaged enough to have the app installed and running, exactly the users least at risk. So the number we would most like, the fraction of intended recipients who actually saw it, is not obtainable, and the honest position is to publish acceptance rate and open rate as two separate metrics rather than to compute a delivery rate that implies more than it knows.

**The per-user rate limit is enforced at the wrong granularity, and fixing it properly conflicts with fan-out.** The token bucket sits at the gate, before expansion into channels and devices, so a cap of five per hour means five logical notifications. A user with push and email enabled and two devices receives up to fifteen physical interruptions in that hour, and the one who feels over-notified is counting interruptions, not logical sends. Moving the bucket after expansion sounds like the fix and is not: the message has already been persisted and enqueued by then, so a channel-level refusal means throwing away work the outbox has already guaranteed, and it makes the cap non-deterministic in a way users will notice, since which channel gets dropped depends on which worker happens to dequeue first. What we actually do is run separate buckets per channel at the gate and accept that the user-facing total is the sum rather than a single number. Broadcast traffic gets its own bucket for the same reason, which stops a marketing send from consuming a user's transactional budget but means the guarantee is "five of these and two of those" rather than a number anyone can explain in a settings screen.

**Nothing coordinates across a user's devices.** A user with a phone, a tablet and a watch is buzzed three times for one event and dismisses it three times. `apns-collapse-id` coalesces repeated sends within one device, not across devices, and there is no protocol hop that reports "the human has seen this". The available mechanism is a client-side dismiss that calls our API, after which we send a silent push withdrawing the notification on that user's other devices, and it is best-effort by construction: the other devices have to be online and awake to act on it, the withdrawal is itself a push subject to the same acceptance-not-delivery gap, and on some platforms a delivered notification cannot be programmatically removed at all. We would build it because it helps in the common case where the devices are all online, and we would not describe it as solving the problem. The clean solution requires the OS to tell us what the user saw, and it does not.
#### Drill questions
1. APNs is down for 30 minutes. What happens?
2. A "send to every user" broadcast lands at 17:00. How do you not melt the providers?
3. How do you prevent duplicate notifications when a client retries on a flaky network?
4. A user opts out. How fast does that propagate?
5. How do you guarantee delivery confirmation?
6. How do you observe and alert on this system?
7. Walk through the delivery state machine. What triggers each transition?
8. How do you implement true exactly-once delivery?
9. A user has 5 devices. How do you fan out to all of them?
10. A user in the EU opts out at 12:01 and ingestion already enqueued a notification at 12:00. What happens?
11. How do you handle scheduled notifications ("send at 9am local time tomorrow")?
12. How do you handle templating and i18n without paying render cost on every send?
13. A user is about to receive their sixth notification this hour. What happens to it, and who decided that?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Circuit breaker opens on repeated failures; the push queue keeps buffering (Kafka retains for days). When APNs recovers, workers drain backlog with rate limiting. *If pushed:* if backlog grows past SLA, fall back to alt channel (push → email) for high-priority notifs; drop low-priority that's already stale.

2. Smear send time across a window (e.g., 30 minutes); the broadcast becomes a stream of small batches into the per-channel queue. Workers naturally pace at provider rate limits. *If pushed:* per-region smearing aligned to user timezones (don't send "Good morning" at 3am locally); stage broadcasts via batch worker, not the synchronous API.

3. A mandatory `idempotency_key` per request, cached as `(caller_id, key) -> notif_id` in Redis for 24h. The retry returns the original ID and nothing is re-sent. The write has to be a conditional insert, not a read then a write, or two concurrent retries both miss and both create a notification. *If pushed:* dedup has to hold inside the worker too, since a crash after the provider call and before the offset commit causes redelivery. Check a `sent:{notif_id}` key before calling, and pass `apns-id` so the provider drops what still slips through. (`apns-collapse-id` is display coalescing, a different feature.)

4. The preference check happens at ingestion, before queueing. Preferences are cached in Redis with a 1-minute TTL and writes invalidate via pub/sub, so the normal propagation is under a second. *If pushed:* a message already in the queue is checked again at worker dequeue, which costs one extra cache read per send and closes the window for users who opted out after enqueue.

5. You do not. You guarantee "accepted by the provider". APNs and FCM return per-message status synchronously; SES and Twilio accept, then post the final state to a webhook minutes later. None of them tells you a human saw it. *If pushed:* the closest thing to display proof is an in-app receipt posted by the client on render, and it is biased toward engaged users, so publish acceptance rate and open rate separately rather than multiplying them into a "delivery rate". Meanwhile consume the error responses and prune dead tokens so the next send does not pay for them.

6. Track everything per channel, because failures cluster by provider: queue depth, provider call latency p99, error rate broken out by status class (4xx permanent, 4xx auth, 5xx and 429 mean four different things), and DLQ growth. Page on DLQ growth and on a per-channel SLO breach. *If pushed:* two metrics that are easy to miss. Publisher lag from the outbox, because a stalled publisher presents as an empty queue and idle workers, which every depth-based alert calls healthy. And a synthetic notification through each channel every minute into a test account, which detects provider degradation before users do.

7. `Queued` to `Attempting`: a worker dequeues. `Attempting` to `Delivered`: 2xx. `Attempting` to `Retry`: 5xx, 429, or a network error, and the backoff timer starts. `Attempting` to `Failed`: a permanent 4xx (410 invalid token, 403 auth, 413 too large). `Retry` to `Attempting`: backoff elapsed. `Retry` to `DeadLetter`: the attempt budget of four is exhausted. `Delivered` to `Confirmed`: a webhook reports terminal success. `Delivered` to `Bounced`: a webhook reports the recipient unreachable, and the token is pruned. *If pushed:* state is persisted on every transition, keyed on `notif_id`, so a worker restart resumes from durable state. Deriving state from queue position breaks the moment a message is redelivered.

8. You cannot, fully. The achievable shape is at-least-once with dedup at four hops, which is observably exactly-once: the caller's idempotency key, the outbox between database and queue, a recently-sent set inside the worker, and the provider's own dedup id (`apns-id` on APNs, `message_id` on FCM). *If pushed:* say where it leaks. Hop three is not airtight, because the crash can land between the provider returning 200 and the dedup key being written, and hop five, provider to device, is not yours at all. Also: `apns-collapse-id` is display coalescing, not duplicate suppression, and conflating them is the usual tell.

9. At ingestion, expand `(user_id, channel)` into one message per registered device token and enqueue each separately. Each carries its own `notif_id` so per-device dedup and retry are independent and one stale token does not block the other four. *If pushed:* FCM's batch endpoint takes up to 500 tokens in one HTTP call with per-token errors in the response body, which matters for broadcasts rather than for one user's five devices. And note the fan-out interacts with the rate limiter: five devices is five interruptions against a cap that counts logical sends.

10. The pre-queue check missed it, because of the lag between the preference write and the ingestion cache invalidating. The worker re-checks at dequeue as a second gate, one cache read, which blocks the send. *If pushed:* for GDPR and CCPA the second check usually has to be the authoritative one, so cache preferences at the worker tier with a 10-second TTL and accept the extra load, since the cost of getting this wrong is regulatory rather than operational.

11. Persist `(notif_id, send_at_ts, payload)` to a scheduled-jobs table partitioned by hour bucket. A scheduler polls the next bucket every 10 seconds and enqueues mature jobs onto the normal channel queues, after which the live retry and dedup path takes over unchanged. Quiet hours and per-user timezone are resolved at schedule time rather than dispatch time, so the scheduler only compares `now >= send_at_ts`. *If pushed:* at millions of scheduled jobs, a sorted set keyed by epoch timestamp gives O(log N) next-due lookups; for horizons months out, keep them in durable storage and lazy-load only the next 24 hours into memory.

12. Templates are versioned objects (Mustache or Liquid), keyed by `(template_id, locale)`. Authoring writes a base template plus per-locale translations, and a render pipeline pre-renders the variant matrix (`welcome × {en,es,fr,ja}`) into a render cache when the template is published, so send-time work collapses to variable substitution in under a millisecond. Locale fallback chain: requested locale, then language family (`en-GB` to `en`), then default. *If pushed:* per-user dynamic content such as names and balances cannot be pre-rendered, so templates split into a static shell plus dynamic slots and only the slots are substituted at send time; the layout and translation work stays on the cold path.

13. It is held, not dropped. The per-user token bucket at the gate is empty, so unless the notification carries a bypass flag for a transactional or security category, it goes to a digest buffer and is delivered as one combined notification at the next allowed slot. The decision belongs to the gate, before the message reaches a channel queue, because once it is queued the only remaining question is when to send. *If pushed:* the interesting failure is bypass inflation. Every team believes their notification is transactional, so if the bypass list is not centrally owned and audited it grows until the cap protects nobody. The usable rule is to treat any category above roughly 20% bypass traffic as evidence the classification has drifted, and to review it against whether the notification is something the user must act on within minutes.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, size it and say what it is not.** Open by taking throughput off the table: 10M sends a day is 120 a second, so this is not a scale problem and nothing in the next forty minutes should be about partitioning. Then name the two things it is: a delivery guarantee against providers you do not control, and restraint, because the binding constraint is how much a person will tolerate before muting you. Ask the three questions that change the answer: which channels, is a duplicate worse than a miss (and note the answer differs by channel), and does anything broadcast to the whole base. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine.** Five boxes: callers, one ingestion service, a per-user gate, one queue per channel, workers per provider. Say the two placement rules as you draw the arrows, because they carry the design. The gate sits *before* the queues, since once a message is queued the only decision left is when to send it. The queues are *per channel*, because providers fail independently and one shared backlog means an APNs bad hour stops email. Then say the guarantee out loud in one sentence: at-least-once with dedup, which is observably exactly-once and is not the same claim. Add the outbox as a small box inside ingestion rather than a new service, and move on.

**15-35, the drill.** This is the interview, so protect it and split it two ways. First the guarantee: walk the four hops (caller to ingestion, ingestion to queue, queue to worker, worker to provider), say what suppresses duplicates at each, and volunteer that hop three leaks because the crash can land between the provider returning and the dedup key being written. Then say the hop you cannot cover at all is provider to device, so every delivery number is an acceptance number. Second, and give it equal time because most candidates give it none, the gate: preferences, quiet hours in the recipient's timezone, five per hour with a digest above that, and a bypass list for transactional categories that is centrally owned or it will swallow everything. Bring the broadcast in here rather than as a footnote: 15M messages is 1.5 days of traffic in one call, smeared over 60 minutes to hit 4,200/s against a 10k/s ceiling, staged through a batch path and never the synchronous API. Keep provider error classification as a one-liner you can expand: retry 5xx and 429 honouring `Retry-After`, prune the token on 410, page on 403.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the gaps first, since they are found anyway: acceptance is not display and client receipts are biased toward engaged users; the rate limit counts logical sends rather than the interruptions the user actually feels; nothing coordinates across a user's three devices. Then two minutes of operations: DLQ growth and per-channel error rate by status class as the pages, publisher lag graphed separately from queue depth because a stalled publisher looks like a healthy queue, and a synthetic notification per channel per minute as the canary.

Cut first: multi-region and DR, which is a generic answer here and changes nothing about the design; then templating and localisation, which is real work and is a different system; then the state machine drawn out in full, since naming the transitions is enough and the diagram eats five minutes. Never cut: the guarantee and its four hops, the per-user gate, and the broadcast arithmetic.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **notifications** (wide-column store partitioned by user_id):
  `(user_id, notif_id, template_id, channels, state, attempts, created_at)`
- **prefs** (transactional store): `(user_id, channel, enabled, quiet_hours)`
- **templates** (object store + in-memory KV cache): Mustache/Liquid templates with i18n
- **dedupe** (in-memory KV cache): `idempotency_key → notif_id`, TTL 24h

**API contract**

```
POST /notify
  body: {
    user_id | user_segment,
    template_id,
    params: {...},
    channels: [push, email],
    priority: high|normal,
    idempotency_key
  }
  → { notification_id, status: queued }

GET /notifications/{id} → { state, attempts, delivered_at }
```

**Observability**

- **`notif.delivery_latency_p99`**: time from API accept to provider 2xx, emitted by the worker. Alert above 30s for high-priority, above 5min for normal-priority.
- **`notif.queue_depth_per_channel`**: messages awaiting send, per channel, emitted by the broker. Alert on sustained growth for 15min, which means worker undercapacity or provider degradation.
- **`notif.outbox_publisher_lag`**: age of the oldest unpublished outbox row, emitted by the publisher. The metric that catches the failure queue depth cannot see, since a stalled publisher looks like an empty queue.
- **`notif.dlq_size`**: dead-letter messages per channel, emitted by the broker. Page on growth, which always means a persistent failure pattern rather than a blip.
- **`notif.provider_error_rate_by_class`**: 4xx permanent, 4xx auth, 5xx and 429 broken out per provider, emitted by the worker. Page on auth, since an expired cert blocks every send on that channel; alert on sustained 429, which is a rate-limit misconfiguration.
- **`notif.gate_suppression_rate`**: fraction of accepted requests held by quiet hours, preferences or the rate limiter, emitted by the gate, split by category. A drop means bypass flags are spreading; a spike means a team has started sending far more than it used to.
- **`notif.dedup_hit_rate`**: fraction of requests suppressed by idempotency key, emitted by ingestion. A sudden drop signals a client SDK regression that stopped sending keys.
- **`notif.bounce_prune_rate`**: stale tokens removed per day from bounce webhooks, emitted by the webhook consumer. Alert above 5%/day, which points at a flagged domain or a damaged sender reputation.
- **SLOs:** high-priority delivery p99 < 30s end-to-end (ingestion to provider 2xx), normal-priority p99 < 5min, availability 99.95% per channel (each provider has its own outage profile; account for provider SLAs).

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** active-active across regions for ingestion (any region accepts requests, geo-routed to nearest); active-passive for shared state (idempotency cache, prefs) with cross-region async replication. Per-region channel queues drain to provider endpoints in the same region (APNs/FCM are global from the client's POV but worker placement affects RTT to provider edge).
- **RTO / RPO:** RTO 1min for ingestion failover (geo-DNS pulls unhealthy region); RTO 5min for queue/worker recovery in standby region. RPO < 60s of in-flight messages (durable Kafka retains; replay from outbox bridges any gap).
- **Failover trigger & cadence:** automatic on regional health-check failure; tested monthly via simulated regional ingestion outage. Quarterly drill kills an entire region and validates queue replay + idempotency-cache cross-region reconciliation.
- **Cross-region cost trade-off:** active-active ingestion costs replication bandwidth for the idempotency cache and preferences, which is small, since preferences are bytes and the idempotency cache is 1.2 GB. The real cost is that dedup becomes a cross-region problem: a request accepted in us-east and its retry landing in eu-west must resolve against shared state, and the alternative of pinning each user to a home region trades availability for simpler dedup. The per-user rate limiter has the same shape and is easier to concede on, since a user briefly getting 6 notifications in an hour instead of 5 during a failover is not worth a synchronous cross-region read on every send.

### 8. Design a News Feed System (Facebook, Twitter)
#### Problem
Build the home feed for a social product: every user sees a stream of posts from the accounts they follow, ranked, paginated, and loading in under 200ms. Reads outnumber posts by roughly an order of magnitude, and the follow graph is a power law, so the same post can need 200 deliveries or 100 million. The entire design turns on where you put that delivery work.
#### Core
A feed is a materialised join between the posts table and the follow graph. The only real question is when you compute it.

Compute it on write and every follower ends up with a prebuilt list, so a feed load is one cache read. Compute it on read and a post costs a single write, but every load has to gather and merge recent posts from 200 accounts. Neither survives the shape of the graph: the median account has a few hundred followers and the top ones have a hundred million. Push breaks at the top of the distribution, pull breaks everywhere.

So do both, split by author size. Push for accounts below a follower threshold, pull for accounts above it. Concretely, 10,000 followers. A post is written to the posts store and acknowledged immediately; a fan-out worker picks it up asynchronously. Under the threshold, the worker inserts the post id into each follower's capped, time-sorted timeline list. Over it, the worker does nothing, and the post stays in the author's own recent-posts list. At read time the feed service reads the user's prebuilt timeline, reads the recent-posts list for each large account they follow, typically eight of them, merges, ranks, and hydrates.

Timelines hold ids, never bodies. That way a delete, an edit, or a block resolves at hydration against the source of truth instead of by rewriting a hundred million cached lists.

Ranking runs on the read path over a bounded candidate set of about 500, because the signals that decide the order, engagement in the last hour, do not exist at write time.

The threshold is the design. Raise it and cache write load doubles; lower it and the read-time merge eats the latency budget.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a newspaper delivery service where the newspaper changes depending on who you follow. For most subscribers a paperboy drops a personalised edition on the doorstep before they wake up, so opening the paper costs nothing. For a few famous columnists with a hundred million readers, printing and delivering that many copies would take longer than the news stays news, so their column is not delivered at all; you pick it up at the newsstand on your way in. Most readers never notice which of their stories arrived by which route.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Do the work when the post is written.* When someone posts, walk their follower list and append the post id to a prebuilt per-user list. A feed load is then one read of an already-ordered list, no join and no merge, and delivery can take as long as it likes because nobody is waiting on it. What it costs is one write per follower, so the cost of a post is set by how popular the author is rather than by how interesting the post is. It wins whenever follower counts are bounded and reads dominate.

*Do the work when the feed is opened.* Store each post once against its author. On load, fetch recent posts from every account the reader follows and merge them by time. A post costs one write whatever the author's size, and there is no derived state to keep correct, so deletes and privacy changes are automatic. What it costs is a read fan-out proportional to how many accounts the reader follows, paid on the path with a user waiting and paid again on every refresh. It wins when follow counts are small or the graph is flat.

*Split the population and run both.* Push for ordinary accounts, pull for the handful too large to push, merge at read time. This bounds the write burst at the top of the graph and the read fan-out at the bottom. It costs two delivery paths, a threshold tuned against real capacity, and a transition each time an account crosses it.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a user with 200 followers posts "just launched my startup". The post service writes the post to the posts database and returns success immediately. Asynchronously, a fan-out service reads the list of those 200 followers from the follow graph. Because the author is under the celebrity threshold, the fan-out service does 200 Redis ZADDs, adding the post ID to each follower's timeline sorted set (a per-user list in Redis sorted by timestamp) and trimming it back to 1000 entries. Total: 200 cache writes, done in a couple of seconds in the background. Later, when follower Alice opens her app, the feed service reads Alice's Redis timeline (one fast lookup for the top 1000 post IDs), pipelines a read of the recent-posts list for each of the roughly 8 large accounts Alice follows, merges the two sets into ~500 candidates, runs the ranking model, hydrates the top 50 from the posts database, and returns Alice's feed in under 200ms.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Posts database.** A wide-column store (Cassandra) holding canonical post content, partitioned by `author_id`. This is the source of truth. Timelines store only post IDs, so deleted and edited posts propagate correctly because the timeline just points here.
- **Follow graph.** A store of `(follower_id, followee_id)` pairs, indexed both ways. The fan-out service reads it forward to find who should receive a post; the feed service reads it backward to find which of the reader's follows are large accounts on the pull path.
- **Fan-out service.** The async worker that pushes post IDs into followers' timeline caches after a post is durable. It skips authors above the threshold, because those are served at read time instead.
- **Per-user timeline cache.** A Redis sorted set keyed by `user_id`, holding post IDs scored by timestamp, capped at 1000 entries. Loading a feed starts here: one read, then hydration of the survivors.
- **Author recent-posts list.** The mirror image, one sorted set per large account holding its last ~200 post IDs. Every follower of that account reads the same key, so it is the hottest and cheapest thing in the cache.
- **Ranking model.** Reorders the ~500 candidates on the read path. Ranking at write time would be wrong: engagement signals change by the hour and the same post ranks differently for two readers.
- **Hydration and visibility layer.** Turns IDs into posts and enforces deletes, blocks, and regional restrictions at read time. This is the only place correctness is enforced, which is why timelines can be treated as disposable.

**The thing that makes it hard:** a post from an account with 100 million followers is 100 million cache writes, and they have to land inside the freshness SLO or the delivery is worthless. At 0.5ms of worker time per insert that is 14 hours of serial work; even fully parallelised across 1000 workers it is ~50 seconds, and for those 50 seconds the cache cluster is saturated with one person's post while everyone else's fan-out queues behind it. The problem is not the total cost, which amortises fine. It is the concentration: one event, one cluster, one moment. Pulling instead turns it into a single hot key that every reader hits, which is the cheapest access pattern a cache has.

**Why this design and what it costs:** hybrid fan-out is the production default at Twitter and Instagram, and it is not free. You now have two delivery paths that must agree on which authors belong to which, a threshold whose correct value depends on your cache capacity and your ranking budget rather than on any universal number, a dual-mode window every time an account crosses it, and a merge that has to be idempotent because during that window a post arrives by both routes. The threshold is the knob everything else hangs off, so the honest version of this design states the number, states how it was derived, and states what happens on either side of it.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Redis cluster, sorted sets per user, capped at 1000 entries, score = timestamp, for the push timeline.
- Cassandra for posts, partitioned by `author_id`.
- Fan-out via Kafka, partitioned by `author_id` so one author's posts fan out in order; workers consume, check follower count against the threshold, write to Redis or skip.
- Read path:
  ```
  def get_feed(user_id):
    push_ids  = redis.zrevrange(f"tl:{user_id}", 0, 999)      # prebuilt
    big_ids   = pipeline_zrevrange(get_big_follows(user_id))  # pull path
    candidates = dedupe(merge(push_ids, big_ids))[:500]
    posts = hydrate(db.batch_get(candidates), viewer=user_id)
    return ranker.score(posts, user_id)[:50]
  ```

#### What this is really testing
Whether you can say why the threshold exists, not just that it does.

The usual story is that pushing to 100 million followers costs more than pulling from one author, and on the arithmetic that story is wrong. Amortise both over a day and the follower count cancels. Pushing costs `F × posts_per_day` writes. Pulling costs `F × active_fraction × loads_per_day` reads. At 10 posts a day, 25 loads a day, and a fifth of followers active, that is `10F` writes against `5F` reads, and the ratio holds at every follower count. There is no crossover in F at all, which is why "push is expensive for celebrities" is a conclusion in search of a derivation.

What actually breaks is concentration. A push is a burst of F writes that has to complete inside a freshness SLO, and at the top of the graph a hundred million of them land on one cluster in one moment while every other author's fan-out queues behind. A pull is one key read by many, which is the pattern a cache is best at. So the threshold is not a per-post cost comparison. It is bracketed from two directions: the write side caps how high it can go, because each tier you add to the push population multiplies the sustained cache write rate; the read side caps how low it can go, because each account you move to pull adds a merge source to every one of that account's followers' feed loads. A candidate who says "10,000 followers" and cannot say which of those two constraints they are near has memorised a number.

The Twitter question runs the same hybrid fan-out, and most candidates give both questions the same answer, which is exactly why the two interviews diverge. Q26 grants you fan-out in the first five minutes and spends the remaining forty on what a microblog adds on top: an inverted index over every post that has to be searchable within seconds, trending term counts over sliding windows, a repost and quote graph where the reposted item is a reference rather than a copy, and reply threads with their own ordering rules. The feed is one of six subsystems there. Here it is the only one, so the fan-out decision has to carry forty minutes on its own: the derivation of the threshold, the crossing transition, the merge and its cap, hydration as the correctness boundary, backfill on follow. Spend this question on search and trending and you have answered Q26 while leaving the actual question untouched.

Closest question: Q26
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Chronological or algorithmic ranking?
- How many follows on average? Outliers (celebrities)?
- Real-time updates (live) or per-page-load refresh?
- Media types? (text, image, video, different sizes)
- Personalization signals available?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Chronological | a simple merge of followees' recent posts, cheap, no ranking tier |
| Algorithmic ranking | a ranking service scoring candidates, backed by a feature store and precomputation |
| Celebrity outliers | hybrid fan-out, push on write for normal users, pull on read for celebrities, to avoid write amplification |
| Real-time live updates | push new posts over websocket or long-poll; otherwise refresh on page load |
| Rich media | store media in an object store plus CDN and keep only references and sizes in the feed |
| Personalization signals | precompute per-user feature vectors and rank at read time from a candidate set |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** post, follow/unfollow, fetch feed, paginate, refresh
- **NFR:** <200ms feed load p95, survive celebrity fan-out, eventually consistent, deletes visible within one hydration

**Scale**

- **Population:** ~2.5B registered accounts, 500M DAU as a mid-scale composite between Facebook (~2B DAU) and Twitter (~250M DAU). Active fraction = 500M / 2.5B = **20% of any follower list is active on a given day**; the 30-day-active fraction is roughly double that, **~40%**. Both numbers are load-bearing below.
- **Post volume:** 20% of DAU post on a given day × ~10 posts each = 500M × 0.2 × 10 = **1B posts/day**. 1B ÷ 86,400s ≈ **~12k posts/s steady**; global events (election night, a World Cup goal) push 5× → **~60k/s burst**.
- **Follow distribution:** ~200 follows per user (public social-graph studies put the median at 150 to 250). Total edges = 500M × 200 = **100B follow edges**. The tail sits six orders of magnitude above that: Cristiano ~600M followers, Taylor Swift ~280M. That skew is the whole problem.
- **Feed reads:** 500M DAU × ~5 sessions/day × ~5 loads/session = **12.5B feed loads/day**. 12.5B ÷ 86,400 = **~145k loads/s average**; diurnal peak ≈ 1.5× → **~220k/s**; a global event ≈ 3× diurnal peak → **~650k/s**. Against 1B posts/day that is 12.5 loads per post, and each load returns ~20 visible posts, so **~250 impressions per post written**. The read-heaviness is what justifies paying on the write path.
- **Push fan-out write rate:** the average follower count of a *posting* account, restricted below the 10k threshold, is ~500 (posting skews toward larger accounts, so this sits above the 200 median). 1B posts/day × 500 = 500B inserts/day ÷ 86,400 = **~5.8M cache writes/s sustained**, ~12M/s at diurnal peak. With ~100 shards at ~150k ops/s each the cluster tops out near 15M/s, so peak fan-out uses ~80% of it. This is the number that caps how high the threshold can go.
- **Post size:** ~1KB metadata (post_id 16B + author_id 8B + text up to ~280 chars ≈ 600B + media refs ~50B + ts 8B + flags). Media bytes live in the object store, not the post row.
- **Posts on disk:** 1B/day × 1KB = **1TB/day** metadata; replication factor 3 → **~3TB/day** on the posts store. 30-day hot tier = 30TB logical, **90TB provisioned**.
- **Timeline cache:** 500M active users × 1000 post ids × ~24B per sorted-set entry (8B id + 8B score + 8B overhead) = 500M × 1000 × 24B = **~12TB hot**, sharded ~100 ways at ~120GB each.
- **What 1000 entries actually covers:** a user following 200 accounts receives posts from the ~20% who post on a given day, 40 authors × 10 posts = **~400 posts/day into a timeline**, so a 1000-entry cap is **~2.5 days of feed**, not weeks. Anyone scrolling past that falls through to the pull path, which is ~1% of reads. If the product promises "everything since your last visit" for weekly users, the cap has to be ~3000 and the cache becomes ~36TB.
- **Cold tier:** posts older than 30 days move to object storage (~10× cheaper per GB); timelines are never archived because they are derived state.
- **Media:** ~500KB average image (compressed WebP at phone resolution), ~5MB average short video (~30s at ~1.3Mbps). 50% of posts carry an image, 5% carry video → 1B × (0.5 × 500KB + 0.05 × 5MB) = 1B × (250KB + 250KB) = **~500TB/day** to the object store, CDN-fronted at ~95% hit rate.
#### Key decisions
**Hybrid fan-out with a follower threshold, versus fan-out on read for everyone**
- Choice: push for authors under 10,000 followers, pull for authors over it, merge at read time.
- Alternative: pull for everyone, with each author's recent-posts list cached hot and the merge done on every feed load.
- Decider: the threshold is bracketed from both sides, and 10,000 is the middle of the resulting band. *Read side sets the floor.* The 200ms p95 budget breaks down as ~35ms ranking, ~60ms hydration, ~40ms network and serialisation, leaving ~30ms for the pull merge. Each pull source contributes ~20 candidates, and the first ranking stage costs ~5ms per 500 candidates, so the merge has to stay under ~25 sources or it doubles ranking cost. At a 10,000 threshold roughly 4% of follow edges point above the line, so a 200-follow user carries ~8 pull sources. Drop the threshold to 1,000 and that share rises to ~20%, so 40 sources, and the budget is gone. *Write side sets the ceiling.* Raising the threshold to 100,000 pulls the 10k-to-100k tier back onto the push path: ~2% of the 1B daily posts at ~30,000 followers each is 20M × 30,000 = 600B extra inserts/day, ~7M writes/s on top of the ~5.8M/s baseline, which more than doubles cache write load against a ~15M/s ceiling. The defensible band is ~1,000 to ~30,000.
- Alternative wins when: the graph is not skewed and follow counts are small. Under ~30 follows per user with no account more than two orders of magnitude above the median, pure pull merges 30 hot keys per load, needs no fan-out fleet, no threshold, no crossing logic, and gets deletes and privacy for free because there is no derived state. That describes a professional or workplace network, and it describes your own consumer product below roughly a million users. Hybrid is genuinely the wrong first build: do not add a second delivery path until you can point at the skew in your own graph.

**Threshold on active followers, versus a static threshold on total followers**
- Choice: skip dormant followers during fan-out and set the threshold on 30-day-active follower count.
- Alternative: one static number applied to total follower count, push to every follower regardless.
- Decider: the share of pushes that are written and never read. At 500M DAU against 2.5B registered accounts, ~60% of an average follower list has not opened the app in 30 days, so 3 in 5 pushes are pure waste, and wasted writes are the entire cost of the push path. Filtering on 30-day activity cuts the ~5.8M writes/s baseline to ~2.3M/s and, more importantly, removes most of the 12TB of cache held for people who will not read it. The price is a last-active timestamp readable at fan-out time for 2.5B users, which is ~20GB in a separate key-value tier plus a counter pipeline to keep it fresh, and a rebuild path for a dormant user who returns to an empty timeline and has to be served entirely from the pull path on their first load, roughly 300ms.
- Alternative wins when: the registered-to-active ratio is near 1, which is true for a young product and for internal tools. There is nothing to filter, and a static number is one config value instead of a counter pipeline plus a rebuild path. It also wins if returning-dormant sessions exceed about 5% of traffic, because at that point the rebuild is not an edge case, it is a second read path you have to make fast, and it will be the slowest feed load in the product. Measure that share before choosing.

**Rank on the read path, versus materialising a ranked feed offline**
- Choice: rank at read time over ~500 candidates, with the ranked result cached per user for 5 minutes.
- Alternative: rank asynchronously on a schedule and store the ordered feed, so a load is a straight read.
- Decider: feed loads per user per day against refresh cycles per day. A rank costs ~35ms of compute (~5ms first-stage over 500 candidates, ~30ms deep model over the surviving 100). At 25 loads per user per day, the 5-minute cache collapses the ~5 loads inside a session to 1, so 500M × 5 = **2.5B ranks/day**. Precomputing to the same 5-minute freshness means ranking every active user every 5 minutes: 500M × 288 = **144B ranks/day**, 58× more compute for an identical result. Precompute only wins once the refresh interval can be stretched far past the session gap, so the break-even is around 1 to 2 feed loads per user per day.
- Alternative wins when: the feed is a digest rather than a stream. A daily email roundup, a weekly summary, or any product opened once a day inverts the ratio, and you get a second benefit: a precomputed feed can use a model far too expensive to run inline. It also wins for the cold-start slice specifically. A user with no pushed timeline cannot hit 200ms from the pull path, so precomputing something for them before they open the app is not an optimisation, it is the only way to meet the SLO.

**How to read the diagram:** the split is between posting and reading. On the write side, a durable post write is acknowledged first and delivery happens afterwards. On the read side, the app fetches a mostly prebuilt timeline, merges in whatever was not delivered, and reranks before returning.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** reads outnumber posts 12.5 to 1, so the design spends work up front to make feed loads cheap. That trade inverts at the top of the follow graph, where one post would cost a hundred million writes, so large accounts keep their posts in one place and readers come to them.

**What this layout buys you:** fast home timelines for ordinary users without the write path melting on huge follow counts. The price is that one product now runs two delivery strategies, the threshold between them is a real tuning knob with capacity on one side and latency on the other, and every account that crosses it needs a transition.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Hybrid fan-out end to end: the threshold, the crossing, and the merge.**

**The write path.** The post service writes the post to the posts store, waits for a durable quorum, and returns success. Only then does it publish a fan-out event, partitioned by `author_id`. That partition key is the design's only ordering guarantee: two posts by the same author are handled by the same consumer in the order they were written, so a follower never sees an author's second post appear above their first. Nothing orders posts *across* authors, which is a conceded gap below.

A fan-out worker consumes the event, reads the author's follower count from a counter maintained on follow and unfollow, and compares it to the threshold. Under it, the worker pages the follower list in blocks of 10,000, filters out anyone with no session in 30 days, groups the survivors by cache shard, and issues pipelined `ZADD` plus `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` pairs, ~500 per round trip. Batched that way a single worker sustains ~50,000 inserts/s, so the ~2.3M inserts/s baseline needs ~50 workers with headroom for the 5× event burst. Over the threshold the worker does exactly one thing: append the post id to the author's own recent-posts list, capped at ~200 entries.

**Why 1000 entries per timeline, and what the cap really is.** A 200-follow user receives ~400 posts a day, so 1000 entries is ~2.5 days of feed at 24KB per user. Beyond that the reader falls through to the pull path for older pages, which is ~1% of loads. The cap is also the garbage collector of last resort: anything wrong that ever gets written into a timeline, a duplicate, a post from an account since unfollowed, an id from a bad deploy, ages out within 1000 entries and roughly two days without anyone having to find it. Raise the cap to cover weekly users and you multiply a 12TB cache by three and extend the lifetime of every mistake proportionally.

**Crossing the threshold.** An account grows past 10,000 followers. The naive behaviour is that its next post is simply not pushed, and this is where the design most often has a hole. Both paths read the same classification: the fan-out worker uses it to decide whether to push, and the feed service uses it to decide whether to add the author to the reader's pull set. If those two reads disagree, and they will, because the counter is recomputed on a daily batch while follows arrive continuously, one of two things happens. Stale in the direction of "still small" on the read side means the author is pushed but not pulled, which is fine. Stale in the direction of "already large" on the write side means the author is neither pushed nor pulled, and they vanish from their followers' feeds for up to a day, silently.

The fix is a dual-mode window. For 24 hours after an account crosses, it is both pushed and included in the pull set. Posts arrive by both routes, and the merge deduplicates by post id, so double delivery is invisible. The cost is one day of double writes for the handful of accounts crossing on any given day, which is nothing. The requirement this creates is that the merge must be idempotent by post id, always, not just during the window.

**The read-time merge.** A feed load is six steps:

1. `ZREVRANGE` the reader's pushed timeline for up to 1000 ids. One round trip, ~2ms.
2. Read the reader's large-account follow set, a small per-user set maintained on follow and unfollow, typically ~8 entries, hard-capped at 25 by predicted engagement.
3. Pipelined `ZREVRANGE` of each of those accounts' recent-posts lists, 20 ids each. One round trip regardless of count, ~2ms.
4. Merge by score, deduplicate by post id, truncate to 500 most recent. ~1ms of CPU.
5. Rank: cheap first-stage model trims 500 to 100 at ~5ms, deep model scores the survivors at ~30ms with feature-store reads.
6. Hydrate the top 50 from the posts store with a per-post visibility check, ~40ms.

That is ~80ms p50 and ~180ms p95. Steps 1 and 3 are separate round trips rather than one because the pushed timeline read gates nothing, so in practice they are issued concurrently and the merge waits on both.

**Hydration is where correctness lives.** The timeline holds ids and nothing else. Hydration reads each post and drops it if it has been deleted, if the author has since blocked the reader, if the post is restricted in the reader's region, or if the account has been suspended. This is the reason timelines never hold bodies: a delete is one write to the posts store and it takes effect everywhere on the next hydration, versus rewriting up to 100 million cached lists and hoping none are missed. The cost is real and gets skipped in most answers: a load whose candidates are 30% unhydratable fetches 70 to return 50, so the hydration step over-fetches by a tuned factor and still occasionally returns short.

**Backfill on follow.** A new follow leaves the reader's timeline with none of that author's history. An async job reads the author's last 100 posts and inserts them; until it lands, the first feed load treats the author as a one-shot pull source. This makes a follow a write of up to 100 entries, which matters at signup: a user who imports 500 follows triggers 50,000 inserts, so onboarding backfill runs at lower priority than live fan-out on the same worker pool.
