Cost equations (per post, F = followers, A = follows per reader, C = large-account follows per reader):
- Push write cost: `F × 0.5ms` of worker time. At F = 100M that is 14 hours serial, ~50s across 1000 workers, and a saturated cache cluster for the duration.
- Pull read cost: `(A − C) × P` posts merged per load, where P is posts fetched per author. Unbounded in A, and paid on every refresh.
- Hybrid read cost: one timeline read plus `C × P` merged, bounded because C is ~8 at p50 and capped at 25.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Celebrity fan-out.** Pushing to 100M followers saturates the cache cluster and blows the freshness SLO for every other author queued behind it. *Mitigation:* the threshold, so those accounts are never pushed; readers pull them instead, bounded by `O(large accounts followed)`, ~8 at p50.
- **Hot post.** A viral post goes from 100 QPS to 100k QPS of hydration within minutes. *Mitigation:* hot-post detection on a per-id counter, then an edge cache with a 30 to 60s TTL, plus request coalescing so 1000 concurrent identical hydrations collapse into one backend read. Note the interaction with hydration-as-correctness: a 60s TTL means a deleted post stays visible for up to 60s, which is the deliberate price and has to be short enough to satisfy moderation SLAs.
- **Cache miss cascade at peak.** A hot key falling out of cache during a spike triggers N concurrent rebuilds. *Mitigation:* single-flight, one request rebuilds and the rest park on it.
- **Ranking latency on the read path.** ~35ms per rank against a 200ms budget, and it is the first thing to degrade under load. *Mitigation:* the 5-minute per-user ranked-result cache absorbs intra-session refreshes, and a timeout falls back to chronological order over the same candidate set rather than a blank feed.
- **Scheduled write storms.** A "post your year in review" prompt at midnight UTC creates a 10× write spike in one second. *Mitigation:* jitter fan-out by 0 to 5 minutes for non-time-critical posts, flattening the curve without touching the durable write path.
- **RAM economics.** 12TB of sorted sets is 10 to 50× more expensive per GB than disk. *Mitigation:* keep the sorted-set tier for the active working set and push the cold tail to the wide-column store, which is exactly the Redis to Cassandra move Instagram made around 2013 at 100M DAU.
- **Workload entanglement.** A viral post's fan-out can trigger compactions that starve follow-graph queries if both live on the same store, which is what pushed Twitter to split timelines out of Manhattan. *Mitigation:* physically separate the timeline tier from the graph tier and size them independently.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Timeline fan-out | Async fan-out workers lag after a bursty post event | Queue-depth and oldest-job age alerts | Post ack returns after durable write only; fan-out drains asynchronously with backpressure and per-author rate shaping |
| Timeline cache | Redis timeline shards evict or lose a user's prebuilt feed | Cache-miss spike and rebuild-rate alarm | Rebuild from author-posts store on demand, cap timeline length, and repopulate lazily rather than blocking the request |
| Celebrity pull path | Recent-post list for a high-follower account is stale or unavailable | Read-time pull latency spike and empty-merge rate | Fall back to an author partition scan for a small recent window and cache the result aggressively |
| Threshold classification | Push and pull paths disagree on whether an author is large, so posts reach nobody | Per-author delivered-impressions canary against post rate | One classification source read by both paths, plus a 24h dual-mode window on crossing and idempotent merge by post id |
| Follow graph | Follow/unfollow propagation lags, so feed composition is stale | CDC lag and post-from-unfollowed-author canary | Treat follow changes as eventually consistent, backfill on follow, and remove on next timeline rebuild or cache expiry |
| Ranking service | Ranker timeout causes slow or blank feeds | Ranker p99 and timeout-rate alerts | Serve chronological order over the same candidate set and refresh the ranked feed asynchronously |
| Delete / moderation | Deleted or moderated posts remain visible | Tombstone-hit rate and delete propagation lag | Timelines store IDs only; hydration consults source-of-truth tombstones, so a delete needs no feed rewrites |

**Unresolved**

**The celebrity-heavy reader gets a measurably worse feed and we have no clean fix.** The merge is capped at 25 pull sources because the ranking budget says so. The p50 reader has 8, but the p99 reader has 60 or more, and that is not an exotic case: it is most new users, because onboarding suggests popular accounts, so a fresh account's follow list is almost entirely above the threshold. For those readers the accounts ranked 26th and below are not deprioritised, they are absent, and the feed is a ranked subset of a subset. Rotating the bottom slots round-robin makes the feed change between two refreshes with no new posts, which reads as a bug. Raising the cap taxes every other reader's latency. What we actually do is rank the 25 by predicted engagement, rotate the bottom 10 slots, and accept a completeness gap that we can measure and cannot close. The clean answer is probably to push large accounts to their small population of highly engaged followers, which is a third delivery mode, and we have not built it.

**There is no causal ordering across authors.** Fan-out is partitioned by `author_id`, so one author's posts stay in order. Two authors' do not. A reply, a quote, or a second account's "as I said above" can be delivered and ranked ahead of the thing it refers to, and with a timestamp score it stays that way until something reorders the feed. The clean fix means either one globally ordered fan-out stream, which reintroduces exactly the throughput ceiling the per-author partitioning exists to avoid, or a dependency check at merge time, which is a second hydration round trip for every candidate against a budget that has 30ms of slack. What we do instead is hydrate the parent inline for posts that declare one, which fixes explicit replies and quotes and does nothing at all for implicit references, which are the majority.

**Nothing notices when a timeline degenerates.** Timelines are capped at 1000 and hydration silently drops deleted, blocked, suspended, and region-restricted posts. A reader whose follows were mass-moderated, or who blocks heavily, can hold a full 1000-entry timeline that hydrates down to 40 usable posts, and the write path is oblivious because fan-out did its job: it delivered ids. The read path sees it as a low hydration yield, but the only remedy is to rebuild that timeline from the pull path, which is the expensive load, for exactly the readers whose feed is already thin. Doing it inline would blow the 200ms budget, so we alert on per-reader yield below 20% and rebuild offline, which means those readers see a short feed until the rebuild lands. We chose the thin feed over the slow one, and it is a choice, not a solution.
#### Drill questions
1. How do you handle a brand-new celebrity, 10M followers overnight?
2. What is the tradeoff of push vs pull vs hybrid?
3. How do you prevent stale feeds when a user follows someone new?
4. How do you handle viral posts that 10x normal traffic?
5. How do you test ranking changes without nuking engagement?
6. How would you scale this 10x to 5B DAU?
7. Why did Twitter unbundle timelines from Manhattan?
8. Why did Instagram move feeds from Redis to Cassandra?
9. Where does the 10,000-follower threshold come from, and what breaks at 1,000 and at 100,000?
10. A reader follows 80 large accounts. What does their feed load actually look like?
11. Two posts from different authors land out of order in a follower's timeline. Does it matter?
12. Would you ever push a post to a follower who has not opened the app in six months?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. The classification is recomputed on a daily batch, so an account crossing 10,000 flips to pull on the next run and existing pushed entries age out of follower timelines within ~1000 entries. *If pushed:* the transition is the interesting part. Run a 24-hour dual-mode window where the account is both pushed and pulled, with the merge deduplicating by post id, because the alternative failure is that a stale counter leaves the account neither pushed nor pulled and it disappears from every follower's feed for a day with no error anywhere.

2. Push: O(1) reads, O(followers) writes, and it dies on the concentration at the top of the graph rather than on total cost. Pull: O(1) writes, O(follows) reads, paid on the latency-sensitive path on every refresh. Hybrid bounds both. *If pushed:* hybrid buys you two code paths, a threshold to tune, and a crossing transition, and it is the wrong first build. A product under a million users with a flat graph should be pure pull and should not add fan-out until the skew is visible in its own data.

3. Async backfill reads the followee's last 100 posts and inserts them into the follower's timeline. *If pushed:* until the backfill lands, the first feed load treats the new followee as a one-shot pull source, so the reader never sees a gap. Watch the signup case: importing 500 follows is 50,000 inserts, so backfill runs at lower priority than live fan-out on the same pool.

4. Per-post QPS counter on the read path; above a threshold the post is promoted to an edge cache with a 30 to 60s TTL, and hydration requests are coalesced so 1000 concurrent identical reads become one. *If pushed:* the TTL fights hydration-as-correctness. A cached post survives its own deletion for up to the TTL, so the TTL ceiling is set by the moderation SLA, not by cache economics.

5. Online A/B on 1 to 5% of traffic with a long-running holdout, plus shadow ranking in production where the new model scores real candidate sets and the results are logged but not served. *If pushed:* counterfactual evaluation on logged impressions gives you an estimate before you spend traffic, but it is biased by the fact that the logged candidates were selected by the incumbent model, so it screens candidates rather than deciding them.

6. Geo-shard timelines and posts by user region, replicate the graph and posts cross-region asynchronously, and let the CDN absorb the read multiplier. *If pushed:* 10× DAU multiplies the fan-out write rate by 10 to ~58M/s, which is well past a single cache cluster, so the threshold has to come down. That is not free: dropping it to 1,000 puts ~40 pull sources on the average reader and forces the ranking budget to be re-derived. Scaling this system means moving the threshold, and the threshold has a floor.

7. A single store carrying both timeline writes and graph reads could not isolate the workloads: a viral post's fan-out triggered compactions that starved graph queries on the same nodes. Timelines moved to a Redis-backed cache tier and Manhattan stayed the graph store. *If pushed:* the general lesson is that shared infrastructure is fine until one workload's bursts correlate with the other's read SLA, and fan-out bursts correlate with everything, because the events that make people post are the events that make people read.

8. RAM economics. Sorted sets work at tens of millions of users; at 100M+ DAU the RAM cost of holding push timelines for high-follower accounts stopped being rational, and wide-column on disk is 10 to 50× cheaper per GB. Redis stayed as the hot cache for the active working set. *If pushed:* sharding Redis harder does not help, because a sorted-set entry costs the same RAM on any shard. The substrate had to change, which is a different fix from the usual "add capacity".

9. It is bracketed, not derived from a single equation. The read side sets the floor: the 200ms budget leaves ~30ms for the merge, each pull source adds ~20 candidates, and the first ranking stage costs ~5ms per 500, so the merge must stay under ~25 sources. At 10,000 about 4% of follow edges point above the line, giving a 200-follow reader ~8 sources; at 1,000 that share is ~20%, giving 40 sources, and the budget is gone. The write side sets the ceiling: at 100,000 the 10k-to-100k tier comes back onto the push path, 20M posts/day × ~30,000 followers = 600B extra inserts/day, ~7M writes/s on a cluster already running 5.8M/s against a ~15M/s ceiling. *If pushed:* neither bound is a law, they are both properties of your capacity, so the number moves when either changes and it should be a config value with an alert on both sides of the band.

10. Badly. The pull set is capped at 25 sources, so 55 of their 80 large-account follows contribute nothing to that load. The merge is 25 pipelined reads in one round trip, ~2ms, plus 500 candidates from the pull side alone, which fills the candidate budget and squeezes out whatever the pushed timeline held. *If pushed:* this is the p99 reader and it is disproportionately new users, because onboarding suggests popular accounts. We rank the 25 by predicted engagement and rotate the bottom 10 slots between loads, which trades completeness for the appearance of freshness. There is no version of this that is both complete and inside the latency budget.

11. Usually not, and occasionally very much. Fan-out is partitioned by `author_id`, so a single author's posts are ordered. Across authors nothing is, and timestamps are assigned at write on different hosts, so a reply from account B can be scored above the post from account A that it is replying to. *If pushed:* for posts that declare a parent, hydrate the parent inline and render them together, which fixes replies and quotes. Implicit references are unfixable at this budget; a dependency check per candidate is a second hydration round trip and there is not 40ms spare. Making fan-out globally ordered would fix it and would give the write path a single-stream throughput ceiling, which is a much worse trade.

12. No, and skipping them is the single largest saving available on the write path. With 500M DAU against 2.5B registered, ~60% of an average follower list has no session in 30 days, so filtering on last-active cuts the fan-out baseline from ~5.8M writes/s to ~2.3M/s and frees most of the 12TB cache. *If pushed:* the cost is the returning user, whose timeline is empty and whose first load runs entirely on the pull path at ~300ms. That is acceptable while returning-dormant sessions are a small share of traffic; above ~5% it becomes a second read path you have to make fast, and then a static threshold on total followers is the simpler system.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, frame it as a placement problem.** Open with the shape, not the components: "a feed is a materialised join between posts and the follow graph, and the only question is when you compute it." Then ask the three things that change the answer: is the feed ranked or chronological, what does the follow-count distribution look like at the top, and what is the read-to-write ratio. State the numbers you are assuming out loud: 500M DAU, 1B posts/day, 200 follows per user, 12.5B feed loads/day, 200ms p95. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine and the fork.** Draw two columns: write path (client, post service, posts store, fan-out worker, timeline cache) and read path (client, feed service, timeline cache, merge, rank, hydrate). Say three things as you draw: the post ack happens at the durable write and fan-out is asynchronous; timelines hold ids and never bodies; the fan-out worker branches on author size. Then take the fork explicitly and give the number: push under 10,000 followers, pull over it. Do not justify it yet, just plant it, because the justification is the next block and interviewers reward you for signposting it.

**15-35, the drill, and protect this time.** Derive the threshold from both sides, because this is the section that separates a memorised answer from a designed one. Read side: 200ms budget, 35ms ranking, 60ms hydration, so ~30ms for the merge, ~5ms per 500 candidates in the first ranking stage, therefore under 25 pull sources, therefore the threshold cannot go below ~1,000. Write side: at 100,000 the middle tier comes back onto the push path and adds ~7M writes/s to a 5.8M/s baseline against a 15M/s ceiling, therefore it cannot go above ~30,000. Then the crossing transition, dual-mode for 24 hours, merge idempotent by post id, and name the failure it prevents: an author neither pushed nor pulled, invisible for a day, with no error. Then hydration as the correctness boundary, which is where deletes, blocks, and moderation all land, and why that decides the ids-not-bodies rule. Keep active-follower filtering and backfill-on-follow in reserve as one-liners.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the gaps before they are found: the celebrity-heavy reader whose merge cap makes their feed incomplete, no causal ordering across authors, no detection when a timeline hydrates to almost nothing. Then the operational surface in two minutes: fan-out lag, hydration yield, per-shard cache write rate, ranker timeout rate, and the point that timeline caches are disposable derived state, so the recovery story for a lost shard is "rebuild lazily", not "restore from backup".

Cut first: media storage and CDN sizing, then the two-stage ranking model internals, then the multi-region layout. All three are real and none of them changes the fan-out decision, and the ranking model in particular is a rabbit hole that will eat the threshold derivation. Never cut: the threshold and where its two bounds come from, ids-not-bodies with hydration as the correctness boundary, and the crossing transition.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **posts** (wide-column store): `(post_id, author_id, content, media_ids, ts, deleted_at)` partitioned by `author_id`
- **follows** (wide-column store): `(follower_id, followee_id, ts)` with both-direction indexes
- **author_stats**: `(author_id, follower_count, active_follower_count, is_large, crossed_at)`, the single classification both paths read
- **timeline** (sorted set per user): `key=tl:{user_id}`, `score=ts`, `member=post_id`, capped at 1000
- **author_recent** (sorted set per large account): `key=ar:{author_id}`, capped at 200
- **big_follows** (set per user): the reader's large-account follows, maintained on follow/unfollow, capped at 25
- **media**: object store plus CDN, referenced by id from the post row

**API contract**

```
POST /post            body: { content, media_ids }  -> { post_id }
POST /follow/{user}                                 -> { ok, backfill_queued }
GET  /feed?cursor=X&limit=20                        -> { posts: [...], next_cursor }
```

**Observability**

- **Fan-out lag**, durable write to last follower insert, p99. The freshness SLO for every non-large author.
- **Hydration yield**, usable posts returned divided by candidates hydrated. Below 20% for a reader means a degenerate timeline; below 20% globally means a moderation event.
- **Per-shard cache write rate.** The number that caps how high the threshold can go, so it is the capacity signal for the whole fan-out decision.
- **Pull sources per feed load, p50 and p99.** The number that caps how low the threshold can go. Watch p99, not the average.
- **Classification disagreement rate.** Authors the write path calls large and the read path does not, or the reverse. Should be zero outside the dual-mode window.
- **Ranker p99 and timeout rate.** Ranking is on the read path, so it directly sets user-facing tail latency.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** posts and the follow graph replicate cross-region asynchronously; timeline caches are region-local and never replicated, because they are derived.
- **RTO:** seconds for stateless feed-service failover; minutes for timeline-cache loss, because caches rebuild lazily from the durable stores and the first load per user runs on the pull path.
- **RPO:** near-zero for posts and follows; total loss is acceptable for timeline caches by construction.
- **Failover cadence:** drills must include a cold-cache feed load, since that is the path nobody exercises and the one that decides whether a regional failover is a blip or an outage.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by media egress and fresh-post replication, not by anything in the timeline tier.

### 9. Design a Chat System (WhatsApp, Messenger)
#### Problem
Deliver messages between users, one to one and in groups, in under a second when both parties are online, and without loss when they are not. Every device must be able to reconnect after an arbitrary gap and end up with exactly the conversation everyone else sees. Presence, typing and read receipts ride the same pipe.
#### Core
Chat is a store-and-forward system wearing a real-time coat. The durable path is the product; the socket is an accelerator bolted on top.

Each device holds one long-lived connection to an edge server. On send, the message goes to a persist path that assigns a conversation-scoped monotonic id and does a quorum write to the conversation log. Only once that write commits does the sender get a tick. That ordering is the delivery contract: the tick means stored, never that one process accepted it. The committed record then goes onto a partitioned bus. A registry maps each user to the edge currently holding their socket, so the owning edge picks the event up and pushes it. If there is no socket, nothing special happens, because the message is already durable, and a platform push wakes the device instead.

Everything else falls out of treating the socket as unreliable. Each device keeps a cursor, the highest id it has applied per conversation, and on reconnect asks for everything after it. That one mechanism covers crashes, deploys, flaky mobile networks and offline users, and it demotes push notifications to wakeups rather than delivery. Delivery is at-least-once and the client applies by id, because exactly-once over a mobile socket is not on offer.

Ordering is per conversation, never global. Nothing a client renders needs more than that.

The number that sizes the fleet is concurrent sockets, not messages per second: 30 million idle connections at roughly 16KB each is 480GB of memory doing nothing, across 60 boxes.

The fork that reshapes the rest is end-to-end encryption. It removes server-side search, content-based abuse detection and server-held history in a single move.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a switchboard operator at an old telephone exchange. Every caller has a live wire plugged into a physical jack at the switchboard. When Alice wants to talk to Bob, the operator sees which jack Bob is plugged into and patches the wires together. If Bob is away, the operator writes down the message and reads it back when Bob plugs back in. The key property: the connection is live and persistent, not something you request fresh each time.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Keep the conversation on the server and deliver it over a live connection.* Every device is a thin view of a copy the operator holds. History on a new device is a download, search is a server query, abusive content is inspectable, and adding someone to a group is one write. The price is that the operator can read everything, which is a policy commitment and a target. This wins wherever discoverability, search and moderation are worth more than secrecy, which covers most workplace and most consumer products.

*Encrypt on the sending device and treat the server as a blind mailbox.* It holds ciphertext addressed to a specific device and forgets it once collected. A breach yields nothing readable and a subpoena yields metadata. The costs land everywhere at once: search must run on the device, history does not follow a new phone without an out-of-band transfer, a group message becomes one encryption per recipient device, and abuse detection is reduced to who talked to whom and how often. This wins when confidentiality is the product rather than a feature.

*Write one copy per conversation and let readers pull, or write a copy into every reader's mailbox at send time.* Pulling keeps writes flat no matter how many people are in the room, and makes very large rooms cheap, at the cost of a cursor per conversation on the read path. Pushing makes a reader's unread set one cheap sequential scan and costs one write per member. Group size decides it, and the answer flips somewhere in the low thousands.

**The single-request walkthrough:** Alice sends "hey" to Bob. Alice's phone holds a WebSocket, a persistent full-duplex TCP connection (unlike normal HTTP, which is request-response and closes after each exchange), to Edge Server A. She hits send and her app emits `{type: send, to: bob, body: "hey", client_msg_id: c123}`. Edge A hands it to the persist path, which assigns a conversation-scoped Snowflake id and does a quorum write into the `chat:alice-bob` conversation log. Only after that commit does an ack come back: `{type: ack, server_msg_id: s456}`, which is Alice's single tick. The committed record goes onto the bus. A routing consumer looks up Bob in the session registry, an in-memory cache answering "which edge currently holds Bob's socket?", finds Edge B, and publishes the event onto Edge B's partition. Edge B finds Bob's open socket and pushes `{type: receive, from: alice, body: "hey", server_msg_id: s456}`. Bob's device applies it, advances its cursor to s456, and emits a delivered receipt, which is Alice's second tick.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Long-lived connections at the edge.** Unlike HTTP, where each request opens and closes a connection, a WebSocket stays open and the server can push at any time without the client asking. Each edge holds hundreds of thousands to a million open sockets on an event-loop runtime built for cheap concurrency, Erlang's BEAM or Go's goroutines. WhatsApp demonstrated 2 million concurrent connections on a single FreeBSD/Erlang box back in 2012, with custom BEAM patches and kernel tuning, so treat that as the ceiling of the class rather than a default.
- **Durable write before ack.** The sender's tick must mean the message exists durably, not that one server process accepted it. If the edge acks first and then crashes, Alice believes Bob has "hey" and it is gone. Commit first, ack second, always.
- **Session registry.** A cache mapping `user_id → edge_id`, written by the edge on connect with a 60-second TTL refreshed by heartbeat every 30 seconds. Routing reads it. A stale or missing entry is not a correctness problem, only a latency one, because the cursor replay on reconnect is the backstop.
- **Partitioned bus.** The routing layer between edges. Edge A does not call Edge B directly, because that needs every edge to know every other edge and it breaks during a deploy. Edge A publishes, Edge B consumes its own partition.
- **Wide-column conversation log.** Partitioned by `chat_id`, clustered by `msg_id`, so one read returns a conversation in send order. Time-bucket the partition key for hot conversations so no single partition grows without bound.
- **Offline and push path.** With no live socket the message is already durable, so the only extra work is waking the device. APNs or FCM sends a notification, the user unlocks, the app reconnects, and the reconnect handler asks for everything after `last_applied_msg_id`. Push notifications are best-effort wakeups, never delivery guarantees.

**The thing that makes it hard:** an edge holding 1 million sockets crashes. All 1 million clients detect the disconnect within a couple of seconds and reconnect at once. Spread across 59 surviving boxes that is 17,000 reconnects per second per box, each carrying a TLS handshake at roughly 1ms of CPU, so 17 cores of pure handshake on a box that was already busy. Latency rises, clients time out, they retry, and the cascade takes the fleet. The fix is jittered backoff on the client: wait a uniform random 0 to 30 seconds before reconnecting. The same million reconnects then arrive at 570 per second per box, which is 0.6 of a core.

**Why this design and what it costs:** commit-before-ack plus cursor replay is the delivery guarantee. Sockets plus registry plus bus are the latency optimisation. They are deliberately independent, so when the fast path fails the slow path still converges: an offline user gets everything on return, an online user gets it in 200ms. The cost is that connection ownership is now architecture. Deploys, failover and capacity planning are all stateful in a way an HTTP service never is.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Cassandra or ScyllaDB for the conversation log: partition `(chat_id, time_bucket)`, clustering key `msg_id` (Snowflake).
- Redis for the session registry: `SET user:{bob} edge_B EX 60`, refreshed on heartbeat.
- Kafka for routing, one partition per edge, plus a routing consumer group that resolves membership and looks up the registry.
- Edge in Go or Elixir for cheap concurrency:
  ```
  on_send(ws, msg):
    if seen(msg.chat_id, msg.client_msg_id): return prior_ack   # idempotent retry
    msg_id = snowflake.next()
    log.quorum_write(msg.chat_id, msg_id, msg.body)             # commit first
    ws.send({type: ack, server_msg_id: msg_id})                 # then ack
    bus.publish(route(msg.chat_id), msg_id)                     # then deliver
  ```
#### Interactive diagram
The whole design as one explorable picture: [open the interactive diagram](/diagram/chat-system).

Every box and every arrow is clickable. Selecting one dims everything it does not touch and opens what it is, why it exists, the numbers worth quoting, the failure it owns, and why that technology rather than the obvious alternative. Start with the Overview button.

#### What this is really testing
Whether you can see that the real-time part is the easy part. The socket is a latency optimisation over a store-and-forward system, and every hard question in the interview lives in the durable path: what the sender's tick actually promises, what a device asks for when it comes back after three weeks, what happens to a message that was written but never pushed. A candidate who opens with WebSockets and connection pooling has picked the layer that scales linearly with boxes and skipped the layer that does not.

The second thing it tests is whether you treat end-to-end encryption as a requirement rather than a feature. Whether the server can read the plaintext decides four other subsystems at once, and none of them can be retrofitted cheaply. Ask it in the first two minutes.

The contrast is with Slack. Same transport, opposite content policy, and the whole design bends around that. In Slack the organisation owns the messages, not the user, so retention rules, eDiscovery, admin export and search across every channel are the product; the server must hold plaintext and the interesting work moves to workspace-scoped authorisation, channel membership with tens of thousands of members, and threads as a second ordering dimension inside a channel. The read path is the hard part there: a user in 200 channels launching a cold client has to reconstruct 200 unread counts and 200 cursors before the UI is usable, which is a fan-in problem this question never has, because a consumer messenger user has a handful of active conversations and a device that is almost always nearly caught up. In the other direction, connection count barely troubles Slack, because seats sit at desks in working hours across a few timezones, while a consumer messenger's socket count is bounded by phones, worldwide, at all hours, and that is the number that sizes this fleet.

Closest question: Q32
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- 1:1 only or also groups? Group size cap?
- End-to-end encryption, and is it a hard requirement or a later phase?
- Presence (online, offline, typing)?
- Read and delivery receipts?
- How many devices per user, and must history follow a new device?
- Voice and video calls in scope? (assume out)
- Message history retention?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| 1:1 only | sender-to-recipient routing is a single registry lookup; no membership resolution on the hot path |
| Groups with a size cap | membership resolution per message, and a cap low enough that fan-out stays bounded |
| Groups above a few thousand | switch to a pull model: readers poll a shared conversation log rather than receive copies |
| E2E encryption | the server stores ciphertext only, keyed per recipient device; no server-side search, no content moderation, no server-driven history sync |
| Presence and typing | ephemeral pub/sub with TTLs and heartbeats, never written to the durable path |
| Read and delivery receipts | a per-device high-water mark, not a row per message, or the reverse channel outgrows the forward one |
| Multi-device with history | per-device cursors plus a device-addressed sync path; with E2EE this becomes an encrypted backup problem |
| Long history retention | storage sizing and legal hold; without it, delete-after-delivery removes most of the store |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** send and receive 1:1 and group (cap 1,024); presence and typing; delivery and read receipts; scrollable history; offline delivery via push; multi-device.
- **NFR:** p99 end-to-end delivery under 300ms for two online users; ordered within a conversation; at-least-once with idempotent client apply; a device offline for months converges on reconnect.

**Scale**

- **DAU and send rate:** size for a serious but not planetary messenger, 100M DAU. WhatsApp's published figures are ~2B users and ~100B messages/day, which is 50 sent per user per day, so use that rate: 100M × 50 = **5B sends/day**. 5B ÷ 86,400 = **~58k sends/s average**. The evening peak stacks three big timezone bands, so 3× average = **~175k sends/s peak**.
- **Delivered copies:** the mix is 85% 1:1 and 15% groups averaging 12 members, so recipients per send = (0.85 × 1) + (0.15 × 11) = **2.5**. 5B × 2.5 = **12.5B delivered copies/day**, 145k/s average and **~435k/s peak**. Every fan-out cost in this design multiplies by that 2.5, not by the group cap.
- **Message size:** ~200B on the wire (chat_id 16B + msg_id 16B + sender_id 8B + body ~120B for average text + ts 8B + state flags 4B + framing ~30B). Media never rides this path; the row carries a 32B blob reference.
- **Conversation log on disk:** 5B × 200B = **1TB/day raw**; replication factor 3 across AZs = **3TB/day**. Hot retention is 30 days, which covers scroll-back for ~99% of sessions: 30 × 1TB = **30TB raw**, **90TB replicated** on SSD. Older buckets fall to object storage at roughly 10× cheaper per GB, with a per-chat TTL so legal hold and disappearing messages coexist.
- **Concurrent sockets, the number that sizes the fleet:** a client holds a socket whenever the OS lets it, which is not the same as being in the foreground. Assume 60% Android and 40% iOS. Android permits a background socket and a device is awake and on network roughly 50% of the day: 60M × 0.5 = 30M. iOS suspends the app, so a socket exists only in the foreground, ~4% of the day: 40M × 0.04 = 1.6M. Peak concurrent = **~30M sockets**.
- **Per-socket memory:** kernel send and receive buffers tuned to their 4KB floor for idle connections = 8KB, TLS record and session state ≈ 4KB once the library is told to release idle buffers, application session struct ≈ 1KB. Round to **16KB/socket**. 30M × 16KB = **480GB of fleet RAM holding nothing**. Untuned this is far worse: OpenSSL's default buffers alone are ~34KB per connection, giving 30M × 50KB = 1.5TB, three times the fleet.
- **Edge fleet:** plan 1M sockets per box, conservative against the 2M WhatsApp demonstrated in 2012 with custom runtime and kernel patches. 30M ÷ 1M = 30 boxes; 2× for rolling deploys and absorbing a lost AZ = **60 boxes**, each carrying 16GB of connection state on a 128GB machine.
- **Session registry:** 100M entries × ~80B (user_id 8B + edge addr 16B + conn_id 16B + last_seen 8B + flags and key overhead) = **8GB**, one in-memory shard, replicated 3×.
- **Push notifications:** ~45% of delivered copies find no live socket, so 12.5B × 0.45 = 5.6B push-eligible events/day. Coalescing per device on a 30-second floor collapses bursts (a phone asleep for eight hours gets one notification, not forty) and removes ~60% on this traffic mix, leaving **~2.2B pushes/day**, 26k/s average, ~78k/s peak, all of it into APNs and FCM, which we do not control.
- **Media:** 5% of sends carry media at ~500KB average (compressed image ~400KB, 30s voice note at 16kbps ≈ 60KB, mix-weighted). Ingest = 5B × 0.05 × 500KB = **125TB/day** to object storage, 45PB/year at a 1-year TTL. Read side = 12.5B × 0.05 × 500KB = 312TB/day, ~85% absorbed by CDN so origin sees ~47TB/day. Media is 125× the text volume, which is why it is a separate system with its own lifecycle rather than a column in the log.
- **Latency budget:** p99 300ms decomposes as mobile radio to edge 60 to 120ms, quorum write 10ms, bus hop 5ms, edge to recipient radio 60 to 120ms, total 135 to 255ms. Roughly 80% of the budget is the last mile on both ends, so shaving milliseconds inside the data centre buys almost nothing and the engineering should go into never losing the message instead.
#### Key decisions
**Persistent connections vs long polling**

- Choice: one long-lived TLS connection per device, held whenever the OS permits, with platform push as the fallback once the app is suspended.
- Alternative: long polling. The client issues an ordinary HTTP request that the server holds open for up to 30 seconds and answers when a message arrives or the timer expires, then reissues it, with a separate POST for upstream sends.
- Decider: concurrent connection count against per-connection memory and per-cycle setup cost. At 30M peak sockets × 16KB tuned state = 480GB of fleet RAM across 60 boxes, and that cost is identical under long polling, because a held request occupies the same socket. What long polling adds is a second connection for the upstream direction, roughly doubling the socket count, and a re-establishment every 30 seconds: 30M ÷ 30 = 1M request setups/s fleet-wide, ~17k/s per box. If 10% miss TLS session resumption, that is 100k full handshakes/s at ~1ms of CPU each, about 100 cores burned on nothing. Above roughly 1M concurrent connections the arithmetic stops being close.
- Alternative wins when: concurrency is small enough that the churn vanishes. At 100k concurrent, the same formula gives 3.3k setups/s fleet-wide and the operational simplicity of plain HTTP (no sticky routing, no drain mode, no connection-count capacity model, load balancers that already work) is worth more than the sockets. It also wins per client rather than fleet-wide, and that case is not marginal: corporate proxies that strip the `Upgrade` header and captive portals that kill idle connections account for a low single-digit percentage of sessions, and every serious client ships long polling as a fallback for exactly those. Build it as a fallback on day one, because retrofitting a second transport into a protocol that assumed full duplex is much worse than designing for both.

**Server-held plaintext history vs end-to-end encryption**

- Choice: store-and-forward with server-side plaintext history, TLS in transit and encryption at rest. This is the default only because the stated requirements include scrollable history, multi-device, and abuse handling, and no confidentiality requirement was given.
- Alternative: end-to-end encryption. Ciphertext addressed to a specific recipient device, keys generated and held on the device, the server as a blind mailbox that forgets a message once collected.
- Decider: whether confidentiality from the operator is a requirement, asked in the first two minutes, because it is not additive. Four subsystems change together. Server-side search over 30TB of hot history stops existing and must become an on-device index over the ~5,000 messages a user holds after 30 days (50 sent plus 125 received per day, the 12.5B delivered copies spread over 100M users), which is about 1MB of text and genuinely fine, but it is a client feature now and it cannot search what the device never had. New-device history stops being a server read and becomes either a device-to-device transfer or an encrypted backup. Group send goes from one ciphertext to one per recipient device: 12 members × 2.5 devices = 30 encryptions per message with pairwise sessions, which is why sender-key schemes (Signal's Sender Keys, shipped from 2014 onward) exist and why you would use one. And content-based abuse detection disappears, leaving rate, graph shape and account age.
- Alternative wins when: confidentiality is the product, or the regulatory posture demands it, and for a consumer messenger in 2026 that is close to the default expectation rather than a niche. The alternative is genuinely the better product choice for WhatsApp and I would take it if asked; the honest cost is that users who lose their only device lose their history unless you build the encrypted-backup escape hatch, and that hatch is a server-held recovery path that partly undoes the claim. Where it clearly loses is workplace messaging, because an employer that cannot run eDiscovery over its own corpus cannot buy the product.

**Shared conversation log vs per-recipient inbox fan-out**

- Choice: one shared log per conversation, plus a per-device cursor. The bus carries a lightweight routing notification, not a copy of the message.
- Alternative: write a row into every recipient's own inbox partition at send time, so a client's unread set across all conversations is one sequential scan.
- Decider: the group size distribution, specifically its tail rather than its mean. At our mix the mean amplification is 2.5, so fan-out would cost 12.5B inbox writes/day against 5B log writes, which is entirely affordable. The tail is what breaks it: one 100k-member room at 10 messages/minute is 1M inbox writes/minute, 16k writes/s from a single conversation, landing on whichever shards its members happen to hash to, so one chatty room degrades unrelated users on those shards. Once p99.9 group size passes roughly 1,000 members the shared log wins, and our cap is 1,024 precisely so that this stays true.
- Alternative wins when: groups are hard-capped small and read latency is the SLO you are measured on. At a 100-member cap the worst case is 100× amplification, still bounded, and the read path becomes one partition scan per device instead of one query per conversation. That matters enormously when a user belongs to 200 conversations and cold-starts a client, which is Slack's shape rather than this one. It also wins if unread counts must be exact and instant across hundreds of rooms, because a shared log makes you compute them and an inbox makes you read them.

**How to read the diagram:** the bus is drawn as one box but carries two distinct flows. The ingest flow takes a message from the sender's edge to the persist service, which assigns the conversation-scoped id and does the quorum write. The routing flow takes the committed record back out, one partition per edge, to whichever edge holds each recipient's socket. The sender's ack is emitted after the write and travels back over the routing flow like any other event. The sequence diagram later in this question compresses ingest into a single persist hop; the invariant both drawings share, and the only one worth defending in the room, is that nothing acks before the write commits.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** a direct mesh between edges needs every edge to know every other edge, and it breaks during a rolling deploy exactly when connections are moving. Routing through a bus makes edge membership a subscription rather than a topology. Coordination is deliberately off the write path: discovery and presence are TTL'd caches, so a stale entry costs a round trip through the push path, never a lost message.

**What this layout buys you:** real-time delivery, durable history, and one code path for offline catch-up. The cost is that connection ownership is now part of the architecture. An edge is not interchangeable while it holds sockets, so deploys need draining, failover needs a reconnect storm plan, and capacity is planned in connections rather than requests per second.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The delivery ladder: what each tick means, and how a device that missed everything catches up.**

This is the mechanism that gets drilled, because it is where correctness lives and where most designs quietly break. A message passes three independent facts back to the sender, each produced by a different actor, each losable on its own: it is stored, it reached a device, a human looked at it. Conflating any two of them is the classic failure.

**Stored.** The persist path assigns a conversation-scoped monotonic id and does a quorum write to the conversation log. Only then is the ack emitted. The temptation is to ack from the edge on receipt and write asynchronously, because it shaves 10ms. Do not: a tick that can be retracted is worse than a slow tick, and against a 60 to 120ms mobile round trip the 10ms is invisible anyway. The quorum matters as much as the write, because a single-replica acknowledgement means a node loss silently deletes acked messages, and the symptom is a conversation where one side sees a message the other never will.

**Idempotency, the step most candidates skip.** The client generates a `client_msg_id` before its first attempt and reuses it across every retry. The persist write is conditional on `(chat_id, client_msg_id)` not already existing, and on a hit it returns the original `msg_id` rather than writing again. Without this, the common case of a lost ack plus a retry produces two genuinely distinct messages, and no downstream dedupe can undo that, because by the time anyone notices both have valid ids and both have been delivered. The window has to cover the client's whole retry horizon, hours on mobile, so this is a real 24-hour index rather than a small in-process LRU, and it costs one extra read on the write path.

**Cursors, per device rather than per user.** Each device stores the highest `msg_id` it has durably applied per conversation, and the server mirrors it as `(chat_id, device_id) → applied_msg_id`. Multi-device is what makes this subtle. A user with a phone, a laptop and a tablet has three cursors in the same conversation. "Delivered" is a per-device fact and is true when any one device has it. "Read" is a per-user fact and is the maximum over that user's devices. Getting this backwards produces the familiar bug where reading on a laptop leaves the phone showing an unread badge forever.

**Reconnect.** The client sends its cursors and the server streams everything after them. This needs a bound. A device returning after three months in a busy group would receive tens of thousands of messages down a socket that times out mid-stream, then retry from the same cursor and fail identically. So if the gap exceeds roughly 500 messages or 7 days, the server answers with a resync marker and the current highest id instead of the backlog; the client jumps its cursor forward, renders the last page, and pages older history through the ordinary paginated read. State the cost out loud: that device never receives the intervening messages as pushes, so it never acks them, and the sender's ticks for those messages never complete. It is the right trade and it is a behaviour change, not a free optimisation.

**At-least-once, never exactly-once.** The socket can die after the server has written the frame and before the client has applied it, and neither side can distinguish that from the frame never arriving. So the server retries and the client applies by `msg_id` with an upsert. Exactly-once at the transport is not achievable over a mobile network; idempotent apply at the client is, and it is cheap. The leak is notifications: a duplicate push produces a duplicate buzz even when the duplicate message is discarded, so the push service dedupes on `msg_id` per device with a short TTL of its own.

**Receipts, the expensive half.** A receipt is a message travelling the other way, and the reverse channel is where the arithmetic goes wrong: in a 500-member group one forward message can produce 500 delivered plus 500 read events, a 1,000× amplification. Three things keep it bounded and they compose. Carry a high-water mark instead of a row per message, so a burst of 40 messages collapses into one update. Debounce per conversation per device on a 5-second window. Above roughly 50 members show a count rather than a per-member list, so the server aggregates. Notice the first of those is the same row as the cursor, so the receipt and the sync state are one write, not two.

**Ordering.** Ids come from the persist path per conversation, so every recipient renders the same sequence regardless of which edge delivered their copy or how the bus interleaved things. Client timestamps cannot be used because phone clocks are wrong by seconds, and global ordering is not needed and would cost a per-user sequencer. Where the guarantee leaks is two devices of the same user sending concurrently into one conversation: they get their ids in the order the persist path happened to see them, which may not be the order the human experienced. Accepted, not solved.

**Message delivery state machine.** Modern chat clients render four user-visible states; each transition is a separate ack from a different actor.

```svg
</svg>
```

Sending is client-local and nothing outside the device knows about it. Sent (one tick) is the persist ack. Delivered (two ticks) is a recipient device raising its cursor. Read (blue) requires an explicit receipt, which most clients only send when the app is actually opened, to save battery, so receipts commonly arrive in batches long after delivery. Failed is not terminal: it is the client's retry loop, driven by the same `client_msg_id`, which is why a retry after a failure that was really a lost ack resolves to Sent rather than a duplicate.
