The build path tolerates minutes of latency because it runs hourly; the serve path budgets ~50ms of server time inside a ~100ms keypress-to-paint target. Note that the diagram draws the personal merge at the origin, which is the alternative in the third fork above; the design as chosen moves that box to the client so the response stays cacheable, and the merge arrow disappears from the origin entirely.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Structure size in RAM** → compile to an FST. A hashmap trie over 100M queries is ~76GB including top-K payloads; suffix sharing brings that to 8 to 16GB, which fits on one box and removes the need to shard at all.
- **Hot prefix** → the CDN plus a whole-structure-per-node layout. Single and double character prefixes take a few percent of all traffic each; the edge absorbs ~95% of requests, and because every node holds the entire snapshot there is no prefix-to-shard mapping left to skew. This is the main practical reason to pay for the FST compile.
- **Build time on log explosion** → sample the tail, keep the head whole. A viral event multiplies log volume and the aggregator falls behind. Sampling at 1% below the frequency floor preserves the head distribution exactly (popular queries still dominate every top-K) and only costs resolution in the tail, which was never going to make anyone's top-10.
- **Stale suggestions for trends** → a 60-second streaming overlay merged at serve time. The base snapshot is up to an hour old. The overlay is small (50 to 100MB per node) and adds ~5μs to a lookup, and it is the only mutable thing on the serving path, which is why it is also the riskiest (see Unresolved).
- **Snapshot distribution** → object storage plus staged rollout. Pushing 12GB to 200 nodes from a build host would saturate its egress; upload once, let nodes pull in parallel at ~670MB/s aggregate, and roll the swap in 10% waves so a bad build cannot take the whole fleet.
- **Tight latency budget** (~50ms of server time) → nothing on the hot path may touch a database. Every ingredient of a response is either in local RAM or already at the edge. This is precisely why personalization moved to the client: a per-user history lookup is the one thing that would put a datastore back on the path.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snapshot distribution | New snapshot is corrupt or incomplete on some nodes | Checksum mismatch and canary-prefix failure before activation | Verify checksum and canary set before the pointer flip, keep the last two known-good snapshots resident, roll back by flipping the pointer |
| Bad build | Snapshot is well-formed but semantically empty or wrong | Canary-prefix diff against the previous snapshot, and top-K emptiness rate | Staged 10% rollout with a two-minute soak, automatic halt on canary regression |
| Hot prefix | A prefix range saturates a node | Per-node QPS skew and p99 spike | Whole snapshot on every node so any node can serve any prefix; add replicas and let the edge absorb short prefixes |
| Trend overlay | Streaming overlay stalls or is poisoned | Overlay age, and a spike in suggestions with no history in the base snapshot | Serve from the base snapshot alone until the overlay recovers; overlay entries are always rate-limited and policy-filtered before merge |
| Edge cache | Cache stampede on popular prefixes after a snapshot roll | Origin QPS spike on short prefixes | Pre-warm the top prefixes ahead of the roll and single-flight origin fills |
| Policy filter | Suppression rules fail and unsafe suggestions leak into top-K | Blocklist-match canary and policy-violation audit | Filter at build time and again at serve time, and keep purge-by-tag on the edge cache tested |

**Unresolved**

**The tail is neither fresh nor good, and the frequency floor is why.** Roughly 15% of Google searches are ones it has never seen before, and the floor of 5 occurrences per day deletes a much larger band than that from the index. For a real fraction of prefixes the system has genuinely nothing to say and returns an empty list, which reads as broken to a user who is typing something perfectly reasonable. Lowering the floor does not fix it; it just imports bot noise into the suggestion list, which is worse than silence. The only real answer is to generate rather than retrieve, completing from an n-gram model or a small language model when the index comes up empty, and that swaps a retrieval system with a bounded output space for one that can invent a suggestion nobody has ever searched for, including defamatory ones. That is a different safety problem with a different review process attached, and we have not built it.

**Popularity ranking is a feedback loop and we cannot measure our way out of it from inside.** Suggesting a query causes people to run it, which raises its count, which causes it to be suggested more. Nothing in the log distinguishes "popular because people wanted it" from "popular because we put it in front of them", and the obvious experiment does not help: engagement metrics are inflated by the same loop they are supposed to evaluate. The partial fix is a small holdout arm that never receives suggestions and ranking the head from its organic frequencies, which costs you a degraded experience for those users and is statistically far too thin to say anything about the tail. So the head is measurable and the rest is asserted. It also means a suggestion that becomes wrong (a person's name attached to an accusation, a product that was recalled) is self-reinforcing until a human intervenes.

**Safety filtering is a build-time blocklist against a serve-time adversary, and the overlay is the hole.** Suppression happens at build time, which is the right place because it costs nothing at request time. But offensive and defamatory combinations are composed continuously, blocklists are string matching against people who are deliberately working around string matching, and the legally required suppression set varies by jurisdiction with a takedown clock measured in hours. The 60-second overlay is the sharpest edge here: a term can go from unseen to served in one minute, which no human review process can match, so the overlay gets a stricter automated filter and a lower trust score than the base index and will still be the path that leaks something. We accept a serve-time filter as second-line defence, costing ~0.2ms, and we accept that a suppression pushed now is still served from the edge for up to 60 seconds afterwards.
#### Drill questions
1. What if a serving node goes down mid-rollout?
2. How do you handle real-time trends, breaking news in the last five minutes?
3. How would you support typo tolerance?
4. How do you personalize without blowing up the shared structure?
5. How do you prevent suggesting offensive or defamatory queries?
6. How would you scale this 10x, to 100B searches/day?
7. Why an FST over a hashmap trie in production?
8. What is the latency budget end to end, and where does each millisecond go?
9. How does this change for Chinese, Japanese or Korean input?
10. Suggesting a query makes it more popular. How do you keep ranking from eating its own tail?
11. What does the client do between keystrokes, and how does that change your QPS estimate?
12. Walk through the moment a new snapshot lands on a serving node.
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Every node holds the whole 12GB snapshot, so there is no state to reconstruct and no shard that becomes unavailable; the load balancer routes around it and the remaining nodes absorb the traffic, which they can because CPU utilisation is ~25%. A replacement warms up by pulling the current snapshot from object storage, a few minutes at 670MB/s aggregate. *If pushed:* during the warm-up window the node must not take traffic, so readiness is gated on the canary prefix set passing, not on the process being up. A node that answers with an empty index is worse than a node that is down, because the load balancer will happily keep sending it requests.

2. A streaming aggregator builds a small overlay trie every 60 seconds from a sliding window of recent queries, and serving nodes merge it with the base snapshot at request time. *If pushed:* the tradeoff is freshness against noise. A short window means one coordinated group can spike a term into the suggestion list within a minute, so the overlay needs per-source rate limiting and bot filtering before counting, and a stricter policy filter than the base index gets. It is the least safe path in the system and it is the one with the least review time.

3. Three options with genuinely different costs. Pre-expand: generate edit-distance-1 variants of each top query at build time and add them as entries, which multiplies index size 5 to 10x but costs nothing at request time. Side index: a BK-tree or n-gram index consulted only when the exact prefix returns zero hits, adding 50 to 100ms on that fallback path, which blows the budget but only for requests that would otherwise show nothing. Or punt: let the user submit and let the search engine's spelling correction handle it. *If pushed:* Google essentially punts on the prefix and corrects post-submit; e-commerce search pre-expands, because "adiddas" returning nothing loses a sale. The choice follows from whether an empty suggestion list is an inconvenience or a lost transaction.

4. Keep the shared structure global, and do the blend on the client from history stored locally. That keeps the response identical per `(prefix, locale)`, which is what preserves the ~95% edge hit rate, and the edge hit rate is what keeps the origin at 100K QPS instead of 2M. *If pushed:* the cost is that a new device has no personalization until it accumulates history, and you cannot personalize for users who clear local storage. If the product genuinely needs cross-device personalization, move the merge to the origin and accept a 20x fleet, which is a fine trade at 5K QPS and an absurd one at 2M.

5. A blocklist applied at build time, before any string can reach a node's top-K, plus a classifier pass over the candidate set. A serve-time filter runs as second-line defence at ~0.2ms. *If pushed:* build-time filtering cannot keep up with the 60-second overlay, so the overlay gets a stricter automated filter and a lower trust weight. Jurisdictional suppression (right to be forgotten, defamation takedowns) is maintained as per-region overlays with a takedown clock in hours, and the edge cache TTL means a suppression is still served for up to 60 seconds after you push it, so purge-by-tag has to be tested before you need it.

6. 10x the searches is 20M peak suggest QPS and ~1M at the origin after the edge. The origin fleet grows linearly, which is fine because it is ~20 cores today. The interesting part is the index, which does *not* grow 10x: query popularity is Zipf, so 10x the volume yields maybe 2 to 3x the distinct strings above the frequency floor, so the FST goes from 12GB to perhaps 30GB and no longer fits comfortably beside the OS page cache on a 64GB box. *If pushed:* that is when you finally shard, and the honest cost is that you reintroduce the hot-prefix skew that holding the whole structure per node had eliminated. Shard by a hash of the first three characters rather than the first one, so "th" and "tw" land in different places.

7. Memory. A hashmap trie over 100M queries at 20 characters is ~1B nodes at ~60B each, ~60GB, plus ~16GB of top-K payloads, so ~76GB, which does not fit a 64GB box. An FST shares suffixes as well as prefixes, so every "-ing" tail is one path, and amortises to ~10B per node, landing at 8 to 16GB. That fits whole on every node, which is what lets you delete the routing layer entirely. FSTs are immutable, but we rebuild hourly, so that costs nothing here. Lucene has used FSTs for term dictionaries since 2011 for the same reason. *If pushed:* the trade is build complexity, since FST construction is a real algorithm while trie insertion is trivial. Build with a trie, compile to an FST for the snapshot, and keep the trie path working so you can debug against it.

8. ~100ms from keypress to painted list, derived from typing cadence: a 40 wpm typist leaves ~300ms between keystrokes and the list must settle well inside that. Mobile round trip is 30 to 50ms, client render ~10ms, leaving the server ~50ms p99. An edge hit uses ~10ms of that and covers ~95% of requests. An origin miss costs ~30 to 40ms: route, FST walk at ~1μs, overlay merge, policy filter, serialise. *If pushed:* the client can hide some of it by prefetching the next likely characters. If the user has typed "th", speculatively request "tha", "the" and "thi", which trades bandwidth for perceived latency and only pays off because those responses are edge-cached anyway.

9. The trie is over characters, and CJK has no spaces and an alphabet in the tens of thousands, which breaks two assumptions. Input is usually romanised before it reaches you (pinyin for Chinese, romaji for Japanese), so the practical answer is to index both the romanised form and the native form and route on input method. Branching factor rises sharply, which makes an array-of-children node layout wasteful and pushes you further toward the FST. *If pushed:* build one structure per locale rather than one global one, because popularity distributions do not transfer and mixing scripts in one structure just adds noise to every ranking. Cost is roughly linear in locales, which is affordable at 12GB each only because you deploy the locales a region actually serves, not all of them everywhere.

10. You cannot fully, and the honest answer says so. Suggesting a query raises its count, which raises its rank. The measurable part is a small holdout arm that receives no suggestions; rank the head from its organic frequencies and you have an unbiased signal for the queries that matter most. *If pushed:* the holdout is statistically useless for the tail, and it costs those users a degraded product. Beyond that, the mitigations are dampening rather than correction: cap how much a single hour can move a term's score, decay old counts so a self-reinforced term decays if organic interest stops, and require a term to appear in the holdout arm at all before it can enter the top three.

11. It debounces, typically at 150ms, and it suppresses requests below two or three characters entirely because those answers are useless and the edge would serve them anyway. That is exactly why the estimate is ~5 calls per search rather than ~20: 20 characters typed, the first two suppressed, most users committing around character 8, and the debounce collapsing one or two of the remainder. *If pushed:* if you assume one request per keystroke you get 20 calls per search and a 2.3M QPS average instead of 580K, and every capacity number downstream is wrong by 4x. Client behaviour is a load-bearing input to this design, not a UI detail, and it is worth stating the assumption out loud before you multiply anything.

12. The node downloads the new FST to a temp path on local NVMe, verifies the checksum, and runs ~1000 canary prefixes against expected results while the file is still invisible to traffic. If the canaries pass, it mmaps the file and flips a single atomic pointer; requests holding the old pointer finish against the old mapping, which is unmapped once its refcount drops to zero. Both snapshots are resident during the overlap, so the box is sized for 24GB rather than 12GB. *If pushed:* the checksum is the easy half. The failure that actually happens is a well-formed snapshot built from an empty log partition, which passes every integrity check and returns empty lists for everything, so the canary set and the 10% staged rollout with a two-minute soak are the real protection, and the pointer flip means rollback is seconds with no download.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, frame it and name the property that decides everything.** Open with the observation, not the components: "the query is a prefix, not a set of terms, so the answer set for every prefix worth serving is small and can be computed before anyone types." Then ask the three questions that actually fork the design: personalization or not, because that decides whether the response is cacheable; refresh cadence, because that decides whether you need a delta path; and whether typos have to work, because that is a separate index with its own budget. State the assumptions out loud: ~10B searches/day, ~5 suggest calls each, ~2M peak QPS, ~50ms of server time. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the two halves.** Draw a horizontal line across the board. Above it: query logs, aggregate, top-K roll-up, compile, snapshot to object store. Below it: client, CDN, serving node holding the whole structure in memory. Say the sentence that justifies the line: everything above runs hourly and tolerates minutes; everything below has 50ms. Then do the arithmetic that makes the design inevitable, because this is the moment that separates candidates: 2M peak QPS, 95% edge hit rate, 100K at the origin, ~50μs per request, so ~20 cores. Compare that with query-time ranking at 1 to 3ms per request, which is 100 to 300 cores. Three orders of magnitude is not a tuning decision.

**15-35, the drill.** Protect this time; it is where the interview happens. Go deep on the build: the bottom-up roll-up, and the correctness argument for why the union of children's top-K is sufficient, and the condition it depends on (scores must be a property of the completion alone, so length normalisation and prefix-position boosts break it). Then the snapshot swap, including that the failure you defend against is a bad build rather than a bad download, which is why the canary set and the staged rollout matter more than the checksum. Then take the FST fork on your own terms: 76GB against 12GB, and say the real prize is that holding the whole structure per node deletes the routing layer and the hot-prefix problem with it. Then freshness: the 60-second overlay, and volunteer that it is the least safe path in the system. Keep typo tolerance and CJK in reserve as one-liners.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the gaps before they are found: the frequency floor means the tail returns nothing and generating instead of retrieving is a different safety problem; popularity ranking is a feedback loop you can only measure through a holdout arm; safety filtering is build-time and the 60-second overlay outruns human review. Then the operational surface in two minutes: what you page on (edge hit rate by prefix length, canary failures during rollout, overlay age, empty-result rate), and DR as "the snapshot is in object storage and the structure is read-only", which makes this one of the easiest recovery stories you will ever draw.

Cut first: typo tolerance and the three ways to do it, then multilingual and CJK, then the personalization mechanics beyond naming where the merge happens. All three are real and none of them changes the shape of the system. Never cut: the precompute-versus-rank arithmetic, the bottom-up roll-up and its correctness condition, and the snapshot swap.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

**Build-time trie node** (in the pipeline, before compilation):
```
struct Node {
  children: map<char, Node>
  top_k:    list<(query, score)>   # populated only to depth 12
  terminal: optional<(query, score)>
}
```

**Served artifact:** a minimised FST mapping prefix to a byte offset, with the top-10 list stored inline at each offset. Immutable, mmapped, replaced whole.

**Overlay:** a small mutable trie rebuilt every 60 seconds from the recent query stream, same node shape, merged with the base result at request time.

**API contract**

```
GET /suggest?q={prefix}&locale={locale}&limit=10
  → 200 { suggestions: [{text, score}] }
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=60
  Vary: none   (the response is a pure function of q and locale)
```

Personal history is never a parameter; the client merges it locally, which is what keeps this cacheable.

**Observability**

- **Edge hit rate by prefix length** - short prefixes must resolve at the edge; a drop here shows up as an origin QPS multiple, not as a latency alarm.
- **Origin p99 by path** - base lookup, overlay merge and policy filter separately, so a regression is attributable.
- **Canary-prefix results during rollout** - the only signal that catches a well-formed but semantically empty build.
- **Snapshot age and rollout wave progress** - freshness plus how much of the fleet is on which build.
- **Overlay age** - how stale the trending path is; the base index can be an hour old, the overlay cannot be five minutes old.
- **Empty-result rate by prefix length** - the direct measure of the frequency-floor gap conceded above.
- **Suppressed-suggestion rate** - catches policy regressions and coordinated query floods.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** the served artifact is read-only, so every region holds an identical copy per locale. There is no replication protocol, only a distribution job.
- **RTO:** minutes for a node, because recovery is "pull the current snapshot and pass the canaries". Seconds for a bad build, because rollback is a pointer flip against a snapshot already on disk.
- **RPO:** bounded by the last successfully published snapshot plus overlay lag, so at most one hour of ranking freshness. No user data is lost because none is stored on this path.
- **Failover cadence:** rehearse snapshot rollback and edge purge-by-tag, not database failover. The data plane is immutable; the risk is publishing something wrong, not losing something.
- **Cross-region cost:** snapshot distribution and edge fill only. 12GB per locale per hour per region, which is noise next to the request traffic it eliminates.

### 11. Design YouTube
#### Problem
Accept video from anyone at roughly 500 hours of new material per minute, and make every upload playable on any device over any connection anywhere in the world. Almost none of it will be watched more than a handful of times, and you have to decide how much money to spend on a video before you know which kind it is. Everything uploaded is also a safety and rights liability from the moment it becomes visible.
#### Core
The design question is not how to transcode video. It is how little you can commit to an upload before you know whether anyone will watch it.

Upload is chunked and resumable, written by the client straight into object storage so the ingest tier never handles bytes. Completion enqueues a job. Upload readiness and playback readiness are separate lifecycle states, and conflating them is the classic mistake.

The pipeline then does the smallest useful thing. Split the source at keyframe boundaries into six-second segments, encode two rungs only, say 360p and 720p, fan the segments across GPU workers, package once into fragmented MP4 with both HLS and DASH manifests over the same bytes, publish. For a 12-minute upload that is under a minute of wall clock. In parallel a cheap classifier pass and a fingerprint match against the rights database decide whether the video may be published at all.

Everything above 720p is earned. A video crosses a view-velocity threshold, or its channel carries a prior, and only then do we spend on 1080p, 4K, per-title ladder analysis and AV1. Around half of uploads never earn anything, and skipping them cuts the encoding fleet roughly threefold and encoded bytes by more than half.

Delivery is pull-through from a CDN with a shield tier absorbing origin fan-in, because one day of uploads is bigger than an edge cache. Only the predicted-hot slice gets pushed out in advance.

Storage tiers on last access, and renditions for cold titles are deleted and regenerated from the source if anyone returns.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a print shop that anyone can walk into. A film studio knows it is printing a hundred titles this year and can afford to make a beautiful negative of each one and ship reels to every cinema in advance. This shop takes 500 hours of new footage every minute from strangers, has no idea which reel will fill a stadium and which will be seen by the uploader's mother, and cannot afford to treat them the same. So it runs off one cheap print immediately, watches the door, and only goes back to make the good version of the reels that people actually queue for.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Do the whole job at ingest.* Every upload gets the full set of quality versions the moment it lands, and every version is kept. This buys one code path, no partial-availability state machine, and playback that never has to wait for a second pass. It costs the full compute and storage bill for the large majority that nobody ever watches. It wins when upload volume is small relative to viewership, or when someone has already decided each item is worth the money, which is exactly the curated-catalogue case.

*Do the least useful thing at ingest, escalate on demand.* Produce one or two cheap versions so the video is playable within a minute, then upgrade a video only once it shows real demand. This cuts encoding and storage sharply on a skewed catalogue. It costs a second pipeline, manifests that change over a video's life, and a quality cliff for anything that goes viral in its first minutes, because escalation is reactive.

*Keep only a high-quality intermediate and generate everything at play time.* Just-in-time packaging and encoding removes derivative storage almost entirely. It costs per-view compute and a start delay for the first viewer, so it only works behind a cache. It wins for the deep archive, where a title collects a few views a year and storing seven renditions of it for a decade is absurd.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a creator uploads a 20-minute tutorial, about 2.5GB. The client splits it into 5MB pieces and uploads them straight to object storage with a pre-signed URL, acknowledging each; a dropped connection resumes at the last confirmed piece rather than at zero. Completion writes a job. The pipeline probes the file, rejects it if the container is broken, and splits it at keyframe boundaries into 200 six-second segments. Only two rungs are encoded, 360p and 720p, so 400 segment jobs fan out across GPU workers and finish in tens of seconds. A packaging step writes fragmented MP4 segments once and emits two manifests over the same bytes, an HLS playlist and a DASH MPD, so iOS and everything else read the same objects. In parallel, frame and audio classifiers plus a fingerprint match against the rights database return a verdict. Both green, and the video flips to visible. A viewer's player fetches the manifest, picks a rung from its bandwidth estimate, and pulls six-second segments from the nearest edge. Three hours later the video has 40,000 views in an hour, crosses the escalation threshold, and a second pipeline run adds 1080p and 4K rungs and rewrites the manifest.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Chunked resumable upload.** The client uploads fixed-size pieces directly to object storage and tracks which are confirmed, so a failure at piece 47 resumes at 47. Bytes never pass through an application server, which is what keeps the ingest tier stateless and cheap. A 2.5GB upload over a mobile connection will fail at least once; the design assumption is that it always fails.
- **Transcoding pipeline, as a DAG of jobs.** Probe, then split, then encode segment by rung, then package, then publish. Segments are independent, so a 20-minute video becomes hundreds of parallel jobs and finishes in wall-clock seconds rather than in real time. Hardware encoders on GPUs run H.264 several times faster than CPU at comparable quality, which is what makes the fleet affordable at 8.3 hours of source arriving per second. An orchestrator owns retries, partial failure, and the readiness state machine, because the pipeline is long-running and must survive worker loss.
- **The escalation controller.** The piece that makes this question different from a curated catalogue. It watches view velocity per video, applies channel-level priors, and decides which videos get the expensive rungs, per-title ladder analysis, and a second codec. Nothing above the floor is produced without its say-so.
- **Adaptive bitrate over a manifest.** The video is cut into short segments and a text manifest lists the segments available at each rung. The player times each download, estimates bandwidth, and picks the next segment's rung itself. There is no server-side session, which is precisely why the whole delivery path can be a dumb cache. A Wi-Fi to cellular handover becomes a quality drop instead of a stall.
- **CDN plus a shield tier.** Segments are immutable once written, so they cache indefinitely at content-addressed URLs. The shield sits between edges and origin and collapses simultaneous misses for the same object into one origin fetch. Manifests are the exception: they change when a rung is added, so they carry a short TTL while segments carry a year. Q51 goes into the CDN itself.
- **Storage tiering and regeneration.** Object storage has tiers roughly 10x to 20x apart in price per byte. Last-access lifecycle rules demote the tail. Below a certain access rate the right move is not a cheaper tier but deletion: keep the source, drop the derivatives, and re-encode if someone ever comes back.
- **Metadata, search and recommendation.** Separate systems with separate scale domains that happen to share a screen with this one. Recommendation ranking is Q28's subject, not this one's.

**The thing that makes it hard:** you must decide how much to spend on a video at the exact moment you know least about it. Assume half of uploads never reach 100 views and the top 1% take roughly 80% of watch time. Producing the full seven-rung ladder for every upload costs on the order of 3,600 GPUs running continuously and 2.9PB of new encoded bytes per day, and the majority of both is spent on video that will never be requested. Producing two rungs and escalating on demand costs roughly 1,200 GPUs and 1.15PB. But the saving is bought with a real defect: escalation is reactive, so the videos that ramp fastest are served at the floor rung during exactly the hours their audience is largest. Every serious version of this design is an argument about how to buy back that first hour with priors rather than with reaction.

**Why this design and what it costs:** separating upload readiness from playback readiness is what lets the expensive work be asynchronous, tiered, and revisable. The system spends almost nothing per view, and in exchange it accepts that a video's quality is a function of its history rather than a property fixed at upload, which shows up as manifests that mutate, caches that hold stale playlists, and a support burden of creators asking why their video is not in 4K yet.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Chunked upload: pre-signed multipart URLs to S3, client writes directly, completion event on the bucket triggers the job.
- Pipeline: Temporal for the DAG and the readiness state machine, Kafka for the segment work queue, GPU workers running ffmpeg with NVENC.
- Packaging: CMAF fragmented MP4 written once, HLS and DASH manifests generated over the same objects.
- Serving: segments at content-addressed URLs with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`; manifests at `max-age=60`.
- Escalation: view-velocity counters in Redis, a threshold job that re-enqueues the video for the upper rungs.
#### Interactive diagram
The whole design as one explorable picture: [open the interactive diagram](/diagram/youtube).

Every box and every arrow is clickable. Selecting one dims everything it does not touch and opens what it is, why it exists, the numbers worth quoting, the failure it owns, and why that technology rather than the obvious alternative. Start with the Overview button.

#### What this is really testing
Whether you notice that the expensive work has to be committed before the information that would justify it exists. Transcoding, storage and edge placement all cost real money per video, and the demand distribution that decides whether that money was well spent is not known for hours or days. A candidate who describes a seven-rung ladder, replication, and global pre-positioning has designed a system that is correct and about three times more expensive than it needs to be, and has not noticed that the interesting engineering is the policy layer deciding which videos deserve which treatment. The second half of the same insight is that this is the only design in the media cluster where the content itself is untrusted, so publication is a gated event rather than a deployment step.

The contrast is with Netflix. Both stream adaptive-bitrate video off a CDN, both need a bitrate ladder, both need per-title analysis, and if you answer only that far the two questions are the same answer twice. The axis that separates them is whether the value of an asset is known when the work is committed. Netflix acquires a title, knows before a single byte is encoded that it will be watched millions of times, and can therefore afford per-shot convex-hull optimisation over the whole catalogue and can push the entire catalogue to appliances inside ISPs overnight, because the catalogue is small enough to fit. Its hard problems are ladder quality, licensing windows, and steering traffic between its own appliances. YouTube gets 500 hours a minute from strangers. One day of uploads is larger than an edge appliance holds, so pre-positioning everything is not a cost decision but an impossibility. Half of what arrives is worthless and you cannot tell which half. And Netflix has no moderation problem at all, because a human bought the content, whereas here the moderation gate sits on the critical path between a creator hitting publish and anyone being allowed to see it. Give the Netflix answer here and you have solved delivery while ignoring the two things that actually make this system hard.

Closest question: Q31
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Live streaming in scope? (assume on-demand only)
- What is the upload-to-playable target, and does it differ by creator tier?
- Resolutions to support, and must every video get every rung?
- Is moderation in scope, and may a video be visible before it clears?
- Average video length and upload rate?
- DRM or forensic watermarking?
- Comments, likes and recommendations in scope?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| On-demand only | an asynchronous transcode pipeline on upload, no low-latency live path, and moderation can gate publication |
| Live is in scope | a second pipeline with segment-by-segment encoding at real time, and moderation becomes strictly after the fact |
| Upload-to-playable under a minute | a cheap floor rung published first, with the rest of the ladder produced later |
| Every video gets every rung | a fixed ladder at ingest, roughly 3x the encoding fleet, and no escalation controller at all |
| Moderation must clear first | visibility gated on classifier verdicts, a risk-tiered human queue, and a stated exposure budget |
| High upload rate | chunked resumable upload straight to object storage, then a queue feeding transcode workers that scale independently |
| DRM or watermark | an encryption step in packaging plus key servers, and per-session URLs that break long CDN caching |
| Comments, likes, recommendations | separate services with separate scale domains; recommendations consume watch-history events |
| Global delivery | pull-through CDN with a shield tier, and pre-positioning only for the predicted-hot slice |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** resumable upload; transcode to an adaptive-bitrate ladder; publish HLS and DASH manifests; gate publication on moderation and rights checks; playback with per-segment quality adaptation; thumbnails; metadata, search, comments and recommendations as adjacent services.
- **NFR:** upload-to-playable under 60s at p50 for a 12-minute video; time-to-first-frame under 500ms at p95; rebuffer ratio under 0.5% of watch time; source bytes durable before the upload is acknowledged; derivatives always recomputable; encoding cost per upload bounded rather than proportional to the full ladder.

**Scale**

- **Upload rate:** take ~500 hours uploaded per minute, the figure YouTube has published since 2019. 500 × 60 = 30k hours/hour, × 24 = **720k hours/day**. Per second: 500 ÷ 60 = **8.3 hours of source arriving every second**, which is the number the whole encoding fleet is sized against.
- **Videos per day:** assume a 12-minute mean. Shorts dominate the count but not the duration and run a separate pipeline; vlogs sit at 5 to 15 minutes and podcasts at 1 to 3 hours pull the mean up. 720k hours × 60 min = 43.2M minutes/day ÷ 12 = **~3.6M videos/day**.
- **Upload concurrency:** assume half of all starts fall in a 6-hour peak window. 1.8M ÷ 21,600s = 83 upload starts/s. Mean in-flight duration on a mobile connection is ~5 min, so 83 × 300s = **~25k concurrent uploads at peak**. These hold object-store multipart sessions, not application-server connections, which is why the ingest tier stays small.
- **Raw ingest:** phone footage after container normalisation averages ~2.2 Mbps, so 2.2 Mbps × 3600s ÷ 8 = 990MB, call it **~1GB per source hour**. 720k hours × 1GB = **~720TB/day of source**, retained forever because every derivative is recomputable from it.
- **Full ladder, if you encoded everything:** for a 1080p source the rungs are 144p 0.15, 240p 0.3, 360p 0.7, 480p 1.2, 720p 2.5, 1080p 4.5 Mbps, summing to 9.35 Mbps, which is 9.35 ÷ 2.2 = **4.25x the source**. Blending in the minority of 1440p and 4K sources, call it ~4x. 720TB × 4 = **~2.9PB/day encoded**.
- **Floor plus escalation, what we actually encode:** floor is 360p + 720p = 3.2 Mbps = 1.45x source, so 720TB × 1.45 = **1.04PB/day**. Assume 5% of videos cross the escalation threshold and take the remaining 6.15 Mbps of ladder, which is 2.8x source: 0.05 × 720TB × 2.8 = **~100TB/day**. Total **~1.15PB/day**, a **60% cut** against the full ladder.
- **Encoding fleet:** take hardware H.264 encode at ~15x realtime for one 1080p rung, so 4 GPU-minutes per source hour. Lower rungs scale with pixel count: 720p 0.44, 480p 0.20, 360p 0.11, 240p 0.05, 144p 0.02 of a 1080p rung. Full ladder = 1.82 1080p-equivalents = 7.3 GPU-min per source hour. At 8.3 source-hours/s that is 8.3 × 7.3 = 60.6 GPU-minutes of work per second of wall clock = **~3,600 GPUs saturated**. The floor is 0.44 + 0.11 = 0.55 equivalents = 2.2 GPU-min/source-hour → **~1,100 GPUs**, plus escalation at 0.05 × 1.27 equivalents → ~125 GPUs. **~1,200 against ~3,600, a 3x fleet difference**, and this is the number that settles the first fork.
- **Diurnal peak:** upload rate peaks around 2x the daily mean, so either provision ~2,500 GPUs or let the queue absorb it. Queue absorption is correct here because the SLO is measured in tens of seconds and the backlog drains in minutes.
- **Watch egress:** ~1B DAU × ~1 hour/day = ~1B watch-hours/day. At a 2 Mbps blend, since most viewing is mobile at 480p to 720p: 1e9 × 3600s × 2 Mbit = 7.2e15 bits/day ÷ 86,400 = **~83 Tbps average**, with a ~3x diurnal peak at **~250 Tbps** and single-event spikes on top of that.
- **The ratio that justifies the whole architecture:** 83 Tbps is 900PB/day of egress against 1.15PB/day of new encoded bytes, so in aggregate the system serves **~800 bytes for every byte it produces**. For the median video the same ratio is close to zero, and holding both numbers at once is the point of the question.
- **Origin load:** at 95% edge offload the origin still serves 5% × 900PB = 45PB/day, about 4 Tbps. Pushing offload to 99% with ISP-embedded caches drops that to ~9PB/day. The shield tier exists because that last few percent is the part that arrives as correlated bursts.
- **Segments and object count:** 6s segments, so 720k hours × 3600 ÷ 6 = 432M source-segments/day × 2 floor rungs = **~900M new objects/day**. A 6s 720p segment is 6 × 2.5 ÷ 8 = **1.9MB**; at 1080p 3.4MB; manifests ~5KB. Object count is a real cost line, not a rounding error: at $5 per million PUTs, 900M/day is **~$4.5k/day** before a byte is stored, which is one of the arguments for not producing rungs nobody asked for.
- **Storage growth:** 1.15PB/day encoded + 720TB/day source = ~1.9PB/day, × 1.4 for erasure-coding overhead = 2.6PB/day, × 365 = **~950PB/year**, call it 1EB/year. Tiering is not an optimisation at that rate, it is the only reason the number is payable: archive tiers run 10x to 20x below standard per byte, and the ~90% of the catalogue that goes untouched after 30 days belongs there.
- **Moderation arithmetic:** 3.6M videos/day at 5 minutes of human review each is 300k reviewer-hours/day, which is **~37,500 full-time reviewers**. That settles the moderation fork on its own. Classifiers are the opposite: sample 1 frame/s of a 12-minute video is 720 frames, at ~1,000 frames/s/GPU is 0.7 GPU-seconds/video, so 3.6M × 0.7 ÷ 86,400 = **~30 GPUs** for the whole classifier pass. Against a 1,200-GPU encoding fleet there is no cost case for skipping it.
#### Key decisions
**Full ladder at ingest vs a cheap floor plus demand-driven escalation**
- Choice: encode two rungs at ingest, 360p and 720p, publish, and produce everything above that only when a video earns it through view velocity or a channel prior. Per-title ladder analysis and a second codec are escalation-only.
- Alternative: the full ladder for every upload, one code path, nothing revisited. This is not a strawman: it is what every curated-catalogue service does, and it removes an entire subsystem, a mutable manifest, and a class of "why is my video not in 4K" support tickets.
- Decider: the fleet arithmetic above. Full ladder is ~3,600 GPUs saturated and 2.9PB/day of encoded output; floor plus 5% escalation is ~1,200 GPUs and 1.15PB/day. A 3x compute difference and a 60% storage difference, against a catalogue where half of uploads never reach 100 views, is not a close call. The second half of the decider is the escalation hit rate: escalation only pays if the fraction crossing the threshold stays under roughly 30%, above which you have paid for two pipeline runs on most videos and should have done it once.
- Alternative wins when: the catalogue is small, curated, or paid for in advance, so every asset is known to be worth the full treatment. It also wins at low absolute volume, where 3x of a small number is cheaper than the engineering and operational cost of an escalation controller. And it wins for any tier where the platform has contracted a quality floor, such as a paid creator programme promising 4K on publish, because there the reactive gap is a contract breach rather than a cost saving.

**Publish then review vs gate visibility on the moderation verdict**
- Choice: gate on the cheap synchronous checks, which is a frame and audio classifier pass plus a fingerprint match against the rights database, both of which finish in seconds and cost ~30 GPUs across the whole platform. Everything slower runs after the video is live, with tombstoning available at any point.
- Alternative: hold every upload private until all checks including human review have cleared.
- Decider: 3.6M videos/day at 5 minutes of review each is ~37,500 full-time reviewers, so a universal human gate is not expensive, it is arithmetically unavailable. What is genuinely open is the classifier gate, and that turns on the false-positive cost: at a 1% false-positive rate a synchronous gate wrongly delays 36,000 legitimate creators a day, which is why the gate is risk-tiered rather than uniform.
- Alternative wins when: the content class makes a single exposure unacceptable and the volume is small enough to pay for. Uploads from accounts under 24 hours old, uploads whose classifier score lands in the uncertain band, and anything matching a known-harmful hash all get held. So does regulated content in jurisdictions with pre-publication obligations. The honest framing is that the choice is not binary: the design picks an exposure budget, and the gate policy is tuned against it.

**Pre-position everything at the edge vs pull-through with a shield tier**
- Choice: pull-through by default. Edges fetch on miss, a shield tier collapses correlated misses into one origin fetch per object, and only a predicted-hot slice is pushed out in advance: scheduled premieres, channels above a subscriber threshold, and videos crossing a velocity threshold in their first minutes.
- Alternative: push the catalogue to edge and ISP-embedded appliances ahead of demand, which is how a curated streaming catalogue is delivered and is strictly better when it fits.
- Decider: daily catalogue growth against edge capacity. One day of encoded output is 1.15PB; an ISP-embedded appliance holds on the order of 100 to 500TB. A single day of uploads is 2x to 10x what one box holds, before the back catalogue exists at all, so pre-positioning everything is not a budget question. What can be pushed is the slice that fits, and 80% of watch time concentrating in about 1% of videos means the slice that fits is also the slice that matters.
- Alternative wins when: the catalogue fits on the appliance, which is the curated case and is why Netflix does it. It also wins per-event: for a scheduled fixture with a known audience, pushing in advance beats any reactive mechanism, and the cost is one planned fill instead of millions of correlated misses. Note this interacts badly with the first fork, because you can only pre-position bytes that exist, and a video escalated reactively has no upper rungs to push. Q51 covers the cache hierarchy itself.

**How to read the diagram:** the left column is the write path and the right column is the read path, and they meet only at the encoded object store. A creator's bytes go in once; a viewer's bytes come out of a cache. Nothing on the playback side ever talks to anything on the upload side, which is why a transcode backlog degrades creator experience and leaves viewers untouched.

**The renditions box is a snapshot, not a batch.** The diagram shows six rungs because that is what a fully escalated video looks like. On the day it is uploaded, only two of those boxes exist. The rest are filled in later, by a second pass triggered by demand, which means the encoded object store is append-only over a video's lifetime and the manifest that indexes it is mutable. That single asymmetry, immutable segments under a mutable manifest, is what drives the cache-control split later on.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** the expensive work is asynchronous because it has to be, and it is revisable because the information needed to size it does not exist yet. Upload acknowledgement, publish visibility, and full-quality availability are three separate events, and the status field has to model them separately or creators will be told a video is ready when it is not.

**What this layout buys you:** upload capacity scales independently of transcode capacity, which scales independently of delivery. The cost is a long-running state machine per video, a manifest whose contents change under cached readers, and an origin that must stay correct for content it may not have served in two years.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The tiered transcode pipeline, and what it costs to change your mind later.**

*The unit of work.* Segment-parallel encoding is what turns 20 minutes of video into tens of seconds of wall clock, and it works only because a segment can be encoded without reference to its neighbours. That is a property you create, not one you find. A source file's keyframes fall wherever the camera put them, so the split step re-cuts the source on fixed 6-second boundaries and forces a closed group of pictures at each cut, meaning no frame inside a segment references a frame outside it. The failure modes are asymmetric and both are quiet. Cut on the wrong frame and the segments do not concatenate cleanly, so the player shows a flash of macroblocks at every boundary. Force keyframes far more often than the segment length and you have paid maybe 10% extra bitrate for nothing. Rung alignment matters as much: if 360p and 720p carry keyframes at different presentation timestamps, a player cannot switch between them mid-stream without a visible stall, so every rung is cut on the same timestamps and that constraint is fixed before any encoding starts.

*The floor pass, timed.* A 12-minute upload is 120 segments across 2 rungs, so 240 jobs, each 6 seconds of source at 720p or below, which at 15x realtime is at most 0.4 GPU-seconds apiece and closer to 0.05 for the 360p rung. Total GPU work is well under two minutes and with a few hundred free workers the encode itself is seconds. Wall clock is then dominated by object-store round trips, not by encoding: 240 reads of source ranges and 240 writes of output. That inversion is worth saying out loud, because the reflexive answer is to add workers and the actual fix is to have each worker pull one contiguous byte range recorded by the split step and batch its writes. Adding workers past that point makes the job slower, since every extra worker is another set of round trips against the same source object.

*What escalation reads.* A per-video counter over a sliding window of views in the last hour, plus the channel's median first-day views as a prior, plus explicit overrides for scheduled premieres and paid tiers. The threshold is not a constant to hardcode. It is set so that roughly 5% of uploads cross it, because that fraction is what the 1,200-versus-3,600 GPU arithmetic assumed, and it has to be re-derived as traffic shifts or the fleet size drifts silently. Escalation is deliberately one-way. A video that spikes and dies keeps its upper rungs until the ordinary storage lifecycle reclaims them, because tearing down a rung a day after building it pays the compute and gets none of the storage back.

*The manifest is mutable and the segments are not.* When escalation completes, the manifest gains rungs, and every edge holding a cached copy keeps serving a video that appears to top out at 720p until that copy expires. So manifests carry `max-age=60` and segments carry a year with `immutable`, and segment URLs are keyed by source hash, rung, encoder build and segment index so a re-encode can never overwrite an object that is already cached somewhere in the world. This split is the concrete price of the escalation design and it is the follow-up an interviewer will actually reach for.

*Idempotency and the encoder build.* Jobs get retried, workers die mid-write, and escalation runs weeks after the floor pass. Two properties keep that safe. A job's output path is a pure function of its inputs, so a retry overwrites itself byte for byte and a duplicate is harmless. And the encoder build is part of that key, because an encoder or driver upgrade between the floor pass and escalation produces subtly different output, and a rung half-encoded on one build and half on another gives quality discontinuities at segment boundaries that nobody finds until a viewer complains. Putting the build in the path turns a rare bug into an impossible one.

*Publishing a rung.* A rung becomes visible only when all its segments exist. The orchestrator writes segments, verifies the count and the summed duration against the source, then rewrites the manifest. A manifest that references a segment which is not there yet hands every player a 404 mid-playback, and players handle that badly: most stall rather than stepping down a rung. The check costs nothing and the failure is expensive, so it is unconditional rather than sampled.

*What escalation cannot fix.* It is reactive by construction. A video going from zero to a million views in ten minutes is served at 720p through the whole ramp, and the upper rungs land after the audience has gone. Priors buy back part of it: a channel with a million subscribers gets the full ladder at ingest regardless of the arithmetic, because its expected value is known before the file arrives. A first-time uploader about to go viral gets nothing, and no signal available at ingest would have told you otherwise. That is a genuine hole and it is conceded below rather than closed.

**The job graph.** Below is one full pass. The floor run executes the same graph with two encode nodes instead of six; escalation re-executes it with the remaining rungs and the split, thumbnail and notify nodes skipped.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 680" role="img" aria-label="Video transcoding pipeline DAG">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ah" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse">
```
