The orchestrator owns the graph, not the workers. It tracks per-node state, retries individual segments rather than the video, and enforces the readiness transitions: uploaded, floor-published, escalated. Two details in the picture carry weight. The pre-warm node fires only for channels above a subscriber threshold, which is the push slice from the third fork. And thumbnails are generated once, on the floor pass, because they are cheap and creator-visible immediately, while everything expensive waits for demand.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Transcode queue depth under an upload spike.** A news event doubles or triples upload rate for a few hours and the floor pass, which is the creator-visible SLO, starts queueing behind it. *Mitigation:* the floor pass is small and uniform, so it autoscales cleanly; escalation work is the shock absorber. Escalation jobs run on a separate, preemptible lane and are shed entirely under pressure, because a video whose upper rungs arrive an hour late is invisible to almost everyone while a video that is not playable for an hour is a support ticket. Priority within the floor lane is by channel tier, not by arrival.
- **Object-store round trips, not GPU, on short videos.** For anything under a few minutes, encode time is dominated by reading source ranges and writing hundreds of small objects. *Mitigation:* the split step records byte offsets so each worker issues one ranged read; outputs are batched. Below roughly 60 seconds of source, segment parallelism stops paying and the video is encoded whole on one worker.
- **Cold-tier restore on a reawakened long-tail video.** A video untouched for two years whose derivatives were reclaimed needs a re-encode before it can play, which is minutes, not milliseconds. *Mitigation:* keep the 360p rung of everything in a warm tier forever, since 360p is 0.7 Mbps and cheap, so there is always something to play immediately while the rest regenerates behind it. This is the mitigation that pays for itself, because it also removes the "preparing video" state from the user-visible path.
- **Correlated cold misses on a fast-rising video.** Thousands of edges miss the same segment within the same second. *Mitigation:* a shield tier that coalesces concurrent fetches for one object into a single origin request, plus a push of the floor rung to major points of presence when a video crosses the velocity threshold. Note the push can only carry rungs that exist, so on a first-time uploader's video the push and the escalation race each other.
- **Storage growth at ~1EB/year.** *Mitigation:* lifecycle by last access, and delete rather than demote below a threshold, keeping only the source and the 360p rung. Storing seven renditions of a video with 40 lifetime views for a decade is the single largest avoidable line item in this design.
- **Format duplication.** Storing transport-stream segments for HLS and fragmented MP4 for DASH doubles the bill for nothing. *Mitigation:* CMAF, standardised in 2018, lets one set of fragmented MP4 segments serve both manifests, and HLS has supported fMP4 since 2016, so there is no remaining compatibility argument for the split.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upload ingest | Resumable upload state is lost mid-file | Offset-mismatch rate and abandoned-upload alarms | Part-level acknowledgement with resumable state keyed by upload id, so clients restart from the last confirmed part |
| Split | Segments are cut off keyframe boundaries or misaligned across rungs | Concatenation check and cross-rung timestamp diff in the packaging step | Force closed GOPs at fixed presentation timestamps and fail the pass rather than publish a stream that stalls on switch |
| Transcode | Segment jobs stall and the video never becomes playable | Queue depth, oldest-job age, per-rung failure rate | Retry per segment, dead-letter permanently bad inputs, and publish the floor rung independently of anything above it |
| Escalation | Threshold drifts and far more or fewer than 5% of videos escalate | Escalation rate against its target, plus GPU-hours per upload | Treat the threshold as a control loop against fleet cost, not a constant, and alarm on the rate before the bill |
| Manifest publish | A manifest references segments that do not exist yet | Segment-404 rate at playback start and a manifest-validation canary | Verify segment count and summed duration against the source before the manifest is rewritten; promote atomically |
| Manifest caching | Escalated rungs stay invisible because edges hold the old manifest | Gap between escalation completion and observed rung usage | Short TTL on manifests, long and immutable on segments, and content-addressed segment paths so a re-encode never collides |
| CDN and origin | Fast-rising content causes correlated cold misses to origin | Origin egress spike and cache-fill amplification | Shield tier coalescing concurrent fetches per object, plus a velocity-triggered push of the floor rung |
| Moderation and rights | Unsafe or infringing content is playable before the slow checks finish | Exposure-hours before takedown, and reviewer-queue age at the top of the priority order | Risk-tier the synchronous gate, order the human queue by predicted reach rather than arrival, and tombstone at manifest hydration |
| Recommendation path | Ranking degrades and the home page empties | Candidate-generation timeout rate and fallback-feed share | Fall back to subscriptions and trending; never let it block playback of a video the user already chose |

**Unresolved**

**Escalation is reactive, and the first hour is the hour that matters.** A video that goes from nothing to a million views inside ten minutes is served at 720p for its entire ramp, which is precisely when the largest audience it will ever have is watching. This is not a tuning problem, it is the shape of the mechanism: the signal that justifies the spend arrives after the spend would have been useful. Priors close part of the gap for creators with history, and a scheduled premiere closes it entirely, but a first-time uploader has no signal at ingest that distinguishes them from the half of uploads that never reach 100 views. It also interacts with the third fork in a way I would not hide: the pre-warm push can only distribute rungs that exist, so for exactly the videos where the push matters most, the bytes worth pushing have not been encoded. The options are all unattractive. Speculatively encoding the top rungs for anything with unusual first-minute velocity re-imports a large slice of the cost we removed. Raising the floor to include 1080p looks like the moderate compromise and is not one: 1080p alone costs more GPU time than every rung beneath it combined, 1.0 against 0.82 in 1080p-equivalents, so a 1080p floor takes the fleet from ~1,100 to ~3,100 and hands back almost the entire saving. What we do is accept a degraded first hour for unknown creators and measure it as a distinct SLO rather than burying it in an average.

**Moderation is a rate, not a gate, and fingerprinting loses an arms race.** Publish-then-review means a nonzero exposure window that cannot be driven to zero at 3.6M uploads a day, so the honest metric is exposure-hours before takedown rather than an incident count, and the target is a number someone has to sign off on rather than zero. Underneath that, rights matching is fingerprint-based, and a re-upload that has been re-encoded, cropped, mirrored, time-shifted or pitch-shifted defeats naive matching. Robust fingerprints handle each of those individually and lose to combinations. There is no version of this that ends; the reachable position is to make evasion expensive enough that it stops being worth doing at volume, prioritise the human queue by predicted reach so the misses that matter get caught first, and be explicit that low-reach infringement is largely uncaught. Live content is worse still, since there is nothing to check before it is visible.

**A takedown does not remove the bytes.** Long segment TTLs are load-bearing for the whole delivery design, and they directly oppose the requirement to stop serving something immediately. Tombstoning at manifest hydration stops players, which handles the overwhelming majority of real traffic, but a segment URL that is already cached at an edge stays fetchable by anyone who kept it until it is evicted or explicitly purged, and a global purge across tens of thousands of edges and third-party ISP-embedded appliances is minutes at best and not something we control end to end. Signed short-lived URLs would fix it and would also destroy the cache hit rate the cost model depends on, so we use them only for content where the requirement is contractual. For the public catalogue the position is that takedown is fast at the manifest, best-effort at the edge, and we can state a bound on the second but not a guarantee. Cold-tier content adds a smaller version of the same problem: purging an object you must first locate across an archive tier is minutes rather than seconds.
#### Drill questions
1. The transcode queue backs up during an upload spike. What gives first?
2. How do you keep storage sane at roughly 1EB/year of new bytes?
3. How would you handle a single-event 100x traffic spike, such as a cup final?
4. Why adaptive bitrate rather than progressive download?
5. How do you secure premium or paid content?
6. How would you migrate from H.264 to AV1 in production?
7. Why a per-title ladder rather than a fixed one, and can you afford it here?
8. How do ISP-embedded caches change the architecture?
9. HLS, DASH, or both?
10. Half your uploads never reach 100 views. What do you skip for them, and what happens when you guess wrong?
11. A court order takes a video down at 14:00. Walk through exactly what stops serving, and when.
12. Escalation adds rungs to a manifest that edges have already cached. How does anyone ever see the new quality?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Split the lanes and shed the right one. The floor pass carries the creator-visible SLO and autoscales on queue depth; escalation runs on a preemptible lane and is shed first, because upper rungs arriving an hour late are invisible to nearly everyone while a video that will not play for an hour is a support ticket. Priority inside the floor lane is by channel tier, not arrival order. *If pushed:* the spike shape decides the response. A 2x diurnal peak is absorbed by the queue, since a backlog drains in minutes against a tens-of-seconds SLO. A sustained 10x is a capacity event, and the only fast lever left is dropping the floor to a single 360p rung, which halves floor cost and is visibly worse.

2. Three levers, largest first. Do not produce rungs nobody asked for, which is the 60% cut. Lifecycle by last access into archive tiers running 10x to 20x below standard. Then, below a low access threshold, delete the derivatives entirely and keep the source plus a 360p rung, because re-encoding costs seconds of GPU and storage costs forever. *If pushed:* dedup by source hash catches identical re-uploads and is worth having, but it is a minor lever. The dominant saving is that most of those bytes should never have been produced.

3. This is the case where pre-positioning wins outright, and it is the exception to the pull-through default. A scheduled fixture has a known audience and a known start time, so push the full ladder to every major point of presence and to ISP-embedded appliances hours ahead and buy the burst capacity in advance. No reactive mechanism helps, because the traffic arrives faster than a cache fills. *If pushed:* for the unscheduled version there is no clean answer. Shield-tier coalescing keeps origin alive, velocity-triggered push starts filling edges, and the first minutes are served at the floor rung to whoever gets there first. Q51 covers the cache hierarchy itself.

4. Because bandwidth changes during playback and the server cannot observe it. ABR moves the decision to the only party holding the measurement, and converts a stall into a quality drop, which viewers tolerate far better. It is also what makes the delivery path cacheable: no per-viewer session state exists anywhere between the player and the object store. *If pushed:* the cost is visible quality oscillation. Modern players damp it with buffer-occupancy control rather than raw bandwidth estimates, an approach that became standard after BOLA in 2016. Progressive download still wins for very short clips, where the whole file lands before the first adaptation decision would have fired.

5. Encrypt segments during packaging and hand keys from a licence server after an entitlement check, with the client DRM stack enforcing output protection. Short-TTL signed URLs stop casual link sharing. *If pushed:* both mechanisms fight the cost model here. Signing makes the URL unstable, so the cache key has to be a signed path prefix with the token excluded from the key or hit rate collapses. Forensic watermarking is worse: per-user marks mean per-user bytes, which removes shared caching entirely, so it is confined to a small high-value tier and never applied to the general catalogue.

6. Attach AV1 to the escalation tier rather than to ingest. AV1 costs roughly an order of magnitude more compute than H.264 in software; hardware AV1 encode arrived on datacentre GPUs with NVIDIA's Ada generation in 2022 and improves that considerably but does not make it free. Encoding it only for the ~5% of videos that carry most of the watch time buys most of the egress saving for a small share of the compute, and the manifest lists both so clients negotiate by capability. *If pushed:* the long tail stays H.264 permanently, and that is correct rather than lazy. Codec migration is an egress optimisation, and a video with 40 lifetime views has no egress worth optimising.

7. A fixed ladder over-provisions bitrate for a static talking head and under-provisions for high-motion content, and the perceptual complexity gap between them is several-fold. Per-title analysis, published by Netflix in 2015 and extended to per-shot optimisation in 2018, buys around 20% bitrate at equal quality. *If pushed:* you cannot afford it on everything here, and that is exactly where this answer diverges from the Netflix one. The analysis pass costs GPU time per title and repays in egress, so it only clears above a watch-hours threshold. It belongs in the escalation tier next to AV1, and the ~95% that never escalate get a fixed ladder that is somewhat wrong and costs nothing to compute.

8. They move where the money goes more than what the system does. An appliance racked inside an ISP serves bytes without crossing a peering link, converting transit cost into hardware and logistics cost, and it is why a large scheduled event does not saturate the public internet. Architecturally it is one more cache tier below the CDN edge. *If pushed:* it also sharpens the third fork, because appliance capacity is the decider in it. A box holding 100 to 500TB against 1.15PB of new encoded output per day means it can hold a slice of the catalogue chosen by predicted demand and never the catalogue, which is the exact inversion of the curated case where the whole library fits on one.

9. Both manifests over one set of bytes. HLS is required on iOS and Safari, DASH is the open standard elsewhere, and since HLS gained fragmented MP4 support in 2016 and CMAF standardised the container in 2018 there is no reason to store two segment formats. One byte-stream, two small text files. *If pushed:* what remains different is manifest syntax and DRM signalling, and the DRM half is the awkward one, because key-system signalling still diverges enough that a single encryption scheme across both takes deliberate work.

10. You skip 1080p and above, per-title analysis, AV1, and any pre-positioning, and you keep 360p, 720p and the source. The reason the mechanism is shaped this way is that guessing wrong is asymmetric. Wrong in the cheap direction means a video that deserved 4K is served at 720p until escalation catches up, costing some watch time on the ramp. Wrong in the expensive direction means 3x the fleet and 2.5x the bytes, permanently, for output nobody requested, and none of it is recoverable. *If pushed:* the threshold is a control loop, not a constant. Track escalation rate against its 5% target and GPU-hours per upload, and move the threshold when either drifts. Above roughly 30% escalation the mechanism has stopped paying for itself and the honest move is to encode the full ladder at ingest and delete the controller.

11. Metadata flips first and it is the only genuinely fast step. The video row goes to tombstoned, and every manifest hydration from that instant returns a takedown response, so anyone starting playback stops within seconds. Sessions already in flight keep pulling segment URLs they hold until they refresh the manifest, which the 60-second TTL bounds. Then a purge propagates across the CDN, minutes across tens of thousands of edges, and across ISP-embedded appliances we do not fully control. Origin objects are deleted last, because deleting them first turns every in-flight fetch into an error indistinguishable from a bug. *If pushed:* the gap between stopped serving and bytes gone is real and I would state it as a bound rather than claim zero. If the order demands a hard guarantee, the only mechanism that delivers one is short-lived signed URLs on that content, and that costs the cache hit rate the whole cost model rests on.

12. Not until the cached manifest expires, which is why the cache-control split is part of the design rather than a detail. Manifests carry `max-age=60`, so an edge holds a stale playlist for at most a minute. Segments carry a year with `immutable`, safely, because their URLs are keyed by source hash, rung, encoder build and index, so adding a rung creates new URLs and never mutates an existing object. *If pushed:* a player that loaded the manifest once and is mid-playback will not see the new rung at all until it refreshes, and most refresh only on a seek or a stall. So the practical effect of an escalation is that the quality improvement lands on the next viewer rather than the current one. That is acceptable, and it is better said out loud than presented as an instant switch.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, name the real problem before drawing anything.** Open with the thesis, not the components: "the hard part is not transcoding video, it is deciding how much to spend on a video before you know if anyone will watch it." Then get the two numbers that decide everything: 500 hours a minute in, and a demand distribution where half of uploads never reach 100 views and the top 1% take 80% of watch time. Ask whether live is in scope, whether moderation is in scope, and what the upload-to-playable target is. Say out loud that this is where the answer diverges from a curated streaming service, because the interviewer is checking whether you noticed.

**5-15, the spine and the fleet arithmetic.** Draw the write path down the left: client, object store, split, encode, package, encoded store. Draw the read path down the right: manifest, edge, player. They touch only at the encoded store. Then do the arithmetic on the board, because it is what justifies everything after: 8.3 source-hours per second, full ladder at 7.3 GPU-minutes per source hour is ~3,600 GPUs and 2.9PB/day; two rungs plus 5% escalation is ~1,200 GPUs and 1.15PB/day. Say the word "escalation" and draw the controller as a box reading view counters and writing back into the pipeline. Add the moderation gate as a second edge into publish, not as a downstream step.

**15-35, the drill.** Protect this time; it is the interview. Go deep on the tiered pipeline: closed GOPs and cross-rung keyframe alignment, why the floor pass is bound by object-store round trips rather than GPU, what the escalation controller reads, and the manifest-mutability consequence with the cache-control split, which is the follow-up that separates people who have shipped this from people who have read about it. Then idempotency and encoder-build pinning, then per-rung atomic publish. Take the moderation fork on your own terms with the reviewer arithmetic, 37,500 full-time reviewers, since that number ends the argument in one line. Then the delivery fork against the appliance capacity number, which is where the contrast with a curated catalogue becomes concrete rather than rhetorical.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the three gaps before they are found: escalation is reactive so the first viral hour is served at the floor rung and the pre-warm push has nothing to push; moderation is a rate rather than a gate and fingerprinting loses an arms race; a takedown stops the manifest fast and the edge bytes slowly. Then two minutes of operations: upload-to-playable at p50 and p95, escalation rate against its target, GPU-hours per upload, rebuffer ratio, exposure-hours before takedown. Close on the cost line, that the system serves roughly 800 bytes for every byte it produces in aggregate and near zero for the median video, and that holding both facts at once is the design.

Cut first: the ABR control algorithm, then HLS against DASH, then storage tier pricing and the recommendation two-stage architecture. All four are real and none of them changes the shape of this answer; the recommendation detour in particular is a different question's material and will eat the pipeline discussion. Never cut: the fleet arithmetic, escalation and what it costs, and the moderation gate.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **videos** (transactional store, sharded by video_id):
  `(video_id, owner_id, title, description, duration, upload_state, publish_state, quality_tier, created_at)`. Three state fields rather than one `status`, because uploaded, published and escalated are independent.
- **video_rungs** (wide-column): `(video_id, rung, codec, encoder_build, segment_count, bytes, produced_at)`. The row exists only once the rung is complete, so the manifest generator has no partial-state case to handle.
- **source blobs**: `src/{video_id}/{source_hash}` in an archive-class tier, retained permanently.
- **segments**: `seg/{source_hash}/{rung}/{encoder_build}/{index}.m4s`, content-addressed so a re-encode never overwrites a cached object.
- **manifests**: `mf/{video_id}.m3u8` and `.mpd`, rewritten on escalation, never cached long.
- **moderation_verdicts**: `(video_id, check, verdict, score, decided_at)`, append-only, since a takedown must be able to show what was known when.

**API contract**

```
POST /upload/init            -> { upload_id, presigned_part_urls[], part_size }
PUT  <presigned part url>    -> { etag }              (client to object store, direct)
POST /upload/{id}/complete   -> { video_id, upload_state: "processing" }
GET  /video/{id}             -> { metadata, manifest_url, publish_state, quality_tier }
GET  /manifest/{id}.m3u8     -> HLS playlist          (CDN, max-age=60)
GET  /seg/{hash}/{rung}/...  -> segment               (CDN, max-age=31536000, immutable)
```

**Observability**

- **Upload-to-playable, p50 and p95, split by ingest, split, encode and package.** The creator-facing SLO, and the only latency number that gates publication.
- **Escalation rate against its target, and GPU-hours per upload.** The control loop for the first fork. Either drifting means the fleet size is silently wrong.
- **Rebuffer ratio and time-to-first-frame, segmented by rung.** Aggregate rebuffer hides the specific case that matters, which is a video stuck at the floor rung under a large audience.
- **CDN offload by content class.** Hot and long-tail content behave nothing alike, and a blended hit rate conceals both.
- **Exposure-hours before takedown, and reviewer-queue age at the top of the priority order.** The moderation SLO is a rate, so it needs a rate metric.
- **Cold-restore rate and latency.** Rising numbers mean the deletion threshold is set too aggressively.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** source bytes replicate cross-region synchronously before the upload is acknowledged. Encoded derivatives replicate asynchronously, because they are recomputable and re-encoding is cheaper than the transfer.
- **RTO:** ingest and the stateless APIs fail over in seconds. Transcode capacity recovery is minutes, and the backlog is bounded because the sources are already durable.
- **RPO:** zero for acknowledged uploads. Non-zero and irrelevant for derivatives, since the pipeline regenerates them deterministically from the source hash and encoder build.
- **Failover cadence:** drills must include a cold-region transcode replay and an origin failover with the CDN in the loop, not just an API restart.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by source replication at 720TB/day, which is the one thing that cannot be recomputed.

### 12. Design Google Drive (Dropbox)
#### Problem
Keep a folder of arbitrary files identical across a user's devices and their collaborators', when devices go offline for days, edit independently, and reconnect expecting to converge. Files run from 1KB config files to multi-gigabyte videos, and a one-byte edit must not cost a full re-upload. Durable storage of the bytes is assumed and buyable; the product is the convergence protocol on top of it.
#### Core
Storage is the easy half and you should buy it. The product is a protocol for making two replicas agree when one of them has been unplugged for a week.

Split every file into chunks and name each chunk by the hash of its bytes. Everything else falls out of that. A file becomes an ordered list of hashes plus some metadata; the bytes live in an object store keyed by hash. Upload becomes a handshake: the client hashes locally, sends the list, and the server replies with the subset it does not already hold. A one-byte edit ships one chunk. An installer that a million users already uploaded ships nothing.

Keep the two stores apart on purpose. Metadata is small, mutable, transactional, and needs ordering. Chunks are large, immutable, and need durability, which is exactly what an object store sells. That is question 21 and I would not rebuild it.

Convergence runs off a per-namespace journal, an append only log of operations with a monotonic id. A client stores its cursor, reconnects, and asks for everything after it. Cost is proportional to what changed, not to how many files exist, which matters when a namespace holds 10 million.

Commit is a compare and swap on the parent version. Two devices committing against version 2 means the second one fails, and that failure is the conflict. There is no correct automatic answer because a Word document has no merge function, so the loser is written alongside as a conflict copy and a human decides.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a postal system where every document is sliced into numbered pages before mailing. When you change one page, you only re-send that page, and every post office along the route keeps a copy of every page it has ever received. When your laptop wakes up after a week offline, it asks the post office "what pages changed since I was last here?" and only downloads those, never the whole document.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Ship the whole file and version it.* Hash the file, and if the server has never seen that hash, send all of it. Every save creates a new immutable version. This is a few hundred lines of client, it is very hard to get wrong, and it still deduplicates identical files across users. It fails on exactly one axis: a one-byte change to a 2GB video costs 2GB. That is fine for a write-once corpus, a phone camera roll or a scanner drop folder, where files are created and never edited.

*Cut the file at fixed offsets and ship only the pieces that changed.* Slice every 4MB, hash each slice, ask the server which hashes it is missing. Overwriting bytes in place touches one slice. One pass over the bytes, and a 1GB file is 256 hashes to track. It breaks on inserts: adding 10 bytes at the front shifts every later boundary, so every hash changes and you re-upload the whole file.

*Cut the file where the content says to.* Run a rolling window over the bytes and start a new chunk whenever the window's fingerprint hits a chosen pattern, so boundaries are anchored to content rather than to offsets. An insert perturbs one or two chunks and everything after it resynchronises on its own. You pay a second pass over every byte and you accept chunks of unpredictable size. This wins when files are edited in the middle: documents, source trees, database files, disk images.

**The single-request walkthrough:** you edit a 200MB video file, changing 4MB near the end. Your laptop's sync agent splits the file into 4MB chunks and hashes each one with SHA-256. It sends the hash list to the Metadata Service: "I have chunks A, B, C, D, E, F." The server replies "I already hold A, B, C, D, E, just send F." Your client uploads F (4MB) to the Block Service, which stores it under its hash. The Metadata Service commits the new version against parent version 2: the file now maps to chunks [A, B, C, D, E, F_new] at version 3. It appends that to the journal and publishes `{ file_id, version: 3 }` to the Notify Service. Your phone wakes, sees the notification, asks for the chunk list, discovers only F changed, and downloads 4MB. Total bandwidth: 4MB instead of 200MB.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Sync agent (client-side).** The program running on your laptop or phone. Watches the local filesystem, splits changed files into chunks, hashes each chunk, compares against the server's list, and uploads only what is missing. It also holds the cursor into the change journal. This is where nearly all the difficulty lives.
- **Metadata Service.** Stores the logical description of your files: folder structure, permissions, version history, and the ordered list of chunk hashes making up each version. It does not store bytes. Backed by a transactional database sharded by namespace.
- **Block Service.** Stores raw bytes keyed by the hash of those bytes. Two chunks with identical content collide by construction and are stored once. This is content-addressed storage, and it is what makes cross-user deduplication free rather than a feature you build.
- **Server File Journal.** An append only log of every operation in a namespace (create, modify, move, delete), each stamped with a monotonically increasing id. A device reconnecting after a week fetches everything after its last-seen id instead of walking the tree. This is the property that keeps sync cheap for a namespace with 10 million files.
- **Notify Service.** A push channel over a persistent socket. On commit, the Metadata Service publishes an event and the Notify Service pushes it to the user's other connected devices. It is an accelerator, never a correctness mechanism: clients poll the journal regardless.

**The thing that makes it hard:** two devices edit the same file while offline. Your laptop edits `report.docx` on Tuesday; your tablet also edits `report.docx` on Tuesday. Wednesday both come online. The laptop commits version 3 against parent 2 and wins. The tablet then tries to commit its own version 3, also against parent 2, and the compare and swap fails. Two branches, one common ancestor, no way to reconcile them: merging byte ranges out of two divergent edits to a binary format produces a corrupt file, not a merged one. So the server does the only safe thing. It keeps the laptop's version as canonical and writes the tablet's bytes alongside as `report (conflict copy from tablet).docx`. Both files now exist and you resolve it by opening both.

**Why this design and what it costs:** the handshake before every upload is what makes the system efficient at scale. Instead of "upload it and we will work it out", the client asks "which of these do you already have" and moves only the remainder. In a corporate tenant that collapses a 1GB installer to roughly 40MB of transfer, because 240 of its 250 chunks already exist from prior uploads. The cost is that the sync engine becomes the hard part of the product: offline edits, interrupted uploads, filesystem watchers that lose events, and cursors that fall out of the journal's retention window.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Metadata in a sharded transactional SQL store keyed by namespace; chunks in an object store with key = SHA-256 of the chunk bytes; notify over a WebSocket fleet fed by a pub/sub bus.
- The handshake on every upload:
  ```
  hashes = [sha256(chunk) for chunk in split_4mb(file)]
  missing = POST /file {hashes}      # server replies with the hashes it lacks
  for h in missing: PUT /chunk/{h} bytes
  POST /file/commit {file_id, parent_version, hashes, metadata}
  ```
- On reconnect: `GET /journal?since={cursor}` then replay operations, transferring only the chunks the local tree lacks.
#### Interactive diagram
The whole design as one explorable picture: [open the interactive diagram](/diagram/google-drive).

Every box and every arrow is clickable. Selecting one dims everything it does not touch and opens what it is, why it exists, the numbers worth quoting, the failure it owns, and why that technology rather than the obvious alternative. Start with the Overview button.

#### What this is really testing
Whether you can tell a storage problem from a replication problem. The bytes are the easy half and you should buy them. The real question is how several replicas, some unplugged for a week, agree on the state of a tree. Every interesting answer is forced by one fact: the system cannot read the files. It sees opaque bytes with no notion of a line, a cell, or a paragraph, so it has no merge function, so concurrent edits cannot be resolved automatically, so the design has to make conflicts rare and hand the survivors to a human. A candidate who spends the hour on erasure coding and replication factor has answered question 21 by accident.

The contrast is with the real-time collaborative editor. Both are convergence problems and they land on opposite answers because of what each one knows about its payload. The editor owns its data model: a document is a sequence of characters with identity, so an insert at position 5 can be rewritten to mean the same thing at position 0, and two divergent histories genuinely merge into one document holding both people's work. It pays for that with a persistent connection, one owning process per document, and per-character bookkeeping, and it only works because there is exactly one format. Here the format is whatever the user dragged into the folder, so there is nothing to transform. The unit of concurrency is the file rather than the character, the unit of transfer is a 4MB chunk rather than a keystroke, and the resolution is a second file on disk rather than a merged one.

Notice which way the offline assumption runs, too. Four hours offline is the editor's hard case, and its output is a consistent document that reads like nonsense. A week offline is the baseline here, and the output is two files and an apology. If you find yourself reaching for operational transformation in this question you have misread which problem you are in.

Closest question: Q37
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Max file size? Per-user storage cap?
- Real-time collab in docs (Google Docs)? (assume separate problem)
- Selective sync? Offline access?
- Sharing model: per-file ACL, link sharing?
- What is actually in the folder: media and installers, or documents and source?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Large max file size | chunk files into blocks, hash each, and store blocks in an object store, which buys resumable upload and dedup together |
| Real-time doc collab out of scope | sync whole-file versions with conflict copies, not operational transforms (that is the Google Docs problem) |
| Selective sync and offline | a local metadata DB plus a sync engine diffing three trees (local, last-synced, server) and moving only changed blocks |
| Files are edited in the middle | rolling-hash chunking so an insert re-uploads only the affected blocks instead of everything after them |
| Per-file ACL sharing | an authorization service consulted on every file and block access, with a cached permission decision |
| Link sharing | capability tokens (signed URLs) that bypass per-user ACLs for read |
| Heavy folder sharing | the shared folder becomes its own namespace and shard, not a subtree replicated into every member's shard |
| Versioning | keep a chunk manifest per version so old versions cost only their changed blocks |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** upload/download, sync across devices, share, versions, conflict resolution, search
- **NFR:** durability (11 9s), efficient sync (delta only), 99.99% availability

**Scale**

- **Users and raw size:** assume 1B active users with an average of 10GB consumed (free tier partly used, paid tiers pulling the mean up). 1B × 10GB = **~10EB raw user data** before dedup.
- **File-size distribution:** average ~1MB. Most files are under 100KB (text, config, notes) with a long tail to multi-gigabyte videos and disk images that drags the arithmetic mean to about 1MB. Small files dominate metadata QPS; large files dominate bytes. Cross-check: 10GB per user at 1MB average is **~10k files per user**, and 1B × 10k = **~10T file rows**, which is the metadata figure below.
- **Chunk size:** 4MB fixed, matching published Dropbox and Drive values. Large enough to amortise metadata and erasure-coding overhead, small enough to bound a retransmit on flaky mobile. Files under 4MB are stored whole; many small files are packed into archive chunks so metadata is not 1:1 with files.
- **Dedup ratio:** content hashing across the corpus catches templates, OS-shipped files and common media. Public Dropbox figures are around 30%, enterprise tenants closer to 50%. At 40%: 10EB × (1 − 0.4) = **~6EB of distinct bytes**.
- **Replication:** hot data is 3× replicated across AZs; cold data is erasure coded at Reed-Solomon 10+4, a 1.4× overhead. Steady state has roughly 30% of bytes hot and 70% cold: (0.3 × 6EB × 3) + (0.7 × 6EB × 1.4) = 5.4 + 5.9 = **~11EB stored**. If nothing had migrated to cold it would be 6 × 3 = 18EB, so the cold tier is worth ~7EB of hardware.
- **Daily churn:** ~10% of users sync on a given day = 100M active user-days. Each averages ~100KB of genuinely new bytes, since most operations are deletes, renames and metadata. 100M × 100KB = **~10TB/day net new**, ×3 replication = **~30TB/day of writes**. Pre-dedup ingest is 3 to 5× that; dedup absorbs the difference at the handshake, before the bytes are sent.
- **Metadata:** a file row is name and path (~200B) + ids (~64B) + timestamps (~32B) + version pointer (~16B), call it **~500B**. 10T rows × 500B = 5PB. Chunk lists live in their own table because they do not fit a row for large files: at 32B per hash and ~3 retained versions, 10T × 3 × 32B ≈ 1PB. So ~6PB logical, ×3 replication = **~18PB of metadata**, which is two orders of magnitude smaller than the chunk store and is why they are different systems.
- **Journal:** 100M active user-days × ~10 file operations each = **~1B journal entries/day**, at ~100B each = **~100GB/day**, spread across 1B namespaces. At 90 days retention that is ~9TB, trivially cheap, and 90 days is the number that decides when a returning device has to fall back to a full tree diff.
- **Sync events:** the same 1B operations/day fan out through notify: 1B ÷ 86,400 ≈ **~12k events/s** steady, with business-hours peaks around 5× = ~60k/s. Fan-out multiplies by devices per user (~2.5) and by shared-folder membership.
- **Conflicts:** a conflict needs two devices committing off the same parent version. At roughly 1 in 10^4 modifications, 1B operations/day × 10^-4 = **~100k conflict copies/day**. Small as a rate, large as an absolute number, and the basis for the merge argument in Key decisions.
- **Hot tier:** chunks touched in the last 30 days are ~5% of the corpus. 5% of 6EB = **~300PB on SSD-backed storage**, provisioned to ~500PB for burst.
- **Cold tier:** everything idle past 30 days moves to infrequent access, past a year to glacial, where reads tolerate seconds of warm-up. The 95% of bytes nobody touches is what pays for the 5% that is hot.
#### Key decisions
**Fixed-offset chunking vs content-defined chunking**
- Choice: fixed 4MB chunks, each hashed with SHA-256, for a general consumer and business corpus.
- Alternative: content-defined boundaries from a rolling hash (Rabin fingerprint or buzhash), cutting at an average of 1MB with a 512KB floor and an 8MB ceiling.
- Decider: what fraction of modified bytes come from edits that change a file's length in the middle. Fixed chunking is correct for in-place overwrites and appends and catastrophic for inserts: a 10-byte insert at offset 0 of a 1GB file shifts all 256 boundaries and re-uploads 1GB, against roughly 2MB for content-defined, a 500× difference on that one operation. Against that, content-defined costs a second pass over every byte: SHA-256 with hardware acceleration runs at 1 to 2 GB/s per core, and a rolling hash roughly halves that, which is battery on a phone preparing a 10GB upload. Below about 5% length-changing edits, fixed wins on cost and simplicity; above about 20% you are losing whole files to single inserts and the CPU is cheap by comparison. Consumer Drive traffic is dominated by photos, video and PDFs, which are written once and never edited, so it sits at the low end.
- Alternative wins when: the corpus is edited in the middle. A source-code or design-asset sync product, or a backup product ingesting VM images and database files where a page insert shifts everything after it. Content-defined chunking is genuinely the better default for backup and has been since the LBFS and Venti work around 2001 to 2002, which is why restic, borg and rsync's delta algorithm all use it. If the corpus mix is unknown, choosing it costs CPU and buys insurance, and that is a defensible call rather than a wrong one.

**Last writer wins with a conflict copy vs a real merge**
- Choice: commit is a compare and swap on the parent version; the loser's bytes are preserved as a sibling file named for the losing device and the user resolves it.
- Alternative: a three-way merge against the common ancestor, which the version history already gives you for nothing, dispatched by format: text and source merged the way a version control system does, structured formats merged field by field, everything unrecognised falling back to a conflict copy.
- Decider: what fraction of conflicting files have a defined merge function, weighed against the asymmetry of being wrong. A conflict copy is a visible annoyance costing a user two minutes. A bad merge is silent corruption of a file the user believes is fine and may not open for six months. So the merge path needs a very high hit rate to earn its keep: below roughly 20% mergeable formats you are carrying a format sniffer, per-format merge code and a whole class of corruption bug in order to help one conflict in five. At the derived ~100k conflicts/day, 20% coverage is 20k merges/day, and a 1-in-1000 bad merge is 20 corrupted user files per day, which is not a rate a storage product survives.
- Alternative wins when: you control the format. A notes app, a code host, or a design tool with its own document model should merge, because coverage is 100% and the merge is testable against a fixed grammar. This is really a fork about product scope rather than about merging: the moment the folder accepts arbitrary bytes, merging becomes a special case rather than the mechanism, and a design that leads with merging has quietly assumed a narrower product.

**Shard metadata by user vs make each shared folder its own namespace**
- Choice: the unit of sharding and of journaling is a namespace, not a user. A private root is one namespace; every shared folder is a separate namespace mounted into the tree of everyone it is shared with. A device syncs the union of its namespaces and keeps one cursor per namespace.
- Alternative: shard by user_id and replicate a shared folder's metadata into each member's shard, fanning writes out to all members on every change.
- Decider: members per shared folder multiplied by change rate. A folder with 500 members taking a 10k-file bulk edit is 5M metadata writes under the alternative against 10k under the choice, and those 5M have to be transactional across 500 shards or members will see different trees. Break-even is around 5 members: below that, per-user replication is simpler and the write amplification is invisible. Above about 50 members it is the dominant cost in the metadata tier.
- Alternative wins when: sharing is rare, small and read-mostly, which describes a purely consumer product. It also buys something real that namespaces give up: with a user's whole tree in one shard, a move between any two folders is a single transaction. Under namespaces, moving a file out of a shared folder into your private root crosses two independently sequenced journals and cannot be atomic. That is the first Unresolved item below, and it is a genuine cost of the choice rather than a detail.

**How to read the diagram:** the system is split between metadata and file contents. Metadata tracks folders, permissions, versions, and change history; the file bytes live in chunk storage and move on their own path. The client talks to all three, and it is the only component that ever holds a whole file.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** the split exists so that reasoning about what changed never requires touching bytes. Devices exchange journal entries and chunk-hash lists, which are kilobytes, and fetch chunks only for what they actually need locally.

**What this layout buys you:** delta sync, version history that costs only changed blocks, and sane offline behaviour across many devices. The price is that the sync agent becomes the hardest component in the system, and it is the one running on hardware you do not control.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The convergence protocol, from a changed byte to a converged device.**

**Three trees, not two.** The client keeps three views of its folder: the local filesystem as it is now, the server state as of its cursor, and `synced`, the last state at which the two were known to agree. Diffing local against `synced` yields local changes. Diffing server against `synced` yields remote changes. A path appearing in both diffs is a conflict, and a path in neither is untouched. Nearly every sync bug is a client that tried to work with two trees, because with only local and server you cannot distinguish "I deleted this" from "they created this".

**Upload is a handshake, not a transfer.** For each locally changed file the client chunks, hashes, and asks the server which hashes it lacks.
