Three properties of that state machine that are not visible in the boxes:

1. **Authorise, not capture.** An authorisation places a hold on the card without moving money and can be voided at zero cost; a capture moves money and reversing it means a refund, which costs the per-transaction fee and creates accounting noise. Holds survive about 7 days, which comfortably covers the saga. Capture happens at check-in for flexible rates and at booking for prepaid non-refundable ones, and that choice is a property of the rate plan, so the saga reads it rather than hard-coding it.
2. **Compensations are keyed to forward steps.** A release that naively runs `sold = sold - 1` gives two rooms back if it runs twice, which is an undersell that nobody notices until occupancy reports disagree. Each compensation writes against `(booking_id, step_id)` and checks that the forward step is still marked applied, so a retry is a no-op. The failure this prevents is silent, which is why it is worth stating explicitly.
3. **Cancellation is not the same path as compensation.** A compensation undoes a saga that never completed. A cancellation reverses a confirmed booking, days or months later, and has to run the refund policy, emit a different set of notifications, and return the room-night into a market whose price has moved. They converge on the same `sold = sold - 1` write and diverge everywhere else, so modelling them as one transition is a common and expensive simplification.

The mechanism above is complete for the happy path and for every failure inside the saga. What it does not cover is the case where the reservation is valid, the payment cleared, and there is still no room, which is the deliberate consequence of the allowance and is handled by people rather than by software. See Unresolved.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hot row.** A stadium event announcement puts 10k attempts on one `(hotel, room_type, date)` row. At ~2ms per transaction the row absorbs ~500/s, so 10k attempts drain in 20 seconds while every one of them holds a connection. The fix is admission control rather than a faster lock: cap concurrent booking attempts per row and reject the excess immediately with a clear "high demand, this may already be gone", because 9,999 of those users are going to fail anyway and failing them in 5ms is better product than failing them in 20 seconds. What does *not* work here is bucketing the counter into sub-rows. Bucketing assumes a single-date decrement; a 3-night stay needs the same bucket free on all three nights, so remainders fragment and the system reports sold out with rooms genuinely available.
- **Search latency** on a multi-million-document index with geo and date filters. Use a dedicated geo index for proximity, cache `(city, date_range, guests)` for 60 seconds at a ~70% hit rate, and pre-render the top few hundred city and date combinations to static JSON at the edge. Date-range availability in the index is coarse by design: it answers "plausibly available", and the booking path answers the real question.
- **Payment provider variance.** Authorisation latency spans 200ms to 30 seconds and providers fail. Idempotency keys on every charge call, bounded retries with backoff on transient errors only, and a circuit breaker so an outage fails fast instead of accumulating sagas stuck in `INVENTORY_RESERVED`. When the breaker is open the right behaviour is to refuse new bookings rather than reserve inventory that cannot be paid for.
- **Saga durability.** Five steps that each fail independently need state persisted at every transition, a dashboard over the state distribution, and an operator path to replay or force-compensate. The metric that matters is the age of the oldest saga not in a terminal state; a rising floor there means the sweeper is losing.
- **Cancellation storms.** A closed airport or a moved festival cancels 10k bookings within minutes. Refunds drain asynchronously under the provider's rate limit while the user is told immediately that the refund has been initiated. The inventory side matters more than the refund side: 10k room-nights return to sale at once, and if the forecast job runs on stale cancellation data it will oversell against a demand estimate that has just collapsed. Suppress oversell for any date whose cancellation rate in the last hour exceeds the daily norm.
- **The single-writer arbiter for pooled inventory.** Funnelling every channel's booking through one process is a bottleneck only if it is one process; shard it by `hotel_id` so a 500-property chain gets 500 independent write paths. The real constraint is fan-out latency: availability must reach every subscribed channel within about 5 seconds, and slow channels must not be able to delay fast ones, so fan-out is per-channel queues with independent backpressure.
- **Slow distribution channels.** Older travel-agent networks tolerate seconds to minutes of staleness by design, so an agent will confirm against a view that is already wrong. Push updates within 5 seconds where the protocol allows, and where it does not, return a specific `INVENTORY_LOST` with alternatives rather than a generic error, so the agent can rebook in the same call.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory store | Hot row serialises bookings on one popular date | Booking p99 climbs; lock-wait time on the row exceeds 50ms | Per-row admission cap that rejects excess attempts in milliseconds instead of queueing them; isolate known-hot properties on their own shard |
| Forecast job | `allowance` written from a stale or broken forecast, oversell far above policy | `allowance - physical` exceeds the per-class policy ceiling on any row | Hard clamp in the write path: reject any `allowance` above physical × 1.2 regardless of what the job says, and alert rather than truncate silently |
| Saga orchestrator | Crash after payment authorisation, before the booking write | Oldest non-terminal saga age exceeds 60s | Resume worker replays from the last persisted step; forward-step idempotency keys make re-running safe |
| Expiry sweeper | Sweeper stops; abandoned checkouts hold room-nights indefinitely | Count of bookings in `INVENTORY_RESERVED` older than 10 min is non-zero and rising | Sweeper is a leader-elected job with its own liveness alarm; on restart it processes oldest-first, and the release is idempotent so double-processing is harmless |
| Payment provider | Provider returns 5xx or hangs for 30s | Per-call p99 climbs; circuit breaker trips | Bounded retry on transient errors only; open breaker refuses new bookings rather than reserving inventory that cannot be paid for |
| Search index | Change-capture lag spikes during a chain-wide inventory push | `cdc_lag_seconds` above 30s | Booking re-checks at commit, so stale search is friction rather than error; alert on sustained lag; rebuild from a snapshot if the pipeline is broken |
| Channel sync | A partner's receiver is down and its view of availability drifts | Per-channel last-sync age climbs | Push plus a periodic full-sync poll; auto-pause a channel after 3 missed syncs and rebuild from the authoritative rows on resume |
| Cancellation storm | 10k bookings cancelled at once, inventory floods back | Cancellation rate for a date exceeds 5× its trailing norm | Refunds drain under the provider rate limit; oversell is suppressed for affected dates until the forecast has seen the new data |
| Idempotency cache | Cache outage loses dedupe for in-flight attempts | Duplicate key rate spikes; cache health alarms | The durable unique constraint is the guarantee and the cache is only a fast path, so a cache outage costs latency and not correctness |

**Unresolved**

**The feedback loop that justifies the oversell runs through a system we do not own.** The allowance is computed from a forecast, but the cost it is traded against is realised at 6pm at a front desk, in the property's own management system, when a clerk decides who gets walked and to where. We can sell the 131st room; we cannot see whether the property had a walk partner with capacity that night, what the walk actually cost, or which guest absorbed it. So the model is calibrated against an assumed $300 rather than a measured one, and the assumption is worst exactly where it matters, on citywide sold-out nights when every comparable property is also full and the true cost is two or three times higher. What I would do is ingest walk events as first-class records per property per night and drive the allowance from realised cost. Until that data exists, and for most intermediaries it never will because the walk is an interaction between the hotel and the guest that we never see, the honest position is a flat conservative cap of a few percent with the critical-fractile calculation as an argument for the shape rather than a live control loop.

**Greedy first-come-first-served is the wrong revenue policy, and we implement it anyway.** A one-night booking on the Friday of a peak weekend can make an adjacent four-night stay unsellable, and the four-night stay is worth more. The industry answer is minimum-length-of-stay and closed-to-arrival restrictions computed per date, which means deliberately rejecting a paying customer to protect a hypothetical better one. We enforce those restrictions when a property sets them, but we do not compute them, and we cannot evaluate the counterfactual because we never observe the stay we turned away. A displacement check at booking time, rejecting a stay whose revenue is below the forecast value of the room-nights it consumes, is implementable but it makes booking success non-deterministic from the user's point of view and it puts a forecast in the synchronous write path. That is a product decision more than an engineering one, and we have not taken it.

**Modification is not a first-class operation, and the workaround has a visible seam.** Changing dates is implemented as reserve-new then release-old, which is the right order because the reverse briefly returns inventory to a pool where a stranger can take it. But when the new dates overlap the old ones, the booking holds room-nights against itself, and a guest extending a sold-out stay by one night can be blocked by their own reservation. We special-case the overlap by computing the delta and only writing the difference, which works and is fiddly, and it interacts badly with rate plans: the extension may only be available on a different plan, so the "same booking" now spans two plans with two cancellation policies. Every intermediary I have seen handles this by cancelling and rebooking with a price guarantee, which is honest about the fact that it is a new reservation, and worse for the guest when the original rate is no longer available.
#### Drill questions
1. How do you guarantee two guests never hold the same room-night, and why is that not the same as never overselling?
2. Who sets the oversell allowance, how often, and what stops it being wrong?
3. A user starts booking and walks away mid-payment. Is that inventory reserved forever?
4. Why is payment outside the inventory transaction, and what does that cost you?
5. Every guest turns up on an oversold night. What is your system responsible for?
6. A one-night booking on the Friday of a peak weekend blocks a four-night stay. What do you do?
7. How would you scale search to 10x the query rate?
8. Booking commits but the confirmation email never sends. Bug or feature?
9. Authorise versus capture: why does it matter for the saga?
10. How does a booking modification work without double-book risk?
11. Multiple channels sell the same rooms. How do you stop them overselling each other?
12. A chain pushes a 500-hotel inventory update and change capture falls five minutes behind. What does the user see?
13. Why a per-row counter here when Ticketmaster uses a per-seat key?
14. How do you stop competitors and scrapers mining your real-time availability?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. One row per `(hotel_id, room_type_id, date)` and a single conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE sold < allowance` covering every night, which either commits for all nights or rolls back. The engine's row locks do the serialisation. That guarantees the system never sells above `allowance`; it does not guarantee `allowance` equals the number of rooms, and deliberately so. *If pushed:* the two failure modes have completely different owners. Selling above `allowance` is a software bug and a postmortem. Selling above physical capacity is a business decision, tracked as walks per 1,000 room-nights against a target, and a rate of zero means the allowance is set too conservatively.

2. A nightly job per property and room-type class, from a demand and no-show forecast. It writes `allowance` only; it never touches `sold`, which is what keeps it from racing bookings. *If pushed:* three guards. A hard clamp in the write path rejects any allowance above physical × 1.2 no matter what the job says. Classes below about 20 units get no oversell at all, because with 8 suites the no-show mean is 0.8 and selling one extra walks a guest on 0.9⁸ = 43% of nights. And a date whose cancellations in the last hour ran 5× above normal has oversell suppressed until the forecast has seen the new data, because the count no longer reflects demand.

3. No. The booking commits with status `INVENTORY_RESERVED`, and a leader-elected sweeper releases anything still in that state after 10 minutes. *If pushed:* the sweeper is a correctness component, not housekeeping, so it gets its own liveness alarm and the alert fires on the age of the oldest non-terminal booking rather than on a queue depth. Note the race it creates: an authorisation can succeed after the sweeper has released the rows, so the confirm step re-checks state and, if the reservation is gone, voids the authorisation rather than confirming a booking with no inventory behind it.

4. Because an authorisation takes 200ms to 30 seconds and lock hold time is the denominator of row throughput. Inside the transaction, the ~2ms critical section becomes 200ms or worse, dropping a single row from ~500 attempts/s to about 5/s and holding a database connection per user filling in a card form. *If pushed:* the cost is a window where inventory is consumed by a booking that never confirms, which is exactly what compensations and the sweeper exist for, and it is a much cheaper problem than the alternative. Two-phase commit is not a way out: payment providers do not participate in it, and a coordinator crash after prepare holds inventory locks with no bound.

5. Detecting it, recording it, and pricing it, not solving it. The system knows at check-in time that confirmed arrivals exceed physical rooms, so it should surface that to the property early in the day rather than at 9pm, prioritise who is protected (loyalty tier, length of stay, prepaid rates) by a published rule rather than by arrival order, and record the walk as a first-class event with its cost. *If pushed:* this is the honest gap. The walk itself happens between a clerk and a guest in a system we usually do not own, so the cost that justifies the whole oversell model is assumed rather than measured, and it is most wrong on citywide sold-out nights when comparable rooms cost two to three times the assumed $300.

6. Today, nothing: it is first-come-first-served per room-night and the short stay wins. The industry answer is a minimum-length-of-stay or closed-to-arrival restriction on that date, which the property sets and we enforce as a predicate in the booking path. *If pushed:* computing those restrictions ourselves means a displacement check, rejecting a stay worth less than the forecast value of the nights it consumes. It is implementable and I would not ship it lightly: it puts a forecast in the synchronous write path, makes booking success non-deterministic to the user, and you never observe the counterfactual, so the model cannot be validated against the outcome it is optimising.

7. Shard the index by city, since almost every query is city-scoped, and cache `(city, date_range, guests)` for 60 seconds for a ~70% hit rate. At 4k/s peak that leaves ~1.2k/s reaching the index. *If pushed:* 10x is 40k/s, and the answer stops being sharding. Pre-render the top few hundred city and date combinations to static JSON at the edge, where the object is shared across all users, and fall through to the index only on a miss. The availability data in the index is coarse anyway, so serving it from a 60-second-old edge object costs nothing the design was not already paying.

8. The booking is committed and durable; email is a downstream effect on a retry queue, so a missing email is not a lost booking. *If pushed:* never let email be how the user learns they booked. Return the reference number on a server-rendered confirmation page, make it retrievable from the account, and expose a resend endpoint. The interesting version of this question is the loyalty accrual, which is also downstream and where users do notice, so it needs a reconciliation job rather than just a retry.

9. An authorisation holds funds without moving them and voids at zero cost; a capture moves money and reversing it means a refund, which costs a fee and creates accounting noise. Holds last around 7 days, which covers the saga comfortably. Capture at check-in for flexible rates, at booking for prepaid non-refundable ones, driven by the rate plan rather than hard-coded. *If pushed:* on a stay spanning mixed rate plans, authorise per plan segment so cancelling part of the stay voids only that segment's hold instead of reversing and re-authorising the whole thing.

10. Reserve the new dates first, then release the old ones. The reverse order briefly returns inventory to a pool where a stranger can take it, which is how a guest loses their own room while extending a stay. *If pushed:* when the ranges overlap, the booking contends with itself, so compute the delta and write only the difference. That works and it has a seam: the extra night may only be available on a different rate plan, so one reservation now spans two cancellation policies. Most intermediaries duck this by cancelling and rebooking with a price guarantee, which is honest about it being a new reservation and worse for the guest if the original rate has gone.

11. Pooled inventory with one arbiter as the only writer to the authoritative row, sharded by `hotel_id` so it is not a single process, with availability pushed to every channel within about 5 seconds. Allocation, meaning a pre-split block per channel, removes the contention but strands 3 to 8% of room-nights when one channel sells out while another has rooms. *If pushed:* real systems run both, because group blocks, tour-operator allotments and negotiated corporate rates are contractually allocated and the hotel has promised those rooms whether or not anyone books them. Under contention within the pooled base, priority by margin is a policy the arbiter can express, and it is a commercial decision rather than an engineering one.

12. Stale prices and availability in results, and occasional "no longer available" at the point of booking. Nothing worse, because the booking path re-checks against the authoritative rows and never trusts the index. *If pushed:* the failure to watch for is not the lag itself but out-of-order application. Change events carry a monotonic log position and the indexer writes idempotently by key, so a slow partition cannot regress a document to an older state. And the alert threshold is on sustained lag rather than on a spike, because a chain-wide push is a normal event and paging on it trains people to ignore the page.

13. Because the buyer is not choosing a unit. Nobody books room 412; they book a standard king, and the assignment happens at check-in, which means the system only needs to answer "how many of this class remain" and a counter is the exact fit. A seat buyer chooses row 5 centre by name, so contention is per identified unit and the state has to be per unit. *If pushed:* the consequences run deeper than the data structure. A counter permits deliberate oversell because units are substitutable; per-seat state does not, since there is no other row 5 centre to move someone into. And a counter creates length-of-stay fragmentation, which has no analogue in a seat map, because seats are not consumed across consecutive dates.

14. Per-key rate limits, scoped views so a partner sees only what it is entitled to, and scoring on query shape, since sequential sweeps of a city and date grid do not look like human sessions. *If pushed:* the durable fix is removing the incentive to scrape by offering push updates to legitimate partners, so the ones with a real need stop polling and the remaining traffic is easier to classify. Note the tension with caching: a 60-second edge cache is what makes the scrape cheap for them and cheap for you, so tightening staleness to defeat scrapers costs you the read economics that make search affordable.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, separate the physical constraint from the business one.** Open with it, before any box: "nobody books room 412, they book a standard king on the 14th, so inventory is a counter per room type per night, and the ceiling on that counter is not the number of rooms. Hotels oversell on purpose and they are right to." That sentence tells the interviewer you are not about to spend 40 minutes defending a lock. Then ask the three questions that actually fork the design: room types or specific rooms, do we own the oversell decision or does the property, and are we the only sales channel. State your numbers out loud: 5M hotels, 43M searches/day against 1M bookings, 3.2 nights average, and the one that decides everything, 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ decrements per inventory row per day. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine, and say the placement rules as you draw.** Six boxes: client, search service, booking service as saga orchestrator, inventory service, payment, notifications. Two stores: the search index on the left, the inventory table on the right. One arrow between the halves, change capture pointing away from the transactional store, and say the contract as you draw it: "search is allowed to be seconds wrong because the booking path re-checks; a stale hit costs one `NO_AVAILABILITY` and nothing else." Never query the booking database from search. Then write the row on the board, because it is the whole answer compressed: `(hotel_id, room_type_id, date) -> sold, allowance`, two columns with two different owners. Say why they are separate before anyone asks: the booking path owns `sold`, a nightly forecast job overwrites `allowance`, and neither reads the other's value, so there is no read-modify-write to race. Say "saga, not two-phase commit" here and give the reason in one line: payment providers do not participate in XA, and a coordinator crash after prepare holds inventory locks with no bound.

**15-35, go deep on the write path and protect this time.** One conditional statement, not select-then-update: `UPDATE inventory SET sold = sold + 1 WHERE ... AND date >= ? AND date < ? AND sold < allowance RETURNING date`, and fewer rows back than nights means roll back the whole stay. Say the two properties that fall out of it. Check and write collapse into one statement so locks live for about 2ms with no application hop inside; and the range predicate forces an ascending index scan, so two overlapping stays visit shared nights in the same order and cannot deadlock, which is a property of the primary key rather than a convention someone has to remember. Then payment outside the transaction with the number: 200ms in the good case and 30 seconds in the bad one against a 2ms critical section, so putting it inside drops the per-row ceiling from ~500 attempts/s to about 5/s and pins a connection per user staring at a card form. Then the price of that: a real window where room-nights are consumed by a booking that never confirms, closed by a compensation on the failure path and a sweeper that releases anything still in `INVENTORY_RESERVED` after 10 minutes. Call the sweeper a correctness component, not housekeeping. Then idempotency, and be specific that the unique constraint is in the database and the cache is only a fast path, because a cache failover during a burst is exactly when clients are retrying. Then authorise rather than capture: voids are free, refunds cost a fee and create accounting noise, and holds last around 7 days. Then compensations keyed to `(booking_id, step_id)` so a retry is a no-op, and note that a naive `sold = sold - 1` run twice is a silent undersell nobody notices until occupancy reports disagree. If time remains, take the contention fork on your own terms: worst observed burst 8/s against a 500/s single-row ceiling, so a queueing tier would add a tier, a failure mode and 10ms to 100% of bookings to help 0.001% of rows, and the fix for a genuine hot row is admission control that rejects in 5ms rather than a faster lock.

**35-45, concede the gaps and close.** Volunteer them, because they are what separates this from a textbook answer. The feedback loop that justifies the oversell runs through the property's own system: we can sell the 131st room but we never see what the walk actually cost, so the model is calibrated against an assumed $300 and is most wrong on citywide sold-out nights. Greedy first-come-first-served is the wrong revenue policy and we ship it anyway, because a displacement check puts a forecast in the synchronous write path and you never observe the stay you turned away. Modification is reserve-new-then-release-old, which is the right order, and it makes a booking contend with itself on overlapping dates. Add pooled versus allocated channel inventory as a one-liner if there is room: pooled recovers the 3 to 8% that fixed blocks strand, allocation wins where a channel is contractually entitled to rooms. Close with the operational surface in ninety seconds: `inventory_lock_wait_seconds` p99, age of the oldest non-terminal saga, count of bookings stuck in `INVENTORY_RESERVED`, `cdc_lag_seconds`, walks per 1,000 room-nights against target.

Cut first: the multi-region and DR detail, then the search index internals and the geo query, then the loyalty and notification fan-out. All three are real and none of them changes the architecture, and the search discussion in particular is a rabbit hole that eats the write path. Never cut: the two-column row and who owns each column, payment outside the transaction, and the conceded gaps.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **hotels** (transactional store): `(hotel_id, name, address, lat, lng, amenities, ...)`
- **rooms** (transactional store): `(hotel_id, room_id, room_type, capacity, base_price)`
- **inventory** (transactional store, sharded by hotel_id):
  `(hotel_id, room_type, date, sold, allowance, price, restrictions)`  PK = `(hotel_id, room_type, date)`.
  `sold` is written only by the booking path, `allowance` only by the nightly forecast job.
- **bookings**: `(booking_id, user_id, hotel_id, room_type, checkin, checkout, status, auth_ref)`
- **idempotency**: `(key, booking_id, state)` with a unique constraint on `key`
- **search_index** (search index store): denormalized hotel docs with current min price

**API contract**

```
GET  /search           params: city, checkin, checkout, guests
                       → [{hotel_id, name, price, room_type, available}]

POST /booking          body: { hotel_id, room_type, checkin, checkout,
                               guest, idempotency_key }
                       → { booking_id, status, total_price }

DELETE /booking/{id}   → { refund_amount, status: cancelled }
```

**Observability**

- `booking_attempts_total` and `booking_success_rate` per hotel (anomaly = oversell or stuck Saga)
- Saga state distribution (`pending`, `compensating`, `completed`, `stuck`); alert on `stuck` count > threshold
- `inventory_lock_wait_seconds` p99 (high = hot-row contention)
- `cdc_lag_seconds` from Postgres WAL to ES indexer
- `payment_auth_latency_p99` and circuit-breaker state per provider
- `compensation_runs_total` by step (track which compensations are firing vs noise floor)

**SLOs:** 99.9% of booking attempts complete within 5s p99; zero bookings accepted above `allowance` (hard target, every incident is a postmortem); walks per 1,000 room-nights within the published oversell policy band; search index lag <5s p95; refund initiation within 24h of cancellation.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** transactional store is regional with sync replicas across AZs and async cross-region replica for DR. Search index is regionally replicated and rebuilt from CDC + initial snapshot in the peer region.
- **RTO:** 15-30min for booking write path failover (DB cutover, Saga orchestrator state migration, channel manager re-pairing). Search reads can fail over in under 5min.
- **RPO:** <5s for booking writes (sync replica); ~30s for cross-region failover (async replica lag). Compliance-tier (financial-grade) topics may use 2-region sync writes for zero-RPO.
- **Failover cadence:** quarterly DR drill with a real cutover of a non-primary region; monthly partial-component failover (search, channel manager) to keep tooling fresh.
- **Cross-region cost:** Postgres async replication egress + ES cross-region snapshot ship + Saga state cross-region replica. Payment is provider-region (Stripe handles its own DR).

### 20. Design a Distributed Email Service (Gmail)
#### Problem
Accept mail from any host on the internet, decide inside a single SMTP transaction whether to take it, and then store it durably and searchably for a billion users for years. The protocol is fixed by specification and cannot be changed, and roughly half the inbound volume is hostile, so ingest is an adversarial classification problem before it is a storage problem. Getting the classification wrong one way fills every inbox with junk; wrong the other way, it silently destroys legitimate mail with no way to recall it.
#### Core
Start with what you do not control. SMTP is fixed, any host on the internet may open a connection and hand you a message, and roughly half of what arrives is unwanted. Every other decision is downstream of where you put the accept-or-reject boundary.

Inbound is an MX fleet that decides in three places, cheapest first. At connection, drop known-bad IPs before a single byte of message arrives. At `RCPT TO`, refuse unknown recipients, never accept and bounce later, because a bounce to a forged return path makes you the spammer. At end of `DATA`, evaluate SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and reject only where the sending domain itself published a policy telling you to. That disposes of roughly 30% of traffic before anything is stored. Everything probabilistic is accepted, scored asynchronously, and filed into inbox or spam, because SMTP has no way to un-reject and a rejection is permanent loss.

Storage splits in two. Metadata, meaning headers, labels, thread id and a body hash, goes to a wide-column store sharded by user, so every mailbox operation is single-shard. Bodies and attachments go to content-addressed object storage keyed by content hash, which is where deduplication actually pays: one newsletter PDF in a million inboxes is one stored object.

Search is per user. Nobody searches anyone else's mail, so there is no cross-user ranking problem, only a packing problem.

Outbound is a durable queue with hours of backoff and reputation-tiered sending IPs, so one compromised account burns a quarantine address rather than the pool everyone else sends from.

The number that governs the design is the false-positive rate. At 0.1% on 100B messages a day you mis-file 100M legitimate messages daily.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a postal sorting facility that is legally obliged to accept a delivery from anyone who turns up, where half the vans at the gate are carrying contraband, and where the rules of the road were written in 1982 and cannot be amended. Mail that gets past the gate is X-rayed, then filed in a personal cabinet with a label and a subject card in the index drawer. Outbound mail goes to a dispatch office that queues letters and retries for days if the recipient's facility is busy. Each cabinet is indexed so ten years of letters can be searched in seconds, and each cabinet is private, so nobody's letters are ever mixed with anyone else's.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Decide at the door.* Everything happens inside the SMTP conversation: authenticate the sender, check reputation, score the content, accept or refuse before the sending server disconnects. This is the cheapest possible disposal of bad mail, since nothing is written and nothing is queued, and the sender learns the outcome and can fix a misconfiguration. It costs you context: you judge one message with no view of the campaign it belongs to, and you can never revise the verdict. It wins when the bad traffic is high volume and cheaply identifiable.

*Take everything, sort it afterwards.* Accept anything syntactically valid, run classification off a queue, then file into inbox or spam. You get unlimited thinking time and batch features a per-connection decision cannot see, such as the same body arriving at forty thousand mailboxes in ninety seconds, and every verdict stays reversible. You pay storage and CPU on traffic that is mostly junk, and you own an abuse surface you invited in. It wins when mis-classifying real mail is more expensive than the compute.

*A cheap gate at the door, a slow judgement behind it.* Refuse at the door only on evidence the sender's own domain published, or on a repeat offender's address, and accept everything else for asynchronous sorting. This is where large providers converge, and the reason is not cost. It is that the door is the only place where a refusal is permanent, so only near-certain signals are allowed to use it.

**The single-request walkthrough:** an external server sends mail to alice@example-mail.com. Our MX host, the address published in DNS for external senders, accepts the TCP connection and immediately checks the connecting IP against a reputation table; a known botnet address is dropped here, before a byte of message body has crossed the wire. The sender issues `MAIL FROM` and `RCPT TO`; if alice does not exist we return a 5xx now, because accepting mail for an unknown user and bouncing it afterwards would send that bounce to a forged return address, which makes us the abuser. The sender then issues `DATA` and we read the message. At end of `DATA` we evaluate three things: SPF (is this IP in the list the sender's domain published?), DKIM (does the cryptographic signature over headers and body verify against a key in the sender's DNS?), and DMARC (does the visible `From:` domain align with whichever of the two passed, and what did that domain say to do if not?). A DMARC failure against a published `p=reject` policy is refused with a 5xx, because the sender's own domain authorised the refusal. Everything else is accepted with a 250, and acceptance is a promise about storage, not about the inbox. The message body is written to content-addressed object storage under `SHA-256(content)`, so the same corporate newsletter PDF arriving in ten thousand mailboxes occupies one object. A metadata row lands on alice's shard of a wide-column store carrying subject, participants, timestamp, thread id and the body hash. The asynchronous classifier scores the message with features the SMTP transaction could not see, including how many other mailboxes just received the same body, and sets the label to `INBOX` or `SPAM`. Indexing, threading and the push notification all consume the same change stream. When alice opens the message, the client reads the metadata row from her shard and the bytes from object storage.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **MX fleet (SMTP inbound).** The internet-facing servers named by the domain's MX records, speaking SMTP (RFC 5321, whose semantics date to RFC 821 in 1982). They hold the only place in the system where a refusal is possible, and they spend that power sparingly: connection reputation, unknown recipient, and authenticated policy failure. Roughly 30% of inbound is disposed of here at close to zero cost.
- **Asynchronous classifier.** Scores every accepted message on headers, body, links against a phishing corpus, attachment hashes, sender velocity, and cross-mailbox campaign signals. Output is a label, never a rejection. Running it off the acceptance path is what buys the batch features, since the tenth copy of a campaign is easy to classify and the first is not.
- **Mailbox metadata (wide-column, sharded by `user_id`).** Message id, subject, participants, timestamp, labels, thread id, body hash, wrapped data key. Not the body bytes, because inlining multi-megabyte attachments into the row that every inbox listing reads destroys the read path once mailboxes reach tens of gigabytes. Sharding on `user_id` makes list, search, label and delete single-partition operations.
- **Body and attachment store (content-addressed).** The bytes, keyed by content hash, so identical content is stored once regardless of how many mailboxes reference it. Deleting a message removes the reference; a reference-counting collector reclaims the object once nothing points at it.
- **Per-user search index.** One logical inverted index per user, physically packed many-to-a-shard. Nobody searches another user's mail, so there is no global ranking or cross-corpus recall requirement, which is the only thing a shared index would buy.
- **Outbound queue and retry.** A send is durable in a queue before the UI says "Sent". A worker does an MX lookup, opens SMTP, and on failure retries with growing backoff for up to 72 hours before returning a bounce. Delivery is never synchronous, because the recipient's server is not our problem to make fast.
- **Reputation-tiered sending IPs.** Outbound addresses grouped by sender trust: established clean accounts, new or unverified accounts, and a quarantine pool. A compromised account is demoted before it can burn the address the rest of the population sends from.

**The thing that makes it hard:** the protocol gives you one bit and no take-backs. At end of `DATA` you either accept or you do not, and the vocabulary for "no" is a three-digit code. There is no way to say "I have taken this but I think it is junk", no way to revise an acceptance, and no way to withdraw a rejection. That asymmetry, and not storage, is what shapes the system: a 5xx on legitimate mail is permanent and invisible to the recipient, so only signals with false-positive rates around one in a million are allowed to produce one. Everything scored by a model, which in practice operates nearer one in a thousand, has to be accepted and then foldered, which means you pay to store the junk and you own an abuse surface you deliberately let in.

**Why this design and what it costs:** the load-bearing separation is metadata from body. Metadata is small at a few hundred bytes, read on every inbox view, and wants strong consistency because marking a message read must show on every device at once. Bodies average around 50KB, are typically read once, and deduplicate well across users. One store cannot serve both without being wrong for one of them. The cost of splitting is that a message is no longer one object: delete, retention, legal hold, encryption-key revocation and index cleanup each have to be correct across two stores plus a search index, and they are only eventually consistent with each other.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Wide-column store (Bigtable or HBase class) sharded by `user_id` for metadata; object storage with content-addressed keys for bodies and attachments; a search cluster with one logical index per user routed by `user_id`; Postfix or a purpose-built MTA for SMTP; a log-structured bus for the change stream that feeds classification, indexing and notification.
- Inbound hot path, with the refuse-or-accept boundary made explicit:
  ```
  # inside the SMTP transaction: only near-certain signals may refuse
  on_connect(ip):
      if ip_reputation(ip) == KNOWN_BAD: return "554 no"
  on_rcpt(addr):
      if not resolve_local(addr):     return "550 no such user"
      if over_rate_limit(ip, addr):   return "421 try later"   # 4xx, not 5xx
  on_data_end(msg):
      auth = evaluate_spf_dkim_dmarc(msg)     # RFC 7208 / 6376 / 7489
      if auth.dmarc_fail and auth.policy == "reject":
          return "550 DMARC policy"           # the sender's domain said so
      if classifier_fleet_unhealthy():
          return "451 try later"              # defer, never guess
      accept(msg); return "250 ok"            # ~70% of arrivals land here

  # after acceptance: reversible, and allowed to be slow
  body_hash = sha256(msg.body)
  dek = hkdf(body_hash)                       # convergent: dedup survives encryption
  object_store.put_if_absent(body_hash, encrypt(msg.body, dek))
  metadata_store.insert(user_id, msg_id, headers, thread_id,
                        body_hash, wrap(dek, kek[user_id]), labels=["UNSORTED"])
  # classifier, indexer and notifier all consume the change stream
  ```
#### What this is really testing
Whether you notice that the interface is not yours. Every other system in this set gets to define its own write path: you choose the API, you authenticate the caller, you version the protocol and you make clients upgrade. Here the write path was specified in 1982, every host on the internet is a legitimate caller, roughly half of them are hostile, and the only vocabulary you have for declining is a three-digit response code inside a transaction you cannot reopen. So the first architectural decision is not what to store, it is which signals are permitted to refuse and which are only permitted to file. A candidate who opens with sharding and storage tiers is designing the second half of the system and will be steered back to the first within ten minutes, because every capacity number they quote is a function of what they let in.

The contrast is with the workplace messaging question. On the surface they are the same system: years of message history for a large population, per-tenant privacy boundaries, full-text search over everything, files stored separately from metadata, and a storage bill dominated by content nobody will read again. Every writer there is an authenticated member of a known organisation, so the write path is an authorisation check that either passes or fails and the hard problem moves downstream, into tenancy, placement, retention and the cost of the index. Here nothing about the writer is known before the message arrives, authentication is voluntary and only tells you which domain is responsible rather than whether the content is wanted, and the expensive decision has to be made inside a connection from a stranger. One of them can also fix its own mistakes: a message delivered to the wrong channel can be deleted, an API contract can be changed, a client can be forced to a new version. Here a refusal is permanent and unappealable and an acceptance cannot be withdrawn, which is why the same storage architecture ends up serving a completely different question.

Closest question: Q32
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- What false-positive rate on legitimate mail is acceptable, and who measures it?
- Are we ever allowed to hard-reject on a model score, or only on deterministic evidence?
- Consumer accounts, or enterprise tenants with an administrator, retention policy and legal hold?
- IMAP and POP, or an HTTP API and our own clients only?
- How long is mail retained, and does the user or an administrator decide?
- Do we have to work correctly behind forwarders and mailing lists?
- Who holds the encryption keys, and what does "delete" have to mean contractually?
- Search over everything, or a recent window?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| A tight false-positive budget | acceptance is generous and sorting is asynchronous and reversible; the door only refuses on deterministic signals |
| Hard-reject on score is permitted | the classifier moves inside the SMTP transaction and the storage tier shrinks, at the cost of unrecoverable losses |
| Enterprise tenants | the tenant, not the user, becomes the unit of retention, hold, residency and key ownership |
| IMAP and POP | stateful protocol servers with per-folder UID sequences and flag sync, which constrains how freely you may re-shard a mailbox |
| Long retention | age tiering on both bodies and the search index, since the index is the more expensive of the two per byte |
| Forwarders and mailing lists in scope | SPF alone is unusable for policy decisions, and ARC (RFC 8617, 2019) becomes load-bearing at the list boundary |
| Customer-held keys and provable deletion | envelope encryption per user with a revocable key, plus a separate index-purge job whose completeness you have to demonstrate |
| Recent window only for search | the index collapses to a hot tier and the largest single infrastructure line item disappears |
| Threading required | group on `In-Reply-To` and `References` chains with subject normalisation as fallback, computed at write time |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** accept and deliver SMTP in both directions; classify and label rather than silently discard; IMAP, POP and an HTTP API; search over the whole mailbox; attachments; threading; labels; user-visible spam folder with a reversible verdict.
- **NFR:** never silently drop an accepted message; false-positive rate on legitimate mail under 0.1%, measured by "not spam" feedback; inbox list and search under 500ms p95; durable before acknowledged; outbound delivered or bounced within 72 hours.

**Scale**

Every number below hangs off two assumptions: 1B active users, and 100 messages per user per day surviving to storage. Both are round numbers chosen so the arithmetic is checkable; published mailbox surveys put the received figure nearer 120, and Google has cited roughly 1.8B accounts against which 1B active is a conservative read.

- **Arrival rate versus accepted rate.** These differ and conflating them is the usual error. Accepted mail is 1B × 100 = **100B messages/day**, which is 100e9 / 86,400 = **1.16M/s average**. If 30% of arrivals are refused at the door, arrivals reaching at least `RCPT TO` are 100B / 0.7 = **143B/day = 1.65M/s average**. Peak is the US morning overlapping the European evening plus scheduled newsletter blasts, roughly 4x average, so **~6.6M SMTP transactions/s peak**. Of the 100B accepted, about 30% is foldered as spam, leaving ~70B/day reaching an inbox.
- **Message size.** Assume ~80% are text or HTML only, mean 5KB, and ~20% carry attachments, mean 200KB. Weighted mean = 0.8 × 5KB + 0.2 × 200KB = 4 + 40 = **44KB, call it 50KB logical**. Content addressing dedupes the attachment slice roughly 7x on real corporate and newsletter traffic, so stored bytes per message = 0.8 × 5KB + 0.2 × 200KB / 7 = 4 + 5.7 = **~10KB**.
- **Daily storage.** 100B × 10KB = **1PB/day stored**, against 100B × 50KB = **5PB/day logical**. The 5x gap is the entire justification for content addressing.
- **Steady-state corpus.** A 15GB quota shared with other products leaves roughly 10GB for mail. At 100 messages/day × 50KB = 5MB/day, a mailbox reaches 10GB in 10GB / 5MB = **2,000 days, about 5.5 years**, at which point the user prunes or pays. So the corpus is not "forever", it is about 5.5 years of ingest: 1PB × 365 × 5.5 = **~2EB stored**, 10EB logical. Cross-check: 1B users × 10GB logical = 10EB, which matches.
- **Messages per mailbox.** 100/day × 2,000 days = **~200k messages** for an average user, and 20x that, ~4M, for the heaviest corporate mailboxes.
- **Metadata.** Row = msg id 8B + thread id 8B + timestamps 16B + participants ~80B + subject ~60B + labels 20B + body hash 32B + wrapped data key 40B ≈ **250B**. Per user 200k × 250B = **50MB**. Total 1B × 50MB = **50PB**, at RF=3 **~150PB** on the wide-column tier.
- **Metadata cache.** The hot set is people currently reading mail, not the whole corpus. At 5% of users active in an hour, each touching their most recent 100 rows: 50M × 100 × 250B = **~1.25TB**, which is a modest cache tier. This is the payoff for keeping bodies out of the row.
- **Search index.** The index covers extracted text, not attachment bytes, so ~4KB indexable per message, not 50KB. Per user 200k × 4KB = 800MB of text; positional postings run about 30% of source text, giving **~250MB/user** and ~2.5GB for a heavy mailbox. Total 1B × 250MB = **250PB**, RF=2 for query capacity → **~500PB on fast storage**. Sanity check on cost: at roughly $5/TB/month for cold object storage and $60/TB/month for SSD, the 2EB of bodies costs 2e6 TB × $5 = ~$10M/month while the index costs 5e5 TB × $60 = ~$30M/month. **The index is an eighth of the bytes and about three times the bill**, which is why age tiering the index matters more than age tiering the mail.
- **Fan-out.** Most inbound is one-to-one or already expanded by the sender's list software before it reaches us, so assume a mean of **1.3 of our recipients per delivered message**. A shared message store would therefore avoid at most 1 − 1/1.3 = **23% of metadata rows**, which is 23% of 50PB = ~12PB, or **0.6% of the 2EB corpus**. That number decides the first fork below.
- **Outbound.** Users send roughly 10x less than they receive: 10/user/day = **10B/day = 116k/s average, ~500k/s peak**. If 3% of sends transiently defer and the mean deferral is 4 hours, in-flight retry state is 10B × 0.03 × 4/24 = **~50M messages** held durably at any moment.
#### Key decisions
**Refuse inside the SMTP transaction, or accept and classify afterwards**
- Choice: refuse only on deterministic evidence, meaning connection reputation, unknown recipient at `RCPT TO`, and DMARC failure against a domain that published `p=reject`. Everything else gets a 250 and an asynchronous verdict that files it into inbox or spam.
- Alternative: run the classifier inside the transaction and answer 5xx above a score threshold, so junk is never written, never indexed and never counted against a quota.
- Decider: false-positive rate against storage cost, and the two are three orders of magnitude apart. A production spam model runs near 1e-3 false positives; a refusal authorised by the sender's own DMARC policy runs near 1e-6. At 100B accepted messages a day, moving the model inside the transaction destroys 1e-3 × 1e11 = **1e8 legitimate messages a day**, permanently, with no bounce the recipient will ever see. What it saves is storing the junk: 30B spam/day × 10KB = 300TB/day, purged at 30 days, so 9PB standing, which at $5/TB/month is **~$45k/month**. $45k against 100M destroyed messages a day is not a close call.
- Alternative wins when: you have nowhere to put the message. An inline filtering gateway sitting in front of somebody else's mail server, under a contract that forbids retaining customer content, has to answer in the transaction because it is not allowed to own a quarantine. The same holds for a single-box deployment where the MTA and the classifier are the same process and there is no queue between them. Note the middle option, which people forget: a 4xx defer is a refusal you can take back, so probabilistic signals are allowed to produce one where they are never allowed to produce a 5xx.

**Per-user mailbox shard, or one canonical message record with thin per-user index rows**
- Choice: shard metadata by `user_id`, one full 250B row per recipient, with bodies deduplicated underneath by content hash. Every mailbox operation is single-partition.
- Alternative: store one canonical record per delivered message, per organisation or globally, and give each recipient a thin pointer row carrying only their labels and read state.
- Decider: mean recipients per delivered message, which for us is **1.3**, because sending list software has already expanded its recipient list before the mail reaches our MX and most consumer mail is one-to-one. A shared record therefore removes at most 1 − 1/1.3 = 23% of metadata rows, 23% of 50PB = ~12PB, or **0.6% of the 2EB corpus**. Against that you give up single-partition reads, since every list and search becomes a join across a partition you own and a record you share, and one user's retention policy can no longer delete a record another user still holds.
- Alternative wins when: mean internal fan-out is above roughly 15, which is the enterprise case (all-hands mail, distribution lists expanded at delivery, 200-recipient threads). At fan-out 15 the canonical record removes 93% of the row bytes, and more importantly the tenant rather than the user becomes the unit of legal hold and purge. Holding one copy is the only version of a legal hold whose completeness you can demonstrate. If the tenancy clarifying question comes back "enterprise", this fork flips.

**One physical search index per user, or `user_id` as a routing key into a shared index**
- Choice: one logical index per user, packed many to a physical shard, with `user_id` as the leading sort key so a user's documents sit contiguously and a query touches one shard and one contiguous run of postings.
- Alternative: one physical index per user, fully isolated, no shared postings and no cross-user skip cost.
- Decider: per-shard floor cost against user count. A search-engine shard costs on the order of 100MB resident plus a slot in cluster state whether it holds 200k documents or 200M, and clusters get unmanageable in the low hundreds of thousands of shards. 1B physical indices is four orders of magnitude past that. Packing ~50k users per shard gives 1e9 / 5e4 = **20,000 shards**, large but operable. The packing cost is that a common term's posting list now spans 50k users, so every query pays to skip other users' postings; sorting the index on `user_id` turns that skip into a block-level seek, which is what makes it affordable. Q47 covers the postings machinery itself.
- Alternative wins when: the population is thousands of tenants rather than a billion users, and isolation is contractual rather than merely correct: customer-managed keys, per-tenant residency, provable index purge on offboarding. At 10k tenants, 10k physical indices is an ordinary cluster and physical separation is worth more than the packing efficiency. Q32 takes this fork for exactly that reason.

**How to read the diagram:** sending, receiving, storing, filtering, and searching email are all separate paths that meet in the mailbox. Outbound delivery is queue-driven and retry-heavy, while mailbox reads and search need index-friendly storage.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** email is unreliable on the network but users expect inboxes to feel crisp and searchable. The architecture keeps slow delivery behavior from leaking directly into mailbox UX.

**What this layout buys you:** durable mail handling with fast inbox reads and strong search. The tradeoff is that one product contains several very different subsystems, each with different correctness and latency priorities.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The accept-or-refuse boundary, and why it sits where it does.**

The SMTP transaction gives you exactly three moments to say no, and they cost radically different amounts. On `connect`, before a byte of message has crossed the wire, you have only the peer IP; a lookup against a reputation table drops known botnet space for the cost of one memory read, and this is where the bulk of raw connection volume dies. On `RCPT TO` you know the intended recipient, so an address that does not resolve locally gets a 550 immediately. Accepting mail for a non-existent user and bouncing it afterwards is the single most common self-inflicted wound in mail operations: the return path on spam is forged, so your bounce goes to the forged victim, that is backscatter, and it gets you listed as a spam source by the same feeds you rely on. At end of `DATA` you have the whole message, and this is the only place a content-aware decision is possible.

**What the three authentication protocols actually establish.** They are usually recited as a stack; the useful framing is that each answers a different question and only the third produces a policy you may act on.

- **SPF** (RFC 7208) asks whether this connecting IP is in the list the *envelope* sender's domain published in DNS. It authenticates the Return-Path, not the `From:` header the user sees, which is why SPF alone is useless as a phishing defence: a message can pass SPF for `attacker.example` while displaying `From: security@yourbank.com`.
- **DKIM** (RFC 6376) verifies a signature over a canonicalised body and a selected set of headers, with the public key fetched from `<selector>._domainkey.<domain>`. Multiple selectors are normal during key rotation and the receiver tries each. Because the signature travels with the message rather than with the connection, it survives forwarding, which SPF does not.
- **DMARC** (RFC 7489) is the only one that yields an actionable verdict. It requires *alignment*: the visible `From:` domain must match whichever of SPF or DKIM passed, either exactly (strict) or on the organisational domain (relaxed, and relaxed is what almost everyone publishes, so `mail.example.com` aligns with `example.com`). It then reads the domain's own published policy: `p=none`, `p=quarantine` or `p=reject`.

That last point is the whole reason the boundary sits here. A 5xx on a DMARC failure against `p=reject` is not our judgement of the message, it is the sending domain instructing us to refuse mail that fails its own authentication. The false-positive risk transfers to the party that can actually fix it. Every other refusal we might want to make is our opinion, and our opinions run at 1e-3 error rates.

Two operational details follow. `pct=` lets a domain roll enforcement out gradually: `p=reject; pct=10` refuses 10% of failing mail and quarantines the rest, which is how a large organisation discovers that its payroll vendor was never in the SPF include list before it starts destroying its own payslips. And `rua` aggregate reports, daily XML to an address the domain publishes, are the feedback channel that makes the rollout navigable; `ruf` per-message forensic reports are largely dead for privacy reasons.
