The diamond in the diagram is drawn as the familiar author-level threshold, which is the version most candidates will sketch. The design above replaces that test with two conditions rather than one, `active_followers(author) < 1M` at the diamond and `active_recently(follower)` inside the fan-out loop, and the rest of the flow is unchanged. Draw it the simple way, then say what the test actually is; changing the shape of the diagram to make that point costs more time than it buys.

The right-hand column is the part worth defending. Its three boxes are the three costs of the choice: an extra graph lookup, an extra fan-in whose width is set by the cut, and a merge that has to deduplicate because the same tweet can arrive by several routes at once.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Aggregate fan-out at a correlated peak.** The push cut bounds what any *one* tweet can spend, at ~200k appends/s. It says nothing about what happens when 50k tweets/s arrive at once. Steady-state fan-out is 1.2M appends/s and the pool is sized at roughly 5M/s, so a 20x tweet-rate spike wants ~24M/s and the queue simply grows. *Mitigation:* shed by tightening the activity window rather than by dropping tweets. A 24-hour window is not enough to matter, because 250M of the 350M weekly actives are also daily actives, so it removes under 30%. Tighten to an hour: 250M DAU × 5 sessions is 1.25B sessions/day, ~52M an hour, so on the order of 40M distinct readers, which is roughly a 9x cut against the 350M weekly set. That sheds exactly the right population, because the least-recently-active reader is the least likely to open the app in the next minute. Those readers fall back to the cold-mailbox rebuild path, which is the third Unresolved item below and is where this mitigation's real cost lands. The tweet write path is untouched throughout; only distribution lags.
- **Retweet cascade.** 500k retweets of one original at ~500 mean followers each is 250M pushed entries at ~200k/s for twenty minutes, from accounts that are all three orders of magnitude below the push cut. *Mitigation:* the rate-triggered cutover in Key decisions. Above ~1,000 retweets/minute on an original, later retweets stop fanning out and become edges in the per-original retweeter index, which the read-side merge already consults. The residual cost is read-side, not write-side: every reader now has one more merge source for the duration of the cascade, and the deduplication step becomes load-bearing rather than cosmetic.
- **Hot tweet counters and hydration.** One viral tweet takes tens of thousands of like and retweet increments per second against a single row, plus millions of hydration reads for the same body. *Mitigation:* counters shard across N keys per tweet, writers pick a shard at random, readers sum across; the count is approximate for a few hundred milliseconds and nobody can tell. Hydration is absorbed by the tweet cache at a 99% hit rate, so 1.2M hydrations/s becomes ~12k store reads/s, and media plus the rendered card sit behind the CDN. Note the interaction with the design above: because timelines store ids and bodies are hydrated late, a hot tweet concentrates load on exactly one cache key, so that key needs client-side replication across cache nodes rather than the usual single-owner hashing.
- **Search ingestion lag.** At a breaking-news spike the indexer falls behind and the freshest tweets are the ones missing from search, which is the worst possible failure ordering. *Mitigation:* the hot index is append-only and does no segment merging, so it has no write amplification to fall behind on, which removes the usual cause. What remains is transport and tokenisation throughput, and that is scaled by adding shards, since the hot index is partitioned by tweet id and any shard can accept any document. If lag still exceeds the 10s target, drop tokenisation of low-value fields (link previews, alt text) before dropping documents, because a document indexed on its body alone is far better than one not indexed at all.
- **Mass-follow events.** A new account gains 10M followers in an hour. The forward record (follower to followee) is cheap and sharded by follower. Two things are not: the inverse index, and the denormalised fetch-path set that step 2 of the read path depends on. *Mitigation:* the inverse index is written asynchronously and smeared over minutes, which is safe because an above-cut account is not fanned out anyway. The fetch-path set is the awkward one, because 10M users each need one small set updated, and the same 10M updates fire again the moment the account crosses the cut. Treat crossing the cut as a batch job rather than an event: write the new membership to a versioned side table, let the read path union the small per-user set with a bounded "recently crossed" list, and fold that list into the per-user sets in the background.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fan-out | Async fan-out backlog delays tweet visibility for normal accounts | Publish-to-visible lag and queue-depth alerts | Keep tweet write ack separate, autoscale fan-out workers, and backpressure only the fan-out path |
| Timeline cache | Large timeline-cache shard loss causes rebuild storm | Cache miss spike and rebuild queue age | Rebuild lazily from author partitions and celebrity pull path, not via global backfill |
| Search indexing | Hot index falls behind during breaking news | Index lag and stale-search canary | Prioritize high-value or trending tweets and keep timeline writes decoupled from search |
| Trending pipeline | Bot spam poisons hashtag counts | Diversity-score anomaly and abuse suppression rate | Apply spam heuristics inline and suppress low-diversity bursts |
| Counter shards | Like/retweet shard totals diverge from event log | Counter-drift reconciliation metric | Reconcile against the source event stream and repair via explicit adjustments |
| Delete / moderation | Deleted tweets remain visible in caches or quote cards | Delete-propagation lag and tombstone-miss alerts | Hydration checks canonical tweet state, and quote cards resolve to tombstones when needed |

**Unresolved**

**Deletion is fast for visibility and slow for erasure, and the gap is architectural.** Storing ids and hydrating late means an ordinary delete is instant: the next hydration finds a tombstone and the tweet vanishes from every timeline at once, without touching a single cached list. That covers the product requirement and it does not cover the legal one. The real-time search index is append-only with sealed segments, which is precisely the property that lets it ingest 200M docs/day with no merge amplification, so a deleted tweet's postings stay in that segment until it ages out of the 7-day window and a query-time tombstone filter hides them. For a GDPR erasure request or a court order the document has to actually be gone, and the only honest answer is a rewrite of the affected sealed segment, which is the one operation the hot index was designed not to do. So we run two deletion SLAs: seconds for visibility, and hours for physical removal, executed as a batched segment rewrite off the hot path with the archive picking it up on its next build. Downstream of the firehose it is worse: once a tweet has been delivered to a licensed consumer, its removal is a contractual obligation on them and we have no technical enforcement at all. We publish the two SLAs rather than pretend there is one.

**We have no design for the reply tree that is both bounded and fair.** A reply is a tweet with a `parent_id`, so a conversation is a tree whose nodes are scattered across every partition of an author-partitioned store. The per-parent reply index makes fetching children cheap, but ranking a thread is not the timeline problem in miniature: a timeline ranks a bounded candidate window, and a thread under a large account can hold 200k replies with no bound at all, where the interesting reply may be a late one with no engagement yet. What we do is cap and score, showing the top few dozen direct replies with lazy expansion, and that is a product decision wearing engineering clothes. It also creates the incentive that makes reply-spam under large accounts profitable, because early position in a big thread is worth real money and our ranking is what allocates it. A design that bounded the read *and* gave a late reply a genuine chance would need something like per-thread exploration budget, and we have not built it.

**The cold-mailbox rebuild fails exactly when it is most likely to be needed.** Activity-gated pushing is what buys the high cut, and its bill arrives on the first load of a returning user: 150 recent-list reads instead of 3, tens of milliseconds when pipelined well and seconds when not. One user at a time this is a fair trade. The failure is correlation. A World Cup final or an election brings tens of millions of lapsed users back inside the same ten minutes, so a cold-rebuild cohort 50x more expensive per load arrives while tweet rate is 10x and the fan-out shedding above has just widened the cold population on purpose. The mitigations we have are both unattractive. Speculative pre-warming, triggered off the trending pipeline, rebuilds mailboxes for users who may never come back and spends write capacity during the spike to save read capacity during the same spike. Graceful degradation serves the cold user a merge over their 20 most-engaged followees instead of all 150, which is a visibly worse timeline on their first impression in a month. We take the degradation and label it, but there is no version of this where the returning user's first load is as good as everyone else's, and that is a direct consequence of the choice that makes the steady state work.
#### Drill questions
1. An account with 100M followers tweets. What actually happens, and is that the expensive case?
2. Ranked timeline rather than chronological. How does that interact with the cache?
3. Search must include tweets posted seconds ago. How?
4. A hashtag is being used by spam bots to trend artificially. How do you catch it?
5. A new account gains 10M followers in an hour. What breaks?
6. Tweet ids need to be sortable by time and globally unique. How?
7. Why did Twitter migrate from Storm to Heron?
8. Why fork Redis rather than use vanilla ZSETs for the timeline?
9. Where do you need strong consistency and where is eventual consistency fine?
10. A user follows 30,000 accounts. What breaks?
11. A tweet is deleted after 200k retweets and 50M impressions. What has to happen, and what is still visible afterwards?
12. The timeline is ranked and the user scrolls to page 3. What does the cursor mean?
13. Why does the real-time index store documents in descending tweet-id order rather than by relevance?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Almost nothing. The row is written, the poster is acknowledged, the id is appended to that author's own recent-tweets list, and fan-out does no work at all: one write, one cache key shared by 100M followers. Each of those followers picks it up on their next timeline load through the fetch path. The point of the question is the second half. That is the *cheap* case, and it is cheap because a single policy line handles it. The expensive case is what happens twenty minutes later, when 500k ordinary accounts retweet it and push 250M entries through the very path you just excluded the original from. *If pushed:* the cut is on active followers at ~1M rather than total followers at ~10k, and the argument is the per-tweet burst budget, 200k appends/s against a 5s freshness SLO. Deriving that number is the answer; quoting 10,000 is the tell that you have reused a generic feed answer.

2. Cache the merged, unranked candidate set per user, not the ranked result. The candidate pool is a few hundred, so ranking on every request is affordable and a model change invalidates nothing. Ranking on the read path is also forced rather than chosen: the strongest signals, engagement in the last hour, do not exist at write time. *If pushed:* this same cache is the mitigation in the first Key decisions fork for when the push cut has to drop into the tens of thousands. A 60-second TTL on the candidate set turns 38 fetch-path reads per page into 38 per minute, at the cost of making fetch-path authors up to a minute stale while pushed authors stay fresh, which is a freshness inversion the merge cannot hide.

3. Two indexes behind one query API. Recent queries hit an in-memory, append-only index holding the last 7 days: 1.4B docs × 15 postings × 4B = ~84GB of postings, under 1GB per shard across 100 shards, so it is RAM-resident and it does no segment merging at all. Older queries hit a batch-built, relevance-ordered index on disk. The indexer consumes the same tweet event stream as fan-out and trending, so a search outage cannot stop anyone tweeting. *If pushed:* the obvious answer, one Elasticsearch cluster with a 1s refresh, is defensible below a few thousand docs/s and stops being so here. 200M docs/day is ~600GB/day of new index, and tiered merging rewrites each document 8 to 10 times, so ~5 to 6TB/day of merge traffic that peaks exactly when ingest peaks and freshness matters most.

4. Score by entity diversity rather than by count: unique posters, unique networks, account-age distribution, content similarity across the matching tweets. A botnet trips the low-diversity signal because its cheapest axis to scale is accounts that look alike. Apply time decay so a spike is suppressed unless organic accounts join it. *If pushed:* this is question 53's problem, not this one's. Trending consumes the same event stream and is a bounded sketch-and-heap per geo partition, a few megabytes of state. The right move in the room is to name it as a separate ranking problem and go back to distribution rather than spend ten minutes on count-min sketches.

5. Three things, of increasing awkwardness. The forward follow records are cheap, sharded by follower. The inverse index takes 10M appends against one key, so it goes through a queue and smears over minutes, which is safe because an above-cut account is never fanned out anyway. The real problem is the denormalised per-user fetch-path set that the read path depends on: 10M users each need a small set updated, and the same 10M updates fire again the moment the account crosses the push cut. *If pushed:* do not treat crossing the cut as an event. Write the new membership to a versioned side table and have the read path union each user's set with a bounded "recently crossed" list, folding that list into the per-user sets in the background. Otherwise every threshold crossing by a fast-growing account is a 10M-write storm triggered by a counter.

6. Snowflake: 41 bits of millisecond timestamp, 10 bits of machine id, 12 bits of sequence within the millisecond. Sortable, monotonic per machine, no coordinator. Sorting by id sorts by time, so the timeline needs no separate timestamp field and merging two sources is a merge of two sorted integer lists. *If pushed:* clock skew across machines breaks strict global ordering; bound it with NTP and accept millisecond fuzziness, because nothing in this product needs a total order. Do not reach for the ZSET-score framing: 8-byte ids in a packed block are what this timeline actually wants, for the reason in the next answer.

7. Storm's shared-thread worker model produced pathological tail latency under burst load, because backpressure propagated unpredictably through shared queues and one slow bolt could stall a whole worker. Heron's process-per-instance model with explicit metadata-managed backpressure isolates operators. The reported gains at the time of the 2015 migration were 6 to 14x throughput, 5 to 10x latency reduction and 3x less hardware. *If pushed:* the migration was API compatible, so existing topologies ran unchanged, which is what made it operationally possible. The transferable lesson is that streaming runtimes built on shared executors hit a tail-latency wall that process isolation avoids, and tail latency is what a fan-out pipeline lives or dies by.

8. The access pattern is append plus range-read of a recent window, and neither Redis primitive fits it. A list is O(N) for arbitrary access; a sorted set maintains a skiplist on every write and, above 128 members, costs roughly 90B per member rather than the 8B the payload needs. That is the 25TB against 2.8TB derivation in the scale section: a 9x difference on the largest cache in the system. A packed block of ids with a small header gives O(1) append and a contiguous range read. Twitter's own answer was a forked Redis with a hybrid list structure holding recent entries in fast blocks and compacting older ones. *If pushed:* forking is only correct when the access pattern is stable and well understood and the team can carry the maintenance for years. Both were true there and neither is true almost anywhere else, so the transferable part is the memory arithmetic, not the fork.

9. Strong consistency exactly once, on the tweet row, because a published tweet must not be lost. Everything after that is derived and eventual: the timeline cache, the search index, the trend list, the retweet index. A follower seeing a tweet 200ms or 5s late is fine and is what the freshness SLO says. Manhattan exposes per-request consistency, so the same store serves the durable write and the high-volume eventual reads. *If pushed:* engagement counters are the extreme case. Sharded counters summed on read are approximate for a few hundred milliseconds, and there is no version of strong consistency that survives tens of thousands of increments per second against one logical row. Say out loud which numbers in the product are allowed to be approximate, because "likes" is and "your tweet posted" is not.

10. Step 2 of the read path, the denormalised fetch-path set. At 30,000 follows even a 1M-follower cut leaves several hundred above-cut authors, so the pipelined multi-get in step 3 stops being 3 keys in one round trip and becomes several hundred spread across every shard. The merge and the candidate window are unaffected, because they are bounded by page size, so the whole degradation is concentrated in one step. *If pushed:* cap the fan-in rather than the follow count. Take the top N fetch-path authors by the reader's own historical engagement, typically 50, and accept that a user following 30,000 accounts is not reading all of them anyway. Two consequences worth conceding: the timeline is now lossy in a way the product never states, and this is the same shape as the cold-mailbox degradation, so build one mechanism and use it in both places.

11. Visibility is easy and erasure is not. Timelines hold ids, so hydration finds a tombstone and the tweet disappears from every timeline at once without rewriting a single cached list; the 250M entries pointing at it become 250M cheap misses. Quote cards resolve to a tombstone at render. What does not happen is physical removal: the real-time index is append-only with sealed segments, so the postings survive behind a query-time tombstone filter until the segment ages out of the 7-day window. *If pushed:* for a legal erasure that is not good enough, and the honest answer is a batched rewrite of the affected sealed segment, which is the one operation that index was designed to avoid, plus a rebuild on the archive's next pass. Past the firehose there is no technical answer at all, only the licensee's contract. Two deletion SLAs, seconds and hours, published rather than blurred.

12. It cannot mean an offset, and it should not mean a timestamp. A ranked list over a candidate set that is being rewritten continuously will duplicate and skip items across pages if the cursor is positional. Pin a snapshot: on the first page, materialise the ranked candidate ids for that session under a session key with a short TTL, and let the cursor be a position within that frozen list. Page 3 then reads the snapshot rather than re-ranking. *If pushed:* the snapshot is per session and per user, so it is real state on a stateless read path, and it has to expire or the store grows without bound. The alternative, re-ranking on every page with a "seen ids" bloom filter in the cursor, avoids server state and costs a re-rank per page plus a false-positive rate that silently hides tweets. Which one is right depends on how deep people actually scroll, and the answer is usually two pages.

13. Because recency queries can then stop early. With documents in descending id order, a query walking the posting lists hits the newest matches first, so once it has k hits it is done and the rest of the postings are never touched; on a relevance-ordered index the same query has to score every match before it knows which are newest. That is the difference between a bounded cost and a cost proportional to how common the term is, which matters most for exactly the queries people run during a breaking event. Descending order also makes indexing an append, which is what removes segment merging. This is the shape of the Earlybird design published in 2012, and nothing since has changed the reasoning. *If pushed:* it is a genuine trade, not a free win. Relevance-ranked queries over the hot index get nothing from the ordering and must score every match, so the archive is relevance-ordered instead. Two orderings for two query types is the whole reason there are two indexes.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, take the input, not the strategy.** Open by naming what makes this question different: "push, pull and hybrid are settled, so the interesting input is the follower distribution, and the first thing I want to know is what fraction of a typical follow set sits above ten thousand followers." Ask it, and if the answer is a shrug, assume a quarter and say you are assuming it. Then state your other numbers out loud: 250M daily active, ~150 follows each, 200M tweets/day so 2.3k/s steady and ~50k/s at a global event, 58k timeline loads/s. Say explicitly that you will spend the time on distribution and on search, and that trending is question 53's problem. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine, then break the diamond.** Draw it in one pass: client, tweet service, tweet store partitioned by author, an event stream, and three consumers hanging off it, fan-out, search indexer, trending. On the right, timeline service reading two sources. Say the three placement rules while you draw the arrows, because they are the answer: the poster is acknowledged when the row is durable and before any distribution; everything downstream is a derived cache that can be rebuilt and is allowed to be stale; search and trending are never in the write path, so a search cluster falling behind cannot stop anyone tweeting. Draw the fan-out decision as the familiar author-level threshold diamond, then immediately say the test is not that: it is active followers at ~1M, checked per edge, and derive it, 200k appends/s per tweet against a 5s SLO is 1M entries. Two sentences on why ids and not bodies: 8 bytes instead of 1KB, and deletes resolve at hydration instead of rewriting 100M lists.

**15-35, the drill, in this order.** First the read path, because it is what the cut is chosen to protect: seven steps, and only step 3 scales with the graph, so raising the cut from 10k to 1M takes fan-in from ~38 fetches to ~3. That number is the single most valuable thing you will say. Second, the retweet cascade: 500k retweets × ~500 mean followers is 250M pushed entries at 200k/s for twenty minutes, which is 2.5x the 100M the celebrity rule existed to avoid, arriving through the path you excluded the original from. Give the rate-triggered cutover at ~1,000 retweets/minute and concede that a trigger firing 90 seconds late has already let most of the peak through. Third, search as a second architecture rather than a component: 1.4B docs × 15 postings × 4B is ~84GB, so the hot week fits in RAM, append-only with no merges, descending id order for early termination, and a relevance-ordered archive behind the same API. Keep read-time deduplication and sharded counters as one-liners you expand only if asked.

**35-45, concede, then operate.** Volunteer the three gaps before they are found: deletion is seconds for visibility and hours for erasure because the hot index is append-only; the reply tree has no bounded-and-fair ranking and we cap it; the cold-mailbox rebuild is 50x the normal read cost and arrives correlated, at exactly the events that caused the fan-out shedding. Then two minutes of operations: publish-to-timeline lag, fan-out queue depth, search freshness, timeline p99 split by stage, counter drift. Close on multi-region as one line, timeline caches are region-local and disposable, so the recovery point objective is near zero for tweets and the real DR cost is cold-cache latency, which is the same cold-rebuild problem again.

Cut first: trending, which is one sentence and a pointer to question 53; then media and the CDN, which nobody is testing here; then the Snowflake bit layout, which is question 4. All three are safe to drop because none of them changes the distribution design. Never cut: the per-edge split with the 38-against-3 number, the cascade arithmetic, and the fact that search is a second index design rather than a box on the diagram.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **tweets** (wide-column store, partition by author):
  `(tweet_id Snowflake, author_id, text, media_ids, parent_id (for reply), created_at)`
- **follows** (wide-column store, two views): `(follower → followee)` and `(followee → follower)`
- **home_timeline** (cache, one key per user): a packed block of 8-byte ids in descending order, capped at 800. Not a sorted set; see the 25TB against 2.8TB derivation under scale.
- **author_recent** (cache, one key per author): the same structure, capped at ~200. The fetch path reads these.
- **fetch_path_set** (cache, one key per user): the above-cut authors this user follows, maintained on follow and on cut crossings.
- **retweeters** (wide-column, partition by original tweet id): `(original_id, retweeter_id, tweet_id)`, plus a rate counter that drives the cascade cutover.
- **search**: two indexes behind one API. Hot, in memory, append-only, 7 days, documents in descending tweet-id order. Archive, on disk, relevance-ordered, rebuilt in batch.
- **trending** (in-memory): top-K topics per geo partition, refreshed every minute. See #53.

**API contract**

```
POST /tweet                body: { text, media_ids? } → { tweet_id }
POST /follow/{user}
GET  /timeline/home?cursor → [tweets]
GET  /timeline/user/{id}   → [tweets]
GET  /search?q=...         → [tweets]
GET  /trending?region      → [topics]
```

**Observability**

- **Tweet publish-to-timeline latency.** The freshness SLO for ordinary accounts, alerted at 5s.
- **Home timeline p99**, split by stage: prebuilt read, fetch-path fan-in, merge, rank, hydrate. The split matters more than the total, because only fan-in scales with the graph.
- **Fetch-path fan-in width**, p50 and p99 count of above-cut authors per load. This is the number that says whether the push cut is still in the right place.
- **Fan-out queue depth and age.** The write-side health signal, and the trigger for tightening the activity window under overload.
- **Cold-rebuild rate.** Fraction of loads with no prebuilt timeline, which spikes at exactly the events that matter.
- **Search freshness.** Age of the newest searchable tweet, alerted at 10s.
- **Counter reconciliation drift** against the event log, which protects engagement integrity on viral content.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** tweets and social graph replicate durably; home-timeline caches are region-local and disposable.
- **RTO:** fast for stateless read services; slower for cache warmup after a regional loss.
- **RPO:** near-zero for canonical tweet writes, relaxed for derived caches and indexes.
- **Failover cadence:** test cold-cache regional failover because that is the real user experience after DR.
- **Cross-region cost:** mostly media/CDN and tweet-store replication rather than timeline-cache replication.

### 27. Design Instagram
#### Problem
Photo and video sharing at billion-user scale: post, follow, feed, profile, stories, search. The distinguishing feature is the payload, because a post is 2MB of pixels rather than 300 bytes of text. That makes the upload pipeline, the derivative ladder and the delivery path the actual design, with the feed bolted on top.
#### Core
The feed half of this is the news feed answer: hybrid fan-out, push post ids into per-follower timeline caches, pull for high-follower accounts, rank at read time. Assume it in one sentence and spend the interview on what is different, which is that the payload is two megabytes of pixels.

Pixels never pass through the API tier in either direction. Upload is a pre-signed PUT straight to object storage, so the API only ever handles metadata. The landed object raises an event onto a queue, and a worker pool that autoscales on queue depth decodes the source (HEIC, JPEG, PNG) and encodes a fixed ladder of derivatives: a 100px thumbnail, 480px, 1080px, and a re-encoded full size, each in AVIF or WebP with a JPEG fallback. That is roughly 2.4MB of derivatives per post, generated once and served indefinitely.

On read, the feed response carries CDN URLs plus dimensions, never image data, and the client chooses the variant that fits its viewport and its network. That one property is what keeps a feed render at a few kilobytes of JSON while the bytes arrive from an edge cache in the viewer's city. Media URLs are immutable and content-addressed so they cache forever at a hit ratio above 95%, and mutation happens by minting a new URL rather than overwriting an old one.

Everything else is conventional. Metadata in a wide-column store partitioned by user, sharded counters for likes on viral posts with the append-only like log as the source of truth, stories on the same pipeline with a 24 hour row TTL and a matching object lifecycle rule.

The price is that publishing is asynchronous, so a post is not viewable until its ladder exists.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a photo lab that develops your picture into four sizes and distributes copies to every pharmacy within five miles of your followers, so when they want to look at it, it is already there. The original negative sits safely in a vault. The product experience is "instant photo" but the reality is an assembly line running before anyone asks.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Prepare every size the moment the picture arrives.* Decode once at upload, write a small fixed set of sizes to a file store, hand out addresses. This buys a constant read cost forever, because no server does any work per view no matter how many views arrive. It costs storage for sizes nobody ever looks at, and it fixes the menu: changing the ladder later means a bulk re-run over everything already uploaded. It wins when views per item are high and the set of shapes is small and stable, which describes a feed.

*Store one copy and cut sizes on demand behind the cache.* Keep a single high-quality master. When a request arrives for a size that is not cached, generate it then, cache it, and serve it. This buys any size on request and pays only for what is actually looked at. It costs a slow first request for each size, and a cache miss on popular content becomes a compute stampede. It wins when the shapes are unpredictable, such as arbitrary crops or a per-surface aspect ratio, or when most items are never viewed at all.

*Push the work onto the phone.* Have the uploading device produce the small sizes and upload all of them. This buys zero server compute and the fastest possible publish. It costs trust, since you are accepting client-produced pixels and cannot guarantee the small size shows the same thing as the large one, and it costs battery and upload bandwidth on exactly the worst networks. It wins as a supplement rather than a replacement: the phone makes the thumbnail so the post appears instantly, the server still produces the canonical ladder.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a user uploads a 4MB iPhone HEIC photo. The app requests a **pre-signed URL** from the API, a temporary web address that lets the phone upload directly to object storage without routing bytes through application servers, which would otherwise make those servers a bandwidth bottleneck. The phone PUTs the file directly. The object store emits an "object created" event to a queue. An **image processing worker** picks up the event, fetches the raw bytes, and re-encodes in parallel into four variants: 100x100 thumbnail (~10KB), 480px-wide small (~80KB), 1080px-wide medium (~300KB), and full resolution re-encoded (~2MB). Each variant is written back and gets a **CDN URL**, an address that routes through a content delivery network so the file is served from a cache close to the user. The post metadata (caption, location, variant URLs) is written to the database. The fan-out service copies the post id into the timeline caches of the poster's followers. The app shows the user their post using the thumbnail that was generated first, while the larger variants finish.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Object storage.** A globally replicated file store holding every raw upload and every processed variant. Near-unlimited capacity, designed for large binary blobs. You never serve images out of a database.
- **Image processing workers.** A fleet that re-encodes photos into multiple sizes and formats, autoscaling on queue depth. It also emits WebP and AVIF variants, modern formats that are 30 to 50% smaller than JPEG at equivalent quality, for clients whose `Accept` header says they can decode them.
- **CDN.** A global network of cache servers in hundreds of cities holding copies of popular media. A user in Tokyo is served from the Tokyo node rather than from a server in Virginia. The CDN absorbs over 95% of media requests, so origin sees very little traffic.
- **Multi-tier CDN.** The cache is layered: city-level edges nearest users, regional nodes backstopping city misses, and origin as the last resort. Posts the ranker scores as rising are pre-warmed to regional nodes so the first viewer in a new city gets a cache hit rather than an origin fetch.
- **Sharded like counters.** A celebrity post taking 5 million likes in 10 minutes is ~8,300 writes per second against one row, which no ordinary row sustains. Split the count across 100 shard keys (`likes:{post_id}:{0..99}`), each write picking a shard at random, so a shard sees ~83 writes per second. Reading the total means summing 100 keys, which is the price.
- **Stories.** A separate wide-column collection with a native 24 hour row TTL, so the store's own expiry removes them with no cleanup job. The object store carries a matching lifecycle rule deleting the media 25 hours after creation.

**The thing that makes it hard, the upload spike:** a global sporting event ends and ten million fans upload at once. Workers process as fast as they can and the queue still grows, users watch "uploading" for minutes, and they abandon. Two fixes, and both are needed. Autoscale workers on queue depth with a scale-up policy that adds capacity within 30 seconds. And generate the thumbnail synchronously at the upload edge before queuing the rest, so the post appears in the user's own grid immediately while the larger variants are still in flight.

**Why this design and what it costs:** pre-encoding at upload rather than resizing at request time is the central efficiency decision, and the arithmetic is not as lopsided as it first looks. Pre-encoding costs roughly 2 CPU-seconds per post and 2.4MB of derivative storage, paid whether or not anyone looks. On-demand resizing costs nothing for a post nobody views, but every cache miss becomes a CPU-bound resize on the read path. At a 95% CDN hit ratio and 600k feed loads per second at peak, that is 30k resizes per second, which is more compute than pre-encoding everything and it lands on the latency-critical path rather than in a background queue. Pre-encoding wins here for the second reason more than the first.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Upload: pre-signed S3 PUT URL, phone uploads directly, S3 event to an SQS queue, image worker fleet as containers autoscaling on queue depth.
- Image processing hot path:
  ```
  raw = s3.get(raw_key)
  decoded = decode_heic_or_jpeg(raw)
  variants = parallel_encode([100x100, 480w, 1080w, full], decoded)
  for each variant: s3.put(variant_key); cdn.prewarm(variant_url)
  db.update(post_id, status=ready, media_urls={...})
  fan_out_queue.publish(post_id)
  ```
- Counters: Redis with 100 shards per post for likes, plus a separate Kafka event stream as the audit-grade source of truth. Exact counts come from the event log, approximate counts from Redis for display.
#### What this is really testing
Whether you can turn a media problem into an addressing problem. Every request path in this system carries addresses, and the bytes travel on a separate, cacheable, asynchronous path that neither the API tier nor the database ever touches. Upload bypasses the API with a pre-signed URL, transcoding happens off a queue, the feed response is JSON containing URLs, and delivery is a cache hit in the viewer's city. Once you see that, the follow-on questions answer themselves: URLs must be immutable so they cache forever, mutation must mint a new URL, and deletion becomes hard precisely because you optimised for cacheability. A candidate who designs the feed carefully and then says "and the images go in S3" has answered the wrong question, because the images are the question.

The one it resembles is TikTok, and they look nearly identical from a distance: a media feed at billion scale with an upload pipeline behind it. The axis that separates them is what decides *what* you see. Here the follow graph decides, and the ranker only orders within a candidate set the graph produced, so the read path is a per-user materialised timeline and the scaling problems are fan-out and derivative delivery. On TikTok the graph is close to irrelevant, candidates come from a retrieval model over the whole corpus, so there is no per-user timeline to maintain at all and the scaling problems are candidate generation and online learning.

Two concrete consequences. Instagram can materialise a timeline hours before the read and TikTok cannot, because the candidate set depends on the user's last thirty seconds of behaviour. And TikTok must prefetch the bytes of the next two or three items because a swipe has a sub-100ms budget with nothing on screen to hide the fetch, whereas a scrolling photo feed gives you a viewport of warning and can lazy-load. The media shape differs too: a photo ladder is a handful of discrete whole files, one fetch each, while video needs a segmented adaptive ladder that switches bitrate mid-playback.

Closest question: Q28
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Stories (24h ephemeral)?
- Reels (short video)?
- Direct messages?
- Image filters / processing in scope?
- Live streaming?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Media is dominant | an upload-transcode-CDN pipeline is the core; the feed stores references and multiple sizes |
| Stories (24h ephemeral) | a separate store with TTL expiry and a lightweight per-follower fan-out |
| Reels (short video) | a recommendation-driven feed and video transcode ladder, distinct from the photo feed |
| Direct messages | a separate chat service |
| Server-side image processing | a processing stage on upload generating thumbnails and filters |
| Billion-user scale | shard by user, cache hot feeds, and hybrid fan-out for high-follower accounts |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** post photo/video, follow, feed, profile, like/comment, stories, search
- **NFR:** fast image load (CDN), worldwide low latency, durable media

**Scale**

- **Userbase:** ~2B MAU (Meta-public 2024), DAU/MAU ~25% → **~500M DAU**.
- **Posts/day:** assume ~5% of DAU posts a feed item daily → 500M × 0.05 = ~25M; round up for multi-post users + Reels duplicating to feed → **~100M posts/day**. ÷86,400 ≈ **~1.2k posts/s avg**, ×5 spike → ~6k/s peak.
- **Stories/day:** stories use rate ~6% of DAU → 500M × 0.06 ≈ **~30M stories/day**.
- **Post metadata size:** post_id (8B) + user_id (8B) + caption (~300B avg of 2200-char limit) + media_url refs (~64B for 1–10 variants) + location (16B) + hashtags (~100B) + ts (8B) + envelope ≈ **~1KB**. Daily metadata = 100M × 1KB = **~100GB/day**; RF=3 → **~300GB/day** on wide-column store.
- **Media, original:** avg ~2MB/post (mix: photos ~500KB, carousel ~3MB, Reels ~5MB) → 100M × 2MB = **~200TB/day raw uploaded** on object store.
- **Media, variants:** server-side transcoded ladder of thumb 100² (~10KB) + small 480w (~80KB) + medium 1080w (~300KB) + full re-encoded (~2MB) ≈ **~2.4MB derivative set per post**. 100M × 2.4MB = **~240TB/day variants**.
- **Total media on object store:** raw + variants = 200 + 240 = **~440TB/day**. CDN-fronted, hot 90d, warm 1yr, then archive class. Hot footprint = 440TB × 90 = **~40PB**, which is also the net add per quarter.
- **Transcode compute:** decode a ~12MP source plus four encodes at fast presets ≈ **~2 CPU-seconds/post**. 100M × 2 = 200M CPU-s/day ÷ 86,400 = **~2,300 cores continuous**, ×5 at the peak hour → ~12k cores burst. This is the number that decides the first fork below.
- **Stories TTL storage:** 30M × ~1.5MB avg (short video ~3MB and photo ~500KB blended) = **~45TB/day ephemeral**. 24h row TTL plus a 25h object lifecycle grace bounds the live footprint at 45TB × 25/24 ≈ **~47TB hot**.
- **Likes/comments:** ~100 likes/post avg × 100M posts/day = **10B likes/day**, and ~5 comments/post → 500M comments/day. Sharding is irrelevant for the median post, which takes tens of likes over its lifetime; it exists entirely for the tail. Worst case seen in practice is 5M likes in 10 minutes = 5M / 600 = **~8.3k writes/s on one post**, which ÷ 100 shards is **~83 writes/s per shard**. Counter state ~100B per (post, shard) pair → 100M hot posts × 100 × 100B = **~1TB counter state**.
- **Feed timeline cache:** 500M DAU × a ~500 post_id candidate set × 8B = 4KB each → 500M × 4KB = **~2TB hot**, ×2 replication → ~4TB.
- **Reads:** average post is rendered ~100 times → 100M × 100 = 10B feed renderings/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **~115k feed-loads/s** steady, ×5 peak → **~600k/s**. A render fetches the medium variant (~300KB), not the whole 2.4MB set. At a >95% CDN hit ratio, origin sees 5% × 600k/s = 30k fetches/s × 300KB = **~9GB/s ≈ 72Gbps origin egress**.
#### Key decisions
**Pre-encode a fixed ladder at upload vs derive variants on demand behind the cache**
- Choice: encode a fixed four-rung ladder in an async worker at upload time, plus AVIF and WebP alternates per rung, and write every result to the object store before the post is publishable.
- Alternative: store one high-quality master, derive any requested size lazily at an image service in front of the cache, and persist the derived result so the second request is a hit.
- Decider: where the compute lands relative to the latency-critical path, and it is not the total that decides it. Pre-encoding is ~2 CPU-s per post × 100M posts = ~2,300 cores continuous, spent in a background queue where a 5 second p95 is invisible. On-demand at a 95% hit ratio and 600k peak feed loads is 30k derivations/s on the read path; even at 150ms each that is ~4,500 cores, and every one of them sits between a user and an image. The storage the lazy approach saves is the ~30% of posts nobody ever views, about 70TB/day, which at archive-class prices is not worth a read-path stall.
- Alternative wins when: the variant space is combinatorially large rather than a fixed menu. If product wants arbitrary crops, per-surface aspect ratios and four device pixel densities, the ladder goes from 4 rungs to 40 and pre-encoding goes from 2.4MB to ~24MB per post, which is 2.4PB/day. At that point you pre-encode two masters and derive the rest lazily, which is what an image-CDN product does and it is the right answer for a long tail of shapes. It also wins outright for any workload where most assets are never viewed, such as a backup or archival product, where the pre-encode is pure waste.

**Immutable public URLs vs per-viewer signed URLs**
- Choice: content-addressed, effectively permanent URLs on an unguessable path for public posts, with signed short-lived URLs used only for private accounts and direct messages.
- Alternative: sign every media URL against the requesting user, so each fetch is individually authorised and individually auditable.
- Decider: cache key cardinality, which sets the hit ratio, which sets origin egress. A signature that varies per viewer makes every URL unique, so unless the CDN is configured to strip it from the cache key the shared cache degrades toward one entry per viewer. Falling from a 95% to an 80% hit ratio takes origin egress from ~72Gbps to ~290Gbps, a 4x infrastructure step for the same traffic. The second half is expiry: a 5 minute signature means a user who scrolls back up, or leaves the app and returns, gets a broken image and forces a metadata re-hydration.
- Alternative wins when: the content is predominantly private, or regulation demands per-access authorisation with an audit record, which is the case for medical imaging, legal discovery, or a closed-group photo product. The middle path is authorisation at the edge, where edge compute validates a token carried outside the cache key, so the object stays shared-cacheable while access is still checked. That costs an edge compute invocation on every request and a token distribution problem, and it is what large platforms actually run for their private surfaces.

**Keep the uploaded original forever vs discard it once the ladder exists**
- Choice: keep the original, tier it to archive storage after 30 days, and treat it as the only re-encode source. The 1080px rung stays in warm storage as a fast fallback master.
- Alternative: generate the ladder, then delete the original and promote the full-resolution derivative to master.
- Decider: 200TB/day of originals is 73PB per year of upload, and archive-class storage at roughly $1/TB/month makes one year of retained originals about $73k/month, growing linearly. Against that, the codec cycle turns over roughly every five years (JPEG through WebP through AVIF, with AV1 and JPEG XL in flight), and every turn is a full re-encode of the corpus. Re-encoding from an already-lossy derivative compounds generational loss, visibly so by the second hop. The retention cost is small and predictable; the quality loss is permanent and unrecoverable, so keep the original.
- Alternative wins when: originals are genuinely enormous relative to what is served, which is the case for raw video and for camera RAW. A 5MB short video that serves a 500KB rendition has a 10x ratio, and at that ratio the archive bill is the dominant line item rather than a rounding error. Discarding is also right when the product's own terms already cap delivered quality at the ladder's top rung, because then there is no future codec migration that can use the extra pixels.

**How to read the diagram:** there are two separate paths and they only meet at a URL. The left column is the byte path, running from the client's pre-signed PUT through the object store and the image processor into the CDN. The right column is the metadata path, running from the post service through the fan-out service into the feed. Nothing on the right ever holds an image.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** deciding who should see a post is a graph problem measured in microseconds per edge, and delivering the post is a bandwidth problem measured in gigabits per second. They have nothing in common except an identifier, so they get separate infrastructure with separate scaling curves. The API tier sits on the metadata path only, which is why it stays a small, cheap fleet while media egress runs at 72Gbps.

**What this layout buys you:** the two halves scale independently, and the read path costs the same whether a post has ten viewers or ten million, because the marginal viewer is a CDN cache hit. The cost shows up in the seam. A post exists in metadata before its bytes are servable, so publish has to be gated on the pipeline finishing, and every new product surface that reuses the media path adds another consumer of that gate.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The path from a pre-signed PUT to a cacheable URL.**

This is the mechanism that gets drilled, because everything else in the design either feeds it or consumes its output.

**Why the API tier never touches bytes.** A 2MB upload through the API tier means every byte crosses an application server that also runs authentication, business logic and database calls. At 1.2k posts/s average that is 2.4GB/s of pass-through traffic sized against a fleet provisioned for CPU-bound request handling, and a slow client on a poor mobile network holds a request thread open for tens of seconds. Instead the client asks the API for a pre-signed PUT URL. The API mints a `post_id`, writes a row with `status=processing`, signs an object key scoped to that id with a short expiry, and returns a few hundred bytes. The phone uploads directly to the object store. The API's throughput is now decoupled from media volume entirely, which is why the same fleet size serves photos and video.

The signature has to be tight or it becomes an upload oracle. Scope it to one exact key, one method, a maximum content length, and a 15 minute expiry. Without a content-length bound a client can upload a 5GB file into your bucket against a URL you handed it.

**Why generation is async, and what that forces.** Object creation raises an event onto a durable queue. A worker pool consumes it, fetches the raw bytes, decodes the source (HEIC from iPhones, JPEG, PNG), and encodes the ladder in parallel: thumbnail at 100x100 for grid views, small at 480px wide for feed cards, medium at 1080px wide for tap-through, and full re-encoded for download. AVIF and WebP are produced alongside a JPEG fallback so clients advertising support in `Accept` get 30 to 50% fewer bytes. A 4MB HEIC produces roughly 10KB, 80KB, 300KB and 2MB in about 5 seconds at p95, on a pool that autoscales on queue depth.

Async is not free. It means a post exists in the database before its bytes are servable, so `status` is load-bearing: the post is excluded from every feed, profile grid and search result until it flips to `ready`. Two things follow. First, fan-out must be triggered by the `post_ready` event and not by the insert, or followers receive timeline entries pointing at 404s. Second, the user's own view is special-cased, because a creator who does not see their post immediately assumes the upload failed. The fix is a synchronous thumbnail generated at the upload edge before the rest is queued, shown only to the author until the full ladder lands.

**Idempotency, because retries are guaranteed.** Queue delivery is at-least-once and mobile clients retry aggressively on flaky networks. Every stage keys off the `post_id` the API minted, and variant object keys are deterministic (`{post_id}/{rung}.{codec}`), so a duplicate delivery overwrites identical bytes rather than creating a second post. The metadata update is a compare-and-set from `processing` to `ready`, so the second worker to finish is a no-op. Without deterministic keys you get orphaned objects that no row references and no lifecycle rule reclaims, which is the most common way this pipeline leaks storage.

**Failure at variant granularity.** A worker that fails one rung requeues with exponential backoff up to a bounded attempt count. It requeues the rung, not the post, because re-decoding a 12MP source to redo one 10KB thumbnail wastes the expensive half of the work. Persistent failure marks the post `processing_failed` and notifies the client. The row stays as a tombstone so a retry resumes from the correct state instead of minting a second `post_id` and orphaning the first upload's objects. A common source of persistent failure is a source format the decoder does not handle, typically a new phone's codec, so the failure metric needs a breakdown by source format or a device launch looks like a generic outage.

**Where the URL comes from, and why it never changes.** Each variant's URL includes the post id and the rung, so `/p/abc123/medium.avif` and `/p/abc123/full.avif` are separate cache entries. That separation matters for lifecycle: the full-resolution rung can tier to archive while thumbnails stay hot forever, and re-encoding one rung does not invalidate the others. The URLs are immutable, served with a one year `Cache-Control: max-age` and an `immutable` directive, because an edit that changes pixels mints a new key rather than overwriting an old one. Immutability is what makes the >95% hit ratio reachable, and it is also the direct cause of the deletion problem conceded below. You do not get one without the other.

**Pre-warming, and its limit.** When the ranker scores a post into the rising bucket, a job pushes the small and medium rungs to every regional cache so the first viewer in a new city gets a hit rather than a cross-ocean origin fetch. Full resolution is never pre-warmed: it is 85% of the bytes and rarely viewed. Nor is pre-warming applied to everything, because 100M posts × 390KB of hot rungs × 50 regions is ~2PB/day of push traffic for content that 49 of those regions will never request. The rising signal is lagging by construction, so the first few thousand viewers of every viral post still pay origin latency.

```
client → API:            POST /uploads              → {post_id, presigned_url}
client → object store:   PUT presigned_url          (2MB, never touches API)
object store → queue:    ObjectCreated{key}
worker:                  decode once, encode 4 rungs × 3 codecs in parallel
worker → object store:   PUT {post_id}/{rung}.{codec}   (deterministic keys)
worker → metadata:       CAS status: processing → ready
metadata → fan-out:      post_ready{post_id}        (not on insert)
```

**Upload, variant generation and publish, as a sequence.** The upload path is decoupled end to end: the API tier sees only metadata, variants are generated off a notification queue, and the post is hidden from every surface until the variants exist. The synchronous thumbnail is the one deliberate exception, and it is visible only to the author.
