The rest of the system is deliberately out of this dive. Feed ranking and hybrid fan-out are the news feed answer and should be cross-referenced rather than re-derived. Stories are this same pipeline with a 24 hour row TTL and a 25 hour object lifecycle rule. Explore is an offline collaborative-filtering job producing a per-user candidate cache, refreshed hourly, filtered and ranked online. Reels reuse a segmented video transcode ladder and merge into the same post path. None of those change the mechanism above.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hot post.** A celebrity post pulls millions of metadata reads in minutes, hammering one row in the wide-column store while feed services hydrate it. *Mitigation:* media reads never reach the metadata path at all, since the CDN absorbs them and origin sees roughly one fetch per edge. The hydrated post card (metadata, URLs, counter values) is cached at the API tier with a 60s TTL, so the store sees one read per miss rather than millions. Read replicas widen the fan-out further, and a per-post rate limit stops one post monopolising the cluster.
- **Storage growth.** At 440TB/day the corpus reaches ~160PB/year, and holding all of it in the hot tier is indefensible when the great majority is never touched after its first month. *Mitigation:* tier by age and by rung, not by age alone. Thumbnail and small stay hot indefinitely because profile grids read them forever; medium tiers to warm at 90 days; full resolution and the original tier to archive at 30 days. This is why URLs are keyed per rung: a rung can move tier without invalidating its siblings. Archive reads take seconds, which is acceptable for a download of a five-year-old full-resolution photo and would not be acceptable for a grid scroll.
- **Image processing queue.** A global event drives 10x the normal upload rate and the queue grows faster than workers drain it. Users watch "uploading" for minutes and abandon. *Mitigation:* autoscale on queue depth with a policy that adds capacity within 30s; run a priority lane so established creators clear ahead of brand-new accounts, which are also the main spam vector; generate the thumbnail synchronously at the upload edge so the author sees their post immediately. Note this makes queue depth, not worker CPU, the alerting signal, because a saturated pool looks healthy per-host.
- **Like write storm on viral posts.** 5M likes in 10 minutes is ~8.3k writes/s against a single counter row, and single-row write throughput in a wide-column store caps in the low thousands. *Mitigation:* sharded counters spread each post across 100 keys, so a shard absorbs ~83 writes/s and the read sums 100 keys behind the same 60s card cache. Readers tolerate eventual consistency on a displayed count; nobody distinguishes 1.20M from 1.199M. Exact counts for advertiser dashboards and audit come from the append-only like-event log, which is the source of truth, with the counters as a derived cache.
- **Mobile data usage.** Serving full resolution to a phone on a slow cellular link wastes bandwidth, slows the render and burns a data cap, which is worst for exactly the users on the worst networks. *Mitigation:* the payload carries URLs for every rung plus dimensions, and the client picks by viewport, pixel density and connection type. It starts at `small` and upgrades to `medium` if the user zooms or dwells past two seconds. AVIF and WebP are served on `Accept`, cutting 30 to 50% of bytes at equal quality. This costs cache entries: four rungs times three codecs is twelve objects per post rather than one, which is a deliberate trade of cache footprint for delivered bytes.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Variant generation | Async media pipeline fails or stalls, leaving broken post assets | Upload-to-ready lag and variant-generation error rate | Retry at variant granularity, keep post in `processing`, and notify user only when required assets are ready |
| Story TTL | Story rows or media objects outlive 24h unexpectedly | Expired-story canary and TTL drift metrics | Use native row TTL plus object-store lifecycle rules, and copy to highlights explicitly instead of exempting originals |
| CDN invalidation | Wrong or stale variant remains cached after moderation/delete | Tombstone-hit mismatch and media-404 after delete | Short cache TTL for mutable surfaces and canonical tombstone checks before serving metadata |
| Counter shards | Like/comment shard skew or drift appears on viral posts | Shard-write imbalance and reconciliation drift | Increase shard count for hot posts and reconcile from append-only event logs |
| Explore / feed hydrate | Metadata DB slowdown makes media URLs unavailable even though bytes are hot on CDN | Hydration p99 and metadata-cache miss spike | Cache hydrated post cards briefly and serve partial fallbacks where possible |
| Moderation | Unsafe content becomes visible before checks finish | Time-to-moderation and block-after-publish metrics | Gate visibility on required trust-and-safety stages for risky uploads |

**Unresolved**

**Deletion is not deletion, and it is the direct cost of the cacheability we chose.** The whole read path depends on immutable URLs with a one year max-age and an unguessable path, because that is what buys a >95% hit ratio at 72Gbps of origin egress. The same properties mean that after a user deletes a post, or moderation removes it, anyone holding the direct URL can still fetch the bytes from an edge until the entry ages out. A purge across hundreds of POPs takes minutes to hours and is best-effort by construction, since a POP that is offline during the purge serves stale content when it returns. Every clean fix breaks something upstream. Short TTLs destroy the hit ratio and the fork above. Per-viewer signed URLs destroy shared cacheability for the same reason. An edge-compute tombstone check on every request adds a call to a central service on the hottest path in the system and makes media availability depend on metadata availability, which is the coupling the whole architecture exists to avoid. What we actually do is tombstone the metadata so the post vanishes from every surface within seconds, issue a best-effort purge, and accept a window during which the raw URL still resolves. Erasure requests under GDPR get a verified targeted purge, which works because the volume is small and would not survive being applied to routine deletes.

**Cold-tier revival has no predictor.** Tiering full resolution and originals to archive at 30 days is what makes 160PB/year affordable, but archive first-byte latency is seconds to minutes. That is fine for a deliberate download and wrong for anything interactive. Keeping thumbnail, small and medium hot forever covers grid scroll and feed render, which is 390KB of the 2.4MB set, so the exposure is limited to tap-through on old content. But old content does resurface: an anniversary feature, a profile deep-scroll, a years-old post going viral after a news event. We cannot predict which archived object is about to be requested, and the prediction problem is genuinely hard because the trigger is usually external to the platform. The partial answer is to promote a whole account's archive tier on the first sign of attention, which helps when the resurfacing is account-shaped and does nothing when a single old photo is linked from elsewhere.

**Moderation and publish latency cannot both be satisfied at 1.2k posts/s.** Perceptual-hash matching against a known-bad fingerprint database runs inline in the worker and costs ~20ms, so that gate is free. The ML classifier is another ~200ms, still affordable against a 5 second pipeline. Human review is minutes to hours, and there is no version of this design where 100M posts a day wait on a human. So the design publishes first for established accounts and reviews asynchronously, which means unsafe content is visible for a window measured in minutes. Holding new and low-reputation accounts pre-publish narrows the exposure, because that is where the abuse base rate is concentrated, but it does not close it and it adds a visible latency penalty to exactly the users being onboarded. This is a policy choice presented as an engineering one, and it should be named as such rather than mitigated away.
#### Drill questions
1. A celebrity post gets 5M likes in 10 minutes. How does the counter survive?
2. The image processing pipeline backs up and the upload queue grows. What do you do?
3. How do you keep stories ephemeral at scale, with a TTL on billions of objects?
4. A user uploads illegal content. How do you catch it before it is seen?
5. How do you handle 10x growth in upload volume?
6. A user blocks someone. How does that propagate to the feed and Explore?
7. A user deletes a post. What actually happens to the bytes, and when?
8. How does the multi-tier CDN handle a post going viral globally?
9. How are sharded counters reconciled against the like-event log?
10. You need to add an AVIF rung to every photo already uploaded. How do you run that?
11. Why does the feed response carry URLs rather than image data, and what breaks if you inline the thumbnails as base64?
12. A post is published in Jakarta and opened one second later by a follower in São Paulo. Trace the bytes.
13. Why is the API's pre-signed URL scoped and short-lived, and what goes wrong if it is not?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Sharded counter: split the post's like count across 100 keys (`likes:{post}:{0..99}`), writes pick a shard at random, reads sum all of them. 5M likes in 10 minutes is ~8.3k writes/s, so a shard takes ~83 writes/s, comfortably inside a single row's capacity. *If pushed:* eventual consistency is fine because nobody distinguishes 1.20M from 1.199M, and the summed read is amortised behind the 60s post-card cache. For exact counts in audit and ads, batch reconcile from the like-event log.

2. Autoscale workers on queue depth, with the alert on depth rather than per-host CPU because a saturated pool looks healthy per-host. If it is still backing up, prioritise: established creators first, brand-new accounts last, which is also an anti-spam control. The client shows an "uploading" state until the variants exist. *If pushed:* generate the thumbnail synchronously at the upload edge so the author sees their own post immediately, and let the remaining rungs fill in asynchronously. That converts a throughput problem into a perceived-latency problem, which is much cheaper to solve.

3. Store the story row with a native 24 hour TTL, so expired rows are reclaimed by compaction with no sweeper job to operate. Object storage carries a matching lifecycle rule that deletes the media at 25 hours, one hour of grace beyond the row so the row never outlives its bytes. *If pushed:* Highlights copies the underlying media into a permanent collection on opt-in rather than exempting the original from its TTL. Copying is the right model because the two have different access patterns and different lifecycles, and an exemption flag on a TTL row is a reliable way to leak storage forever.

4. Match a perceptual hash of the upload against a known-bad fingerprint database inline in the worker, roughly 20ms, and block on a hit before the post is ever publishable. An ML classifier scores the other risk dimensions at ~200ms, still cheap against a 5 second pipeline, and high scores route to human review. *If pushed:* human review is minutes to hours and cannot gate 1.2k posts/s, so established accounts publish first and are reviewed after, while new and low-reputation accounts hold pre-publish. That narrows the exposure window rather than closing it, and it is a policy decision, not a design one. Matched content also carries mandatory reporting obligations.

5. Transcoding is embarrassingly parallel and the object store does not notice, so upload volume itself is a budget question rather than an architecture question. The metadata store is where 10x actually lands: pre-shard posts by user so hot partitions split independently. CDN scales on its own. *If pushed:* metadata write QPS per post is trivial; it is read QPS on hot posts that spikes, and read replicas plus the 60s post-card hydrate cache absorb it. The one thing that genuinely does not scale linearly is the archive tiering job, which has to keep up with 440TB/day of new objects.

6. Block lists are per-user, small, and cached in the feed service, applied as a filter over candidates at read time. Search and Explore consult the same filter so there is one place to get it right. *If pushed:* for accounts blocking thousands, use a Bloom filter for the fast negative and the full set only to confirm a hit. Eventual consistency across services is acceptable here, since a blocked post visible for a few seconds is not catastrophic, but the same is not true for a block applied after harassment, so the propagation path needs a bounded and measured lag rather than a best-effort one.

7. The metadata row is tombstoned immediately, so within seconds the post is gone from every feed, grid, search result and Explore surface. The bytes are a different story. URLs are immutable with a one year max-age precisely so they cache forever, so a purge has to fan out across hundreds of POPs, takes minutes to hours, and is best-effort because an offline POP serves stale content when it returns. Object deletion at origin is immediate; edge deletion is not. *If pushed:* concede that anyone holding the direct URL can fetch bytes during the purge window, and that this is the price of the hit ratio rather than an oversight. Erasure requests under GDPR get a verified targeted purge, which works only because that volume is small.

8. When the ranker scores a post into the rising bucket, a pre-warm job pushes the small and medium rungs to every regional cache. Edge POPs then hydrate from their region on first request, so a first viewer in a new city gets a sub-100ms load and origin sees one fetch per region rather than one per city. *If pushed:* full resolution is never pre-warmed, since it is 85% of the bytes and rarely viewed. And the signal is lagging by construction: a post only enters the rising bucket after enough people have already viewed it, so the first few thousand viewers of every viral post pay origin latency regardless.

9. Every like is an append-only event keyed by `(post_id, user_id, ts)`, which is both the source of truth and the idempotency mechanism, since a duplicate like from the same user is a no-op insert on an existing key. The sharded counters are a derived cache. An hourly job sums the event log per post, compares against the sum of the shards, and writes an audit-trailed adjustment for any drift. *If pushed:* drift is normally zero because the increment and the event insert are issued together, and it appears mainly on cross-region propagation failures. When they disagree the log always wins. Advertiser dashboards read a batch-refreshed materialised view over the log directly rather than the counters.

10. Do not do it as one bulk job over 500 billion objects. Two phases. First, add AVIF to the worker so every new upload gets it, which stops the gap growing from the moment it ships. Second, backfill lazily and in ranked order: the client sends `Accept: image/avif`, the delivery layer serves the existing WebP when no AVIF rung exists, and enqueues a low-priority backfill for that object. Popular content converts within hours because popularity is what drives requests, and the archive tail converts never, which is correct because nobody is asking for it. *If pushed:* the reason a bulk backfill is wrong is not just runtime, it is that re-encoding an archived original means a restore from archive first, so a naive bulk job turns a compute bill into a much larger retrieval bill. Cap the backfill's share of the worker pool so it cannot starve live uploads, and it is one of the few jobs worth pausing entirely during a traffic peak.

11. Because a feed render is 20 posts and the images are 300KB each. Inlining them makes a single response 6MB, which cannot be cached per-post since the composition is per-user, cannot be range-requested, cannot be progressively rendered, and has to pass through the API tier, putting 72Gbps of media through a fleet sized for JSON. URLs keep the response at a few kilobytes and let the bytes travel on a path that is cacheable, resumable, and independently scalable. *If pushed:* inlining a 2KB blurhash placeholder is the exception worth making, because it removes a round trip on the very first paint and it is small enough not to change the response's character. Base64 also inflates by 33%, so inlining a 10KB thumbnail costs 13KB, and the break-even against a separate cached request is worse than it looks.

12. The Jakarta client PUTs to the nearest object store region. The worker there produces the ladder and writes it to that region. The metadata row flips to `ready` and fan-out pushes the post id into the São Paulo follower's timeline cache, which is metadata and replicates in tens of milliseconds. The follower's feed request returns the URL almost instantly, and then the image request misses the São Paulo edge, misses the South America regional cache, and pulls from the Jakarta origin: a cross-ocean fetch with 300 to 800ms to first byte instead of the ~30ms a warm edge gives. *If pushed:* this is the seam the design does not close. Pre-warming every post to every region is ~2PB/day of push for content that the median post's audience will never request from 49 of 50 regions. Cross-region object replication of the small and medium rungs for accounts with a geographically distributed follower base is the targeted fix, and it works because the follower distribution is known at post time even though the viral trajectory is not.

13. Scope it to one exact object key, one method, a maximum content length and a 15 minute expiry, all bound into the signature. Without the key scope the URL writes anywhere in the bucket. Without the content-length bound a client uploads a 5GB file against a URL you handed out, which is an unmetered write into your storage bill and a decode bomb for the worker. Without a short expiry the URL is a durable capability that can be shared, and revoking it means rotating the signing key for everyone. *If pushed:* the expiry has to cover a slow upload on a poor network, so 15 minutes rather than 60 seconds, and the client re-requests rather than resuming past expiry. Also validate the decoded image server-side in the worker, because a signature bounds the bytes and says nothing about whether they are actually an image.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, name the axis and refuse the obvious trap.** Open with "the feed is the easy half and it is the news feed answer, so let me assume hybrid fan-out in one sentence and spend the time on the payload, because a post here is 2MB of pixels rather than 300 bytes of text." That single move buys you the rest of the interview, because the default candidate spends twenty minutes rediscovering fan-out. Then ask the two questions that change the design: is video in scope (which changes a discrete ladder into a segmented adaptive one), and are posts public or private (which decides the signed-URL fork). State the numbers you are working from: 500M DAU, 100M posts/day, ~1.2k posts/s, 10B renders/day, 440TB/day of media. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, two columns, not one diagram.** Draw the byte path down the left: client, pre-signed PUT, object store, event queue, worker pool, object store again, CDN, viewer. Draw the metadata path down the right: client, API, post row, fan-out, timeline cache, feed service. Say the rule as you draw the gap between them: the two paths meet at a URL and nowhere else, the API tier never touches a byte in either direction, and that is why the API fleet is sized for JSON while media egress runs at 72Gbps. Then say the ladder out loud with sizes (10KB, 80KB, 300KB, 2MB) so the numbers are on the board before anyone asks. Finish the band by naming the seam you have just created: the post row exists before the bytes are servable, so publish is gated on `status=ready`.

**15-35, the pipeline, and protect this time.** This is the question. Walk the pre-signed URL and say why it is scoped and content-length bounded. Walk async generation and say what it forces: fan-out fires on `post_ready` and not on insert, or every follower gets a 404; the author gets a synchronous thumbnail because a creator who cannot see their own post assumes failure. Walk idempotency, since at-least-once delivery plus mobile retries makes deterministic variant keys the difference between overwriting identical bytes and leaking orphaned objects nobody references. Then take the pre-encode fork on your own terms, with the number: on-demand is not cheaper, it is ~4,500 read-path cores against ~2,300 background cores, and it moves compute from a queue where 5 seconds is invisible to a path where 150ms is not. Then URL immutability and per-rung keys, which is what lets a rung tier to archive without invalidating its siblings, and which is also the reason deletion is hard. Keep the original-retention fork and pre-warming as one-liners you expand only if asked.

**35-45, concede, then operate.** Give the three gaps before they are found: deletion is best-effort at the edge and that is the price of the hit ratio, not a bug; cold-tier revival has no predictor; moderation cannot both gate publish and clear 1.2k posts/s, so exposure is a policy window. Then two minutes of operations: alert on queue depth rather than worker CPU, watch upload-to-ready p95, CDN hit ratio broken down by rung, and counter drift against the like log. Close on cross-region, where metadata is region-homed and media is global, and the honest consequence is that a post published in Jakarta and read in São Paulo one second later pays a cross-ocean origin fetch.

Cut first: Explore and the collaborative-filtering candidate job, then stories and their TTL mechanics, then the client-side variant selection logic. All three are real and none of them changes the architecture; Explore in particular is a recommendation question wearing a media question's clothes and it will eat the pipeline discussion. Never cut: bytes never touch the API tier, the async publish gate and what it forces, and URL immutability with its deletion cost.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **posts** (wide-column store, partition by user): `(post_id, user_id, caption, media_urls{thumb,small,med,full}, location, ts)`
- **likes** (sharded counter store + wide-column log): per post
- **comments** (wide-column store): `(post_id, comment_id timeuuid, user_id, text)`
- **follows / feed** (same as Twitter)
- **stories** (wide-column store, TTL 24h): `(user_id, story_id, media_url, ts, viewers[])`
- **media** (object store + CDN), accessed via CDN URL signed if private

**API contract**

```
POST /upload                body: image bytes, caption, location, tags
GET  /feed?cursor           → [{post, author, likes, comments_preview}]
GET  /profile/{user}        → posts grid
POST /like/{post_id}
POST /comment/{post_id}     body: { text }
GET  /stories/feed          → ranked by recency × relevance
```

**Observability**

- **Upload-to-ready p95.** The creator-facing SLO for the whole pipeline.
- **Variant-generation failure rate, broken down by source format.** Without the breakdown, a new phone's codec looks like a generic outage.
- **Queue depth, not worker CPU.** A saturated worker pool looks healthy per-host, so depth is the signal that catches a backlog.
- **CDN hit ratio per rung.** Thumbnail and small should be near 99%; a drop in the medium rung is what moves origin egress.
- **Story expiry correctness.** The fraction of stories still retrievable past their TTL, covering both the row and the object.
- **Counter drift against the like-event log.** Protects engagement numbers on exactly the content people scrutinise.
- **Feed media bytes per render.** The mobile-performance and egress-cost metric in one number.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** media objects replicate broadly behind CDN; metadata is region-homed but globally readable via caches.
- **RTO:** media delivery survives most origin issues via CDN; metadata-region failover is slower but manageable.
- **RPO:** near-zero for post metadata and uploaded media after commit; story expiry is derived and can be recomputed.
- **Failover cadence:** asset-pipeline and metadata failovers both matter; pure API drills are insufficient.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by media replication and CDN egress, not by metadata rows.

### 28. Design TikTok (Short Video)
#### Problem
Serve an endless personalized short-video feed where every swipe plays in under a second, from a corpus of billions of videos that grows by 100 million a day. The follow graph barely matters: most of what a user watches comes from strangers, chosen by a model. Upload, transcode, and moderation exist to keep that model supplied with candidates.
#### Core
There is no fan-out here. The feed is a retrieval problem over the whole corpus, and the follow graph is one weak input among several.

Every swipe resolves against a two-stage funnel. Retrieval narrows roughly 10B videos to a few hundred candidates by querying an approximate-nearest-neighbour index with the user's precomputed 256-dimensional embedding, in parallel with four cheaper channels: trending in region, fresh from follows, sound and hashtag affinity, and an exploration channel of under-observed videos. Ranking then scores those few hundred with a multi-task model predicting completion, like, share and follow, collapses the predictions into one number, and re-ranks for variety so the same creator does not appear three times in six swipes. Top 50 go back to the client.

Two stages rather than one because neither works alone. Scoring 10B candidates per request is arithmetically impossible. Retrieval alone has no notion of what you will actually finish watching, only what looks like what you watched before.

The product constraint is that a swipe must start playing in under 100ms, which no network round trip can meet. So the client preloads the first segment of the next two or three videos while you watch the current one, and playback is local by the time your thumb lands.

The interesting scale problem is not the celebrity. It is the unknown. 100M videos arrive daily with zero engagement signal, and a video that gets no impressions never earns any signal, so a fixed fraction of feed inventory is reserved for under-observed content and a new video's first embedding is computed from its pixels, its audio and its creator rather than from engagement it does not have yet.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a jukebox that watches you. Every song it plays, it studies whether you fast-forwarded, replayed, or danced. The next song is chosen from everything it has observed about you and everyone like you. But this jukebox serves a billion people at once, and if the next song takes more than a fraction of a second to start, they walk out.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Narrow cheaply, then score expensively.* Two stages: a geometric shortlist that costs almost nothing per candidate, then a real model over a few hundred survivors. This buys the ability to consider a corpus of any size at fixed serving cost, because the expensive stage's work is bounded by the shortlist rather than by the catalogue. It costs you a blind spot: anything the cheap stage fails to surface, the expensive stage never sees, and that failure is silent because you only measure what you served. It wins above roughly ten million items, which is nearly always for this product.

*Build each user's next few hundred videos on a schedule and serve from a list.* A batch job every hour writes a personalized queue per user; serving is a list read. Latency becomes trivial and predictable, and the expensive computation happens off the request path where you can use whatever hardware is cheap. It costs within-session reactivity: it cannot notice that you just skipped three cooking videos in a row, which for a product where a session is 40 swipes is most of the signal there is. It wins when sessions are short and inventory turns over slowly.

*Rank only what the graph gives you.* Take everything from accounts the user follows and order it. No models, no vector index, explainable to a regulator. It fails here structurally rather than technically: the median user follows too few accounts to fill a session, and the content that keeps them is from strangers. That approach is the right answer to a different product, and it is the one described in Q8.

**The single-request walkthrough:** you open the app and swipe up. Your client sends `user_id` plus context (time, location, device, what you did in the last 60 seconds) to the Feed Service. The Feed Service retrieves your **user embedding**, a 256-dimensional vector encoding your viewing history, precomputed from past interactions and refreshed hourly. It then runs **ANN retrieval**, an approximate nearest neighbour lookup that finds the videos whose embeddings sit closest to yours in that 256-dimensional space, out of a pool of 10 billion, in under 10 milliseconds. Five channels run in parallel: the two-tower ANN result, trending in your region, recent uploads from creators you follow, exploration candidates with few lifetime impressions, and videos using sounds you have engaged with. The roughly 300 survivors go through a **ranker**, a neural network that predicts your probability of watching each to completion, liking it, and sharing it. The top 50 video ids come back. Your client starts playing number one and simultaneously downloads the first chunk of two and three. When you swipe, number two plays from local storage.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Two-tower model.** Two halves of one architecture. A user tower encodes a user's history into a 256-dim vector; a video tower encodes a video's features into the same space. The critical property is asymmetry: the video tower runs offline, once per video, and the result is stored, so at serve time only the cheap user-tower forward pass runs live. You look up your vector, then find nearby video vectors in an index.
- **ANN index (HNSW or IVF-PQ).** Approximate nearest neighbour finds the closest vectors to a query without checking all 10 billion. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a graph connecting similar vectors; searching it is like navigating a city by always moving toward the destination. IVF-PQ (Inverted File with Product Quantization) compresses each vector from 1KB down to about 16 bytes, accepting a small accuracy loss, and clusters them so only the relevant cluster is searched. At 10 billion vectors HNSW needs roughly 10TB of RAM; IVF-PQ needs roughly 160GB. That gap is the first fork below.
- **Online learning.** Interaction events (watched 80%, skipped after 2 seconds, liked) flow back as a stream. A continuous training process refreshes the ranker every few minutes, so a video going viral right now is boosted within minutes rather than tomorrow. Retrieval embeddings update more slowly, hourly, to keep the model's own outputs from distorting the space it retrieves from.
- **CDN with HLS.** Video is encoded into multiple quality rungs (240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p) and chunked into 4-second segments. HLS tells the player which chunks exist at which rungs. The player fetches the next chunk before it needs it and adjusts quality to network speed. The CDN keeps those chunks close to viewers.
- **Client preload.** The app downloads the first segment of the next two or three videos while playing the current one, on background bandwidth. When you swipe, the video is already on the device and starts in under 100ms. Without it, every swipe pays a round trip plus buffer time.

**The thing that makes it hard, feedback loops in online learning:** if the ranker updates every few minutes on what it just recommended, and users watch whatever is recommended, the model's training data becomes a reflection of its own outputs. Suppose the ranker starts slightly over-weighting cat videos. It shows more. Users watch them, because cat videos are decent. The model sees cat-video engagement. It shows more still. Within hours every feed is cats. The mitigation is to update retrieval embeddings slowly, hourly from a 30-day window, as a stability anchor. The ranker only reorders a candidate set it did not choose, so it can update fast without changing what is eligible to be considered at all.

**Why this design and what it costs:** the two-stage funnel is not a preference, it is forced. Running the ranking network over 10 billion videos per request is more compute than exists. Retrieval narrows 10 billion to about 300 in under 10ms using cheap vector arithmetic; ranking scores 300 in about 30ms with an expensive model. Two cheap operations compose into something one expensive operation cannot do. The cost is that retrieval is now a correctness-critical component whose failures are invisible, because you can only measure the quality of what you served.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Retrieval: a vector database (Milvus, Vespa, or a self-hosted FAISS shard fleet) holding 10B video embeddings as IVF-PQ; ANN query for top-1000 in roughly 5ms, five channels in parallel.
- Ranking: TensorFlow Serving or Triton; a multi-task model with sparse embedding tables scoring ~300 candidates; accelerator fleet autoscaling on request rate.
- Hot path pseudocode:
  ```
  user_vec = embedding_store.get(user_id)  // precomputed, 256 floats
  candidates = union(
      ann_index.search(user_vec, k=200),
      trending_cache.get(region, k=50),
      follows_feed.get(user_id, k=30),
      exploration_pool.sample(user_id, k=20),
      sound_affinity.get(user_id, k=20)
  )
  candidates = safety_filter(candidates, user_id)
  scores = ranker.predict(user_vec, candidates)
  top50 = diversity_rerank(sort_by_score(scores))[:50]
  return hydrate(top50)  // manifest URLs, metadata, prefetch hints
  ```
- Interaction events to Kafka, streaming consumer joining them against logged request-time features to produce `(user_id, video_id, label)` training pairs, online ranker checkpoint every 5 minutes.
#### What this is really testing
Whether you notice that the follow graph has stopped being the data structure the feed is built from. Every other social feed question is, underneath, a question about propagating an item to a known set of recipients: the graph tells you who, and the engineering is about doing that cheaply for the users with pathological degree. Here the graph tells you almost nothing. Most watch time comes from creators the user has never heard of, the candidate set for any single request is the entire corpus, and there is no set of recipients to propagate to. The moment you accept that, fan-out is not a design option that you rejected, it is a mechanism with nothing to do. What replaces it is a retrieval index, and the interesting property of an index is not how fast it serves but what is allowed into it and on what evidence.

That reframing is what the question is for, and it is why the hard scale problem inverts. In a graph feed the pathological case is one account with 100 million followers. Here it is 100 million accounts with no followers and no history, uploading a video the system has zero observations about. A candidate who spends the interview on fan-out, celebrity thresholds and timeline caches has answered Q8 and will have nothing to say when asked how a first-time creator's video ever reaches anybody.

The contrast is with Instagram. Both are billion-user media products with the same transcode-and-CDN spine, and if you draw only the upload path the two diagrams are the same diagram. They diverge on what decides the feed. Instagram's feed is graph-driven: the set of things you could be shown is bounded by who you follow, which is thousands of items, so it can be materialised per user, ranked on read, and the engineering pressure lands on the media pipeline and on fan-out economics. TikTok's feed is model-driven: the set of things you could be shown is 10 billion items, it cannot be materialised per user at any price, and the engineering pressure lands on retrieval recall, exploration budget, and the cadence at which models may safely learn from their own output. Instagram's hardest question is what to do about an account with 500 million followers. This one's hardest question is what to do about a video with none. Same media pipeline, opposite ranking problem.

Closest question: Q27
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Video duration limits? (15s to 10m typically)
- Live in scope?
- Comments/likes/duets?
- Region-specific content (China vs global)?
- Cold-start (new users, no signal)?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Recommendation-driven feed | a candidate-generation plus ranking service is the heart, not a follow graph |
| Sub-second swipe-to-play | pre-fetch and pre-buffer the next few videos and serve segments from edge CDN |
| Short fixed durations | aggressive transcoding to small segments and heavy edge caching |
| Cold-start for new users | fall back to trending/popular content until enough interaction signal exists |
| Cold-start for new videos | a reserved exploration quota and feature-only video embeddings, since engagement priors do not exist yet |
| Region-specific content | per-region content pools and compliance-aware routing |
| Comments, likes, duets | separate interaction services feeding engagement signals back to ranking |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** upload video, browse "For You" feed, like/comment/share, follow, search by sound/effect/hashtag.
- **NFR:** sub-second video start (target under 100ms on swipe), smooth preload, feed relevance that survives an hour-scale trend, scale to 1B daily users.

**Scale**

- **Userbase:** ~1.5B MAU (TikTok-public 2024 order of magnitude); assume DAU ~1B given the engagement profile.
- **Impressions:** 1B DAU × ~100 videos watched or skipped per day = **~100B video impressions/day**. That is the denominator for everything below.
- **Feed calls:** a feed response carries ~50 ids and the client refetches near the halfway mark to stay fresh, so ~25 impressions are consumed per call. 100B / 25 = 4B calls/day; 4B / 86,400 ≈ **~46k feed calls/s average**, and evening peak at ~4x average = **~200k/s peak**. Note this is 25x smaller than the impression rate, which is the whole point of returning a batch.
- **Ranking cost:** 200k calls/s × ~300 candidates = **60M candidate-scorings/s at peak**. A multi-task ranker with sparse embedding tables sharded into accelerator memory sustains roughly 150k candidate-scorings/s per accelerator, so 60M / 150k ≈ **~400 accelerators** for the ranking tier before redundancy, call it 600 with headroom. This is the cost dominator and the reason candidate-set size is a budget line, not a tuning knob.
- **Uploads/day:** ~5% of DAU posts, so 1B × 0.05 = 50M; round up for power creators and cross-posting to **~100M videos/day**. Average raw ~10MB (60s at ~1.3Mbps source) gives 100M × 10MB = **~1PB/day raw**.
- **Transcoded variants:** an ABR ladder of 240p/480p/720p/1080p in H.264 plus H.265, a thumbnail (~50KB) and a poster (~200KB), totalling ≈2.5x raw. 100M × 25MB = **~2.5PB/day of variants**.
- **Hot storage:** raw masters are read only for re-encoding, so they go straight to cold. Variants stay hot for 14 days at full volume (14 × 2.5PB = 35PB), and ~40% of uploads receive under 100 views and tier to cold at day 14, so days 15 to 30 hold 16 × 2.5PB × 0.6 = 24PB. Total **~60PB hot**. Cold grows at ~2.5PB/day of variants, ≈900PB/year, which makes long-tail retention a product decision rather than an engineering one.
- **Metadata per video:** video_id (8B) + creator_id (8B) + duration (4B) + sound_id (8B) + hashtags (~200B) + manifest_url (64B) + thumbnail_url (64B) + moderation flags (16B) + ts (8B) + envelope ≈ **~2KB**. 100M × 2KB = **~200GB/day**; at RF=3 that is ~600GB/day on a wide-column store.
- **Interaction events:** each impression emits roughly 10 fine-grained events (impression, start, 25%, 50%, 75%, complete, like, skip, share, pause). 100B × 10 = **~1T events/day**. Each ~150B (user_id 8B + video_id 8B + type 4B + watch_pct 4B + session_id 16B + ~100B of context features + ts) gives 1T × 150B = **~150TB/day** on the partitioned event log. Seven-day hot retention for online learners = 7 × 150TB ≈ **~1PB hot**.
- **Feature lake:** 30 days × 150TB = 4.5PB raw; columnar Parquet with ZSTD at ~5x gives **~900TB on object store**.
- **User embeddings:** 1B users × 256 dims × 4B = **~1TB**, refreshed hourly in batch.
- **Video embeddings:** eligible pool ~10B videos, since the long tail stays retrievable. 10B × 256 × 4B = **~10TB uncompressed**, which is the number that rules out an uncompressed in-RAM index and forces the first fork below. Product-quantised to 16B per vector: 10B × 16B = **~160GB**, which fits comfortably across a modest shard fleet.
- **Exploration arithmetic:** to estimate a completion rate near 40% to within ±5 percentage points needs n ≈ 0.4 × 0.6 / 0.025² ≈ **400 impressions per video**. 100M uploads/day × 400 = **40B impressions of demand** against 100B total inventory. Reserving 1 slot in 10 supplies 10B, so exploration demand runs at **4x supply**. That ratio is the single most consequential number in this design.
- **CDN:** 100B impressions/day at ~2MB of segments actually watched per impression is 200PB/day of egress, or ~2.3TB/s average. Edge hit ratio above 95% keeps origin egress near 100GB/s, which is why the CDN tier is not optional.
#### Key decisions
**Which ANN index the retrieval pool uses**
- Choice: IVF-PQ, sharded across hosts with a coarse quantizer routing the user vector to the relevant shards, and over-retrieval to buy back the recall lost to compression (pull top-1000 from IVF-PQ, re-rank to top-200 by exact distance against full vectors fetched from a separate store, then hand those to the ranker).
- Alternative: HNSW, which holds full vectors in RAM and gives materially better recall at the same query latency.
- Decider: corpus size against memory budget. At 256 dims and float32 a vector is 1KB, so 10B vectors is ~10TB of RAM for HNSW against ~160GB for IVF-PQ at 16B per vector, a 60x difference. The switching condition is the bottom row of the table below, and it is not close here: 10B is two orders of magnitude past the point where HNSW's memory stops being fundable.
- Alternative wins when: the retrieval pool is under ~100M vectors, which happens more often than the headline number suggests. A recency-restricted channel over the last 30 days of uploads is 3B, still too big, but the trending pool for one region is under 10M and a hot-subset index over it is cheap. The honest production answer is both: IVF-PQ over the full catalogue for reach, HNSW over a hot recent subset where recall matters most and where IVF-PQ is weakest anyway, because its rebuild cadence handles streaming inserts badly.

| Property | HNSW | IVF-PQ |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Hierarchical small-world graph | Inverted file (Voronoi cells) plus product quantization |
| Recall@10 | ~95% at typical settings | 85 to 93%, tunable, lower than HNSW at equal speed |
| Query latency | 1 to 2ms at 95% recall | 0.5 to 2ms at 90% recall |
| Memory per vector | Full vector, ~1KB at 256-dim float32 | ~16B PQ code |
| 10B vectors at 256-dim | ~10TB RAM | ~160GB RAM |
| Index build | Slow graph construction | Fast clustering plus quantization |
| Update cost | Insert touches graph layers, manageable | Periodic re-clustering, poor at streaming inserts |
| Best for | Under 100M vectors, latency-critical and recall-critical | 100M+ vectors, memory-constrained, small recall loss acceptable |

These recall and latency figures track the ann-benchmarks results as of 2024. Both index families are actively researched and the numbers move, so quote the mechanism rather than the percentages.

**How a brand new video earns its first impressions**
- Choice: a reserved exploration quota. One feed slot in ten is filled from a pool of videos with under 500 lifetime impressions, served as its own retrieval channel rather than as an adjustment inside the ranker, with entry to the pool gated by a cheap content-and-creator prior.
- Alternative: no reserved slots. Add an uncertainty bonus to the ranker score, larger the fewer impressions a video has (a UCB-style optimism term), so under-observed videos compete inside the normal candidate set on a boosted score.
- Decider: exploration demand against inventory. Measuring a video's completion rate to ±5 points needs ~400 impressions; 100M uploads/day × 400 = 40B, against 100B total impressions. You cannot explore every upload even if you spent 40% of the product on it, so exploration must be rationed, and rationing needs an explicit budget you can see and cap. An uncertainty bonus has no budget: its spend is an emergent property of the score distribution, it changes silently whenever the ranker is retrained, and there is no dashboard on which "we are spending 18% of inventory on exploration today" appears.
- Alternative wins when: upload volume is small relative to inventory, roughly under 5% of daily impressions needed to fully explore every new item. A niche vertical-video app with 1M uploads/day needs 400M exploration impressions against, say, 20B of inventory, which is 2%, and at that level the bonus is genuinely better: it is one fewer moving part, it explores continuously rather than in a quota that can go unused, and it naturally spends more on items the ranker is uncertain about rather than uniformly. The reserved quota is the right call at TikTok's ratio and the wrong call at that one.

**Model update cadence: split or uniform**
- Choice: split. The ranker checkpoints every 5 minutes from the online interaction stream; retrieval embeddings rebuild hourly from a 30-day window.
- Alternative: one cadence for both, either both hourly (a single training pipeline, one artifact to reason about) or both continuously online.
- Decider: the timescale of the thing you are chasing against the time constant of the feedback loop, and the two layers differ on both. A sound goes from unknown to top-of-region in 2 to 6 hours, so the scoring layer needs sub-hour freshness or it misses the event entirely. What a user likes moves over weeks, so the embedding space has no such deadline. More importantly the loop closes at retrieval, not at ranking: the ranker reorders a candidate set it did not choose, so a bad update costs one session's ordering, whereas a bad retrieval update changes what is eligible and is self-reinforcing across every session afterwards. Concretely, with an hourly rebuild over a 30-day window a single anomalous hour is 1/720 of the training signal; make retrieval fully online on a 5-minute window and that same hour becomes essentially all of it.
- Alternative wins when: both hourly is correct when the corpus turns over on a daily rather than hourly cycle, such as a long-form video service or a music catalogue, where a second training pipeline is pure operational cost for freshness nobody perceives. Both online is defensible in exactly one case: when retrieval embeddings are not learned from engagement at all, for instance a frozen content encoder over pixels and audio with no interaction features. Then there is no loop to close and the stability argument evaporates. That is a real architecture, it is weaker at personalization, and some platforms deliberately choose it for auditability.

**How to read the diagram:** two loops run together. The left loop uploads, transcodes and serves bytes. The right loop observes watch behaviour and feeds it into the models that decide the next swipe. They meet at the candidate pool, which is the only place a video crosses from "processed" to "recommendable".

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** serving bytes fast is necessary and nowhere near sufficient. The platform has to choose the next item well, 100 billion times a day, from a corpus nobody has watched. So the recommendation loop is drawn as core infrastructure with its own feedback edge, not as a scoring step bolted onto the read path.

**What this layout buys you:** tight coupling between what users do and what they are shown next, and a playback path that is almost entirely edge-served. The cost is that the recommender is now on the critical path for the product working at all, which is why the failure table below spends most of its rows on degraded recommendation rather than on media delivery.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**How a brand new video gets its first thousand impressions.**

The two-stage funnel is easy to draw and easy to describe. What the diagram does not show is how anything enters it. Every stage below is a filter that a video with engagement history passes and a video uploaded four minutes ago fails, so the interesting mechanism is not the funnel, it is the door.
