`CALENDAR_LOCKED` on the diagram is the committed `held` state, not an open transaction, which is why every state after it can take seconds or days. Read the right-hand column as the release paths: each one runs the same compare-and-set, and each one is reachable more than once. `RE_AUTH` exists because a card authorisation expires after about 7 days and check-in can be 90 days out, so a job re-authorises roughly 5 days before arrival; a failed re-auth cancels toward `CANCELLED_PAYMENT` and releases the nights, which is the one release the guest did not ask for.

What the state machine does not contain is the thing that actually breaks: there is no transition out of `CONFIRMED` triggered by the host walking away, because the system has no way to detect it and no lock that prevents it. That gap is dealt with below. *[Source: Airbnb engineering, Orpheus, 2017]*
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hot listing on an event date.** 200 attempts on the same three rows in 60 seconds. They serialise behind a 2ms transaction, so the queue drains in about 400ms and 199 get `AVAILABILITY_LOST`. That is correct but a poor experience, so return a remaining-nights hint and let the client short-circuit, and invalidate the search document synchronously on commit for listings flagged hot rather than waiting for the 60s CDC cycle. For genuine mega-events, a lottery with an entry window is better than first-come-first-served, because at that contention first-come rewards whoever has the lowest network latency to our region and nothing else.
- **Search freshness under booking bursts.** 12k QPS against an index that must reflect 120 calendar mutations/s. CDC keeps the availability summary within 60s, and popular `(city, date_range)` queries cache for 5 minutes in front of the cluster, which absorbs most repeat traffic on a hot weekend. The freshness target is set by the acceptable `AVAILABILITY_LOST` rate, not by an abstract SLA: at 0.1 bookings per listing per day a 60s window costs almost nothing, and shortening it uniformly to 5s would multiply re-index cost for no measurable gain.
- **Channel-sync polling load.** 2M externally-listed properties polled every 15 minutes is ~2,200 requests/s against partners who rate-limit in the tens per second per account. Make the interval adaptive: poll a listing with a booking in the next 7 days every 5 minutes, a listing with no near-term demand daily, and prefer webhook or push integrations where the partner supports one. Back off on 429 per partner account rather than globally, or one badly-behaved integration throttles all of them.
- **Payment hold expiry.** A card authorisation lapses after about 7 days and check-in can be 90 days out. A job re-authorises ~5 days before arrival. Failure means a cancelled or expired card, so notify the guest with a deadline, then release the nights and offer them back to the market. This is the only automated path that cancels a `CONFIRMED` booking, and it needs a generous grace period because the failure is usually a bank, not a guest.
- **Cancellation refund storm.** A cancelled event refunds 10,000 bookings at once. Synchronous refunds hit gateway rate limits immediately. Queue them asynchronously with retries and per-payment-method quotas, and show "refund in progress" until the gateway acknowledges rather than optimistically claiming it is done. The calendar release is independent of the refund and happens immediately, because holding inventory hostage to a payments queue is strictly worse.
- **Leaked holds.** A crashed orchestrator leaves nights `held` until the reaper catches them, up to 16 minutes. Alert on the count of `held` rows older than 20 minutes rather than on the reaper's liveness, so a silently dead job pages before a host notices their calendar is frozen.
- **Review gaming.** Dual-blind release with a 14 day deadline stops naive retaliation, because neither side sees the other's text while writing. It does not stop a host flooding a guest's profile after release, or coordinated rings. Weight by reviewer reputation and verified-stay status, run anomaly detection on per-host review patterns, and give victims an appeal path. Concede that this is detection after the fact, not prevention.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calendar lock | Deadlock between overlapping date ranges | Postgres deadlock log, booking retry counter | Always `FOR UPDATE ... ORDER BY date`; a bounded retry on serialisation failure catches the residue |
| Calendar lock | Holds leaked by a crashed orchestrator | Count of `held` rows older than 20 min | Expiry reaper on a 60s cycle using the same `hold_id` compare-and-set |
| Saga | Payment authorisation fails after the hold commits | Compensation queue depth, `PAYMENT_FAILED` rate | Compare-and-set release on `hold_id`; idempotent, so retries and the reaper cannot conflict |
| Saga | Retry starts a second saga and double-authorises | Duplicate authorisations per booking id | Idempotency table read and written on the primary only; deterministic per-step sub-keys |
| Search index | CDC stream stalled | Consumer lag above 60s | Page, fail the connector task over; the commit re-validates, so a stale hit costs one `AVAILABILITY_LOST` |
| Channel sync | Partner returns a stale or empty calendar and we unblock sold nights | Ratio of released-to-blocked nights per partner, per poll | Ingestion may only block, never release a night carrying a confirmed booking; quarantine a partner whose diff exceeds a threshold |
| Payment hold | Authorisation expires before a distant check-in | Re-auth failure rate | Re-auth ~5 days out; on failure, guest deadline then release and requeue the nights |
| Calendar shard | Home-region primary lost | Write 5xx rate, replica lag | Promote the in-region synchronous replica; ~10 min RTO; bookings for that shard fail closed rather than routing elsewhere |
| Cancellation | Refund storm exceeds gateway rate limits | Refund queue depth, 429 rate | Async refund queue with per-method quotas; release the calendar immediately and independently |
| Reviews | Retaliation after dual-blind release | Anomaly detection on per-host review patterns | Reputation weighting, verified-stay weighting, appeal flow |

**Unresolved**

**A confirmed booking is not binding on the host, and nothing in this design makes it one.** Every mechanism above guarantees at most one guest per listing-night. None of them guarantees a guest gets a room, because the host is a human outside the system who can cancel the week before, and the failure looks identical to a double booking from the guest's side. The tools are economic rather than technical: a cancellation fee, blocking those nights on the host's calendar so they cannot relist at a higher price, removing Superhost status, and a human rebooking desk. The gap is that the penalty is a fixed schedule while the incentive to cancel is the arbitrage between the booked price and a peak-event price, which on a Super Bowl weekend can be several times the fee. A penalty scaled to that spread would fix the incentive and we do not have it, because pricing it per listing per date requires a demand model we would then be asked to defend to hosts. What we do instead is detect and rank down repeat cancellers after the fact, which helps the next guest and not this one.

**Out-of-band supply changes leave a real exposure window that we have chosen not to close.** A host who also sells on another site can sell a night there and we will not know until the next poll, 5 to 60 minutes later depending on the adaptive interval. In that window we will happily confirm a booking for a night that no longer exists. Closing it means putting the partner's API in our commit path, which the third fork rejects on availability grounds and which we should keep rejecting. So the residual is permanent: some number of bookings per day are confirmed against inventory that is already gone, and to the guest it looks exactly like our bug. The partial mitigations are shortening the poll for listings with near-term demand, treating channel-conflict rate as a host-quality signal that affects ranking, and instrumenting it honestly so we know the size. We do not have a way to drive it to zero and I would not claim one.

**Nothing in the system is atomic across more than one listing.** A three week trip stitched from three listings, a group taking two units from the same host, a booking that only makes sense with a specific flight: each leg is an independent saga and the guest can finish with legs one and three. This is the same shape as cross-symbol atomicity in the exchange question, and it has the same non-answer. A cross-listing coordinator holding all the legs before authorising any of them is buildable, but it means holding inventory across multiple shards and multiple home regions for the duration of a human's checkout, which is a distributed transaction over units owned by different people in different regions. We push it to the client instead: book sequentially, and cancel the earlier legs under the free-cancellation window if a later one fails. That works because the cancellation policy usually gives a 48 hour grace period, and it stops working precisely for the last-minute and peak-event bookings where a guest most needs it.
#### Drill questions
1. How do you prevent double-booking when two guests hit Book within milliseconds?
2. A guest cancels 2 hours before check-in. What happens to the host?
3. How does search stay fresh when a calendar update happens?
4. What if the card authorisation expires before check-in, more than 7 days out?
5. How do you stop hosts and guests from gaming the dual-review system?
6. 50k searches and 200 booking attempts on one Super Bowl listing in an hour. Where is the bottleneck?
7. A user mashes the Book button five times before the spinner clears. How do you guarantee one booking?
8. How does this differ from a hotel reservation system at the data-model level?
9. Two guests book overlapping but different date ranges on the same listing at the same instant. Walk me through the deadlock and how you avoid it.
10. Why put the hold in the calendar table instead of a short-lived key in Redis?
11. A host sells the same night on a rival site. What does our system do, and what can it not do?
12. Why not run the calendar active-active across regions so European guests get a local write?
13. The guest's card is declined, but the release of the held nights fails too. What is the state, and who fixes it?
14. A host has six identical studio flats in one building. Does your data model change?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. One short transaction takes `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on every `(listing_id, date)` row in the range, in ascending date order, verifies all read `available`, flips them to `held`, and commits in about 2ms. The second transaction blocks, then sees `held` and returns `AVAILABILITY_LOST`. *If pushed:* optimistic concurrency with a version column is the usual alternative and it is worse here. At 0.1 bookings per listing per day, lock waits essentially never happen, so you would be paying retry complexity to optimise a case that does not occur, and on the rare hot listing optimistic retries turn into a thundering herd where pessimistic locking degrades into an orderly queue.

2. The listing's cancellation policy decides the payout, and strict policies still pay the host a share. The nights return to `available` immediately, independently of the refund, which goes through an async queue. A last-minute release may be suppressed from ranking rather than hidden, because a night that goes free at short notice is genuinely lower quality inventory. *If pushed:* for extenuating circumstances such as a hurricane, a batch flow refunds the guest in full and the platform absorbs the host compensation, which makes it a finance decision rather than a policy-engine one.

3. CDC ships committed calendar changes into the index with sub-minute lag, and the commit re-validates, so a stale hit costs exactly one `AVAILABILITY_LOST`. *If pushed:* the interesting part is why 60s is the right target rather than 5s. The cost of staleness is the availability-lost rate, which at 0.1 bookings per listing per day is negligible; tightening it uniformly multiplies re-index cost for no measurable gain. Do it selectively instead: synchronous document invalidation on commit for listings flagged hot.

4. A re-authorisation job runs about 5 days before check-in and refreshes the hold. On failure, usually a cancelled or expired card, the guest gets a notification with a deadline and then the booking cancels and the nights are released. *If pushed:* the simpler alternative is capturing at booking and refunding on cancellation. It removes the re-auth machinery entirely and it is strictly worse for the guest, who is out real money for 90 days on a booking that might not happen, and worse for the platform, which now holds funds it may have to return with interest in some jurisdictions.

5. Neither side sees the other's text while writing; both are released the moment the second submits or at the 14 day deadline. Edit windows are short. *If pushed:* this only stops naive retaliation. Post-release flooding of a guest's profile and coordinated rings still work, so you need reviewer-reputation weighting, verified-stay weighting, anomaly detection on per-host patterns, and an appeal path. Concede that all of that is detection after the fact.

6. Not the lock. 200 attempts serialising behind a 2ms transaction drain in about 400ms. The bottleneck is the 50k searches, and the user-visible problem is that 199 people get told no after committing to a checkout flow. Return a remaining-nights hint so clients can short-circuit, and invalidate the search document synchronously for hot listings. *If pushed:* at genuine mega-event contention, first-come-first-served rewards network proximity to our region and nothing else, so a lottery with an entry window is fairer and also removes the load spike.

7. One idempotency key per checkout session, sent on every retry. The booking service writes `(key -> booking_id, state)` before the saga starts and returns the recorded outcome on a duplicate. Every downstream call carries a deterministic sub-key of `booking_id + step`, so a retry mid-saga resumes rather than restarts. *If pushed:* the idempotency table must be read and written on the primary. A replica read here means the retry does not see the in-progress record, starts a second saga, and authorises the card twice, which is the exact bug the mechanism exists to prevent. Airbnb published this as Orpheus in 2017. *[Source: Airbnb engineering, Orpheus]*

8. A hotel sells room types, so its inventory is a count per `(hotel, room_type, date)` and a booking is a guarded decrement. Here inventory is a row per `(listing_id, date)` and a booking is a lock. Everything else follows from that. The hotel can oversell by 5 to 10 percent against a known no-show rate and walk the overflow to a comparable property at a budgeted cost; we have no substitute unit, so oversell has no price and is simply forbidden. The hotel assigns a physical room at check-in, which gives it slack we do not have. *If pushed:* three more differences worth naming. Price is per night and host-set, so the calendar row carries `price_override` where a hotel carries a rate card per class. Payment is authorised and held until after check-in rather than captured on arrival. And reviews are dual-blind two-way, because the host is also being rated, which a hotel system does not model at all.

9. Guest A books June 14 to 16, guest B books June 15 to 17. If A locks 14 then 15 while B locks 16 then 15, they wait on each other; Postgres detects the cycle and kills one, which the user sees as a random failure under exactly the load where failures are least acceptable. The fix is to make lock acquisition a total order: always `FOR UPDATE ... ORDER BY date`. Then B simply waits for A and gets a clean `AVAILABILITY_LOST` on June 15. *If pushed:* keep a bounded retry on serialisation failure anyway. Ordering fixes the deadlocks you caused; it does not cover a lock taken by an unrelated maintenance job or a host calendar edit, so the retry catches the residue.

10. Because the hold is inventory state, not a coordination hint. Putting it in a separate store means two systems have to agree about whether a night is free, and the classic failure is that the cache expires or is evicted while the booking is still in flight, at which point a second guest is told yes. Keeping the hold as a status on the row makes it one atomic decision in the store that already owns the truth, and expiry becomes a column rather than a distributed lease. *If pushed:* an external lock service is defensible when the inventory store cannot do row locks at all, for example a wide-column store with no transactions. Then you are running a distributed lock, and you inherit every fencing problem that comes with one, which is a real design and it is question 35, not this one.

11. We find out at the next poll, 5 to 60 minutes later depending on how near-term the demand is, and until then we will confirm a booking for a night that no longer exists. When the poll arrives, ingestion may block nights but may never release one carrying our confirmed booking, so the conflict resolves in favour of the guest we already sold to and the host gets an alert. What we cannot do is prevent it, because preventing it means a synchronous call to the partner in our commit path, which makes our booking availability the product of every partner's. *If pushed:* the honest mitigations are adaptive polling, preferring push integrations where the partner offers one, and treating a host's channel-conflict rate as a ranking signal. The residual is permanent and it looks like our bug to the guest.

12. Because a night cannot be split. Active-active for fungible inventory works by giving each region a disjoint slice, 40 of 100 seats to Europe, and that trick has no analogue here. What is left is async multi-master, which admits a double-booking window equal to replication lag, typically 100ms to several seconds, with no way to reconcile afterwards because the unit is unique. So the calendar is sharded with one home region per shard and European guests pay a round trip, about 90ms to a US primary. *If pushed:* the real alternative is a consensus-replicated store where any region commits at quorum latency, 60 to 100ms. That is defensible; it trades a 10ms commit for eliminating a 10 minute shard-failover RTO, and at 100 times our booking rate I would take it.

13. The nights stay `held` and the guest has no booking and no charge. That state is recoverable by construction: the release is a compare-and-set on `hold_id`, so the saga retries it, and if the orchestrator itself has died the reaper releases the nights when `hold_expires_at` passes, up to 15 minutes plus the 60s scan later. Nobody fixes it by hand. *If pushed:* the thing to watch is not the reaper's liveness but the population it should have cleared, so alert on `held` rows older than 20 minutes. A dead reaper produces no errors at all, it just quietly freezes inventory, and a host noticing their calendar is stuck is a bad way to find out.

14. Yes, and it becomes easier, which is worth saying out loud because it shows you know why the hard version is hard. Six identical studios are interchangeable, so they can be modelled as a count per `(unit_group_id, date)` with a guarded decrement, and physical assignment deferred to check-in. That is the hotel model and it supports overbooking against a no-show rate. *If pushed:* I would still not do it, because "identical" is a claim by the host and guests book from photographs of a specific unit. The moment a guest can tell the difference, the substitution you relied on is a complaint. Keep the row-per-unit model and let the host group them for pricing and search deduplication only.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, name the property that makes this question different.** Open with it: "every unit here is unique and owned by a third party, so I cannot count inventory, I cannot oversell, and I cannot reconcile afterwards." That one sentence rules out the hotel answer and tells the interviewer you know which question you are in. Then ask the three questions that actually fork the design: is any inventory interchangeable, do hosts also sell these nights elsewhere, and is it instant book or request-to-book. State your numbers out loud: 10M listings, 1M bookings/day, 12k searches/s, and the one that matters, 0.1 bookings per listing per day. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine and the one arrow that matters.** Four boxes: client, search, booking orchestrator, calendar. Two stores: the index and the calendar. Draw exactly one arrow between the discovery side and the reservation side, CDC pointing away from the calendar, and say the contract as you draw it: "search never decides, the commit decides, a stale hit costs one `AVAILABILITY_LOST`." Then the row: `(listing_id, date)` as primary key, and say why a row rather than a counter, because that is the whole answer compressed. Add payment and notifications hanging off the orchestrator, not off the calendar.

**15-35, go deep on the commit, and protect this time.** The hold transaction in detail: `FOR UPDATE` in ascending date order, all-or-nothing over the range, commit in 2ms. Say why the payment is outside it, with the number: 2s p99 authorisation against a 2ms lock, a factor of 1,000, and connection-pool exhaustion coupled to a third party if you get it wrong. Then compensation as compare-and-set on `hold_id` rather than rollback, and why that predicate is what makes it safe against the reaper and against a late retry. Then the reaper, and immediately concede its 16 minute worst case and that you alert on stale `held` rows rather than job liveness. Then idempotency, primary-only, deterministic sub-keys. If time remains take the home-region fork with the arithmetic: 10ms commit against a 10 minute failover RTO costing about 2,400 attempts, and why per-region inventory slices are unavailable when a night cannot be split.

**35-45, concede the two things a lock cannot reach.** Volunteer them before you are asked, because they are what separates this from a textbook answer. Host cancellation: nothing makes a confirmed booking binding, the penalty is fixed while the arbitrage is not, and the honest fix needs a per-listing demand model you do not have. Channel conflict: a 5 to 60 minute window where a host has sold the night elsewhere, permanently open because closing it means putting a partner's API in your commit path. Add multi-listing atomicity as a one-liner if there is room. Close with the operational surface in ninety seconds: `availability_lost_rate`, `calendar_lock_wait_p99`, stale-`held` count, CDC lag, and daily reconciliation of calendar against the payment ledger.

Cut first: reviews and the dual-blind release mechanism, then Smart Pricing, then the search ranking and personalisation detail. All three are real product surface and none of them changes the architecture, and the review discussion in particular is a trap that eats the commit path. Never cut: row rather than counter, the payment sitting outside the lock, and the two conceded gaps.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **listings** (transactional): `(listing_id, host_id, title, address, lat, lng, amenities[], cancellation_policy, instant_book)`
- **calendar** (transactional, sharded by `listing_id`, one home region per shard):
  `(listing_id, date, status: available|held|booked|blocked, hold_id?, hold_expires_at?, price_override?)`, PK `(listing_id, date)`. Rows pre-materialised 500 days ahead by a rolling job so the booking path never inserts.
- **bookings**: `(booking_id, guest_id, listing_id, checkin, checkout, price_snapshot, state)`
- **idempotency**: `(idempotency_key, booking_id, state, result)`, primary reads and writes only
- **channel_sync**: `(listing_id, partner_id, last_poll_at, last_conflict_at, poll_interval_s)`
- **search_index**: denormalised listing document with price and an availability summary
- **reviews**: `(review_id, booking_id, author_role, rating, text, submitted_at, released_at?)`

**API contract**

```
GET  /search           params: location, checkin, checkout, guests, filters
                       → [{listing_id, name, price, photos[], avail}]
GET  /listing/{id}     → details + calendar
POST /booking          body: { listing_id, dates, guests, payment_method, idempotency_key }
                       → { booking_id, status }
POST /review           body: { booking_id, rating, text }
```

**Observability**

- `availability_lost_rate`. The single most useful number: commits rejected after a search said yes. Above about 2% means index drift or a channel-sync problem, and it is the guest-frustration proxy.
- `held_rows_older_than_20min`. Detects a dead reaper, which produces no errors and silently freezes inventory. Alert on the population, never on job liveness.
- `calendar_lock_wait_p99_ms`. Target under 50ms given a 2ms transaction. Anything higher means either a hot listing or that something slow has crept inside the transaction.
- `booking_saga_success_rate`, broken down by step. Target above 99.5%. The step breakdown is what tells you whether it is cards, the calendar or a partner.
- `cdc_lag_seconds`. Target under 60s, page at 5 minutes.
- `channel_conflict_rate`, per partner and per host. Sizes the exposure window that the third fork consciously leaves open.
- `payment_reauth_failure_rate`. Target under 1%; the population at risk is long-lead bookings.
- SLO: zero double bookings, verified by a daily reconciliation of confirmed bookings against calendar rows and the payment ledger. A count, not a percentage, because the acceptable number is zero.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** stateless services and search run active-active in every region. The calendar does not: it is sharded by `listing_id` with one home region per shard, a synchronous in-region replica for durability, and async cross-region copies that are read-only and never serve the booking path.
- **RTO:** ~2 min for stateless services; ~10 min for a calendar-shard failover, which promotes the synchronous replica and redirects writes. Bookings for an unavailable shard fail closed rather than routing elsewhere, because routing elsewhere is the double booking.
- **RPO:** zero within the home region thanks to the synchronous replica. Non-zero on loss of the whole region, bounded by async replication lag, and that bound is a published number rather than a claim of zero.
- **Failover cadence:** monthly per-shard drill, quarterly full-region. The drill must include a reconciliation pass, because a failover that loses a hold is invisible until a host complains.
- **Cross-region cost:** small in bytes at ~250 GB of calendar. The real cost is the round trip a distant guest pays to reach their listing's home region, about 90ms US to EU and about 180ms to APAC, against a ~1s booking flow.

### 31. Design Netflix (Video Streaming)
#### Problem
Stream a curated catalogue of long-form video on demand to hundreds of millions of subscribers worldwide, at a quality that adapts to whatever connection each viewer has, with playback starting in under a second and effectively no rebuffering. The catalogue is finite, licensed country by country, and known weeks before anyone asks for it. Delivery runs to roughly 900 PB a day, so the cost of moving bytes dominates every other cost in the system.
#### Core
This is a placement problem wearing a streaming problem's clothes. The catalogue is small, finite and known weeks in advance, so nearly every byte can already be sitting inside the viewer's own ISP before they press Play.

Split the system in two and never let the halves touch. The control plane runs in the cloud: authentication, entitlement, the per-country catalogue view, the manifest listing available renditions and the edge URLs to fetch them from, and a DRM licence bound to the device. That is a few kilobytes per session. The data plane is video bytes, and they come from an appliance sitting physically inside the viewer's ISP on a settlement-free port. Bytes never traverse the cloud.

Content is prepared offline. Every title gets a content-aware encoding ladder, eight to twelve rungs across three codecs, with bitrates chosen from that title's own complexity rather than from a fixed table, then sliced into segments of a few seconds.

Placement is the interesting decision. A per-region popularity forecast decides what each appliance holds and a nightly job pushes the delta in the ISP's quiet window. The arithmetic is unusually kind: a country's licensed catalogue is about 300 TB of encoded output and a storage appliance holds 200 TB, so most of it is simply resident. Misses go to a peer appliance, then to an exchange, then to origin, and origin fill rate is a paged metric because every origin byte is one you pay for.

The player picks a rung per segment from buffer occupancy rather than once per session, because networks change mid-stream.

Every appliance is independent, so there is no shared hot path to scale.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a library where, instead of borrowing a book and carrying it home, you read one page at a time from a copy that was placed at the branch nearest your house before you asked for it. Netflix is that library at planetary scale. Storing the films is not the hard part. Making sure the right pages are already at your branch before Friday night is.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Put copies of the popular catalogue inside the networks your viewers are on, before anyone asks.* You install storage in each access network, forecast what its subscribers will watch, and push it there overnight. It buys a peak-hour byte that never crosses a paid link, and a launch that generates almost no origin traffic. It costs a hardware programme, field logistics in thousands of buildings, and a forecast that has to be roughly right. It wins when the catalogue is finite and known ahead of time and the volume is large enough that a box in a rack beats a per-byte bill.

*Rent delivery and let the caches fill themselves on first request.* You pay someone per byte, and the first viewer at each location pulls content through from origin, warming the cache for everyone behind them. It buys near-zero fixed cost and no forecasting, and it is the only option when the corpus is too large or unpredictable to place. It costs a bill that scales linearly forever and it moves fill traffic into the peak hour instead of the quiet one. It wins below the volume where owning hardware pays back, and outright when the corpus is user-generated.

*Serve from a handful of your own regional sites and buy transit.* One topology, no partners, full control. It costs latency to distant viewers and transit at retail prices. It wins for a regional or early-stage service, and stops winning the moment one network's traffic alone justifies a box inside it.

**The single-request walkthrough:** you press Play on a series episode. The app sends `POST /play` to the control plane in the cloud. That service authenticates you, checks your country's licensing rights for the title, and asks the **manifest service** for the available quality levels and the edge URLs to fetch them from. It also calls the **DRM licence server** (Digital Rights Management, the system that encrypts segments so they can only be decoded on an authorised device) for a short-lived key bound to your device. Your app receives an **HLS manifest** (HTTP Live Streaming, a standard that describes a video as a set of four-second segments at several quality levels, listed in a `.m3u8` text file), listing three or four ranked appliance URLs. The app picks a starting rung from historical statistics for your network, fetches the first segment, and starts playing. Every 30 seconds it sends a heartbeat with your position, which is how Continue Watching works. Meanwhile it watches its own buffer: 40 seconds of video buffered and growing means it can step up a rung, 8 seconds and falling means it steps down immediately.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Open Connect Appliances (OCA).** Netflix's own servers, installed free inside ISP data centres. A storage-class appliance carries about 200 TB of SSD holding most of that country's licensed catalogue. When a subscriber in Chicago plays a show, the bytes come from a box in Chicago inside their own ISP, never from the cloud. That is the economic story: Sandvine's 2022 report put Netflix near 15% of global downstream traffic (the 2023 edition has it closer to 10% as short-form grew), and paying commercial egress on that volume runs to hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
- **Pre-positioning.** Between 02:00 and 06:00 local time, a popularity forecast decides what each appliance should hold and a job pushes the delta. When Friday night arrives and millions start the same series, the bytes are already local. The fill is about 100 times smaller than the delivery it enables.
- **ABR (adaptive bitrate).** The title is encoded at several quality levels, each sliced into segments of a few seconds. The player chooses the next segment's rung from how full its buffer is, not from a decision made at session start, because networks change mid-stream.
- **Content-aware encoding.** Rather than one fixed bitrate table for everything, each title's complexity is analysed and its ladder chosen accordingly. Animation with flat colour fields looks perfect at 1080p where an action film with grain and motion needs three times the bitrate. Netflix's published figure for per-title encoding (2015, refined into per-shot encoding in 2018) is around 20% fewer bytes at the same perceptual quality score.
- **Control and data plane split.** Auth, manifest and licence run in the cloud and cost a few kilobytes per session. Video bytes run entirely through appliances inside ISPs. The two paths never mix, because making the cloud serve video destroys both the economics and the routing.

**The thing that makes it hard, the surprise hit:** a title nobody forecast trends on a Saturday morning. The appliances near you do not hold it, so every Play causes a fill from a peer or, worst case, from origin. At this scale that is terabits per second of unplanned traffic through paid paths, arriving during the peak hour rather than at 3 a.m. **Origin fill rate per appliance** is therefore a paged metric rather than a dashboard one. A spike means the forecast missed, and the response is an emergency push to the affected appliances before the curve steepens.

**Why this design and what it costs:** owning the delivery hardware is what makes the rest affordable. At 900 PB a day, even a deeply discounted commercial rate of $0.002 per GB is roughly $650M a year, against something like $150M a year all-in for a fleet of order 18,000 appliances. The partnership is genuinely mutual: the ISP sheds load from its expensive upstream transit, Netflix sheds egress. What it costs is a hardware supply chain, field operations in thousands of buildings, and a business-development function in every market, none of which is a software problem and all of which is on the critical path.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Origin: an object store holding the master encoded catalogue, roughly 2.4 PB of servable renditions plus tens of petabytes of cold mezzanine masters.
- Appliances: Linux boxes running a caching HTTP server, driven by a central controller that knows each appliance's inventory and pushes nightly deltas.
- Playback hot path:
  ```
  POST /play -> auth + entitlement + geo
  manifest_service.get(title_id, country, asn, device) -> ranked OCA URLs + rung list
  drm.issue_key(device_id, content_key_id, country)
  return {manifest, licence}
  // client then:
  GET {oca_url}/{title}/{codec}/{rung}/seg_00042.m4s
  // OCA: pinned hit -> serve from SSD; miss -> peer OCA, then IXP, then origin
  ```
- ABR: step up when the buffer exceeds 40 seconds and has been growing for two segments; step down immediately below 10 seconds; never move more than one rung per segment.
#### What this is really testing
Whether you notice that the catalogue is finite and known in advance, and then follow that fact all the way through. Once the set of bytes anyone might ask for is small enough to enumerate and stable enough to forecast, delivery stops being a routing problem and becomes a placement problem. Everything distinctive follows from that. You can afford to own the hardware, because you know how much of it you need. You can pre-position, because you know what will be watched. You can spend thousands of CPU hours on a bespoke encoding ladder per title, because there are only tens of thousands of titles. You can steer clients from the manifest, because you know what is resident where. A candidate who describes a cache hierarchy with anycast routing has described Q51 and has not answered this question.

The contrast is with YouTube. There the corpus is user-generated, unbounded, and arriving continuously, hundreds of hours a minute, most of it watched by almost nobody. You cannot enumerate it, so you cannot forecast it, so you cannot place it. The answer has to be a pull-through hierarchy that fills on first request and evicts on LRU, and the hard engineering moves off the placement controller and onto an ingest and transcode pipeline that must keep pace with the upload rate. The two systems also fail differently, which is the cleanest way to show you understand the difference. This design's characteristic failure is a scheduled global launch that the forecast prepared badly: a planning failure, with hours of warning and a known deadline. YouTube's is a video going viral in an hour: a reaction problem, with minutes of warning and no deadline at all. If you find yourself explaining LRU eviction here, or a popularity forecast there, you have swapped the two questions.

Closest question: Q11
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Is the catalogue finite and known in advance, or user-generated?
- Can we place our own hardware inside ISPs, or is that off the table commercially or legally?
- DRM required?
- Live in scope? (assume VOD only)
- Offline downloads?
- Multi-device profiles?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Catalogue finite and known ahead | forecast-driven pre-positioning; the resident set is planned, not evicted into |
| Catalogue user-generated | pull-through caches with LRU; no forecast to build on, and the design becomes Q11 |
| Hardware allowed inside ISPs | own appliances on settlement-free ports; egress cost stops scaling with viewers |
| Hardware not allowed | commercial CDN per byte, and cost becomes the dominant design constraint |
| VOD only | pre-transcode an ABR ladder on ingest; no low-latency live pipeline |
| DRM required | a packaging and encryption step plus licence servers (Widevine, PlayReady, FairPlay) |
| Offline downloads | downloadable encrypted renditions with an offline licence lease |
| Multi-device profiles | per-profile watch state and recommendations keyed under one account |
| Personalised recommendations | an offline model plus a feature store serving per-profile ranked rows |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** browse the catalogue, play, pause and resume across devices, search, per-profile recommendations, offline downloads.
- **NFR:** playback start under 1s at p99; rebuffer under 0.5% of playback time; global reach; the byte cost per delivered hour must not scale with subscriber growth.

**Scale**

- **Members and viewing:** ~300M paid memberships (Netflix's own reporting, end of 2024). Netflix's biannual engagement report gives roughly 94B hours viewed in a half year, so 94e9 / 182 days = **~515M hours/day**, round to **500M hours/day**. Cross-check: 500M / 300M = 1.7 hours per member per day, which matches the commonly quoted "about two hours a day".
- **Concurrency:** 500M hours/day / 24 h = **~21M streams running at any average instant**. The global curve is flattened by timezones, so assume peak is 1.5x average: 21M × 1.5 = **~32M concurrent at peak**. A single global launch or a live event stacks on top of that; the November 2024 live boxing event peaked around 65M concurrent streams, so headroom is provisioned to **~50M** steady with burst above.
- **Weighted bitrate:** assume a delivered mix of 55% at 1.5 Mbps (mobile, SD, 720p on small screens), 35% at 5 Mbps (1080p) and 10% at 15 Mbps (4K HDR): 0.55 × 1.5 + 0.35 × 5 + 0.10 × 15 = 0.83 + 1.75 + 1.50 = **~4 Mbps average**.
- **Peak egress:** 32M × 4 Mbps = 128 Tbps, call it **~130 Tbps at peak**, the same order as the "over 100 Tbps" Netflix has publicly described Open Connect serving.
- **Bytes delivered per day:** 4 Mbps = 0.5 MB/s = 1.8 GB per viewing hour. 500M hours × 1.8 GB = **~900 PB/day**, about 27 EB/month.
- **Catalogue:** ~20,000 titles globally, averaging ~4 content-hours each (films around 2 h, a series season around 8 h): 20,000 × 4 = **80,000 content-hours**. A given country licenses roughly **6,000** of those titles.
- **Encoded footprint:** a full ladder is 8 to 12 rungs across three codecs. The rungs are roughly geometric, so the ladder sums to about twice its top rung; a 4K HDR top rung at 12 Mbps is 12e6 × 3600 / 8 = 5.4 GB/hour, so one codec family is ~11 GB/hour and three families are ~33 GB/hour. Trim H.264 (no 4K rung) and add audio and subtitles at ~15%, and it lands at **~30 GB per content-hour**, so **~120 GB per title**.
- **Origin:** 80,000 content-hours × 30 GB = 2.4M GB = **~2.4 PB of servable renditions**, plus mezzanine masters at ~500 GB/hour = 80,000 × 500 GB = **~40 PB of cold archive** that never leaves origin.
- **Regionally relevant slice:** 6,000 licensed titles, and only the codecs and language tracks that country's device mix actually requests, call it 40% of the per-title bytes: 6,000 × 120 GB × 0.4 = 288,000 GB = **~300 TB per country**. Against a 200 TB storage appliance, **two thirds of a country's catalogue fits in one box**, and a four-box cluster holds all of it with replication. This single ratio is what makes everything else in the design possible.
- **Coverage from a small appliance:** VoD popularity is close to Zipf with exponent near 1 (measured repeatedly on VoD catalogues since the mid-2000s), so the demand share of the top k of N titles is ln(k)/ln(N). A 20 TB flash appliance at a small PoP holds 20/300 = 6.7% of the regional catalogue, which is the top ~400 of 6,000 titles: ln(400)/ln(6000) = 6.0/8.7 = **~69% of viewing hours** served locally. A 200 TB box takes that to essentially all of it.
- **Nightly fill:** roughly 20 content-hours of genuinely new material enter the catalogue per day. At ~12 GB per content-hour of regionally relevant renditions that is 20 × 12 = 240 GB per appliance, and forecast churn (titles moving in and out of the resident set) roughly doubles it, so **~500 GB per appliance per night**. Over a fleet of order 18,000 appliances: 18,000 × 500 GB = 9,000 TB = **~9 PB/day of fill against 900 PB/day delivered, a ratio of 100 to 1**. Spread over the four-hour window: 9e15 × 8 / 14,400 s = **~5 Tbps of fill**, which is 4% of the 130 Tbps peak and happens when the networks are empty.
- **Telemetry:** 32M concurrent × 1 heartbeat / 30 s = **~1.1M events/s** at ~200 B each = 1.1e6 × 200 = **~220 MB/s**, or ~19 TB/day raw before compaction.
#### Key decisions
**Pre-position by forecast, or pull through on first request**
- Choice: a central controller computes a target resident set per appliance from a regional popularity forecast and pushes the delta nightly in the ISP's 02:00 to 06:00 window. The resident set is pinned; only the remainder of the disk runs LRU.
- Alternative: treat every appliance as an ordinary pull-through cache. The first viewer at each location fetches from origin, the segment is cached, and everyone behind them is a hit. No forecast, no controller, no nightly job.
- Decider: catalogue size against edge storage, and the shape of the demand curve. A country's licensed catalogue is ~300 TB of relevant renditions and a storage appliance holds 200 TB, so the forecast is not choosing 2% of the catalogue out of a haystack, it is choosing which third to leave off. When a forecast only has to be right about the bottom third, it is right. The second half of the decider is the launch: a scheduled global drop puts tens of millions of plays on one title within an hour, and under pull-through the fill volume is identical (18,000 appliances × ~96 GB for an eight-hour season = ~1.7 PB either way) but it lands during the peak hour rather than at 3 a.m., which is 3.8 Tbps of origin egress at the worst possible moment, and the first viewers behind every appliance eat an origin round trip on every segment until the cache warms.
- Alternative wins when: the resident fraction is small enough that forecasting has nothing to bite on. For a user-generated corpus in the exabytes, 200 TB is well under 0.1% of the library, the popularity curve at that depth is unforecastable at the granularity of a single access network, and pull-through with LRU is simply correct. It also wins for a young service with no launch calendar and no marketing to make the forecast self-fulfilling, where the honest answer is that you do not yet know what people will watch. Pull-through is not the naive option; it is the right option under a different catalogue.

**Own appliances inside ISPs, or rent commercial delivery**
- Choice: build the hardware and place it inside access networks on settlement-free ports, giving it away to the ISP.
- Alternative: buy delivery per byte from one or more commercial CDNs and stay out of the hardware business entirely.
- Decider: annual delivered volume against fleet cost, evaluated per site rather than globally. Per appliance: ~$20k of hardware over a five-year life is $4k/year, call it $500/month fully loaded with logistics and field support. At an aggressive bulk CDN rate of $0.002/GB that pays for 250 TB/month, which is 250e12 × 8 / 2.6e6 s = ~770 Mbps of sustained delivery, roughly 200 concurrent streams. Any ISP with a few tens of thousands of streaming households clears that comfortably, so the box wins. Globally the same arithmetic gives ~$650M/year of CDN spend at that rate against ~$150M/year all-in for the fleet.
- Alternative wins when: you are below the crossover, which is most of the world's networks by count even though it is a small share by traffic, so the tail genuinely does stay on commercial CDN and IXP presence rather than in-network boxes. It also wins when placement is not available at any price: markets where hosting a content provider's hardware raises net-neutrality or regulatory objections, ISPs that see you as a competitor to their own video product, and any service too small to fund hardware, logistics and per-market business development. A service delivering 1 PB/month pays about $2k/month for CDN and would need a decade to justify one field engineer.

**Buffer-occupancy ABR, or throughput-estimate ABR**
- Choice: once the session is past startup, choose the next segment's rung from how full the buffer is. Step up when the buffer exceeds ~40 seconds and is growing, step down immediately below ~10 seconds, never move more than one rung per segment.
- Alternative: estimate recent download throughput from the last few segments and pick the highest rung whose bitrate fits under that estimate.
- Decider: buffer depth relative to segment duration. A VOD player holds 120 to 240 seconds of buffer with four-second segments, so occupancy integrates 30 to 60 segments of history and is a low-variance signal, whereas a per-segment throughput estimate on the same path can have a coefficient of variation above 50% on cellular and will oscillate the ladder. Netflix's buffer-based work (published 2014) reported large rebuffer reductions from exactly this substitution. Above roughly 20 seconds of buffer, occupancy dominates.
- Alternative wins when: the buffer is too shallow to carry information. Low-latency live runs a 2 to 4 second target buffer, which is one segment, so occupancy is either full or empty and you have no choice but to predict from throughput. The same applies to the first few segments of any session, which is why the starting rung comes from historical per-ASN statistics rather than from a buffer that does not exist yet. A hybrid is standard: throughput for startup, occupancy thereafter.

**How to read the diagram:** the vertical axis is time, not just topology. Everything on the left happens days or weeks before playback, everything in the middle happens once per session and costs kilobytes, and everything on the right happens continuously and costs petabytes. Draw it in that order.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** the encode and the placement are offline because they can be. Moving all the expensive work in front of the request leaves the runtime path doing something simple: pick a rung, fetch a segment from a box that already has it. The control plane never touches a video byte, which is why it can live in one cloud region set and still serve a system delivering 130 Tbps.

**What this layout buys you:** predictable playback, and a delivery cost that stops scaling with subscribers once the boxes are placed. The costs are real and worth naming: a large storage overhead for renditions nobody watches, a media pipeline that must finish encoding well before launch rather than just before it, and a control plane that becomes the single thing standing between a viewer and a stream, even though every appliance is healthy.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Pre-positioning: the forecast, the delta push, and what happens on a miss.**

Most of this design is conventional. This is the part that is not, and it is where the interview will actually go.

**What the controller decides.** For each appliance the controller produces a ranked target list of segment groups, where a segment group is one (title, codec, rung, audio track) tuple. It is not a list of titles. Two appliances in the same country hold materially different bytes because their device mixes differ: an ISP whose subscribers are mostly on smart TVs needs the high rungs in HEVC and AV1, one whose subscribers are mostly on Android phones needs the low rungs in H.264 and VP9, and holding the wrong half of a ladder is the same as holding nothing. Language is the second splitter, since audio and subtitle tracks are a meaningful fraction of a title's bytes once you carry thirty of them.

**Inputs to the forecast.** Per-region historical play counts by title, the release calendar, the device and language mix observed behind that specific appliance, and, weighted most heavily, the merchandising plan. The strongest single predictor of what a country watches tomorrow is what its home screen will show, and that is decided in-house. This makes the forecast look better than it is, which is the second Unresolved item below.

**The push.** Each appliance reports an inventory manifest. The controller diffs it against the target list and the appliance pulls the difference during its local 02:00 to 06:00 window. The volumes are small relative to delivery: ~500 GB per appliance per night against ~9 PB of fleet fill and ~900 PB of daily delivery, so every byte pushed to an edge is served roughly a hundred times. That ratio is the justification for the whole programme, and it is worth saying out loud, because the instinctive objection to pre-positioning is that it wastes bandwidth on content nobody watches. At 100 to 1 amortisation there is a great deal of room to be wrong.

**Pinning, not LRU.** The resident set is not a cache in the ordinary sense. Segments placed by the controller carry a pin and only the unpinned remainder of the disk runs LRU. This matters most exactly when it is most tempting to skip: during a global launch, a plain LRU would evict the pre-positioned set to make room for whatever is being requested right now, which is the pre-positioned set arriving late through the expensive path. The pin is what stops the cache policy from quietly undoing the placement policy.

**Fill hierarchy on a miss.** Peer appliance on the same network, then an appliance at an internet exchange where the ISP peers, then a Netflix backbone site, then origin. Q51 covers why delivery hierarchies are shaped like this in general. What is specific here is that the first two tiers sit inside networks we do not own, so promoting a tier is a commercial negotiation rather than a capacity decision, and the hierarchy is deepest exactly where the business relationship is strongest, not where the traffic is heaviest.

**Steering happens in the manifest, not in DNS.** When a client requests a manifest, the control plane resolves its address to an ASN, looks up the appliances serving that ASN, filters to those that are healthy, have headroom, and actually hold the requested title, and returns three or four ranked URLs. A generic CDN steers with anycast or DNS, neither of which can see inventory, so it will cheerfully route a client to a node that does not hold the object and let the miss sort itself out. Issuing the manifest ourselves makes steering inventory-aware, and inventory-aware steering is the reason a miss is rare rather than merely cheap. The cost is specific and worth conceding before it is found: manifest issuance is now a stateful, uncacheable, per-play control-plane call that must know the health and contents of the entire fleet. If that service is down, nobody can start a stream, even though every appliance is healthy and every already-running stream continues undisturbed.

**Immutability, and where rights actually live.** Segments are addressed by (title, codec, rung, segment index) and never change, so there is no cache invalidation problem for bytes. Rights changes are not byte changes. When a title leaves a country the manifest stops listing it and the licence server stops issuing keys, and the bytes can sit on the appliance until the next target list drops them. Segments are stored encrypted under CENC and the appliance never holds the content keys, so an ISP hosting the box has ciphertext and nothing else. That property is what makes it commercially acceptable to put a copy of the catalogue in a partner's rack, and it is also why a leaked manifest is harmless.

**What a scheduled launch actually requires.** A global drop at Friday 00:00 UTC means every appliance must be complete before its own last useful fill window, which for the earliest timezone is Thursday morning. Working backwards, the encode has to be final and locked by Wednesday. That couples the encoding fleet's delivery date directly to the delivery economics: a title whose encode finishes on Thursday evening cannot be pre-positioned and will be pulled through at peak, at full price, in front of the largest audience it will ever have. The scheduling constraint on the encoder farm is therefore not "before launch", it is "before the last fill window in the earliest timezone", which is roughly 36 hours earlier than people assume and is a deadline that regularly gets missed by teams who have only ever seen the launch date.
