Every byte the client sees as video comes from an appliance inside its own ISP. The control plane handles auth, manifest issuance and the DRM key, all of which are small and infrequent enough that cloud egress on them is irrelevant. Telemetry is the only return path and it is tiny, about 200 B every 30 seconds per stream. The pre-positioning job at the bottom is the only thing on the diagram that moves large volumes without a user waiting on it, which is precisely why it can be scheduled into the quiet hours.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **A launch the forecast prepared badly.** If pre-positioning completed, tens of millions of simultaneous plays produce no hot spot at all, because every appliance serves its own ISP independently. The failure is the appliances that missed the push, which fall back to peer or origin fill during the peak hour. *Mitigation:* origin fill rate per appliance is a paged metric with a 5% threshold; the response is an emergency targeted push, and commercial CDN capacity stands by as an expensive backstop for appliances that cannot be filled in time.
- **The manifest and steering service.** Every play is an uncacheable call into a service that must know fleet inventory and health. It is the one component whose loss stops new sessions worldwide. *Mitigation:* active-active across regions, inventory state served from a read-optimised replica that tolerates staleness of a few minutes, and a degraded mode that returns a static per-ASN appliance list without the inventory filter. Degraded mode raises the miss rate and therefore the bill, which is the correct thing to trade for availability.
- **Licence server at launch.** Every play needs a key, so licence issuance has the same instantaneous spike as playback. *Mitigation:* keys are cacheable per device for the session so a resumed or seeked stream does not re-issue; servers are stateless and horizontally scaled with headroom sized to the launch calendar rather than to steady state.
- **Encoder fleet backlog.** An analysis pass plus an encode pass across ~10 rungs and three codecs runs to thousands of CPU hours per title, and the fleet is shared across the whole release slate. *Mitigation:* priority queue ordered by the last fill window rather than by launch date, and a documented fallback of shipping a reduced ladder (drop AV1 and the top 4K rung) for a title at risk. A title that ships with two codecs is a quality regression; a title that ships unpositioned is a cost incident.
- **ISP last-mile congestion.** The appliance removes the upstream transit link from the path but not the access network itself. *Mitigation:* nothing on our side beyond aggressive downward ABR, which turns a stall into a quality drop. This is genuinely the ISP's problem and the third Unresolved item explains why that is unsatisfying.
- **Telemetry backpressure.** ~1.1M heartbeats/s at peak feeds the quality-of-experience loop that tunes ABR. *Mitigation:* heartbeats are fire-and-forget with a small client-side buffer and best-effort delivery. The player must never block on telemetry, and the resume position that matters to users is written on pause and on exit, not on the heartbeat path.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Appliance | An OCA inside a major ISP dies | Per-appliance health probe plus client-reported error rate | Manifest already lists 3 to 4 ranked edges; player fails to the next one mid-session |
| Fill | An appliance falls back to origin during peak | `origin_fill_rate` per appliance, paged above 5% | Targeted emergency push; peer and IXP fill ahead of origin in the priority order |
| Forecast | The model misses a surprise hit | Live-fill rate spike across many appliances in one region | Live-fill until the next window, with a reserved egress budget sized for this case |
| Manifest / steering | Inventory state stale or service degraded | Manifest latency and miss rate diverging | Degraded mode: static per-ASN edge list, accept a higher miss rate |
| Licence server | Key issuance errors during a launch | Licence error rate and p99 issue latency | Per-device session caching, stateless horizontal scale, multi-region |
| Control plane | Regional cloud outage | Health probes across services | Active-active; already-running streams are unaffected because they touch no cloud service |
| ABR | Rung oscillation after a network handoff | Client rebuffer rate and switch frequency per network type | Per-network heuristics, one rung per segment, conservative startup rung from per-ASN history |
| Rights | A title's licence expires mid-session | Manifest 403 rate for that title in that country | Licence server gates key issuance on country; expiry is enforced at the next key request |
| Encoding | Fleet behind on the launch slate | Encode backlog measured against last-fill-window, not launch date | Priority by fill deadline; reduced ladder for at-risk titles |

**Unresolved**

**Live is a different system and this design does not become it.** Everything here depends on the bytes existing before the request. A live event has zero warmth by definition, so pre-positioning is not merely unavailable, it is meaningless. The buffer-based ABR from the third fork carries no signal at a 2 to 4 second target buffer, and the fill hierarchy inverts: instead of each appliance serving independently from local storage, every appliance is pulling the same segment in the same second from one packager, which is the fan-out problem this architecture was specifically built to avoid. What we do is run a parallel path for live, with tiered fan-out from the packager through the same fleet's hardware, throughput-based rung selection, a deliberately conservative ladder, and a rebuffer rate an order of magnitude worse than VOD. It shares racks with this design and almost nothing else, and presenting live as "the same thing with shorter segments" is the fastest way to lose credibility on this question.

**The forecast is self-referential and we cannot measure the counterfactual.** The strongest input to the popularity model is what we intend to merchandise, and merchandising is influenced in turn by what is cheap to serve. That loop makes the model's accuracy metrics look excellent while quietly penalising anything that was never promoted: a title with no edge residency starts slower and opens at a lower rung on first play, which depresses its engagement, which depresses its next forecast. There is no clean experiment available, because randomising edge residency means deliberately degrading real viewers to measure the effect. The partial fix is a residency floor: hold the first episode of everything in the country's catalogue at two mid rungs regardless of forecast, which is 6,000 titles × ~3.6 GB = ~22 TB, about 10% of a 200 TB appliance. That bounds the worst case, it does not remove the feedback loop, and I would not claim otherwise.

**We cannot independently see the last mile, and the box is in someone else's building.** The appliance sits in a partner's rack, on their power, behind their internal routing policy. Every measurement we have of that path comes either from the box itself or from clients on the far side of it, and both are inside the trust boundary we would want to check. An ISP that de-prioritises the appliance's egress ports during congestion looks identical, in our telemetry, to an ISP whose subscribers simply have slow lines, and the subscriber blames us either way. There is no independent measurement point between the appliance and the home. What we actually do is publish a per-ISP speed index so the comparison is public and the pressure becomes commercial rather than technical. That is a policy answer to an engineering gap and it should be presented as one.
#### Drill questions
1. An Open Connect appliance inside a major ISP fails mid-session. What does the client experience?
2. How do you decide which content to pre-position per region, and what are the inputs?
3. A new season launches and 50M people press Play in the first hour. Where does it hurt?
4. Why choose the rung per segment rather than once at session start?
5. Your appliance holds 200 TB and the country's catalogue is 300 TB. What do you leave off, and how do you decide?
6. Why does the manifest service pick the appliance, instead of using DNS or anycast the way a commercial CDN does?
7. How is region-locked content enforced when rights expire at midnight and 40,000 people are mid-episode?
8. What stops the ISP hosting an appliance from reading or copying the catalogue?
9. How would you handle live sport, given this is architected for VOD?
10. Why is the ABR decision driven by buffer occupancy rather than measured throughput, and where does that break?
11. The encoder fleet is behind and a Friday global launch is at risk. What do you ship?
12. Justify per-title encoding to someone who says a fixed ladder is simpler and good enough.
#### Answers to drill questions
1. The manifest already listed three or four ranked appliance URLs, so the player fails over to the next one, possibly in a peer network or at an internet exchange. The visible effect is a brief quality drop while ABR re-converges on the new path, not a stall, because the buffer covers the switch. *If pushed:* if every nearby appliance is gone, the fallback is commercial CDN, where the service stays up and the cost per byte jumps by an order of magnitude. Control-plane health checks stop listing the dead appliance within seconds, so new sessions never see it.

2. A per-region forecast combining historical play counts by title, the release calendar, the device and language mix observed behind that specific appliance, and the merchandising plan. The output is a ranked list of (title, codec, rung, audio track) groups, not a list of titles, because holding the wrong half of a ladder is the same as holding nothing. The delta is pushed during the appliance's local 02:00 to 06:00 window. *If pushed:* the merchandising input is the strongest one and it is self-fulfilling, which flatters the model's accuracy. See the second Unresolved item.

3. If pre-positioning completed, nowhere: every appliance serves its own ISP from local SSD and there is no shared component in the path. The real exposure is the appliances that missed the push, which fill from peer or origin during the peak hour, and the licence server, which sees the same instantaneous spike as playback because every play needs a key. *If pushed:* origin fill rate per appliance is paged at 5%; licence servers are stateless with per-device session caching so a seek or resume does not re-issue. The cost of a missed push is measured in transit dollars, not in downtime.

4. Because the network changes underneath the session: wifi contention, a cellular handoff, someone else in the house starting a download. A rung chosen at second zero is either too low for the next two hours or too high for the next ten seconds. *If pushed:* per-segment decisions also let you be asymmetric, stepping up cautiously and down immediately, which matters because a stall costs far more perceived quality than a rung does.

5. You leave off the bottom third of the popularity curve for that country, and you leave off renditions the local device mix does not request: 4K rungs where few subscribers have 4K panels, AV1 where the installed devices cannot decode it, audio tracks in languages nobody there selects. The forecast is not picking 2% of a haystack, it is choosing which third to omit, which is a much easier problem and is why it works. *If pushed:* the missing third is not unavailable, it is one hop away at a peer appliance or the IXP. Being absent from a box costs a few milliseconds of first-segment latency, not a failure.

6. Because anycast and DNS cannot see inventory. They route on network proximity and will happily send a client to a node that does not hold the title, turning what should be a hit into a miss plus a fill. Since we issue the manifest ourselves, we can filter to appliances that are healthy, have headroom, and actually hold that title's renditions for that device. *If pushed:* the price is that manifest issuance becomes a stateful, uncacheable, per-play call that must track fleet inventory, and it is the single component whose failure stops new sessions globally. The degraded mode is a static per-ASN edge list with no inventory filter, which trades a higher miss rate for staying up.

7. The catalogue service serves a per-country view and the manifest is scoped to the viewer's server-verified geography, never to a client-supplied value. At expiry the manifest endpoint stops listing the title. In-flight sessions continue until their current licence expires, because keys are short-lived and the licence server refuses to reissue for a title no longer licensed in that country. *If pushed:* the bytes stay on the appliance and that is fine, because they are stored as ciphertext and the appliance has never held a key. Rights live entirely in the control plane, so a rights change is a metadata change, not a delete across 18,000 boxes.

8. The segments are encrypted at rest under CENC and the appliance never receives the content keys; only the licence server issues those, and only to an authorised device. The ISP is hosting an opaque blob store. *If pushed:* this is not incidental, it is the property that makes the commercial deal signable. Without it, asking thousands of partners to host an unencrypted copy of the catalogue would be a non-starter with every rights holder.

9. A different pipeline running on the same hardware. Low-latency segmenting at a 2 to 4 second target buffer, tiered fan-out from the packager to the fleet in real time, throughput-based rung selection because the buffer is too shallow to carry a signal, and a deliberately narrow ladder. *If pushed:* the fan-out is the hard part and it is exactly the problem pre-positioning exists to avoid, since every appliance now wants the same segment in the same second. Expect a rebuffer rate an order of magnitude worse than VOD and design the product around that rather than pretending otherwise.

10. With four-second segments and a 120 to 240 second buffer, occupancy integrates 30 to 60 segments of throughput history, so it is a low-variance signal. A per-segment throughput estimate on a cellular path can vary by more than 50% segment to segment and will oscillate the ladder, which viewers notice more than a stable lower rung. Netflix's buffer-based work, published in 2014, reported large rebuffer reductions from exactly this substitution. *If pushed:* it breaks when the buffer is shallow enough to carry no information, which is the first few segments of any session and the whole of low-latency live. Both cases fall back to throughput, and the startup rung comes from historical statistics for that ASN and device rather than from a measurement that does not exist yet.

11. Ship a reduced ladder, and prioritise by fill deadline rather than by launch date. Drop AV1 and the top 4K rung, keep H.264 and HEVC across the middle rungs, and get that into the fill window. A title that launches with two codecs is a quality regression that most viewers will not notice; a title that launches unpositioned is a cost incident that pulls terabits through paid paths during peak. *If pushed:* the real fix is upstream. The encoder farm's deadline is the last fill window in the earliest timezone, roughly 36 hours before the launch timestamp, and teams that schedule against the launch date itself will keep hitting this.

12. Because the ladder is chosen once and the bytes are delivered forever. Analysis plus encode across ~10 rungs and three codecs is thousands of CPU hours per title, paid once against a catalogue of only ~20,000 titles. The published saving is around 20% of bytes at the same perceptual quality (per-title encoding, 2015; per-shot, 2018), and 20% of 900 PB a day is 180 PB a day that never moves. *If pushed:* the argument does invert. For a catalogue of millions of items where most are watched a handful of times, the encode cost per delivered byte is enormous and a fixed ladder is correct, which is one more place where the user-generated version of this problem gives a different answer.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, establish that this is a placement problem.** Say it in the first sentence: "the catalogue is finite and known weeks in advance, which means almost every byte can be inside the viewer's ISP before they press Play, and that single fact drives the whole design." Then ask the two questions that actually change the answer: is the catalogue curated or user-generated, and can we place hardware inside access networks. State the numbers you will use out loud, because they will do the arguing later: ~500M viewing hours a day, ~32M concurrent at peak, ~4 Mbps average, ~900 PB a day delivered, ~20,000 titles and ~6,000 licensed per country. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine and the one ratio.** Four boxes left to right: encode and package, origin, appliance inside the ISP, client. Then a fifth above the client for the control plane, with two thin arrows to it and one fat arrow from the appliance. Say the split as you draw it: control plane in the cloud, kilobytes per session; data plane inside the ISP, petabytes a day; the two never touch. Then put up the ratio that justifies the design: a country's licensed catalogue is ~300 TB of relevant renditions, an appliance holds 200 TB, so two thirds of it is simply resident and the forecast is choosing which third to leave off. That one number is worth more than any three components you could add to the diagram.

**15-35, the drill.** This is the interview, so protect it. Go deep on pre-positioning: what the controller decides (segment groups, not titles, split by device and language mix), the nightly delta push, and the ratio of 9 PB of fill to 900 PB delivered, which is 100 to 1 amortisation. Then pinning versus LRU, and why a plain LRU undoes the placement during exactly the launch it was built for. Then the fill hierarchy, and cross-reference the generic CDN question rather than re-deriving it. Then steering from the manifest instead of anycast, and volunteer the cost immediately: uncacheable per-play call, single point for session start, degraded mode is a static edge list. Then take the pull-through fork on your own terms: same fill volume, different hour, and it is the right answer for a user-generated corpus. Keep the ABR control law and the encoding ladder in reserve as one-liners you can expand on request.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the gaps before they are found: live is a different system sharing the racks and not a variant of this one; the forecast is self-referential and the residency floor bounds rather than fixes it; we have no independent visibility into the last mile and the speed index is a policy answer to an engineering gap. Then two minutes of operations: the metrics you would page on (origin fill rate per appliance, pre-position completion before the earliest fill window, playback start p99, rebuffer ratio, licence issue latency), and the observation that already-running streams survive a full control-plane outage, which is a deliberate property rather than luck.

Cut first: the recommendation system, then offline downloads, then the codec and DRM ecosystem detail. All three are real, none of them changes the shape of the answer, and recommendations in particular is a separate question that will eat twenty minutes if you let it. Never cut: the finite-catalogue insight, the placement arithmetic, and the concession that the manifest service is a single point for session start.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **titles** (wide-column store): `(title_id, title, year, genres, cast, ratings, ...)`
- **rights** (per country): `(title_id, country, window_start, window_end)`
- **renditions** (object store plus index): `(title_id, codec, rung, lang, segment_idx) -> object key, content_key_id`
- **appliance_inventory**: `(appliance_id, segment_group_id, pinned, bytes, filled_at)`
- **playback_history** (wide-column store): `(profile_id, title_id, position_sec, completed, ts)`
- **recommendations** (precomputed per profile, in-memory cache): `profile_id -> [title_id, score]`

**API contract**

```
GET  /catalog?row=trending|continue|recommended  -> titles for this country
GET  /title/{id}      -> metadata + availability window
POST /play            -> { manifest (ranked OCA URLs + rung list), licence }
POST /heartbeat       body: { title_id, position_sec, profile_id }
GET  {oca}/{title}/{codec}/{rung}/seg_{n}.m4s    -> segment bytes (CENC encrypted)
```

**Observability**

- `origin_fill_rate_per_oca`, target under 5% at peak, pages above 10%. The single most important metric in the system, because it is where the cost model fails first.
- `pre_position_completion_by_window`, target 99% of the target set resident before the appliance's own last fill window. Measured against the fill deadline, not against launch.
- `play_start_p99_ms`, target under 1,000 ms from Play to first frame.
- `rebuffer_ratio`, target under 0.5% of playback time, broken out by network type so the ABR heuristics can be tuned per environment.
- `manifest_issue_p99_ms` and manifest error rate, since this is the one call that gates every new session.
- `licence_issue_p99_ms`, target under 200 ms, with a separate launch-day threshold.
- SLO: 99.95% playback start success globally, and a per-title perceptual quality floor maintained across the ladder.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** control plane active-active across cloud regions. The data plane is global by construction, since every appliance is independently servable and shares no state with any other.
- **RTO:** ~30 s for control-plane regional failover; zero for streams already in progress, which touch no cloud service until their licence expires.
- **RPO:** minutes for catalogue metadata and watch position; zero for delivered bytes, since the appliance cache is not authoritative state.
- **Failover cadence:** continuous fault injection in production rather than scheduled exercises, on the reasoning that a failover path exercised once a quarter is a failover path that does not work.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by origin to appliance fill, which is ~9 PB/day but runs off-peak and is amortised roughly 100 to 1 against delivery. Control-plane cross-region traffic is negligible.

### 32. Design Slack (Workplace Messaging)
#### Problem
Run messaging for hundreds of thousands of organisations at once: channels, threads, DMs, files and full-text search, with each organisation's data held as a separate, auditable unit. History is durable and searchable by default rather than encrypted away, because the product is organisational memory. Customer size spans four orders of magnitude, from a five-person startup to a 150,000-seat enterprise, on the same code.
#### Core
The organising decision is that the workspace, not the user and not the channel, is the unit of placement. Each workspace is homed on a named shard: a gateway pool, a database keyspace, a search index home, an object-store prefix and an encryption key. A small global directory maps workspace to shard, and the edge resolves it before any other work happens. Nothing else in the system is globally scoped, and keeping that true is the discipline the design rests on.

That buys what enterprise buyers actually pay for. Deleting a customer, applying their retention policy, keeping their data in one region, revoking their key, exporting for litigation and restoring from backup are each one operation against one bundle, rather than a scan across every tenant's rows with no way to prove completeness.

Delivery is the standard chat shape and deserves five minutes. A persistent socket per client, one publish per message to a per-channel topic, each gateway holding a subscriber consumes once and pushes locally, so fan-out costs the number of gateways involved and not the number of channel members. Persist before acknowledging; the socket is an accelerator, not the record.

Search is what people underestimate. Full text over five years of an organisation's history is a first-class feature, the index costs about as much as the message store and is far more expensive to host, and results must respect channel membership as it stands now rather than as it stood at index time.

Scale comes from packing tens of thousands of small tenants onto shared shards and giving the largest their own. The skew is the design problem: one placement strategy cannot serve both ends.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** an office building where each floor is a different company. Every floor has its own rooms, its own filing cabinets, its own locks, and its own shredder running to its own schedule. The building shares plumbing and lifts, which is the only reason any of it is affordable, but a tenant on the third floor must never be able to open a cabinet on the seventh, and when a tenant leaves you have to hand them a certificate saying their floor was emptied. Occasionally two tenants want a shared meeting room, and whose floor it sits on turns out to be the hard question.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Everything in one pool, with the tenant as a column.* Every table carries an organisation id, every query filters on it, capacity is managed generically. Utilisation is the highest of any option, there is one deployment to operate, and adding a customer costs a row. What you give up is that tenant-scoped operations stop being cheap: deleting one customer, applying their retention policy or proving where their data lives becomes a scan across everybody's data, and a heavy customer's traffic lands on infrastructure shared with everyone else. This is the right answer while customers are within an order of magnitude of each other and nobody has signed a residency clause.

*Home each tenant on a named bundle of infrastructure.* A routing layer resolves the tenant first, and from then on a request can only reach that tenant's storage. Isolation becomes physical rather than a filter someone can forget, and every per-customer obligation collapses into an operation on one bundle. It costs a placement problem: tenants grow, so live migration between bundles has to be routine maintenance, and utilisation drops because a bundle has a floor cost.

*A dedicated stack per customer.* Separate deployment, separate everything. This is what regulated buyers ask for and occasionally what they will pay for. It costs the ability to ship once, and per-customer operating cost stops amortising, so it works only for a handful of accounts at enterprise prices.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a user in a 4,000-seat workspace types in #general and hits send. The client already holds a persistent socket, opened against a gateway chosen by resolving the workspace to its shard, so the message never has to decide where it is going. The gateway writes it to the shard's message store, partitioned by channel and sorted by message id, and acknowledges only once that write commits, which is what turns the sender's tick from a hope into a fact. It then publishes once to the channel's topic on the shard's bus. Every other gateway in that shard holding a subscriber to #general consumes once and pushes down the sockets it owns locally, so the cost is one push per gateway rather than one per member. Two consumers hang off the persist stream rather than off the bus: the indexer, which adds the message to the workspace's search index within a few seconds, and the notification dispatcher, which pushes to anyone mentioned who has no live socket. Send to visible on another screen in the same region: under 200ms.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Tenant directory.** One small, strongly consistent table mapping workspace to shard, region, plan and key alias. 750k rows, about 150MB, cached in full on every edge node. It is the only globally scoped store in the system, and keeping that list at one entry is what makes every other guarantee checkable.
- **Shard.** A named bundle of a gateway pool, a database keyspace, a search index home, an object-store prefix and an encryption key alias. They are bundled because every enterprise obligation (delete, retain, hold, re-key, prove residency) is an operation across all five at once.
- **Gateway pool.** Long-lived servers holding sockets for the tenants homed on that shard, sticky by workspace so a reconnect lands where the channel list and presence are already warm.
- **Per-channel topics.** The bus between gateways. One publish per message, one consume per gateway that has a subscriber. Fan-out cost is the number of gateways involved, not the number of channel members, which is what makes a 100,000-member channel affordable at all.
- **Message store.** Partitioned by channel and sorted by message id, with a second table partitioned by (channel, thread parent) so loading a thread is one range read rather than a scan of the channel. This is the record. The bus is not.
- **Search.** Shared physical indices with the workspace as a routing key for the long tail, dedicated indices above roughly 50M documents, dedicated clusters for the top tier. Hits are filtered at query time against current channel membership, because indexed ACLs go stale the moment somebody leaves a channel.
- **Bridge for shared channels.** A row on the visiting workspace's shard carrying membership and local naming for a channel homed elsewhere. It never carries messages.

**The thing that makes it hard:** the customers are not the same size. The median workspace has ten daily actives and the largest has a hundred and fifty thousand, and both run the same code. Anything that assumes uniformity breaks at one end: hash tenants across a pool and one tenant swamps its bucket; give every tenant its own infrastructure and the long tail costs more to run than it pays. Search sharpens it, because the natural unit of a search engine is an index and an index has a floor cost measured in shards. One index per workspace is 750,000 shards, roughly a thousand machines holding a median of 110MB each. So the answer is bimodal on purpose: pack tens of thousands of small tenants onto shared infrastructure behind a routing key, give the top two percent their own, and accept that you now own a placement problem and a live-migration path.

**Why this design and what it costs:** homing a tenant turns compliance from a query problem into a routing problem, and that is the entire trade. The cost is real and paid continuously. Utilisation drops because bundles have a floor, placement is a forecast that goes stale as tenants grow, and you have to build and keep exercising the machinery to move a live workspace between shards. A pooled design carries none of that overhead and offers none of the guarantees. The moment a contract says "our data stays in the EU and you will destroy it within 30 days of termination", the pooled design owes an answer it cannot give cheaply, and the routing layer stops being overhead and starts being the product.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Directory in a small strongly consistent store, full copy cached at every edge node behind a version counter. Resolve the workspace before authentication does any real work, and reject anything that does not resolve. No default tenant, no fallback shard.
- Per shard: a wide-column keyspace for messages with the two-table thread pattern, a topic per channel on the shard's bus, an object-store prefix, and a key alias in the customer's own key store for the tiers that pay for it.
- Search indexed off the persist stream, not the bus. Shared indices routed on workspace id below ~50M documents, dedicated above. Hydrate hits from the message store so a stale index cannot serve deleted content.
- On receiving a message:
  ```
  handle(conn, msg):
    shard = conn.shard             # resolved at connect, never per message
    id    = ulid()
    shard.store.write(messages, thread_replies, msg, id)   # durable first
    conn.ack(id)
    shard.bus.publish(topic=msg.channel_id, msg, id)       # then deliver
    # indexer and notifier consume the store's change stream, not the bus
  ```
#### What this is really testing
Whether you put the tenancy boundary before the query or inside it. Everything an enterprise buyer pays for is expressed per organisation rather than per user: delete our data within 30 days and attest to it, keep it in the EU, hold these channels for litigation, revoke our key and make us unreadable, export five years for a regulator, prove no other customer can read us. Each of those is one operation when a tenant is a physical bundle you can point at, and each is an unprovable scan across a shared corpus when a tenant is a column. A candidate who describes a chat system and adds `workspace_id` to the tables has answered a different question, because every follow-up is about the operations that column cannot make cheap.

The contrast is with the consumer chat system. There the population is uniform: every user is roughly the same size, so hashing users or conversations across a pool works forever, and there is no administrative entity above the user that can demand a set of conversations be exported, retained or destroyed together. Content is end-to-end encrypted, which means the server holds ciphertext, search is a client-side problem over what the device already has, and history beyond the device is frequently out of scope. Here the opposite holds in every respect. History is durable and searchable by default because organisational memory is the product, so the server must hold plaintext, which means the server also inherits the ACL problem, the index bill and the entire compliance surface. And the size distribution spans four orders of magnitude, so one placement strategy is wrong at one end or the other. Consumer chat is a delivery problem with a storage tail. This is a tenancy and retrieval problem with a delivery front end, and the delivery part is the five minutes you spend before the interview actually starts.

Closest question: Q9
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- How hard is the tenant boundary contractually: shared infrastructure with logical separation, or physical separation the customer can audit?
- Per-customer data residency, or one region for everyone?
- Who sets retention, and does legal hold override it?
- Search across all history, or a recent window?
- Cross-organisation shared channels in scope?
- Third-party apps and bots?
- What is the largest customer we must support, and what is the median?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Auditable physical separation | one tenant per shard for that tier, and the pooled tier stops being offerable to them |
| Per-customer residency | region becomes part of the placement key, and a shared channel can straddle two regimes |
| Customer-set retention with legal hold | deletion is a per-channel policy job with an override list, not a table-level TTL |
| Search over all history | the index is a first-class store sized like the message store, not a bolt-on |
| Recent window only | search collapses to a per-channel scan and the index tier largely disappears |
| Cross-organisation channels | one authoritative home per channel plus a bridge, and the tenancy invariant gains a documented exception |
| Third-party apps | per-app, per-tenant rate limits at the edge, because a runaway integration spends a shard budget shared with thousands of others |
| A 150,000-seat customer | a dedicated-shard tier, and live tenant migration as routine maintenance |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** public and private channels, DMs, threads, mentions, file upload, full-text search over history, presence, third-party apps, cross-organisation shared channels.
- **NFR:** delivery under 200ms in region; tenant isolation provable to an auditor; search over five years in under a second; per-customer retention, residency and key control; no message lost across a deploy.

**Scale**

- **Tenants and users:** ~35M DAU across ~750k workspaces, so the mean is 35M / 750k ≈ 47 DAU per workspace. The mean is useless here because the distribution is the design problem: **median ~10 DAU**, 98th percentile ~1,400 DAU, **largest single customer ~150k DAU**. That is a 15,000x spread between median and maximum. Sanity check: if the top 2% (15,000 workspaces) average 1,500 DAU they hold 22.5M, leaving 12.5M across the other 735,000, which is ~17 each against a median of 10. Consistent with a long tail.
- **Messages sent:** in a workplace tool people read far more than they write. Assume 20 sent and ~200 read per active user per day. 35M × 20 = **700M messages/day**. Flat that would be 700M / 86,400 ≈ 8.1k/s, but traffic collapses into each region's working day, so take the effective window as ~10h of global overlap = 36,000s: 700M / 36,000 ≈ **19k msgs/s busy hour**. A 3x spike at the top of the hour in a large region gives **~60k/s peak**.
- **Message size:** ~500B = text ~200B + ids and timestamps (workspace, channel, message ulid, user) ~80B + reactions and edit metadata ~50B + attachment references ~50B + rich-layout blocks and framing ~120B. Fully laid-out messages reach ~2KB but are under 5% of volume.
- **Message store:** 700M × 500B = **350GB/day raw**; replication factor 3 gives ~1TB/day. A year is 350GB × 365 ≈ **128TB raw**, ~385TB replicated. Five years of paid-tier history is ~640TB raw. The message store is not the cost centre.
- **Search index:** indexed footprint is roughly 0.6 × the row once you count an inverted index with positions plus stored fields for highlighting, so ~300B/message. Five years of everything is 700M × 365 × 5 = 1.28T documents × 300B ≈ **380TB**, comparable to the message store in bytes and far worse per byte, because it lives on nodes with heap rather than on cheap disk. Search, not messaging, sets the cost floor.
- **Search shard count:** a node holds on the order of 500 to 1,000 shards before cluster state and heap overhead dominate. One index per workspace is 750,000 shards, hence ~1,000 nodes holding a median of 10 × 20 × 365 × 5 × 300B ≈ **110MB each**. Sizing a shard at 50M documents (~15GB) puts the crossover at 50M / (20 × 365 × 5) ≈ **1,370 DAU**, which is the 98th percentile. So ~15,000 workspaces justify a dedicated index and 735,000 share.
- **The largest customer, checked against the same model:** 150k DAU × 20 = 3M msgs/day = 1.5GB/day raw, and 150k × 36,500 = 5.5B documents × 300B ≈ **1.65TB of index** over five years. That is a dedicated cluster of a handful of nodes, not a distributed-systems problem. The largest tenant is an operational and blast-radius problem, not a capacity one, which matters for how you argue the placement fork.
- **Concurrent connections:** ~40% of DAU are in a client during their working day: 35M × 0.40 = **14M concurrent sockets** at global peak. At 100k sockets per gateway box (event-loop runtime, ~40KB of socket, TLS and subscription state each, so 4GB per box) that is 14M / 100k = 140 boxes, at 2x for rolling deploys and zone loss = **~300 gateway boxes**.
- **Fan-out:** each connected user actively subscribes to ~8 channels, so 14M × 8 = **112M live subscriptions**. A message in a 100,000-member channel spread across 300 gateways costs 1 publish + 300 consumes, not 100,000 pushes. That 300x is the entire reason a large #general is affordable.
- **Files:** 35M × 0.2 files/day = 7M files/day × ~800KB (screenshots, PDFs, short clips) = **5.6TB/day**, ~2PB/year to object storage. Larger than the message store in bytes and the cheapest tier per byte.
- **Notifications:** ~8% of messages are a DM or carry a mention: 700M × 0.08 = 56M/day; 56M / 36,000 ≈ **1.6k/s busy hour**, ~5k/s peak. Small, and sized off the persist stream rather than the socket path because it must fire whether or not the recipient is connected.
- **Tenant directory:** 750k rows × ~200B = **150MB**. The only globally scoped store, and it fits in memory on every edge node, which is what makes tenant resolution free rather than a hop.
#### Key decisions
**Where the tenancy boundary lives: homed shards or a tenant column**
- Choice: home each workspace on a named shard (gateway pool, keyspace, search index, object-store prefix, key alias), resolved at the edge from the 150MB directory before any other work runs. Keep the `workspace_id` predicate on queries too, as a second line rather than the only one.
- Alternative: one pooled fleet with `workspace_id` as the leading key on every table and generic autoscaling, no placement layer at all.
- Decider: how many tenant-scoped operations must be complete and provable, weighed against the corpus you would otherwise scan. At 750k tenants and 128TB of new messages a year, "delete this customer within 30 days and attest to it" on a pooled fleet is a full-corpus scan per request with no way to demonstrate completeness. Homed, it is a keyspace drop plus a key destruction, minutes, with an artifact. The second half of the decider is the 15,000x size spread: pooled capacity planning has no answer to one tenant that large except provisioning for it everywhere.
- Alternative wins when: tenants are within roughly 10x of each other and no customer has contracted for residency, key control or attested deletion. That describes most products before their first enterprise deal, and pooling is genuinely better there: higher utilisation, one deploy, no placement decisions to get wrong and no migration machinery to build. The mistake is not starting pooled. It is failing to budget the migration for when the first enterprise contract lands.

**Search: an index per tenant, or shared indices with a tenant routing key**
- Choice: hybrid, split on document count. Workspaces above ~50M documents get a dedicated index and the top tier gets a dedicated cluster; everyone below shares physical indices with `workspace_id` as the routing key plus a mandatory tenant filter, injected by a query builder that exposes no way to construct an unscoped query.
- Alternative: one index per workspace uniformly, so tenancy in search is physical like everywhere else.
- Decider: shard count against node capacity. A search node holds on the order of 500 to 1,000 shards before cluster state and heap overhead dominate, so 750,000 workspaces at one shard each is ~1,000 nodes carrying a median of 110MB. The threshold falls out of the same arithmetic: a shard is comfortable at ~50M documents, which at 20 messages per user per day over five years is a workspace of ~1,370 daily actives, the top 2%.
- Alternative wins when: the tenant count is in the thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands, which is the usual shape for a product sold only to large enterprises, or when a specific customer contracts for physical index separation. Regulated buyers do ask for exactly that and it is reasonable to sell it; the cost is a shard that is 99% empty, affordable at a few thousand tenants and not at 750,000. The shared path is where cross-tenant leakage would actually occur, so it needs a live canary: plant a document in one tenant and assert on a schedule that a search executed as another tenant never returns it.

**Cross-organisation shared channels: one home, or a copy on each side**
- Choice: every shared channel has exactly one home shard, the workspace that created it. The visiting side holds a bridge row with membership, local naming and notification preferences, and no messages. Reads and writes from the visiting side route to the home shard.
- Alternative: replicate the channel's message log into both workspaces' shards so each side reads and writes locally.
- Decider: whether two logs may disagree about order. Replication needs a single ordering authority for every message anyway, or concurrent posts, edits and deletes interleave differently on the two copies with no basis for reconciling afterwards, and once you have accepted an ordering authority you have single-home with extra copies. Single-home costs one cross-shard hop on writes from the visiting side, 20 to 80ms cross-region, on roughly 1% of message volume. Slack shipped replication first and moved off it for exactly this reason.
- Alternative wins when: the two organisations sit in different regulatory regimes and each is contractually required to hold its own copy of the record. Then you must replicate, and the honest shape is one side authoritative for serving with the second copy written from that authoritative stream as a compliance archive. That is a materially different system from two live peers, and it is worth naming which one you are being asked to build.
#### High-level design

**How to read the diagram:** every box below the clients sits inside one workspace's shard. This is one tenant's slice of the platform, and the platform is a few hundred copies of it plus a directory that says which copy you are talking to. There are two paths through it: a live path, socket to bus to socket, and a durable path, persist and everything hanging off it.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** the message is durable before it is acknowledged, so a sent tick means the record exists rather than that one process accepted it. Everything that must not be lost consumes the persist stream rather than the bus: search indexing, notifications, compliance export, integrations. The bus carries only what is being delivered right now, which is what makes a rollout that drops every socket in the pool a reconnect event instead of a data event.

**What this layout buys you:** the shard is the unit of backup, restore, retention, key revocation, residency and blast radius, because all of those are drawn inside the same box. The cost is a placement problem the diagram does not show. Tenants grow, shards fill, and moving a live workspace between them has to be routine rather than an incident.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The tenancy boundary: how it is made physical, where it is deliberately punctured, and what it costs to move a tenant.**

**The directory.** One strongly consistent table maps `workspace_id` to `(shard_id, region, plan, key_alias, state)`. 750k rows at ~200B is 150MB, so every edge node holds the whole thing in memory behind a version counter and refreshes on change. Writes are rare: new tenants, plan changes and migrations, on the order of a few thousand a day. It is the only globally scoped store in the system, and keeping it the only one is the discipline everything else rests on. Resolution happens before authentication does any real work: terminate TLS, take the workspace from the hostname or the token, look up the shard, route. A request that does not resolve to a tenant is rejected at the edge. There is no default tenant and no fallback shard, because both are how cross-tenant bugs get in.

**What a shard actually is.** A named bundle of five things that must stay together: a gateway pool holding the sockets, a database keyspace, a search index home, an object-store prefix, and a key alias. They are bundled because every enterprise obligation is an operation over all five at once. Deleting a customer means dropping a keyspace, dropping an index, deleting a prefix and destroying a key, and the last of those is what makes any backup you failed to enumerate unreadable, which is the difference between "we deleted it" and something you can attest to. Applying a 90-day retention policy is a compaction setting on one keyspace and a lifecycle rule on one index. Proving residency is reading one row. Split the five across differently partitioned systems and each of these becomes a distributed transaction across systems with no shared coordinator, which is how "delete my data" turns into a six-week manual project with a spreadsheet.

**The property this buys.** Tenant-scoped correctness stops being a predicate in a query and becomes a routing decision made once, at the edge, by code no feature team touches. On a pooled fleet a forgotten `WHERE workspace_id = ?` returns another company's messages, and the only defences are review and testing, both probabilistic. Homed, the connection the request holds cannot reach another tenant's keyspace, so the same bug returns the same tenant's data. Keep the predicate anyway, as defence in depth, but be clear about which of the two is load-bearing.

**The three punctures, and why they are enumerated.** "Shard-scoped by default" only means something if the exceptions are a finite list somebody can read. Ours is three. First, the directory itself. Second, identity: one email address belongs to thirty workspaces, so the user-to-workspace mapping and the credential are global while the profile, presence and history are per shard. That split is why signing in and choosing a workspace are two steps in the product; it is the tenancy boundary showing through the interface. Third, shared channels between organisations. Anything that wants to be a fourth exception argues its case in review, and the list being short is the point.

**Crossing the boundary on purpose.**
