#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hot document.** Fan-out from one owner is N² in editors, and at ~1,000 concurrent typists that is 2M frame-sends/s, which saturates four cores against a single-threaded owner. *Mitigation:* cap active editors at 50 and downgrade the rest to suggestion or view mode. Note what we deliberately do *not* do: sharding a document by section so each section gets its own owner is the obvious scaling move and it is ruled out here, because a second owner is a second transform site and the transform function does not satisfy TP2. Choosing the cap over the shard is choosing a product limit over a correctness risk.
- **Op log growth.** Every bundle is a row; a long-lived document accumulates millions, which slows loads and burns storage. *Mitigation:* snapshot every 1,000 operations and keep only `last_snapshot_rev` minus a safety buffer online, archiving the rest as compressed columnar for version-history queries. This is also why version history stores coalesced revisions rather than raw operations: 20TB/day raw against 500GB/day coalesced.
- **Large document load.** A 5MB document with deep history takes seconds to deserialise and lay out. *Mitigation:* fetch the latest snapshot only and lazy-load history (revision list, per-range attribution) on request; stream the snapshot so the editor renders the visible viewport before the tail arrives. This does not fix editing performance on a 5MB document, only opening it.
- **Server crash mid-broadcast.** Some clients received the newest operation, others did not, so client revisions diverge. *Mitigation:* the log was written before the broadcast, so on reconnect each client sends `last_received_rev` and the new owner replays the gap. The exposure is the read-only window during lease reassignment, 10 to 30 seconds, during which clients keep typing into their local buffer and the buffer keeps growing.
- **Costs that belong to the alternatives, not to this design.** If you took the CRDT fork, the pressure moves to client memory and tombstone reclamation: mark-and-sweep over deleted identities once deletion is agreed, plus run-length encoding of consecutive identities from one author on the wire. If you took the structured-object fork, fractional indices between siblings lose precision on repeated insertion at the same point and eventually underflow, so you need rational representations or a periodic rebalance triggered off a precision-bits metric. Both are real and neither is a problem we have, which is worth saying out loud rather than listing them as if they were.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Document owner | Owning process dies mid-broadcast; some clients have the newest op, others do not | Lease heartbeat to the coordination service; divergent `last_received_rev` on reconnect | New owner acquires the lease, replays the log to `current_rev`; clients send `last_received_rev` and receive the gap; read-only window of 10 to 30 seconds |
| WebSocket | Connection drops mid-edit with local operations unsent | Ping/pong timeout; client-side socket close | Client keeps buffering against `last_known_server_rev` and reconnects with jittered backoff; the buffer is rebased against the gap on reconnect |
| Op log store | Majority write fails (disk full, replica lag) after the client already saw the edit on screen | Append latency p99 alert; replication-lag SLO; a detector for acks issued without a completed write | Write to majority before broadcast, never the reverse; on failure reject the operation and hold the client in a "saving" state rather than acknowledging it |
| Snapshot service | Writer dies mid-write, leaving a partial blob | Manifest verifies the content hash before `latest` is advanced; orphan-blob sweeper | Write under a temporary key, verify, then atomically advance `latest`; retain the previous snapshot for one cycle so a bad one can be rolled back |
| Auth / ACL | Access revoked while the user holds an open session | Revocation event published to the document's channel | Re-check authorisation on every operation, not only at handshake, so a stale token cannot keep writing; close the socket; keep a per-revision record of who edited what |
| Presence channel | Cursor flood from a buggy or hostile client | Per-client frame-rate alert | Throttle to ~10 frames per second per client and drop the excess at the socket edge, before it reaches the document's process |
| Transform correctness | A transform bug or a doubly-applied operation diverges one client from the rest | Server broadcasts `{rev, hash}` every 200 operations; clients at that revision with an empty buffer compare | Force the offending client to discard state and reload snapshot plus tail, costing it at most one composed operation; no incremental repair exists because nothing says which side is wrong |
| Comment anchors | The range a comment is anchored to is deleted by a concurrent edit | Anchor resolution fails at render time | Store anchors as a range plus surrounding text fingerprint; on failure, orphan the thread into a "resolved from deleted text" list rather than silently dropping it or reattaching it somewhere wrong |

**Unresolved**

**Convergence is not intention preservation, and nothing in this design closes that gap.** Two people rewriting the same sentence converge on an interleaving of both rewrites that reads as neither. This is not an OT bug that a CRDT would fix; both are defined to produce *a* consistent state, and neither has any notion of what the text was supposed to say. What we actually ship is a heuristic: if an incoming operation's range overlaps a range another user touched in the last 10 seconds, prompt the second author into suggestion mode, where the edit lands as a reviewable change rather than into the document. That is a UX patch on a semantic problem. It will miss cases, it will fire on people politely editing adjacent sentences, and the guarantee we can honestly publish is "you will never see a different document than your collaborator", not "the document will say what either of you meant". Track changes as the default for multi-editor sessions would be more honest and would also make the product feel much heavier, so we did not do it.

**The transform is correct only while a document has exactly one owner, and that is a scaling wall we have no plan for.** The whole design leans on there being a single transform site, which reduces the correctness requirement to TP1; we do not satisfy TP2 and no practical implementation on this codebase would. That forbids the two things you would naturally reach for under load: sharding a hot document across owners, and giving a second region its own owner so distant editors are not paying a cross-ocean round trip on every keystroke. Today European editors on a US-homed document eat 140ms of that 200ms budget in transit and we simply accept it. The only escapes are moving to a CRDT, where the property is not needed because there is no transform, or implementing a TP2-correct transform, which the literature suggests is a research project rather than a sprint. We have neither, so the honest position is that this system does not scale along the axis it is most likely to be asked to.

**Long offline rebases produce a result the user cannot meaningfully review.** 200 local operations against 1,500 remote ones is 300,000 pairwise transforms, which is microseconds of CPU and entirely the wrong thing to worry about. The problem is that the output is expressed as character-level operations, so the "preview" we can show past the gap threshold is a before-and-after of the merged text, not "your third paragraph moved and lost its second sentence". Users accept or reject something they do not understand. The right product answer for a genuinely long gap is a fork and merge model, where offline work becomes a branch the author reconciles deliberately, the way source control does it. We did not build one, because the p99 offline gap is under two minutes and maintaining two merge models to serve the tail is not worth it. That is a resourcing decision, not a solution, and the flight case stays bad.
#### Drill questions
1. OT or CRDT, which would you actually pick today?
2. What happens with 1,000 concurrent editors on one document?
3. A user edits offline for a week, then reconnects. What could go wrong?
4. How do you load a 10MB doc with 5M operations of history fast?
5. How do you handle authorisation revocation mid-edit?
6. Comments and suggestions: same channel as edits, or separate?
7. Why does Figma get away without OT or CRDT for text?
8. Yjs and Automerge are both CRDTs. What actually differs?
9. Why must the operation be written to the log before it is broadcast, and what specifically breaks if you reverse it?
10. A remote operation arrives while the client still has unacknowledged local operations. Walk through exactly what the client does.
11. How do you find out that two clients have diverged, and what can you do once you know?
12. Does the log store the operation as the client sent it or as the server transformed it, and why does the answer matter?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. It depends on whether you already have a server on the edit path. We do, for authorisation re-checks, durable append and presence, so OT costs us nothing we were not already paying and keeps the stored document at 1x the text. Greenfield with no server, I would take a CRDT: the correctness burden moves into a library many products have exercised, and offline stops being a special case. *If pushed:* do not argue the metadata point. The 16 to 32 bytes per character figure describes 2006 to 2011 designs; run-length encoded implementations from roughly 2019 land near 1.5x plain text on the standard 182k-operation trace. The live decider is topology and staffing, not bytes.

2. Fan-out is N² and at ~1,000 typists that is 2M frame-sends/s, roughly four cores, against a single-threaded owner. We cap active editors at 50 and downgrade the rest to suggestion or view mode. *If pushed:* the interesting part is what we refuse to do. Sharding the document by section would fix the fan-out and would also create a second transform site, and our transform satisfies TP1 only. We take a product cap over a correctness risk, and if 1,000 simultaneous editors were a real requirement the answer is a CRDT, not a shard.

3. The transforms are cheap; the result is the problem. 200 local operations against 1,500 remote ones is 300,000 pairwise transforms and microseconds of CPU, but if both parties rewrote the same section the merged text interleaves two versions of it. *If pushed:* past a gap threshold we show a before-and-after preview and let the author accept or reject, which is weak because the diff is character-level and does not read as "your paragraph moved". The right answer for multi-day gaps is a fork and merge model, and we do not have one.

4. Snapshot every 1,000 operations to object storage and keep only the tail of the log online behind it. A document open is one snapshot fetch plus the operations since `snapshot_rev`, so open cost is independent of history depth: a 50KB document with 800k operations of history loads the same 50KB blob plus ~50 operations. *If pushed:* version history is served separately and from *coalesced* revisions, roughly one per minute of editing, not from raw operations. Raw would be 20TB/day against 500GB/day coalesced, and no user wants a revision list with 400 entries per session.

5. Check authorisation on every operation, not at handshake. On revoke, the access service publishes to the document's channel, the owner closes that socket and rejects the next operation. *If pushed:* the connect-time-only check is the classic bug, and it is worse here than in a request/response system because the socket can live for hours. Also keep a per-revision record of author, because "who wrote this sentence" is a compliance question in enterprise deployments and the op log is the only place that answer exists.

6. Separate. Comments live in their own store, anchored to a range in the document, so editing a paragraph does not disturb the thread attached to it. *If pushed:* anchor survival is the whole difficulty. Store the range plus a fingerprint of the surrounding text so the anchor can be re-found after edits, and define an explicit policy for when the anchored text is deleted outright: orphan the thread into a visible "resolved from deleted text" list. Silently dropping it loses data and silently reattaching it to the nearest survivor puts a comment on text it was never about.

7. Because a Figma file is not prose. It is a tree of objects with discrete properties, so concurrent edits to different properties never interact, and concurrent edits to the same property are resolved last writer wins, which means someone's input is discarded. That is acceptable when two people typing into the same label at the same moment is rare. In a document, the same paragraph is exactly what two people contend for, so the same rule would feel broken. *If pushed:* Figma is not authority-free either. Sibling order uses fractional indexing, which is a conflict-free technique, and the server still picks the canonical order for last-writer-wins and rejects reparenting cycles. It is CRDT-flavoured, not peer-to-peer.

8. Data structure and intended workload. Yjs uses a linked-list structure (YATA) tuned for text: fast incremental updates, compact wire format, lazy garbage collection of tombstones. Automerge models the document as its full history, which makes forking, merging and time travel natural but costs more per keystroke. *If pushed:* pick on the dominant operation. High-frequency live typing favours Yjs; an offline-first application where reconciling weeks of divergence is the main event favours Automerge's history model. The two have converged considerably since 2021, so benchmark rather than repeat a comparison you read.

9. Because the broadcast is irreversible and the write is not. If you broadcast first and the process dies before the append completes, the edit is on three screens and in no log, so the replacement owner reconstructs a document that is missing text users watched appear. There is no way to un-show it, and the clients that saw it will keep transforming against it. Reverse the order and the worst case is an operation nobody was told about, which the client simply retries because it never got an acknowledgement. *If pushed:* the acknowledgement has to come after the majority write too, not just the broadcast. An ack is a promise of durability, and a client that has been acked drops the operation from its pending buffer and can no longer resend it.

10. Two transforms, and the second is the one people forget. The remote operation was transformed against server state, but the screen shows server state plus the client's own pending operations, so applying it raw is wrong. Compute `remote' = T(remote, pending)` and apply that to the document, then compute `pending' = T(pending, remote)` and replace the buffer, so that when the server transforms it later both ends are working from the same premise. Then shift every local cursor and selection anchor by the same arithmetic. *If pushed:* omitting the buffer rewrite fails silently. The next acknowledgement arrives, the client believes it is level with the server, and the documents differ by exactly the operations that were never rebased. The symptom is one user with a character in the wrong place that never self-corrects, which is why the checksum in the next answer exists.

11. Every 200 operations the server broadcasts `{rev, hash}` of its own document at that revision. A client sitting at that revision with an empty pending buffer compares hashes; anything else ignores it. Once a mismatch is seen there is no incremental repair, because nothing in the protocol identifies which side is wrong. The client discards its state and reloads snapshot plus tail, losing at most one composed operation, roughly half a second of typing. *If pushed:* the value is diagnostic, not corrective. Without it, a transform bug shows up months later as an unreproducible support ticket; with it you get a metric you can alert on and a revision number to replay from. It should be shipped in the first version, not added after the first incident.

12. Store the transformed operation, because that is what defines the document. The log is the authoritative sequence, and replaying it from the snapshot must reproduce `current_rev` exactly; the client's original refers to a state that may no longer be reachable. *If pushed:* keep `base_rev` and the client's operation id alongside it, because the original is what you need to debug a transform bug and to answer "what did this person actually type", which is not the same question as "what does the document say". The compromise is one extra field per row, roughly 12 bytes on a 200B record, and it is the difference between a divergence report you can investigate and one you can only apologise for.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, name the problem, not the components.** First sentence: "we never send the document, we send operations, and every operation is a function of a state that has probably already changed by the time it arrives." That single line separates this from a CRUD editor and it is what the interviewer is listening for. Then ask the three questions that genuinely fork the design: is there a central server on the edit path anyway (yes, for authorisation and durability), how long can a client be offline (hours, not weeks), and is it prose or structure (prose, with tables). State your assumed numbers out loud: p50 of 1 editor, p99 of 20, cap at 50, 200ms end to end. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine and the two placement rules.** Five boxes: clients, the owning collaboration process, the op log, snapshots, the presence path branching off before the log. As you draw each arrow, say the rule it encodes rather than what the box is. One owner per document, because ordering inside a process is free and ordering across processes is a distributed consensus you do not want on every keystroke. Log before broadcast, because a broadcast cannot be undone and a missing acknowledgement can be retried. Presence never touches the log. Then say "operational transformation" and immediately say what it is for: rewriting a stale operation so it still means what its author meant.

**15-35, the drill, and protect this time.** This is the interview. Go deep on the convergence protocol and cover both halves, because most candidates only have the server half: server folds the incoming operation through the gap from `base_rev` to `current_rev`; client transforms an incoming remote operation against its pending buffer *and* the buffer against the remote operation, then shifts its cursors by the same arithmetic. Volunteer the failure mode of skipping the second transform, because it is the strongest signal available in this question. Then TP1 against TP2: state that you need only TP1 because there is exactly one transform site, and that this is the property sharding would destroy. Then the checksum, and that its repair is a forced client reload rather than an incremental fix. Keep the OT against CRDT fork in reserve as a compact two-minute answer, and if you give it, date the metadata numbers rather than repeating the 20x figure.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the gaps before they are found: convergence is not intention preservation and a heuristic suggestion-mode prompt is all we have; the single transform site is a scaling wall, so a European editor on a US-homed document pays 140ms of the 200ms budget and we accept it; long offline rebases produce a diff no user can meaningfully review. Then two minutes of operations: snapshot every 1,000 operations so open cost is independent of history depth, version history from coalesced revisions rather than raw operations, and the metrics you would page on (round trip acknowledgement p99, checksum mismatches per hour, snapshot lag in operations, lease reassignment time).

Cut first: the rich-text representation fork, then comment anchoring, then the storage arithmetic. All three are real, none changes the shape of the answer, and the storage numbers in particular are where a nervous candidate hides from the algorithm. Never cut: log before broadcast, the client half of the transform, and the fact that one transform site is the assumption everything rests on.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **documents** (KV store): `(doc_id, snapshot_blob, current_rev, last_modified)`
- **operations** (append-only log per doc): `(doc_id, rev, client_id, ops_json, ts)`
- **snapshots** (object store): periodic full-document snapshots for fast load

**API contract**

```
WebSocket per editing session:
  → { type: op, doc_id, ops: [...], rev: int }
  ← { type: ack, server_rev: int }
  ← { type: remote_op, ops, by, rev }
  ← { type: presence, user, cursor_pos }

REST:
  GET /doc/{id}                → snapshot + version
  GET /doc/{id}/history?cursor → revisions
```

**Observability**

- **Round-trip acknowledgement latency**, client sent to client acked. SLO p99 < 200ms. This is the number users feel as keystroke lag.
- **Server revision gap**, `current_rev` minus a client's `last_known_rev`, over active editors. SLO p99 < 50 operations; a growing gap means broadcast is back-pressured.
- **Convergence checksum mismatches per hour.** Hard alert at any non-zero value. Every mismatch is a transform bug or a corrupted client, and it is the only signal that the core algorithm is misbehaving.
- **Op log append latency**, majority-write completion time. SLO p99 < 20ms; every operation blocks on it and it is the only part of the latency budget that is not physics.
- **Snapshot lag**, `current_rev` minus `last_snapshot_rev`. SLO < 1,000 operations. When snapshots fall behind, document open time is what degrades.
- **Lease reassignment time**, owner death to new owner serving. SLO p99 < 30s; this is the read-only window users experience as a frozen document.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** every document has one home region, because one owner implies one home. Clients elsewhere connect to a regional socket edge that forwards frames to the home region, which costs them the cross-region round trip on every keystroke. Op log and snapshots replicate synchronously within a metro availability-zone pair and asynchronously to remote regions for read-only standby.
- **RTO:** ~10-30 seconds for actor failover within a region (op-log replay from last snapshot + reassert pin). Cross-region failover is an operator decision: ~5-10 minutes including DNS/TLS cutover.
- **RPO:** ~0s within a region (sync majority write before broadcast). Cross-region: up to a few seconds of unreplicated ops (async lag); a forced cross-region failover surfaces to the user as "your last few keystrokes were lost, please review", because we never acknowledge ahead of durability.
- **Failover cadence:** automatic actor restart on host loss; cross-region game-days quarterly. Snapshot stores are replicated to standby regions continuously so cold-start in a new region is bounded by op-log delta replay.
- **Cross-region cost:** the dominant egress is op-log streaming (~7TB/day live tail) plus snapshot replication (~200GB/day delta). WS proxy traffic is small compared to the op stream.

### 38. Design Tinder (Dating / Match)
#### Problem
Show each user a stream of nearby candidates, record a swipe on every one, and open a chat when two people swipe right on each other. The candidate pool is bounded by geography and consumed as it is used, so a candidate seen once is gone. Interest that is not reciprocated must never be visible to its target.
#### Core
This is an inventory problem dressed as a recommender. Other ranked feeds can show you the same item twice; here a swipe spends a candidate permanently, the pool is bounded by a radius, and nothing happens until both sides agree. Design for depletion and allocation, not only for relevance.

The read path is a narrowing funnel. Start with a geo query for everyone inside the radius, roughly ten thousand people in a dense city. Filter on stated preferences, age band, gender and activity recency, down to about three thousand. Subtract everyone this user has already swiped, leaving about fifteen hundred. Only then rank, because ranking is the expensive stage and must never see the whole population. Return twenty, inside a 300ms budget, half of which the ranker takes.

The write path is one row and one lookup. Record the swipe partitioned by the swiper, then read the reverse index to ask whether the target already swiped right on this user. If yes, insert a match keyed on the ordered pair so that two simultaneous swipes converge on a single row, notify both sides, open the chat. If no, write nothing the target can observe. The privacy rule and the match rule are the same rule.

What people miss is that exposure is a product constraint rather than an optimisation. A profile everyone wants gets more interest than its owner can answer and crowds every feed in the city. Cap impressions per profile, penalise repetition in the ranker, and accept that some interested users never see that profile. A match nobody can act on is not a match.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a speed-dating event where you rotate through hundreds of people in a few minutes, except a very careful organiser pre-screens who reaches your table based on where you are and what you have said you want. Two rules make it unlike any other queue. Once you have met someone they are struck off your list forever, so the list only ever gets shorter. And when you hold up a "yes" paddle, nothing happens unless that person has also held up a "yes" paddle for you, at which point the organiser opens a private room. Nobody is ever told who flashed a "yes" at them before a match exists. Privacy of unreciprocated interest is a core rule, not a feature.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Build the list live on every request.* Narrow by distance, then by stated preferences, then subtract what this user has already swiped, then rank whatever survives. Nothing persists between sessions except the swipe log. It buys freshness, so someone who landed in the city an hour ago is in the next page, and it buys correctness of the location predicate, which is the one predicate that changes while the user is holding the phone. It costs a model pass inside the user's latency budget, so the funnel has to get the ranked set into the low thousands before the model runs.

*Build the list ahead of time.* A batch job assembles each user's next few hundred candidates offline and the app reads them off the top. The read becomes a single lookup and the model can be arbitrarily expensive because nothing is waiting on it, which buys real ranking quality. It costs staleness, and the thing that goes stale first is location.

*Treat it as allocating a scarce pool rather than answering independent queries.* Instead of every user pulling their own list, decide centrally who is shown to whom across a whole local market, so that a popular profile's limited attention goes to the people most likely to reciprocate. It buys the fairness property directly instead of approximating it with per-profile counters, and it is the only shape that can reason about both sides at once. It costs a lot of coordination, and it pays only where the pool is genuinely scarce, which describes most towns and no large cities.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a user in London opens the app. The Feed Service receives a `GET /feed` tagged with the user's last known coordinates. Stage 1, geo query: the service asks the geo index (a Redis `GEORADIUS` call, or a lookup over S2 cells, which divide the globe into a hierarchy of cells each with a compact id) for everyone within 10km, returning ~10,000 candidate user ids. Stage 2, preference filter: age band, gender, online recency, trimming to ~3,000. Stage 3, exclusion: a Bloom filter, a compact bit array that answers "have I probably swiped this person already?", removes everyone this user has seen and leaves ~1,500. It occasionally says yes for someone never actually swiped, a false positive at around 1%, which costs one candidate out of 1,500 and nobody notices. Stage 4, ranking: the survivors are scored by a model predicting mutual interest. Top 20 come back, the whole pipeline in ~250ms.

When the user right-swipes on candidate B, the Swipe Service records `(user_A, user_B, right, timestamp)` in a wide-column store partitioned by `swiper_id` for write speed. It then asks one question of the reverse index, which is the same swipe data indexed by `target_id`: has B already swiped right on A? If yes, create the match, notify both, unlock the chat room. If no, record the swipe and emit nothing. B never learns that A swiped right unless B swipes right too.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Geo index.** Stores each user's location as a coordinate that supports radius queries, updated when the user moves materially. Sharded by country, so a query for "within 10km of this London coordinate" never touches a US shard. This is one stage of four, not the system.
- **Exclusion filter (per user, cached at the edge).** A compact bit array answering "has A swiped B before?" without holding every swipe pair in hot memory. Sized for a 1% false positive rate at 9.6 bits per element, the standard construction from Bloom's 1970 paper. Loaded into the feed server at session start so the check is local rather than a database round trip.
- **Swipes table.** Every swipe as `(swiper_id, target_id, direction, timestamp)`, partitioned by `swiper_id` so writes spread evenly, with a secondary index by `target_id` that exists only to answer the reciprocity question in a single row read.
- **Ranker (two-tower model).** Precomputes a 128-dimensional embedding for every candidate offline. At request time it computes only the current user's embedding and takes a dot product against each candidate, which is orders of magnitude cheaper than running a joint network over every pair.
- **Match Service.** On a reciprocal right-swipe, creates a match keyed on the canonical pair `(min(a, b), max(a, b))`. Two simultaneous swipes hit the same row and the second write is a no-op, so exactly one match exists.

**The thing that makes it hard:** a very popular profile is right-swiped by an enormous number of people. Every one of those writes lands on the reverse index keyed by `target_id`, turning one row into a write hotspot at thousands per second while the primary copy, partitioned by swiper, stays perfectly balanced. The same profile is simultaneously in millions of feeds, so its owner gets an inbox of matches they cannot meaningfully act on and everyone else in the city sees the same handful of faces.

**Why this design and what it costs:** two mitigations together. Sub-shard the reverse index on `(target_id, hash(swiper_id) % N)`, spreading one hot target's writes over N partitions. Then give every profile an impression budget per day; once spent, its score multiplier in the ranker decays toward zero. Both cost something real. The sub-shard turns the reciprocity check from one read into N, so N stays small and is applied only to targets that trip a hot-key threshold. The budget means some genuinely interested users never see that profile, which is the right trade only because a match its owner will never answer was worth nothing to either party.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Redis Cluster sharded by country for the geo index. Cassandra for swipes, which suits append-only write-heavy traffic. PostgreSQL for users and match metadata. Exclusion filters in Redis with an in-process cache per session.
- Feed hot path:
  ```
  candidates = geo_index.radius(user.lat, user.lng, radius_km, limit=10000)
  candidates = filter(candidates, user.prefs)
  candidates = [c for c in candidates if not bloom.possibly_swiped(user_id, c)]
  scores = ranker.dot_product(user_embedding, candidate_embeddings[candidates])
  return top_k(candidates, scores, k=20)
  ```
- Swipe hot path: write to Cassandra partitioned by `swiper_id`, read the reverse index for `target_id`, and if reciprocal run `INSERT INTO matches (...) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and publish a match event.
#### What this is really testing
Whether you notice that the candidate set is consumable, mutually exclusive and two-sided, and design for that rather than for ranking quality. Every distinctive part of the answer falls out of those three properties. The exclusion structure exists because a candidate can be spent only once, which makes it the only stage of the funnel whose selectivity gets worse every day the user keeps swiping. The exposure budget exists because the scarce resource is attention on the other side of the market, not compute. The reciprocity lookup and the privacy rule are the same mechanism, because the product's atom is agreement rather than consumption. A candidate who treats this as "recommendations, with a geo filter" will build something that ranks well on day one and is empty by month two.

The contrast is with the proximity service. That question is geo end to end: choose a cell scheme, size cells to the radius, query the target cell plus its eight neighbours, refine with exact distance, cache. The decisive property there is that the answer is shared. Everyone standing in Times Square searching for coffee gets the same list, a 60 second cache absorbs around 70% of traffic, and a popular result being popular is a pure win, because the restaurant does not mind being returned a million times. Here geo is stage one of four and consumes 10 to 30ms of a 300ms budget. Nothing caches, because the exclusion set, the preference predicate and the ranker are all per user, and the correct answer is different a minute later once the user has swiped. Popularity inverts from a cache win into the central problem, because a person does mind being returned a million times. Answer this one with a geohash scheme and a haversine refinement and you have answered the smaller question.

Within the feed cluster the separation is just as sharp: a video feed has effectively unlimited, re-showable inventory and optimises watch time on one side only, whereas here the inventory is finite, single-use and has to be allocated across two sides that both have to say yes.

Closest question: Q13
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Distance, age and preference filters?
- Super-likes, boosts, other paid ranking levers?
- Image only, or also video?
- Is "who liked you" a visible product surface, and is it paid?
- What is the thinnest market we have to serve well?
- Can a swipe be undone?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Distance, age and preference filters | a per-user candidate query over a geo plus attribute index, narrowed in cardinality order before ranking |
| Swipes at scale | store right-swipes and answer reciprocity with a single-row reverse-index read, never a scan |
| "Who liked you" is a product surface | materialise an incoming-likes list per target, which is the same write as the reverse index but ordered, unbounded and read in bulk |
| Super-likes and boosts | a priority multiplier injected into ranking, which then collides with the exposure budget and needs an explicit precedence rule |
| Match then chat | a match event unlocks a chat channel owned by a separate messaging service (see Q9) |
| Image or video | media in object storage behind a CDN, moderated on upload, with the feed returning URLs only |
| Thin markets in scope | pool exhaustion becomes a first-class SLO, and every exposure control has to degrade gracefully rather than remove candidates |
| Swipes can be undone | the exclusion structure needs deletes, which a Bloom filter cannot do, so a small exact overlay sits in front of it |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** profile, swipe left or right, match on mutual right, chat after match, preference filters, ranked recommendations.
- **NFR:** feed p99 under 300ms; reciprocity never lost; unreciprocated interest never observable; thin markets stay usable.

**Scale**

- **Cohort and swipe rate:** Tinder reports around 75M MAU (Match Group earnings). Take 50M as the active cohort. 1.6B swipes/day is the public figure. 1.6B ÷ 86,400 = 18,500/s, round to **20k/s steady**. Evening peak, US prime overlapping EU evening, runs about 3x the daily average over a four-hour window: 20k × 3 = **60k/s peak**.
- **Per user:** 1.6B ÷ 50M = **32 swipes/user/day**, consistent with the reported 30 to 50 swipes per session at roughly one session per day. By construction the whole cohort is daily active, so MAU and DAU are the same 50M here and nothing in this design gets to assume idle users.
- **Feed requests:** 20 candidates per page, so 1.6B ÷ 20 = 80M pages/day = 80M ÷ 86,400 = **~925/s average, ~2.8k/s peak**. This is the number that sizes the ranker, and it is three orders of magnitude below the swipe rate because one request serves twenty decisions.
- **Concurrency:** one 10-minute session per user per day gives 50M × (10 ÷ 1,440) = **~350k concurrent sessions**, peaking near **1M**. Everything cached per session is sized off that number, not off 50M.
- **Right-swipes and matches:** right-swipes run about 46% of swipes (public figure, heavily skewed by gender), so 1.6B × 0.46 = **~750M right-swipes/day** = 8.7k/s average, 26k/s peak. Mutual rate about 4%: 750M × 0.04 = **30M matches/day**. Cross-check: Tinder has publicly cited roughly 26M matches/day, so 30M is the right order and slightly generous.
- **Profile record:** user_id 16B + demographics 200B + preference JSON 1KB + last_active 8B + geo 32B + verification and premium flags 300B + index padding 3KB ≈ **5KB**. 50M × 5KB = 250GB; RF=3 → **~750GB**. Small enough to be uninteresting.
- **Media:** a photo's resolution ladder is 300px ~30KB + 600px ~80KB + 1200px ~300KB = **410KB**. Profiles allow 6 photos but average about 3 uploaded, so 3 × 410KB ≈ **1.2MB/user**. 50M × 1.2MB = **60TB**, erasure coded at 1.5x → **~90TB stored**. Media never touches the feed path; a feed page is ~5KB of JSON carrying URLs.
- **Swipe events:** swiper_id 16B + target_id 16B + direction 1B + ts 8B + session_id 16B + geo-at-swipe 16B + padding 7B = **80B**. 1.6B × 80B = 128GB/day raw, round **130GB/day**; RF=3 → **~390GB/day**.
- **Hot retention:** 12 months, which is the window in which an old swipe can still produce a match before the other party has moved or gone dormant. 1.6B × 365 × 80B = **~47TB raw**, ~140TB replicated. Older rows tombstone into a columnar archive.
- **Exclusion structures:** at a 1% false positive rate a Bloom filter needs 9.6 bits per element. A three-year user at 32/day holds 32 × 365 × 3 = 35k swipes → 35k × 9.6 ÷ 8 = **42KB**. A power user at a 500k ceiling → 500k × 9.6 ÷ 8 = **600KB**. Weighting across the population gives ~80KB per session, so 1M peak concurrent sessions × 80KB = **~80GB of hot filter cache**. The exact alternative, one 8-byte id per swipe, is 6.7x larger at the same weighting: ~530KB per session, **~530GB**. Both are affordable, which is why the first fork below turns on something other than memory.
- **Match records:** match_id 16B + user_a 16B + user_b 16B + created_at 8B + state 4B + last_msg_at 8B + flags 4B + padding 28B = **100B**. 30M/day × 100B = **3GB/day**, ~1.1TB/year.
- **Chat backlog:** see Q9. 30M matches × 10% that actually converse × 20 messages/day × 300B = **~18GB/day**.
- **Exposure arithmetic, the number that reframes the problem:** a metro of 500k active users emits 500k × 32 = **16M impressions/day** spread over ~500k profiles, so the **mean profile is shown 32 times/day**. A cap of 50k impressions/day is therefore about 1,500x the mean. That cap is a circuit breaker for the few hundred profiles that would otherwise melt a partition; it is not the fairness mechanism, and anyone presenting it as one has not done this division. Redistribution starts at roughly 10x the local mean, so around **320 impressions/day**, and it has to be a decaying penalty rather than a cliff.
- **Pool depletion, the number that decides whether any of this matters:** a dense metro yields ~10k candidates inside 10km, so at 32 swipes/day the runway is 10,000 ÷ 32 = **~10 months**, and new arrivals refill it faster than that. A town with 3k active users yields ~1.5k after preference filtering, so 1,500 ÷ 32 = **~7 weeks**. Every widening and exploration mechanism in this design is buying weeks against that second number.
#### Key decisions
**Build the candidate list online, or precompute it in batch**
- Choice: run the full funnel at request time, roughly 925 times a second and 2.8k/s at peak, and store nothing between sessions except the swipe log.
- Alternative: a nightly batch job that ranks a few hundred candidates per user into a stored deck, so the read path is one lookup and the model can be a full cross-encoder rather than a dot product.
- Decider: how fast the defining predicate goes stale, and the predicate here is location. A deck is anchored to where the user was when it was built, and a large fraction of dating sessions happen away from that point, on a commute, at work, or while travelling. If under about 5% of sessions start more than 10km from the previous session's origin, precompute and repair the exceptions; measured on mobile dating traffic it is closer to a third, and a deck whose entire premise is a stale origin is not repairable, only rebuildable. Note that batch is genuinely cheaper on raw compute: 50M nightly decks × 1,500 scored candidates = 75B scorings, against 80M requests × 1,500 = 120B online, a ~40% saving. Compute is not what decides this.
- Alternative wins when: matching is not geo-anchored. Products that surface a small curated set per day on an interest or questionnaire basis, which is how Hinge's Most Compatible and Coffee Meets Bagel work, have a stable predicate, so the deck is a daily artifact by design and the expensive model is free quality. It also wins when exposure has to be allocated globally rather than approximated, because you can only distribute a scarce profile's attention fairly if you can see all the demand for it at once, and a per-request design structurally cannot.

**Probabilistic exclusion, or an exact seen-set**
- Choice: a Bloom filter per user at 1% false positive rate in the feed path, with an exact check against the swipes table at swipe-write time to catch the false positives that would otherwise mask a duplicate write.
- Alternative: an exact set of swiped ids per user, held as a compressed bitmap and kept in the same cache.
- Decider: the cost of a false positive against 6.7x the memory, and both numbers are small. A false positive drops about 15 of 1,500 candidates and no user can observe it. The memory is ~80GB against ~530GB at 1M peak concurrent sessions. At this scale the exact set is genuinely affordable, so this is a preference rather than a forced move, and the Bloom wins on two secondary properties: its size is fixed at allocation so a 500k-swipe power user does not fragment the cache, and the probe is a constant seven hash lookups regardless of set size.
- Alternative wins when: the market is thin, or swipes can be undone. Dropping 1% of 1,500 candidates is free; dropping 1% of 300 is three real people out of a pool the user will exhaust within weeks, and those are exactly the users you cannot afford to disappoint. Undo is the harder one, because a Bloom filter has no delete short of a counting variant at 4x the space, so shipping rewind means keeping an exact overlay in front of the filter anyway. Once that overlay exists, the argument for not simply holding the whole exact set gets thin.

**Fairness on the supply side, or on the demand side**
- Choice: constrain supply. Count impressions per profile per day and apply a decaying multiplier in the ranker once a profile passes roughly 10x its local mean, which the arithmetic above puts near 320 impressions/day, with a hard circuit breaker at 50k to protect the partition rather than the market.
- Alternative: constrain nothing on the supply side. Instead guarantee demand: reserve a fixed number of slots per page, say 5 of 20, for candidates below an exposure threshold, and let the ranker do whatever it likes with the other 15.
- Decider: which side is actually scarce, measured as the share of right-swipes absorbed by the top decile of profiles. Above roughly 50%, the binding constraint is on the supply side and throttling is the only thing that moves the number. Below it, throttling degrades relevance for no fairness gain, and reserved slots are strictly better because they never remove a good candidate, they only displace a marginal one.
- Alternative wins when: markets are thin, which is precisely where supply-side caps do most damage. With 1,500 candidates after filtering, throttling the top 150 profiles removes the reason people opened the app; reserved slots degrade to "you also see these five" and cost nothing structural. Reserved slots are also far easier to explain and to audit, which matters under algorithmic transparency rules such as the EU Digital Services Act, in force since 2024. The honest position is that large operators run both and tune the mix per market, so the fork is really about which one you make load-bearing.

**How to read the diagram:** one path builds the candidate feed and a second path records swipes and decides whether one became a match. The feed path narrows and ranks; the swipe path does the cheap reciprocity lookup and the state change.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** recommendation and matching are related but not the same problem, and they have opposite cost profiles. Showing good candidates is expensive and approximate. Creating a match is cheap and must be exact, because it is the only irreversible thing the system does and the only one with a privacy guarantee attached.

**What this layout buys you:** a fast swipe response and a match check that costs a single row read no matter how popular the target is. The cost is that quality lives entirely in the feed pipeline, so a ranker outage degrades the product without breaking it, and a bug in the funnel's ordering is invisible in every correctness test you would write for the swipe path.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The narrowing funnel, and why the candidate pool behaves like inventory.**

Four stages, and their order is the design. Approximate cardinalities at p50 in a dense metro: geo radius returns ~10k, the preference filter trims to ~3k, exclusion leaves ~1.5k unswiped, the ranker scores all 1.5k, and diversification with a freshness boost picks the top 20. The p99 budget is 300ms: geo and exclusion cost 10 to 30ms each, the ranker 100 to 150ms and dominates, the remainder is network and serialisation.

**Why ranking cannot come first.** A joint model scoring `f(user, candidate)` has to run once per pair. At 1.5k candidates per page and 2.8k pages/s peak that is 4.2M model invocations per second, and against the unfiltered pool it would be four orders of magnitude worse. The two-tower factorisation is what makes it tractable: a candidate tower produces a 128-dimensional embedding offline, once per profile, and the request path runs one user-tower pass plus 1,500 dot products, which is 192k multiply-accumulates and takes microseconds. What you pay is expressivity, because every interaction between a user feature and a candidate feature has to squeeze through a single inner product. If that costs too much quality, the standard repair is a second pass: rerank only the top 50 with a joint cross-encoder, which is 50 × 2.8k = 140k invocations per second and merely expensive rather than impossible.

**Why exclusion must come before ranking and not after.** Filtering after the ranker looks equivalent and is not. You would have to over-fetch by the reciprocal of the unswiped fraction, and that fraction is not a constant, it decays per user as they consume their local pool. A user 80% through their market needs 100 ranked results to yield 20 fresh ones, and a user at 95% needs 400. Putting exclusion ahead of the model makes the model's cost independent of how depleted the user is, and makes depletion observable as a single number: the cardinality surviving stage 3.

**What the model is trained on.** Labels are behavioural, not declared. The positive label that matters is not a right-swipe but a conversation, defined as a match that reached five or more exchanged messages; negatives are left-swipes and matches that produced nothing. That deep label is scarce and slow: 30M matches/day at roughly 10% converting gives 3M positives, delayed by hours to days. So the model is split by signal speed. A slowly retrained retrieval tower learns from conversation labels, which is the honest objective, and a fast ranker retrains on swipe labels, which are plentiful and immediate but measure attraction rather than compatibility. Features are shared interest tags, mutual-friend overlap where a social graph exists, photo embeddings from a vision model, response latency after a match, and activity recency.

**The ELO story, and why the shape of the mistake matters more than the mechanism.** Early Tinder ran an ELO-derived desirability scalar: every right-swipe on a profile raised its score by a delta proportional to the swiper's own score, every left-swipe lowered it, and high-scored users were preferentially shown to other high-scored users, preserving matching pools by attractiveness tier. Tinder publicly deprecated pure ELO in 2019 in favour of behavioural ranking. The signal underneath it, right-swipe rate per impression, survives as one feature among many and is a strong predictor of match success. The lesson is about the collapse to a scalar rather than about ELO. One global ordinal makes exposure a monotone function of a single number, which produces a monoculture at the top, a dead pool at the bottom, and no way to express that two people are a good match for each other rather than good in general. Keep the signal, refuse the total order.

**Where the exposure budget attaches.** After scoring, before diversification. Applying it at retrieval instead, by removing budget-exhausted profiles from the candidate set, is tempting and wrong in exactly the markets that need fairness most: in a pool of 1,500, removing the top 150 empties the feed, whereas a decaying multiplier degrades smoothly. The arithmetic keeps this honest. In a metro emitting 16M impressions/day across 500k profiles, the mean profile is shown 32 times a day, so the 50k/day hard cap is 1,500x the mean and exists to protect a database partition, not to redistribute attention. Redistribution begins around 320 impressions/day, at 10x the local mean, and the mean has to be computed per market because the same absolute number is generous in London and absurd in a town of 3,000.

**Depletion, which is the property no other feed has.** Stage 3 is the only stage whose selectivity worsens over time, monotonically, for a user who stays in one place. Track candidates surviving stage 3 per user as the primary health metric and start widening at ~200 rather than at zero, because a feed that changes character overnight reads as a broken product while one that drifts does not. Widen in cost order: activity recency first, from 7 days to 30, which breaks no promise the user made; then the age band, ±2 years to ±5; then radius, doubling from 10km to a 500km cap. Radius goes last because it is the only widening the user can see and the only one that produces matches nobody will travel for. In a market of 1,500 filtered candidates at 32 swipes a day, all of this buys weeks against a seven-week exhaustion clock, which is the honest ceiling on what engineering can do here.
