Read the diagram as three regions. Steps 1 to 4 are routing and are stateless: any proxy, any retry. Steps 5 to 11 are the transaction, and the quorum marker is the commit point; everything above it can be abandoned safely and everything below it is committed history. Steps 12 to 15 are consequences, deliberately after the ack, because a webhook receiver or a runner pool having a bad day must never be able to fail a push.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **A hot repository cannot be split.** A megaproject gets hammered by clones and fetches, saturating the primary's disk and network. Add 5 to 10 read-only replicas for the top repositories and load-balance fetches across them; cache `git-upload-pack` responses keyed by the requested ref state, since most clones ask for the same default-branch HEAD; edge-cache recent packfile snapshots so cold-region clones never reach the origin. None of this helps the write side, which stays on one primary.
- **A very large repository.** A 30GB clone is gigabytes of transfer and, before reachability bitmaps, an O(commits) graph walk just to enumerate what to send. Protocol v2 with `--filter=blob:none` defers blob download until checkout; sparse checkout limits what is materialised; server-side multi-pack bitmaps make enumeration effectively constant-time; for the genuinely largest, a virtual filesystem (GVFS, now Scalar) fetches on demand.
- **CI fan-out.** A monorepo push can trigger thousands of workflow jobs, each of which clones. Per-org concurrency caps bound parallelism, queue priorities separate paid from free, and workflow-level dedup collapses repeat triggers on the same SHA into one run plus a rebuild-on-completion. Runners are placed in the same region as the replica they will clone from, because at 870 jobs/s the clone traffic, not the compute, is what saturates first.
- **Repack pressure.** Geometric repacking made maintenance cheap per repository, but a file server hosting tens of thousands of repositories can still saturate its disk if many repack at once. Cap concurrent repacks per server, prioritise by activity, and schedule against per-server I/O metrics rather than a fixed cron.
- **Unauthenticated clone traffic.** Anonymous clones are bandwidth-heavy and free to request, which makes git endpoints an attractive target. Separate rate-limit buckets per IP and per authenticated user, abuse detection on clone patterns, and the ability to require authentication for expensive operations on specific repositories under load.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Git primary | Primary file server fails mid-push; client connection dies | Replica heartbeat to the consensus store; missing ack within timeout | Promote the replica with the highest applied ref state, bump generation to fence the old primary, client retries (safe: objects dedupe, ref CAS is idempotent or correctly rejects) |
| Replica skew | One replica falls behind; a second failure would lose write quorum | Per-replica lag SLO (max lag above N seconds is unhealthy) | Drain reads from the lagging replica, re-replicate from a healthy peer, page if 2 of 3 are unhealthy because the next failure loses quorum |
| Git proxy | Stateless proxy crashes; in-flight git stream interrupted | L4 health checks; per-connection error rate | Client retries against another instance; both smart-HTTP and SSH are safe to retry at the request level; fleet sized N+2 per region |
| Routing lookup | `repo_id → primary` lookup unavailable | Lookup p99; consensus-store error rate | 30s TTL cache at the proxy; serve stale and probe in the background; degraded mode routes to last-known primary, which is safe because the generation stamp fences a stale target |
| Metadata vs git divergence | Merge writes the git ref but crashes before the PR row updates | Reconciler comparing PR `head_sha` and merge state against actual ref state | Background reconciliation keyed on ref state, with git treated as authoritative; the UI can be wrong for seconds to minutes, which is conceded below |
| Webhook delivery | Receiver returns 5xx or times out repeatedly | Per-receiver success rate; per-target queue depth | Exponential backoff within a 24h retention window; circuit-break persistently failing receivers and surface to the repo admin; HMAC-signed payloads so receivers can dedupe retries |
| CI runner pool | Runners fail to start, or throughput collapses under fan-out | Job-queue depth per org; runner-launch p99 | Per-org concurrency caps, queue priorities, SHA-level dedup, hard ceiling with graceful queueing |
| Search index | Shard hot or stale | Query p99 per shard; index-build lag | Replicas per shard; rebuild stale shards from the git store; degrade to "search unavailable" rather than return silently stale results |
| LFS pointer without blob | Pointer committed but blob missing from the object store | LFS fetch 404 at checkout | Validate pointer-to-blob existence at push time; re-upload from any source holding that SHA, since LFS is content-addressed; audit-log every mismatch |

**Unresolved**

**Shared object pools leak across the fork network, and the mitigations are all partial.** A pool means an object pushed to any member is physically present for every member, and git will serve any object by its raw SHA whether or not a ref points at it. That is the mechanism behind the well-known behaviour where a commit pushed to a private fork can be fetched through the public parent by anyone who learns the hash, and the same mechanism means deleting a repository does not delete its objects if a sibling still needs the pool. We partition pools by visibility class, which stops private objects entering a public pool but throws away deduplication at exactly the point where forks are most numerous, and it does nothing for the public-to-public case. Full isolation means one object graph per repository, which costs the 1,000x storage factor from the second fork above. We have chosen storage over isolation and documented the behaviour, which is a policy decision dressed up as an architecture, and a security-minded interviewer will say so.

**There is no transaction spanning the git store and the metadata database.** A merge writes a git ref on the file server and a state change in a relational database, and nothing makes those two atomic. A crash between them leaves a branch that is merged with a pull request that says open, or a pull request marked merged whose merge commit never landed. Worse, the metadata is not even a reliable mirror of git: a force-push moves `head_sha` out from under an open review, so a review comment can be attached to a commit no ref reaches any more. We run a reconciler that treats git as authoritative and repairs metadata behind it, which means the UI is eventually consistent with the repository on a horizon of seconds to minutes, and that during that window the API can return a state no client should act on. The honest fix is a two-phase protocol with an intent record written before the ref update and cleared after, which converts silent divergence into a visible in-progress state but does not make anything atomic.

**Availability is a fleet number and outages are per repository.** Three replicas serving one repository means that repository's availability is independent of the other 100M, so a 99.99% fleet SLO can coexist with a specific customer being fully down while two of their three replicas re-replicate a 30GB working set. Statelessness elsewhere does not help; the data has to be somewhere specific. Re-replication of a large repository takes minutes to tens of minutes and consumes the very disk bandwidth the surviving replicas need to serve reads, so recovery competes with availability. We prioritise re-replication by repository activity and cap its bandwidth, which means the tail of unlucky repositories has a materially worse experience than the SLO advertises. Raising the replication factor to five improves this and costs 67% more storage on 15PB, which is the trade we have not made and would revisit if per-repository availability ever became the thing customers measured.
#### Drill questions
1. Git LFS or just raise the repository size limit?
2. How do you do code search across millions of repositories?
3. A push triggers 1000 CI workflows. How do you stop the runner pool collapsing?
4. A 30GB monorepo. What is the clone strategy?
5. How do you handle a hot repository hammered by clones?
6. How do you migrate a repository to a new file server without downtime?
7. Two people push to `main` at the same moment. What does the server do?
8. Why can you not erasure-code a repository across the fleet the way an object store does?
9. Why three replicas with a cross-DC majority rather than five within one DC?
10. How does code search enforce private-repository access control without scanning every result?
11. A user forks a public repository into a private one and pushes a secret. What is exposed?
12. How does geometric repacking handle a force-push that orphans a million objects?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. LFS for binary assets that change often (designs, datasets, model weights), because git's delta compression is built for line-based text and balloons on binaries, so every clone downloads every historical version forever. *If pushed:* LFS costs an extra round trip per blob and makes a clone two protocols instead of one; for a repository with a handful of static large files, partial clone plus sparse checkout is simpler and needs no separate server.

2. A separate ngram inverted index, sharded by repository, with the query rewritten into an index lookup and a verification pass over the candidates. Q47 has the inverted-index mechanics. *If pushed:* the size driver is unique text, not repository count, because fork pooling and file-level dedup collapse the corpus; GitHub reported ~115TB of content deduplicating to ~28TB in 2023. The hard operational part is keeping the index fresh at ~175 pushes/s while a full rebuild takes days.

3. Per-org concurrency caps, priority queues, and autoscaling runners with a hard ceiling. *If pushed:* workflow-level dedup on SHA is the biggest win, collapsing repeat triggers into one run plus a rebuild-on-completion. Also place runners in the same region as the replica they clone from, because at 870 jobs/s the clone bandwidth saturates before the compute does.

4. Protocol v2 plus `--filter=blob:none` for a partial clone, and sparse checkout to limit what is materialised on disk. *If pushed:* server-side, multi-pack reachability bitmaps make the enumeration phase effectively constant-time instead of O(commits), which is what stopped very large clones timing out. For the genuinely extreme cases (a 270GB Windows-class repository) a virtual filesystem such as Scalar fetches objects on directory access.

5. Extra read-only replicas with fetches load-balanced across them, response caching for `git-upload-pack` keyed by the requested ref state, and edge caching of recent packfile snapshots. *If pushed:* none of that touches writes. Pushes stay on one primary, so a repository whose write rate exceeds one machine has no answer in this design short of splitting the repository, which is a product decision rather than an infrastructure one.

6. Add the new server as an extra replica, let it catch up, verify by hash walk, flip the routing pointer in the consensus store, bump the generation, drop the old replica. Pushes during the flip get a few seconds of rejection and retry. *If pushed:* this is safer than a typical database migration precisely because content addressing makes verification total rather than sampled, and rollback is flipping the pointer back. The expensive part is bandwidth: moving a 30GB repository competes with live traffic on both endpoints.

7. The first push's ref compare-and-swap succeeds. The second arrives claiming an `old_sha` that no longer matches, so the server rejects it as a non-fast-forward and the client must fetch and rebase or merge. The server never merges and never picks a winner. *If pushed:* `--force` defeats this by sending all-zeros as `old_sha`, which is why it loses work; `--force-with-lease` sends the last observed SHA so the CAS still fires. Multi-ref atomicity requires `--atomic` plus a ref backend that supports a real transaction, which is one of the motivations for the reftable format.

8. Because a git operation walks a reachable subgraph and needs every object it reaches present locally. Erasure coding assumes the unit of access is the unit of storage, which holds for an object store where a GET touches one key. Here a single clone touches hundreds of thousands of objects, so spreading them turns every operation into a distributed traversal, and the durability unit is not the object but the reachability closure: a repository missing one reachable object is corrupt, not slightly degraded. *If pushed:* you can erasure-code the packfiles as opaque blobs for cold or archival repositories, where nobody runs live git operations against them, and some hosts do exactly that for dormant storage.

9. Cross-DC majority means no single data centre holds enough replicas to lose write quorum when it fails, so a DC outage costs latency rather than availability. Five within one DC is cheaper to write to (no cross-DC round trip on the quorum path) but a DC-level event is then a data-loss event. *If pushed:* the cost is real and paid on every push: 1 to 3ms of metro round trip. It is tolerable only because pushes are ~175/s fleet-wide and each is dominated by upload time, not by the quorum. On a write path with different economics this trade flips.

10. Shard the index by repository and compute the user's accessible-repository set at query time from the auth service, then restrict the query to those shards so inaccessible shards are never read at all. Filtering after retrieval leaks existence through timing and result counts. *If pushed:* very large organisations break this, because the accessible set itself is millions of entries. Roll access up to the org or team level and filter at that granularity first, descending to per-repository only within the orgs the user belongs to.

11. If the private fork shares an object pool with the public parent, the secret's objects are physically present in storage shared with public repositories, and git will serve any object by its SHA regardless of reachability, so anyone who obtains the hash can fetch it through the parent. *If pushed:* the mitigation is to partition pools by visibility so a private fork is detached into its own object storage, which costs a full copy of the history. That is the right call and it is why forking a public repository into a private one is slower and more expensive than a public-to-public fork. The residual risk is public-to-public: a commit pushed to a public fork and then deleted remains fetchable from the network by hash, which is documented behaviour rather than a bug, and is the reason "force-push to remove a leaked credential" is not a remediation. Rotate the credential.

12. It does not handle it immediately, and that is deliberate. A force-push leaves the orphaned objects unreachable but present; they stay recoverable through the reflog for the retention window (90 days by default) and only then become eligible for collection. Geometric repacking only ever packs reachable objects, so the orphans sit in the loose pool consuming disk until GC. *If pushed:* a team that uses force-push as a normal workflow can inflate the loose pool faster than scheduled GC drains it. The controls are per-org reflog retention, an emergency GC trigger on a disk-usage threshold, and alerting on repositories whose loose-object count grows monotonically.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, name the storage unit and take the fork.** Open with the thesis before any box: "the unit of storage is a git repository, and a repository is already a content-addressed database, so this is a placement problem for stateful shards, not a blob-storage problem." Then ask the three questions that actually change the design: private repositories as well as public, is code search global or repository-scoped, and is CI in scope. State the numbers you are working from out loud: ~100M repositories, ~5PB unique, ~2,000 git ops/s average with ~175 pushes/s, and CI generating more read traffic than humans do. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine.** Four boxes, not one: git storage, metadata, search, CI, joined only by repository id and SHAs. Then zoom into git storage and draw the replica set: one repository, three file servers, no majority in one data centre, one elected primary. Say why the servers are stateful and hold local disks, using the random-read number rather than an adjective. Then draw the proxy above them and say it is stateless and resolves `owner/name` to `(repo_id, primary, generation)`. Say "a fork is not a copy" while drawing the object pool, because it is the cheapest way to show you know what git is.

**15-35, the drill.** Protect this time; it is where the interview happens. Go deep on the push as a transaction: objects first because unreferenced objects are garbage rather than corruption, then the ref compare-and-swap as the commit point, quorum before the CAS and not after, and what the client's `old_sha` buys you (concurrency control with no server-side merge, and free retry semantics). Volunteer split brain and say that content addressing does not save you from it, so you fence with a generation number and accept seconds of write unavailability. Then take the fork-pool decision on your own terms, including the leak, before they raise it. Then code search as a separate index with the corpus-times-QPS number, cross-referencing the search question rather than re-deriving inverted indexes. Keep hot-repository read replicas and partial clone as one-liners ready to expand.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the three gaps before they are found: pools leak across the fork network and every mitigation is partial; there is no transaction across the git store and the metadata database, so the UI is eventually consistent with the repository; availability is a fleet number while outages are per repository. Then the operational surface in two minutes: what you would page on (quorum success ratio, replica lag, push p99 by size class, runner queue depth), and the multi-region shape, which is a home region for writes with read-only mirrors elsewhere.

Cut first: LFS, then the CI runner internals (cross-reference Q54 and move on), then the audit-log and retention arithmetic. All three are real and none of them changes the shape of the answer. Never cut: the repository as the placement unit, the push transaction, and fork pooling.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **repos** (transactional store): `(repo_id, owner_id, name, visibility, default_branch, pool_id, replica_set, generation)`
- **users / orgs / teams / permissions** (transactional store)
- **issues / prs** (transactional store): `(id, repo_id, state, head_sha, base_sha, author, assignees[], labels[], body)`
- **comments / reviews** (transactional store, sharded by repo_id)
- **git data** (local filesystem on each file server): bare git repositories, three replicas each, with a shared object pool per fork network mounted as an alternate
- **LFS objects** (object store, content-addressed by SHA-256)
- **search index** (ngram inverted index, sharded by repo_id so access control is a shard filter)

**API contract**

```
git protocol over HTTPS + SSH                  (upload-pack, receive-pack)
REST + GraphQL:
  GET  /repos/{owner}/{repo}
  POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls
  POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/merge   → 409 if head_sha moved
  GET  /search/code?q=...
Webhooks: push, pull_request, check_run        (HMAC-signed, at-least-once)
```

Merge takes the expected `head_sha` and returns 409 if it moved, mirroring the ref compare-and-swap rather than papering over it.

**Observability**

- **Quorum success ratio on pushes.** SLO above 99.99%. A quorum failure is a user-visible push error and is the most direct reliability signal in the system.
- **Replica lag distribution.** SLO p99 under 5s. Growth is a leading indicator of quorum risk, since a lagging replica plus one failure is an outage for those repositories.
- **Push and clone latency by repository size class.** SLO p99 push under 5s for repositories below 1GB. Bucket by size, because a single global number is entirely determined by the tail.
- **Per-repository availability, not just fleet availability.** The count of repositories with fewer than two healthy replicas is the metric that matches what a customer experiences; the fleet number hides it.
- **CI runner queue depth and time to start.** SLO p99 under 30s for paid tiers. Queue depth is the leading indicator of pool exhaustion during fan-out spikes.
- **Webhook delivery success and lag per receiver.** SLO above 99% delivered within 60s, broken down per receiver so one slow integrator is visible before it starves others.
- **Search index build lag.** How far behind the index is against the git store, since stale results are worse than slow ones.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** three replicas with a cross-DC majority inside a home region, plus asynchronous read-only mirrors in other regions. Reads prefer a local replica; writes always route back to the home-region primary.
- **RTO:** ~30s for in-region primary failover (elect, bump generation, republish routing). Losing a whole region is operator-triggered at ~30 minutes including DNS cutover and promotion of async mirrors.
- **RPO:** effectively zero in region, since the 2-of-3 fsync quorum precedes the ack. Cross-region, up to the async lag, mitigated by the fact that re-pushing a lost packfile is idempotent, so recovery is often a client retry rather than a data-loss event.
- **Failover cadence:** automatic in region; cross-region game days quarterly. Runner pools are regional and scaled on demand.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by git replication. Seeding a new region is a full ~5PB mirror plus roughly 50 to 100GB/day of live delta. LFS blobs replicate lazily: the first remote access pulls and caches at the remote object store.

### 40. Design Spotify (Music Streaming + Recommendations)
#### Problem
Serve a 100-million-track catalogue to hundreds of millions of listeners, decide what plays next, and pay rights holders for every qualifying stream. A track is a few megabytes rather than a few gigabytes, so the whole popular catalogue fits at the edge and delivery becomes a caching problem rather than a chunking one. The harder problem is choosing what to play for someone who mostly wants to hear things they have already heard.
#### Core
Two facts drive everything: the objects are tiny, and people replay them.

Tiny objects. A four-minute track at 160kbps is 4.8MB, so the three lossy rungs of the entire catalogue are ~1.7PB and the top 1% is 17TB, which fits on one edge node. That collapses the delivery problem. You do not chunk a 5MB file and adapt bitrate mid-track; you pick a rung at track start, fetch the object whole, and prefetch the whole next track 20 seconds before the current one ends. The device becomes a real cache tier: a phone with 4GB spare holds 830 tracks, which is most of a heavy listener's rotation. Pre-pushing a mega-release to every edge is a 17MB write across three rungs, not a capacity event.

Replay. Roughly four plays in five are of a track the listener has played before. That inverts the recommender you would build for a video feed. Completion stops being a label, because a track you already love completes; the signal is a skip inside the first 30 seconds. Already-played stops being an exclusion filter and becomes the default candidate pool, which for most listeners is under 10,000 tracks and needs no vector index at all. Recommendation is not the main surface. It is a rationed novelty budget, spent in a few offline-computed discovery surfaces rather than blended into playlists the listener deliberately chose.

Third, every qualifying play is money. Thirty seconds or more triggers a fractional split among rights holders at per-country rates. That path is a ledger: payable numbers come from a deterministic batch over the immutable event log, and the streaming aggregate is a dashboard.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** three businesses sharing one front door. A distribution company that keeps every song at several qualities close to every listener; a recommender that decides what plays next; and an accounting firm that counts every stream and splits the money. The distribution business is the easy one, because a song is five megabytes and the whole popular catalogue fits on a single disk at the edge. The recommender is the strange one, because unlike every other feed you have built, its customers mostly want to hear things they have already heard.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Precompute a fixed list per listener on a schedule.* A batch job writes each person a list of tracks; serving is one key read. It buys unlimited model cost off the request path, and it makes the result a stable object the listener can return to, share, and argue with, which is a product property and not only an engineering one. It costs within-session reactivity: it cannot notice you skipped four songs in a row this evening. It wins when the surface is deliberately an event rather than a feed.

*Extend whatever is already playing.* Treat the current queue as the query and predict the next few tracks from the last few. Almost all listening starts from something the listener chose, so the strongest available signal is sitting in front of you, and it handles the fact that one person has several unrelated moods without forcing them into a single taste vector. It is cheap and works with almost no history. It costs reach: it never leaves the neighbourhood it started in.

*Rank the listener's own history and ration the unfamiliar.* Accept that most plays are repeats, make ordering the familiar the main job, and let unfamiliar tracks enter at a rate you set as an explicit policy number. It buys predictable satisfaction and a novelty spend you can see on a dashboard and cap. It costs long-term discovery, and that cost is invisible in any experiment short enough to run.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a listener in Berlin presses play. The client calls `GET /track/{id}`, which returns metadata, the entitlement decision for this account, and signed edge URLs for each rung the account may use. The client knows its tier (premium, so 320kbps is available) and its measured throughput, picks 320kbps, and issues one HTTP GET against the Frankfurt edge for the whole 9.6MB object, starting playback from the first bytes as they arrive. First audio at about 120ms; the rest of the file lands inside the first 15 seconds of playback. Twenty seconds before the track ends the client fetches the *entire* next track in the queue, so the gap between tracks is zero and the next track's start does not depend on the network at all. Meanwhile three events go to the play-event log: `start` at t=0, `qualified` at t=30s (the royalty threshold, stamped with event time rather than arrival time), and a terminal event carrying the position at which playback stopped. Two independent consumers read that log: the royalty archive, which is the source of the monthly ledger, and the training pipeline, which turns the same events into labels.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Audio storage and edge cache.** Each track is encoded once at upload into four rungs (96, 160, 320kbps and lossless) and stored as four whole objects, not chunked. ~4.4PB at origin. Edges pin the two mainstream rungs of the top 10M tracks, ~144TB, which is one storage node and covers ~90% of plays. A new release is pre-pushed to every edge as ~17MB across its three lossy rungs, cheap enough to be a routine part of the release process rather than a capacity event.
- **Catalogue service.** Metadata, rung pointers, ISRC codes (the identifier the royalty path keys on) and the rights ownership map. Read on every play, almost entirely cacheable, ~450GB replicated whole into each region.
- **Entitlement service.** Decides at every play start what this account may do: which rungs, on-demand selection or shuffle only, offline allowed, skip budget. Separate from the catalogue because it is per-account and changes on billing events rather than on content events.
- **Play-event log.** A partitioned durable log taking ~500k events/s at peak. Everything downstream reads it: the royalty archive, the training pipeline, artist analytics. Hot for 7 days, then archived in columnar form for the contractual audit window.
- **Discovery precompute.** Batch jobs that write each listener a fixed list: weekly for the main mix, Friday for new releases from followed artists, daily for the mood mixes. The request path is a key read. No model runs when the listener opens the app.
- **Royalty ledger.** A deterministic batch over the archived events that applies the 30-second rule on event time, the per-country rate, and the fractional split across recording owner, publisher and writers, producing one statement row per rights holder per period.
- **DRM and offline.** Offline downloads are the same whole objects, encrypted, plus a licence with a 30-day lease bound to device and account. This is also why an event can legitimately arrive four weeks after it happened, which is the constraint that decides the shape of the royalty pipeline.

**The thing that makes it hard, the safe choice always wins:** every measurable signal prefers familiarity. A track the listener already loves completes at over 95%, is almost never skipped, and lifts every engagement metric you can read inside a two-week experiment. An unfamiliar track completes at roughly 60% and is skipped inside 30 seconds about a third of the time. So any ranker trained on those labels, and any A/B test used to tune it, drives the system toward playing the same 40 tracks forever. The listener does not complain for months and then churns for a reason they describe as "it got boring". The cost of novelty is immediate and measurable; the benefit lands outside every experiment window you can afford to run. That asymmetry, not the CDN, is what actually makes this system hard.

**Why this design and what it costs:** the answer to that asymmetry is to stop trying to learn the novelty rate and set it as policy instead. A fixed floor on the fraction of impressions that go to unfamiliar tracks, spent in surfaces that announce themselves as discovery so the listener has consented to the risk. That buys a spend you can see on a dashboard and cap, and it keeps unrequested tracks out of playlists the listener explicitly chose. It costs the ability to claim the number is optimal: it is chosen by argument and by long-horizon holdout cohorts rather than by the experiment framework everything else uses. Anyone who says they optimised their exploration rate with a two-week test has measured its cost and none of its benefit.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Origin on an S3-compatible object store, ~4.4PB. Commercial CDN with an explicit pin API for the hot 10M tracks and a pre-push hook wired into the release calendar.
- Whole-object GET for the lossy rungs; HLS only for lossless and podcasts, selected by an object-size threshold of about 25MB declared in the manifest.
- Play events to a partitioned log keyed by `user_id`; columnar archive on object storage; the payable ledger is a nightly and then monthly batch over the archive, deduplicated on `(user_id, track_id, play_start_ts)`.
- Discovery precompute as a weekly batch; results in a replicated key-value cache, ~400GB.
- Retrieval index: HNSW over 100M track vectors, ~140GB across 8 shards, with incremental inserts for new uploads.
- Hot-path pseudocode:
  ```
  meta = catalog.get(track_id)
  rung = pick_rung(entitlement(user), measured_bandwidth, meta.rungs)
  play(stream_whole_object(edge_url(meta, rung)))   # first bytes start playback
  at(track.duration - 20s): prefetch_whole(next_in_queue)
  emit(start); at(30s) emit(qualified); on_stop emit(terminal, position)
  ```
#### What this is really testing
Whether you notice that repeat consumption inverts the recommender. Every recommendation system a candidate has practised assumes an item is consumed once and that serving it twice is a bug. Here serving it for the two-hundredth time is the product, and four things reverse at once. The exclusion filter becomes the candidate pool: what the listener has already played is the highest-value thing to play next. Completion stops being a usable label, because a familiar track completes at over 95% and carries almost no variance, so the target moves to a skip inside the first 30 seconds and to whether the track gets played again a week later. Retrieval shrinks out of the hot path, because for the surfaces carrying most listening the candidate set is one person's own history and playlists, under 10,000 rows. And the scarce resource in exploration stops being inventory and becomes the listener's patience.

The contrast is with TikTok. The two systems draw the same picture: embeddings, an approximate-nearest-neighbour index, cheap retrieval feeding an expensive ranker. They diverge on the word "again". TikTok never serves the same video twice, so the candidate set is the whole corpus and every impression must be spent on something unproven. Its scarce resource is inventory, and the arithmetic is that 100M new videos a day each need ~400 impressions to be measured, which is 40B of demand against 100B of supply. Here the catalogue grows by 60k tracks a day, it is 100 times smaller, and at 100M vectors (100GB at 256-dim float32) the index fork TikTok agonises over does not even bind: HNSW fits in RAM, where TikTok's 10B vectors is 10TB and forces quantisation. The scarce resource here is the listener's tolerance for a song they did not ask for. TikTok's hardest question is how a video with zero observations reaches anybody. This one's hardest question is how anything unfamiliar wins a slot against a track the listener already loves, when the safe choice scores higher on every metric measurable inside a two-week experiment. Both answers are "reserve a fixed fraction of impressions", and they are the same words about two different problems.

Closest question: Q28
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Free tier with ads, or subscription only?
- Offline downloads?
- Lossless tier?
- Podcasts in scope?
- Social features (follows, friend activity, collaborative playlists)?
- Royalty accounting in scope?
- What share of listening is discovery rather than repeat?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Free tier with ads | an ad-insertion path, a lower rung ceiling for free accounts, and a second royalty pool funded by ad revenue rather than subscription pro-rata |
| Offline downloads | encrypted whole objects plus a time-limited licence lease, and event lateness measured in weeks rather than seconds, which decides the royalty pipeline shape |
| Lossless tier | chunked delivery for that rung only, since a 27MB object breaks whole-object prefetch on cellular |
| Podcasts | long-form chunked objects with resume position, a separate ranking objective, and a rights path that is direct deals rather than the per-stream pool |
| Social features | a follow graph with read-time pull for friend activity, plus a private-session flag that suppresses the social echo without suppressing the royalty count |
| Royalty accounting in scope | an immutable per-play event log and a deterministic batch recomputation as the payable ledger, with the streaming aggregate demoted to dashboards |
| Mostly repeat listening | ranking a listener's own sub-10,000-track universe on the hot path, with discovery rationed onto separate offline-computed surfaces |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** play, pause, skip, queue; library and playlists; search; discovery surfaces (weekly mix, release radar, mood mixes); offline download; per-stream royalty accounting.
- **NFR:** under 300ms tap-to-first-audio at p99; under one rebuffer per 10 minutes of play; discovery surfaces present on Monday morning at 99.9%; royalty ledger reproducible to the cent from the event log.

**Scale**

- **Listeners:** ~600M MAU and ~250M subscribers (2024 reported order of magnitude). Daily actives run ~40% of monthly for a habit product: 600M × 0.40 = **~240M DAU**. Concurrency peaks on the Friday-evening overlap of European and US prime time at roughly 12% of DAU streaming at once: 240M × 0.12 = **~29M concurrent streams**.
- **Catalogue:** ~100M tracks, growing ~60k/day. Average duration ~4min = 240s (pop skews to 3.5min, classical and electronic pull it up).
- **Bytes per track:** the bitrate *is* the compressed rate, so size is bitrate × duration / 8. 96kbps → 96,000 × 240 / 8 = **2.9MB**; 160kbps → **4.8MB**; 320kbps → **9.6MB**; lossless at ~900kbps → **27MB**. All four rungs = **~44MB/track**.
- **Origin:** 100M × 44MB = **~4.4PB**. Lossy rungs only: 100M × 17.3MB = **~1.7PB**.
- **Edge working set:** plays follow a steep Pareto, with the top 10% of tracks taking ~90% of plays. An edge pins the two mainstream rungs for the top 10M tracks: 10M × 14.4MB = **~144TB**, one storage node. The top 1% at those rungs is 1M × 14.4MB = **~14TB**, which fits in any PoP including small ones. A single 4K film is ~15GB, so this whole line has no analogue in video.
- **Device cache:** a phone with 4GB free at 160kbps holds 4GB / 4.8MB = **~830 tracks**. A heavy listener's active rotation is a few hundred tracks, so the device is the highest-hit-rate tier in the system, and it exists only because the objects are small and the same ones recur.
- **Catalogue metadata:** 100M × ~1.5KB (title 64B + artist ids 80B + album id 16B + duration 4B + ISRC 16B + four rung pointers 256B + tags 200B + audio features 500B + envelope) = **~150GB**; RF=3 → **~450GB**. Small enough to hold a full replica in every region, which removes a cross-region hop from the play path.
- **Plays:** 240M DAU × 2.5h listening / 4min per track ≈ 37, round to **~35 plays/DAU/day**. 240M × 35 = **~8.4B plays/day**.
- **Play events:** each play emits a `start`, a `qualified` marker at 30s, and a terminal event; skips under 30s emit two. ~2.2 events per play. 8.4B × 2.2 = **~18B events/day**. 18B / 86,400 = **~210k/s average**; evening peak at ~2.5x = **~500k/s peak**.
- **Event bytes:** ~150B (user_id 16B + track_id 16B + session_id 16B + type 1B + played_at 8B + position 4B + country 2B + device 16B + rung 1B + surface 2B + envelope ~70B). 18B × 150B = **~2.7TB/day raw**; RF=3 → **~8TB/day** on the log.
- **Royalty archive:** the same events in columnar form with dictionary encoding on track_id, country and device compress ~8x: 2.7TB / 8 = **~340GB/day**. Over a seven-year contractual audit window, 340GB × 365 × 7 = **~870TB**, call it **~1PB**. Retention is cheap; the constraint is that the archive stays deterministically re-runnable, not that it is large.
- **Repeat ratio:** first hears arrive at roughly 200/month per listener (30 from the weekly mix, 30 from release radar, ~140 from radio, autoplay tails, search and shares) against 35 × 30 = 1,050 monthly plays, so **~19% first hear, ~81% repeat**. That one ratio is the reason this design differs from a video feed.
- **Common-case candidate set:** a listener's saved library plus playlists plus followed artists' recent releases is **under 10,000 tracks** for the large majority, so the dominant surfaces rank ~10⁴ rows, not 10⁸.
- **Embeddings:** 100M tracks × 256 dims × 4B = **~100GB**; HNSW graph overhead ~40% gives ~140GB across **8 shards of ~18GB**, comfortably in RAM. Listener vectors: 400M weekly actives × 1KB = **~400GB**, refreshed daily.
- **Discovery precompute:** 400M weekly actives × 30 entries × ~32B (track_id 16B + score 4B + reason code 2B + rank 1B + envelope) ≈ 400M × 1KB = **~400GB**, replicated to regional caches. URLs and metadata are hydrated from the catalogue at read time rather than stored per listener, which is what keeps this at hundreds of gigabytes instead of tens of terabytes.
- **CDN egress:** average bytes actually delivered over the network per play sit below the full object because of skips and device-cache hits; assume ~4MB. 8.4B × 4MB = **~34PB/day** = 34PB / 86,400 = **~390GB/s average**, peak ~2x = **~780GB/s**. Cross-check by the other route: 29M concurrent × ~200kbps blended rung = 5.8Tbps = **~725GB/s**, the same order, so the two derivations agree. Origin sees only the misses: at a 97% edge hit ratio, 780GB/s × 0.03 = **~23GB/s**.
#### Key decisions
**Whole-object delivery against chunked adaptive streaming**
- Choice: pick a rung once at track start, fetch the track as one range-able object, and prefetch the entire next track about 20 seconds before the current one ends. Chunk only where the object is large: lossless (~27MB for four minutes) and podcasts (60MB+ for an hour).
- Alternative: HLS or DASH throughout, ~10-second segments, with mid-track bitrate switching exactly as a video service does it.
- Decider: object size against how much you are willing to download speculatively. A 160kbps four-minute track is 4.8MB; on a 5Mbps connection that is under 8 seconds, so the whole file has landed inside the first 3% of playback and mid-track adaptation has nothing left to adapt to. Video cannot do this because a two-hour title is 5 to 15GB. The threshold sits around 25MB, above which you are speculatively spending bandwidth on something the listener may skip past.
- Alternative wins when: the rung is lossless, the content is long-form, or the market is one where a wasted 5MB is a real cost to the listener, which is a metered-data question rather than an engineering one. The two are not exclusive and the production answer is a size threshold rather than a protocol allegiance: the manifest declares the delivery mode per object, and the client already implements both because podcasts are in the catalogue.

**What counts as a training label when the same track recurs**
- Choice: skip-before-30-seconds is the negative, repeat-play-within-7-days is the positive. Completion is recorded and is not the target.
- Alternative: predicted play-completion probability, the objective every video recommender uses.
- Decider: base rates. A familiar track completes at ~95%, a first hear at ~60%, and 80% of impressions are familiar, so the blended completion rate sits near 88% and almost all its variance comes from the 20% of impressions that are first hears. Optimising it trains a model to predict familiarity, which the listener's own history already tells you for free. Skip-before-30s has a base rate near 15%, and being the royalty threshold it is already computed exactly on the money path, so it costs nothing extra to emit.
- Alternative wins when: the surface is exclusively first hears. Inside the weekly discovery mix every track is unfamiliar by construction, repeat has had no time to happen, and completion is the sharpest signal available. That makes this a per-surface choice rather than a global one, and running two objectives on two surfaces is the honest answer rather than a compromise.

**Where the payable royalty number comes from**
- Choice: the monthly ledger is a deterministic batch recomputation over the immutable archived events, deduplicated on `(user_id, track_id, play_start_ts)`. The streaming aggregation exists, is at-least-once, feeds artist dashboards and anomaly alerts, and pays nobody.
- Alternative: one exactly-once streaming pipeline (transactional producer plus checkpointed operator state) whose output is the ledger.
- Decider: how late a legitimate event can be. Offline licences run 30 days, so a play with an event time of the 3rd can legitimately arrive on the 30th. A window that must tolerate 30 days of lateness is a batch job with a watermark bolted onto it, and holding streaming state open for a month costs more than recomputing the month. The second half is scope: exactly-once in a stream processor means exactly-once *inside the processor*, not from a retrying mobile client, so the client-supplied dedup key is doing the real work in both designs.
- Alternative wins when: there is no offline mode and the p99.9 of event lateness is minutes, or the business genuinely needs payable numbers hourly. Neither holds when payouts are monthly. Where the alternative is genuinely stronger is operational simplicity: one pipeline instead of two, and no risk of the dashboard and the statement telling an artist two different numbers, which they will notice and will ask about.
#### High-level design
**must-say**

**How to read the diagram:** three paths leave the catalogue and never meet again. Playback moves bytes, recommendation decides order, royalty counts money. The only thing they share is the play-event log, and everything difficult about the system is a consequence of one event being read by three consumers with incompatible requirements.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** the three have opposite failure tolerances. Playback may drop an event and nobody notices. Recommendation may drop a thousand and nobody notices. The ledger may not drop one, ever, and must be able to prove it years later. Pushing all three through one pipeline forces the loosest consumer to pay the ledger's correctness cost and, worse, tempts you into making the ledger depend on a pipeline nobody can audit.

**What this layout buys you:** each consumer picks its own delivery semantics off a shared immutable log. The cost is that the log's schema is now a contract three teams depend on, and an event field added for ranking is an event field the royalty batch will be asked about in an audit.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Recommending into a stream that is already mostly repeats.**

Start with the ratio, because it decides what the machinery is for. An active listener plays ~35 tracks a day. First hears arrive at roughly 200 a month across every surface: 30 from the weekly mix, 30 from release radar, and ~140 from radio, autoplay tails, search and shares. Against 1,050 monthly plays that is 19% unfamiliar, 81% repeat. So the pipeline below, which is what most candidates spend the whole interview on, decides under a fifth of the plays, and the weekly mix alone decides about 3%.
