The other four fifths need no model at all. A listener's realistic universe is their saved library, their playlists and the artists they follow: under 10,000 tracks for almost everyone, a few hundred kilobytes of rows. Ordering that is a scan with a scoring function over recency, lifetime play count, time of day and what is already queued. No vector index on that path, no candidate generation, no accelerator fleet. Saying this out loud early is worth more than any detail that follows it, because it is the sizing decision that keeps the recommendation tier at a few hundred hosts rather than a few thousand.

**The budget, and why it is concentrated.** Novelty is spent, not maximised. Fix the rate as an explicit policy number, roughly 15 to 20% of impressions, then decide where to spend it. Spreading it uniformly puts one unfamiliar track in every five inside playlists the listener deliberately chose, which is the most reliable way to make someone abandon a playlist. Concentrating the same spend into a small number of surfaces that announce themselves as discovery attaches consent to it: 30 tracks on a Monday that the listener opened on purpose. The arithmetic is identical either way, 200 first hears a month. The difference is entirely in expectation-setting, which is why this is a product decision that the architecture then has to serve rather than the reverse.

**Retrieval, and why the hard index question does not arise.** Three sources feed the candidate pool, for the reason Q28 sets out: no single source covers every data regime. Collaborative filtering over the (listener, track) matrix produces embeddings and is strongest where a track already has plays. An audio encoder over mel-spectrograms produces a vector for a track uploaded four minutes ago, which is the only path by which 60,000 daily uploads become reachable at all. A text model over editorial writing, reviews and playlist titles carries the cultural context neither of the other two can see, which is what lets "sounds nothing alike but belongs in the same room" work.

Index sizing is where music separates from video. 100M tracks at 256 dimensions and float32 is 100M × 1KB = 100GB, plus roughly 40% graph overhead, so ~140GB across 8 shards. HNSW fits in RAM and you simply take its recall. Q28 runs the same funnel over 10B vectors, which is 10TB, and that is what forces product quantisation and its recall loss there. The fork is real; it does not bind two orders of magnitude smaller. Say that explicitly rather than reciting the comparison, because a candidate who recites the HNSW-versus-IVF-PQ table here has not checked whether the constraint applies. (Recall and memory figures track the ann-benchmarks results as of 2024; both index families are actively researched, so quote the mechanism rather than the percentages.)

**Cold start is the easy half here.** A new track has no plays, so collaborative filtering has nothing, but the audio embedding exists from the moment of upload and places it near tracks that sound similar, and release radar routes it to people who already follow the artist. Both work, and neither is exotic. The genuinely hard case is the opposite one and it is specific to this product: a track the listener heard once, three years ago, and would love again. Collaborative filtering sees a play and reads it as satisfied demand. Nothing in retrieval distinguishes "exhausted" from "due for revival", and the feature that expresses the difference, time-since-last-play crossed with lifetime play count, has to be handed to the ranker deliberately because no embedding encodes it.

**Sequence, not only taste.** A single taste vector is a poor summary of a person who runs to one thing and cooks to another. The cheap fix that earns most of the benefit is to condition on the current queue rather than on the profile: the last five tracks predict the next one far better than a 90-day average does. That runs client-side on a small model over the session, which also removes a network round trip from the autoplay path, and it degrades gracefully because the fallback is the server-computed list already sitting on the device.

**The failure mode this creates.** A ranker trained on repeat plays learns that the safest prediction is whatever the listener plays most, and every metric available inside a two-week experiment agrees with it. Left alone the system converges on a rotation of 40 tracks. Two guards, neither satisfying: a hard floor on the novelty rate that no model output may override, and a per-track exposure cap so one hit cannot occupy the same slot in millions of surfaces for a week. Both are policy constants chosen by argument rather than by measurement, for the reason in the first Unresolved item below.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Coordinated midnight release.** Every active listener requests the same object within minutes. The saving grace is size: 9.6MB at 320kbps, 4.8MB at 160, so pre-pushing a whole album to every edge before release is a few hundred megabytes and takes seconds. *Mitigation:* wire pre-push into the release calendar so scheduled releases are never a cold start. For unscheduled virality the edge fills on the first miss and serves everything after, so the herd costs one origin fetch per edge per rung, not one per listener. Origin is sized from the miss rate, not the play rate: 780GB/s of peak delivery at a 97% hit ratio is ~23GB/s at origin. What actually saturates first at midnight is the catalogue and entitlement read path, not the bytes.
- **Shuffle defeats prefetch.** The device cache is the highest-hit-rate tier and it only helps when the next track is predictable. A listener shuffling a 5,000-track playlist turns every track into a network fetch and collapses the cache hit rate toward zero. *Mitigation:* resolve the shuffle order server-side for the next N tracks and ship it with the queue, so the client knows what to prefetch. Shuffle in practice is a seeded permutation delivered ahead of time, not a random draw at play time.
- **Royalty archive determinism.** The ledger is only as good as the archive's ability to be re-run. A schema change, a rate table updated in place, or a rights correction that overwrites history all silently change what a rerun produces. *Mitigation:* rate tables and rights maps are versioned and effective-dated, and the batch takes the version as an input, so re-running last March uses last March's rates. A rerun that disagrees with the original run is an incident, not a correction.
- **Long-tail storage growth.** 60k tracks/day × 44MB = **2.6TB/day** of eager encoding, ~1PB/year, most of which never plays. *Mitigation:* generate only the 160kbps rung eagerly for tracks with no plays and transcode the other rungs on first request, which cuts eager growth to 60k × 4.8MB = ~0.3TB/day. The cost is a few hundred milliseconds on the very first play of a long-tail track at a non-default rung, which is the right trade because that play is rare by definition.
- **Vector index freshness.** 60k tracks/day must become retrievable quickly or release radar misses Friday. *Mitigation:* HNSW takes incremental inserts cheaply, which is the main operational reason to prefer it here beyond the memory sizing; new tracks enter the live graph within minutes, with a weekly full rebuild to control graph degradation.
- **Recommendation cold start for a new listener.** No history, so both the repeat path and collaborative filtering have nothing. *Mitigation:* onboarding picks seed a coarse profile, blended with region and age-band popularity priors, switching to personalised ranking at ~50 plays. The repeat path bootstraps fastest, because those first 50 plays immediately become the candidate pool that carries 80% of everything afterwards.
- **Event lateness from offline playback.** A device offline for three weeks uploads three weeks of events at once. *Mitigation:* because the ledger is a batch, lateness costs nothing structurally: events land in the archive with their event time and the affected period is recomputed if still open, or credited forward with a statement note if closed. The streaming aggregate does drift, so per-source watermarks stop one late device stalling the dashboard for everyone, and the dashboard is labelled provisional.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| CDN edge | Cold miss on a scheduled release; origin egress spikes | Origin egress alarm; edge hit-ratio drop | Pre-push whole objects to every edge from the release calendar; size origin for the 3% miss rate (~23GB/s at peak) rather than for play volume |
| Catalogue service | Metadata lookup unavailable; play start blocked | Per-track lookup p99 and error rate | Client caches metadata for everything in the queue for 24h; whole-catalogue read replicas per region at 450GB; degrade to playing tracks already resident on the device |
| Entitlement service | Cannot decide what the account may play | Entitlement p99; reject-rate anomaly | Fail to the last known entitlement cached on device with a short TTL, because briefly over-serving a paid rung is cheaper than blocking playback |
| Licence server | Offline licences cannot be issued or renewed | Issue error rate per region | The 30-day lease makes transient outages invisible; renewal is attempted from day 20, so there are ten days of slack before any listener is affected |
| Play-event log | Broker partition unavailable | Producer enqueue lag; ISR shrink | Clients buffer locally and replay, which the offline path already requires; multi-region mirroring; the archive rather than the stream is the ledger, so an outage delays dashboards and not payouts |
| Royalty batch | A rerun produces a different total than the original run | Rerun diff against the paid period | Effective-dated rate and rights tables passed as explicit batch inputs; any nonzero diff blocks payout and opens an incident |
| Discovery cache | Weekly mix cache cold on Monday morning | Hit-ratio collapse; surface render time | Precompute Sunday and replicate to every regional cache before the Monday wave; on a miss serve last week's list, since a stale mix beats an empty surface |
| Vector index | Shard offline, or embedding versions skewed across shards | Per-shard query p99; embedding version counter | Replicated shards with fan-out and top-K merge; degrade discovery to popularity-within-genre, which is visibly worse and still a product |
| Device cache | Shuffle defeats prefetch; rebuffering on weak networks | Rebuffer rate segmented by shuffle on/off | Server-resolved shuffle order so the client can prefetch; step down a rung before rebuffering rather than after |

**Unresolved**

**The novelty rate cannot be optimised by any experiment we can afford to run.** A skip today is measurable. The value of having introduced someone to an artist they will play for the next three years is not attributable to the session that introduced them, and it lands far outside any test window. So every online metric penalises novelty: its cost is inside the window and its benefit is outside it. We hold the exploration rate as a fixed policy constant rather than a tuned parameter, which is an admission that we cannot tune it. The only honest instrument is a long-horizon holdout, a cohort held at zero novelty for six months, and that is slow, expensive, and ethically uncomfortable because it deliberately degrades a real cohort's product for half a year to measure a number. We run a small one. It is underpowered, and we would not defend the specific value of 15 to 20% on evidence, only the decision to make it a visible constant rather than an emergent one.

**Royalty correctness is bounded by the client, not by the pipeline.** Everything downstream of ingest is reconcilable: the log is immutable, the batch is deterministic, the dedup key is stable, and the rerun diff proves it. What none of that verifies is whether a reported play happened. The event is produced by a client we ship but do not control on a rooted device or an emulator, and a farm playing tracks on real accounts with real subscriptions and real licences generates events indistinguishable from a listener at the event level. Detection is statistical at the account and payee level, which means we catch the crude and pay the careful, and the fraction we pay is unknown by construction because there is no ground truth to measure a false-negative rate against. This also interacts badly with the batch-as-ledger decision above: excluding suspect plays after a period has been paid means restating a period, and rights holders reconcile against statements they have already booked, so in practice fraud found late is netted off a future period rather than corrected where it occurred.

**The count is exact and the split is not, and the split is where the money is.** The pipeline treats the rights table as authoritative. It is not. Recording ownership is usually clean; composition ownership is asserted by publishers and collecting societies, arrives incomplete for a meaningful share of the catalogue, and is revised retroactively, sometimes years later, sometimes as the outcome of litigation we are not party to. We hold a reserve against unmatched compositions and true up as claims resolve, which means our own books carry a liability of unknown size against streams we counted perfectly. No amount of exactly-once machinery in the aggregator touches this, and a candidate who says the royalty path is "solved" by exactly-once semantics has solved the smaller half of it.
#### Drill questions
1. How does a discovery surface work for a brand new listener with no history?
2. Ten million listeners hit play on the same new release at midnight. What fails first?
3. How do you compute royalties for streams that cross a billing-period boundary?
4. A listener plays a song for 5 seconds, then 5 seconds again. Does that count?
5. Offline mode: what stops a listener copying the encrypted file off the device?
6. How do you stop play farms inflating royalties?
7. Two-stage retrieval plus ranker: why not one big model?
8. How does the system stay fresh between weekly batches?
9. Four plays in five are repeats. What does that do to your training label and your exclusion filter?
10. Why not chunked adaptive streaming for music, the way video does it?
11. Your streaming aggregate and your monthly batch disagree by 0.3%. Which one pays, and what do you do?
12. A listener is offline for three weeks on a long trip. What breaks?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Onboarding artist and genre picks seed a coarse profile, blended with region and age-band popularity priors, switching to personalised ranking at ~50 plays. The repeat path bootstraps fastest, because those first 50 plays immediately become the candidate pool that carries 80% of subsequent listening. *If pushed:* the harder cold start is not the new listener but the returning one whose taste moved while they were away. A stale profile is worse than no profile, so decay the embedding on inactivity rather than preserving it intact.

2. Not the bytes, and that is the point. The object is 9.6MB at 320kbps, so pre-pushing the album to every edge before midnight is a few hundred megabytes. Even without pre-push, each edge takes one origin fetch per rung and serves everything after it, so origin sees thousands of requests rather than ten million. *If pushed:* what saturates first is the catalogue and entitlement read path, ten million clients calling `GET /track` inside sixty seconds. That is an admission-control and caching problem, and the fix is a jittered release-visibility window plus an edge-cached catalogue response, not more origin bandwidth.

3. Every event carries `played_at`, never arrival time. Period boundaries are resolved by the batch: March's ledger is a recomputation over every archived event whose event time falls in March, run after a cutoff long enough to have collected the offline stragglers. *If pushed:* events arriving after a period is paid are credited to the next period with an explanatory line on the statement. Under-counting one month and over-counting the next is acceptable; restating a paid period is not, because rights holders have already booked the statement.

4. No. The threshold is 30 contiguous seconds, applied on event time inside the ledger rather than in the UI. Two 5-second plays are two skips, and they are useful negative labels for the ranker. *If pushed:* the abuse vector runs the other way, a track looped all night. Royalty calculation caps streams counted per listener per track per day, typically around one, and the cap is applied in the batch where it can be re-run rather than at ingest where it would destroy the raw signal the ranker needs.

5. The downloaded object is encrypted and useless without a licence bound to device and account, leased for 30 days and renewed automatically from day 20 on any connection. *If pushed:* this is deterrence, not proof. Anyone determined will capture decoded audio at the output stage, and that is accepted. The licence exists to make casual copying pointless and to make revocation possible on a lost device or a cancelled subscription.

6. Behavioural detection at the account and payee level: uniform inter-play timing, plays concentrated on one payee's catalogue, IP and device clustering, and a ratio between plays and every other product action that no real listener produces. Suspect plays are excluded before the ledger runs. *If pushed:* concede the shape. A farm on real accounts with real subscriptions produces events indistinguishable from a listener at the event level, so detection is statistical and there is no ground truth against which to measure the false-negative rate. The honest position is that the caught fraction is unknown.

7. Scoring every listener against every track is 400M × 100M = 4×10¹⁶ evaluations per refresh. Retrieval narrows to a few hundred candidates with cheap vector arithmetic and a richer model scores those; Q28 covers the pattern in full. *If pushed:* what differs here is scale, and it makes the classic index fork disappear. 100M vectors at 256-dim float32 is 100GB, so HNSW fits in RAM and you take its recall, where Q28's 10B vectors is 10TB and forces quantisation. Note also that this funnel only serves the ~19% of plays that are first hears.

8. Different surfaces on different cadences. The weekly mix is deliberately weekly, because being an event is part of what it is. Mood mixes recompute daily from a shorter window. Release radar is event-driven off the follow graph. Within a session, a small on-device model reorders the next few tracks from the last five plays with no server round trip. *If pushed:* recomputing everything continuously is not merely expensive, it is wrong for this product. A weekly mix that changes when you refresh stops being a thing you can talk to a friend about, and that is a substantial part of why it works.

9. Both flip. The exclusion filter becomes the candidate pool: what the listener has already played is the highest-value thing to play next, the reverse of every video feed. And completion stops being a usable target, because a familiar track completes at ~95% against ~60% for a first hear and 80% of impressions are familiar, so nearly all the variance in the blended rate comes from a fifth of the data and the model mostly learns to predict familiarity. Train on skip-before-30s as the negative and repeat-within-7-days as the positive. *If pushed:* keep completion as the objective on the discovery surfaces specifically, where every track is unfamiliar by construction and completion is the sharpest signal available. Two objectives on two surfaces is correct here, not a compromise.

10. Because the object is 4.8MB. On a 5Mbps connection the whole file arrives in under 8 seconds, so mid-track bitrate adaptation has nothing left to adapt: the decision was made and executed inside the first 3% of playback. Chunking buys the ability to change your mind partway through an object you cannot buffer, which matters at 10GB and does not at 5MB. *If pushed:* the real rule is an object-size threshold around 25MB, declared per object in the manifest, not a protocol allegiance. Lossless at 27MB and podcasts at 60MB+ get chunked delivery from the same client, which is why the manifest carries the delivery mode.

11. The batch pays. The streaming aggregate is at-least-once and is labelled provisional on artist dashboards for exactly this reason. A 0.3% gap is large enough to chase before it becomes a support conversation, and the usual causes are late offline events the stream never saw, duplicate delivery the stream did not dedupe, and a fraud exclusion applied only in the batch. *If pushed:* what you must never do is reconcile by adjusting the batch to match the stream. The batch is deterministic over an immutable log, so if it is wrong then either the input or the code is wrong and both are inspectable, whereas the stream's state is a checkpoint nobody can audit after the fact.

12. Three things, in increasing order of how much they matter. Licences: the 30-day lease covers it, with renewal attempted from day 20, so a 21-day trip is inside the slack and a 35-day one is not. Royalty: events land in the archive with correct event times, and any period already paid gets those plays credited forward. Recommendation: three weeks of listening arrive at once with old event times, and a training pipeline that windows on arrival time will treat three weeks of behaviour as a single day and badly distort the profile. *If pushed:* the recommendation case is the one people miss. Anything windowed by arrival time is wrong for this product, and offline playback is the reason. Use event time everywhere and accept that a profile can be updated with three-week-old evidence.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, state the two facts and take the fork.** Do not open with boxes. Open with "a track is five megabytes and four plays in five are repeats", and say what each one collapses: the first makes delivery a caching problem, the second inverts the recommender. Then ask the two clarifiers that actually change the design: is there a lossless tier or are podcasts in scope, which decides whether delivery is whole-object or chunked; and is royalty accounting in scope, which decides whether there is a ledger at all. State your numbers out loud: 600M monthly, 240M daily, 100M tracks, 8.4B plays a day, 18B events a day.

**5-15, the spine.** Five boxes: client, catalogue plus entitlement, edge cache over object origin, the play-event log, and two consumers hanging off the log (the ledger and the training pipeline). Draw the prefetch arrow explicitly and say it fetches the *whole* next track, because that single arrow carries the entire delivery argument. Say the edge working set out loud: top 10M tracks, two rungs, 144TB, one storage node. Do not draw the recommendation funnel yet.

**15-35, the drill.** Spend it on the recommender, because that is where the question lives. Open with the ratio: 80% repeat, so the funnel you are about to draw decides a fifth of the plays and the weekly mix decides about 3%. Then the four fifths: a listener's universe is under 10,000 tracks and ranking it is a scan, with no index on the hot path. Then the funnel, three retrieval sources, and note explicitly that at 100M vectors the HNSW-versus-quantised fork does not bind, unlike the 10B-vector case. Then the label argument, which is the strongest thing you have: completion is useless when 80% of impressions complete, so the target is skip-before-30s and repeat-within-7-days. If time remains, the ledger: a batch over an immutable log, event time, the 30-second rule, and versioned rate and rights tables.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the three gaps before they are found: the novelty rate cannot be optimised by any experiment you can afford to run, fraud detection has no ground truth so the caught fraction is unknown, and the rights split is asserted by third parties and revised retroactively, so the pipeline is exact on the count and approximate on the money. Then the operational surface in two minutes: what you page on (time to first audio, rebuffer rate segmented by shuffle, edge hit ratio, ledger rerun diff, Monday discovery cache hit rate) and DR as whole-catalogue regional replicas, which is affordable precisely because the catalogue metadata is 450GB.

Cut first: the ad-insertion path and the free-tier feature matrix, then podcasts, then social features and collaborative playlists. All three are real product surface and none of them changes the architecture. Never cut: the repeat ratio and what it does to the label, the whole-object delivery argument, and the fact that the ledger is a batch rather than the stream.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **tracks:** `(track_id, isrc, title, artist_ids[], album_id, duration_ms, rungs{bitrate → object_key, bytes}, audio_features, tags[])`. ~1.5KB/row, 100M rows, replicated whole per region.
- **rights:** `(isrc, effective_from, effective_to, holders[{holder_id, role, share}])`. Effective-dated and never updated in place, because the royalty batch takes the version as an input.
- **playlists:** `(playlist_id, owner_id, entries[{track_id, position_key}], collaborators[], visibility)`. Positions are fractional keys so two collaborators inserting at the same spot do not collide.
- **library** (per listener): saved tracks, albums and artists, plus `(track_id, play_count, last_played_at)`, which is the feature that separates "exhausted" from "due for revival".
- **play_events:** `(user_id, track_id, session_id, type, played_at, position_ms, country, device, rung, surface)`. Append-only, partitioned by `user_id`, archived in columnar form.
- **discovery:** `(user_id, surface, generated_at, entries[{track_id, score, reason}])`, ~1KB per listener per surface.
- **embeddings:** track vectors in an HNSW index (100M × 256 × 4B); listener vectors in a key-value store.

**API contract**

```
GET  /search?q=...
GET  /track/{id}                  -> metadata + entitlement + per-rung edge URLs
GET  /track/{id}/audio?rung=160   -> whole object (range-able); HLS manifest above 25MB
GET  /queue/next?context=...      -> next N track ids, resolved shuffle order included
GET  /discovery/{surface}         -> precomputed list, key read
POST /events                      body: [{ track_id, type, played_at, position_ms, ... }]
POST /offline/license             body: { track_ids[], device_id } -> 30-day lease
```

`POST /events` takes batches because the offline path has to upload weeks at once, and every event carries its own `played_at` so the server never infers time from arrival.

**Observability**

- **Time to first audio, p99.** Tap to first decoded sample, SLO under 300ms. The latency listeners actually feel.
- **Rebuffers per 10 minutes of play, segmented by shuffle on/off.** Shuffle defeats prefetch, so an unsegmented number hides the one case that is genuinely bad.
- **Edge hit ratio, hot catalogue against long tail.** SLO above 97% hot, above 80% tail. Origin capacity is sized from this number rather than from play volume.
- **Ledger rerun diff.** Recompute a closed period and diff it against what was paid. SLO exactly zero; anything nonzero means the batch is not deterministic, which is an incident rather than a rounding difference.
- **Stream-against-batch gap.** How far the provisional dashboard sits from the payable number. Expect under 0.1%; a widening gap usually means duplicate delivery or a fraud rule only one side applies.
- **Novelty rate actually served.** The fraction of impressions going to tracks the listener has never played. It is a policy constant, so drift in the served value means a model is overriding policy.
- **Discovery cache hit rate on Monday morning, plus payload age.** SLO above 99.9% with age under 7 days.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication:** catalogue and rights replicated whole into every region, affordable at ~450GB and worth it because it removes a cross-region hop from the play path. Audio origin is multi-region behind edge caches. The play-event log is mirrored across regions. The royalty batch runs in one canonical region over the archive; discovery precompute is centralised with its output replicated to regional caches.
- **RTO:** seconds for edge failover, since the next edge simply misses and fills. Minutes for catalogue and entitlement, which are read-mostly replicas. Hours is acceptable for the royalty batch, because nothing user-facing depends on it.
- **RPO:** zero for audio, which is immutable content. For play events, zero in practice rather than by construction, because clients buffer and replay, which the offline path already requires, so a log outage delays events rather than losing them. For the ledger, zero, enforced by the rerun diff rather than by replication.
- **Failover cadence:** automatic for edges; quarterly game days for the event log; a rehearsed annual drill for the royalty batch, the only path whose failure is financial rather than experiential.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by edge egress at ~780GB/s peak. Everything else is small: 450GB of catalogue, ~8TB/day of event mirroring, and ~1PB for the whole seven-year archive.

### 41. Design a Stock Price Notification System
#### Problem
Let users subscribe to price rules on financial instruments ("AAPL crosses above $200", "BTC drops 5% in 1h") and deliver a push or email alert within seconds of the condition firing. Broker scale: millions of users, tens of thousands of instruments, hundreds of thousands of price ticks a second.
#### Core
This is a predicate matching problem wearing a notification costume. Ten million standing rules, fifty thousand instruments, a quarter of a million ticks a second: the only question that matters is how a tick finds the handful of rules it could trigger without touching the other ten million.

The answer is to invert the loop. Do not iterate rules and look up prices; that costs one lookup per rule per poll and floors latency at the poll interval. Iterate ticks and look up rules. Route the tick stream by instrument so each evaluator process owns a fixed set of instruments, and keep those instruments' rules in that same process's memory. At roughly 500 bytes a rule, all 10M rules are about 5GB, so they fit across sixteen shards with room to spare. Inside a shard, hold the threshold rules sorted by trigger price, so a tick moving AAPL from 199.95 to 200.05 range-scans only the rules whose threshold lies in that interval rather than scanning every AAPL rule.

Two correctness details do most of the remaining work. Fire on the crossing, not the level: `prev < 200 && now >= 200`, or every subsequent tick above 200 refires. And carry an arm epoch on each rule that increments when it re-arms, so a tick replayed after a crash produces a fired event the dispatcher recognises as a duplicate and drops.

Everything downstream is an ordinary notification pipeline and it is the easy half. The hard half is one instrument holding 500,000 rules and moving 8% in a minute.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a trading floor with 50,000 price boards, each flickering every second. Millions of customers have pinned sticky notes to boards: "call me when AAPL crosses $220", "text me if BTC drops 5% in an hour". The job is to watch every board and honour every note, at 250,000 board updates a second. One employee rescanning all 10 million notes on every flicker is obviously wrong. Assign boards to employees instead: each one owns a set of boards and has already copied that set's notes into their own notebook, sorted by price. When a board moves from 199.95 to 200.05, the responsible employee reads only the notes filed between those two numbers.

**The approaches people actually take:**

Strip the delivery layer away and the question is how you evaluate ten million standing predicates against a quarter of a million events per second.

*Re-evaluate everything on a timer.* Every minute, walk the rule table, fetch each rule's instrument price, compare. Trivial to build and to reason about, and genuinely correct while you have tens of thousands of rules and a tolerance measured in minutes. Its cost scales with the number of rules rather than the number of price changes, which is backwards once rules outnumber ticks, and the poll interval is a hard floor under latency.

*Wake only the rules a tick could touch.* Route rules and ticks by instrument so the process receiving an instrument's ticks already holds that instrument's rules, then order those rules by trigger price so a move from 199.95 to 200.05 examines only the rules sitting in that interval. Cost now scales with ticks and with rules actually crossed, not with rules held. This is the standard answer above a few hundred thousand rules, and it buys single-digit-millisecond evaluation.

*Index the price line itself.* The same idea taken further: a rule is a point or a range on the price axis, so a price move is a range query, and structures built for that (interval trees, segment trees over bucketed price levels) handle two-sided rules and bulk reloads naturally. Worth the machinery when many rules are two-sided bands. Overkill when 80% of rules are one-sided crosses that a sorted list already serves.

**The single-request walkthrough:** AAPL is trading around $199. A tick arrives from the exchange feed: `{ instrument: "AAPL", price: 200.05, ts: "14:32:01.342", seq: 10422 }`. The gateway drops it if it has already seen `(AAPL, seq 10422)` from the second vendor, stamps an ingest timestamp, encodes it in a compact binary format rather than JSON (at 250k ticks/s, 100 wasted bytes per tick is 25MB/s of pure overhead), and puts it on the tick stream. Ticks are routed by instrument, so every AAPL tick reaches the same evaluator process, and that process already holds AAPL's state: `last_price = 199.95` and a threshold-sorted list of armed rules including `{ alert_id: "a77", user: "u42", cross_above: 200.00 }`. The evaluator range-scans the rules with thresholds in [199.95, 200.05], finds a77, confirms `prev < 200.00 <= now`, emits a fired event, and flips a77 to FIRED in local state so the next tick at $200.10 does not refire it. Tick to fired event: under 50ms. The dispatcher picks the event up, finds no `idem:a77:epoch7` key, applies u42's channels and quiet hours, records the fire against the triggering sequence number for audit, and sends the push. Tick to phone: under 3 seconds.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Market data gateway.** Receives raw feeds from exchanges and vendors, deduplicates on the exchange's own sequence numbers, normalises to one binary tick format, stamps ingest time, and publishes onto the tick stream. Also the reliability buffer: if a feed drops for 30 seconds it reconnects, pulls a price snapshot, and marks the gap so downstream knows not to trust a jump across it.
- **Partitioned tick log.** A durable append-only stream keyed by instrument, so all of an instrument's ticks land on one partition and therefore one evaluator. Retaining 24 hours lets a crashed evaluator replay from its checkpoint instead of losing market data, and gives compliance a same-day replay.
- **Rule evaluator.** A stateful stream processor holding, per instrument it owns: last price, the rules indexed by threshold, and window buffers for percent-change rules. Rules arrive from the transactional store as a change stream keyed the same way, so a new AAPL alert lands on the shard that evaluates AAPL, typically within a second. Evaluation is a local memory operation with no network hop, and it fires on the crossing edge rather than the level.
- **Alert dispatcher.** Consumes fired events, checks the idempotency key, applies user preferences and quiet hours, writes the audit record, moves the rule's durable state to FIRED, and hands off to the notification service.
- **Idempotency layer.** A short-TTL key-value store holding `idem:{alert_id}:{arm_epoch}`. The evaluator can replay ticks after a crash and re-emit a fire; the dispatcher drops the second one.

**The thing that makes it hard:** NVIDIA reports blowout earnings and NVDA jumps 8% in 60 seconds. Every rule with a threshold between the old price and the new one fires at once. Say 500,000 rules sit on NVDA. By construction they are all on one partition, handled by one process, because that is what made the cheap local lookup possible. A flat scan of 500,000 rules against 200 ticks/s is 100 million comparisons a second, which at 10ns a comparison is a fully saturated core doing nothing but compares, before deserialisation, state updates, or emitting anything. During the actual event the tick rate on that one name goes to 1,000/s, so it needs five cores that the partitioning model will not give it. Consumer lag builds, alerts land minutes late, and the move is over.

**Why this design and what it costs:** two mitigations, both with a real price. First, the threshold index. Rules sorted by trigger price turn "scan 500,000" into "range-scan [prev, now]"; a tick moving 0.01% wakes single digits instead of half a million. The cost is a sorted structure to maintain on every rule create, delete, and re-arm, and the fact that it only covers rules with a fixed numeric trigger. Second, for pathologically hot instruments, split the instrument across N sub-shards by hashing `alert_id`, publishing each tick to all N. Each sub-shard holds 1/N of the rules and CPU spreads across N cores. The cost is that the tick is now written and read N times, and last-price state has to be maintained identically in every sub-shard, so the "one owner per instrument" invariant that made this simple is gone for exactly the instruments where you can least afford confusion.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Kafka for the tick stream, partitioned by `instrument_id`. Apache Flink for evaluators, with RocksDB local state and 10-minute checkpoints to S3. Postgres as the source of truth for rules, Debezium streaming its changes onto a co-partitioned topic. Redis for the dedupe cache. The existing notification service for delivery.
- Core evaluator loop per tick:
  ```
  on tick(instrument_id, price, ts):
    prev = state.last_price.get(instrument_id)
    state.last_price[instrument_id] = price
    for alert in state.subs[instrument_id].range(prev, price):
      if alert.state == ARMED and crosses(prev, price, alert.rule):
        emit(fired_alert(alert.id, alert.arm_epoch, price, ts))
        alert.state = FIRED
  ```
- On restart: restore the Flink checkpoint and replay the tick log from its offset. Cold start with no checkpoint: load rules from Postgres, then replay. RTO target under 90 seconds.
#### What this is really testing
Whether you notice that the notification is the easy half. The system's cost is set entirely by how a price change locates the rules it could trigger. A candidate who spends the first ten minutes on push tokens, provider retries, and quiet hours has answered a different question. The insight to reach for is the inversion: stop iterating rules times price lookups, start iterating ticks times rules that could fire, then make "rules that could fire" small by ordering rules along the same axis the price moves along.

The second thing being tested is smaller and missed more often: fire on an edge, not a state. `price >= 200` is a level. A rule is a crossing.

Q7 looks like the same problem from the outside and is a different one underneath. There, the input is already one notification per recipient, and the work is fan-out and delivery: per-channel isolation so a push-provider outage does not block email, idempotency keys so a client retry does not double-send, smearing a 10M-user broadcast so you stay under a provider rate limit. Nothing in Q7 decides *whether* to notify; that decision arrived with the request. Here the decision is the entire design, and the volumes invert with it. Ten million rules produce on the order of twenty notifications a second in normal markets, which is small enough that the delivery tier is a dependency you reuse rather than a thing you design. Answer this question with Q7's answer and you get the classic failure: a beautifully isolated per-channel delivery tier fed by an evaluator that cannot keep up with NVDA.

Closest question: Q7
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- What rule types? (threshold cross, % change over window, volume spike, custom expression)
- How fresh do alerts need to be? (seconds p99, or is a minute fine?)
- Per-user subscription limit? (retail brokers: ~50 alerts/user typical)
- Fire once and disable, or re-arm after cooldown?
- Market hours only, or 24/7 (crypto)?
- Do we also show alerts in-app, or only push and email?
- Are rules allowed to reference derived data (moving average, RSI) or only raw price?
- Regulatory: audit trail required? (yes, for a broker)

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Simple threshold-cross rules | index rules by (instrument, threshold) so a tick range-queries only the rules that could fire |
| Percent-change or windowed rules | maintain per-window state (rolling reference price) per rule, scanned in full on each tick |
| Derived-data rules (moving average, RSI) | a precompute layer publishing indicator streams the evaluator subscribes to, not raw price only |
| Seconds-p99 freshness | an in-memory streaming evaluator keyed by instrument; a per-minute tolerance allows cheaper batch checks |
| Fire-once vs re-arm | a per-rule state machine (armed, fired, cooling down) so one crossing does not spam repeatedly |
| Per-user subscription cap | shard rule storage by instrument and enforce the cap at subscribe time |
| 24/7 (crypto) vs market hours | a session and calendar service gating evaluation windows per instrument |
| Audit trail required | append-only log of rule fires and deliveries for the broker's compliance |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:**
    - Users CRUD price rules on any instrument in the catalogue
    - Rule types: threshold cross (above/below), % change over window (1h/1d), volume spike
    - Fire within a few seconds of the triggering tick
    - Fire once then disarm, with optional re-arm cooldown
    - Respect user notification preferences and quiet hours
    - Audit trail of every fire with the triggering tick
- **NFR:**
    - p99 end-to-end latency, tick to push, under 5s
    - Handle 10M active rules, 50k instruments, 1M ticks/s peak
    - 99.9% of alerts delivered within SLA; no duplicate alert for the same crossing
    - Survive a market-data feed disconnect without losing armed state

**Scale**

- **Rules:** retail broker of roughly Trade Republic class, ~4M active users. Free-tier quota 50 alerts, observed average usage ~2.5 (one or two on instruments held, one or two on the watchlist). 4M × 2.5 = 10M active rules.
- **Instruments:** ~10k equities + ~5k ETFs + ~10k bonds + ~20k derivatives + ~5k crypto + ~5k FX pairs = ~55k, call it 50k tickable.
- **Rules per instrument:** 10M / 50k = 200 average, but the distribution is what matters. Heavily skewed: the top 20 names plausibly carry 5% of all rules each at peak interest, so 10M × 0.05 = 500k on a single instrument is the number to design against.
- **Tick rate, sustained:** ~5k liquid names quoting ~40 updates/s = 200k/s, plus ~45k long-tail names at ~1/s = 45k/s, so ~250k ticks/s during the EU and US overlap.
- **Tick rate, peak:** the first 60s after a US open or an ECB decision runs ~4x sustained, so ~1M ticks/s.
- **Tick rate, daily average:** 8h active at 250k/s = 8 × 3600 × 250k = 7.2B ticks, plus 16h of crypto and FX only at ~20k/s = 16 × 3600 × 20k = 1.15B. Total ~8.4B ticks/day, so 8.4B / 86400 = ~97k/s averaged over the day. Note this is well below the 250k/s sustained figure: sizing the evaluator fleet uses 250k, sizing storage uses 97k.
- **Fire rate:** if 5% of rules fire on a given day, that is 10M × 0.05 = 500k fires, almost all inside the 8h active window: 500k / 28800 = ~17/s average. The burst is what sizes the dispatcher: an index dropping 3% in ten seconds can trip 100k rules, so 100k / 10 = 10k fires/s, roughly 600x the average.
- **Rule state in memory:** ~100B of fields (ids 48B, rule type and value 12B, window 4B, state and epoch 8B, timestamps 16B, channels ~16B) plus index and object overhead (sorted-structure pointers ~32B, per-entry map and header overhead ~150B, channel list indirection ~64B, safety margin) = ~500B per rule loaded. 10M × 500B = ~5GB. Across 16 evaluator shards that is ~310MB each, comfortably in RAM alongside window buffers.
- **Tick size:** ~150B serialised (instrument_id 16B + price 8B + bid 8B + ask 8B + ts 8B + volume 4B + vendor_id 4B + exchange_seq 8B + flags 4B + schema header ~30B + padding ~52B). JSON would be 3 to 4 times larger; binary encoding is not optional at this rate.
- **Tick volume:** 8.4B/day × 150B = ~1.3TB/day logical. At replication factor 3 that is ~3.8TB/day on the hot log cluster.
- **Hot retention:** 24h of replay covers evaluator restart plus same-day audit, so ~3.8TB on SSD. Twelve brokers with 1TB SSD each sits at ~32% utilisation, which leaves headroom for a peak day.
- **Cold archive:** MiFID II requires 7 years. Columnar files on object storage with dictionary encoding on `instrument_id` and `vendor_id` and delta encoding on price and timestamp gives roughly 8x, so 1.3TB / 8 = ~160GB/day, × 365 = ~58TB/yr, × 7 = ~410TB. Tier to glacial storage after 90 days.
#### Key decisions
**Where the rules live relative to the ticks**
- Choice: co-partition. Route ticks and rule-change events by the same `instrument_id` key so an evaluator holds every rule for every instrument it consumes, and evaluate against local memory with no network call on the tick path.
- Alternative: keep rules in a shared low-latency store (Redis, Aerospike) and query per tick. Evaluators become stateless and horizontally trivial, rule changes take effect immediately rather than after change-stream lag, and rule count stops being bounded by evaluator RAM. This is a genuinely reasonable design, not a straw man.
- Decider: total rule footprint against fleet RAM, and the per-tick latency budget. 10M rules × 500B = 5GB fits in 16 shards at 310MB each. A shared store adds ~0.3ms per lookup, and 250k ticks/s of blocking lookups is 75 core-seconds of wait per wall second, which needs a large fleet purely to absorb network latency.
- Alternative wins when: rules outgrow RAM, roughly past 100M rules or 50GB, or rule churn is high enough that a 1s change-stream lag is a correctness problem (institutional clients programmatically arming and disarming rules), or you need any evaluator to answer for any instrument during a partial outage.

**Scan every rule on the instrument, or index by threshold**
- Choice: keep the fixed-threshold rules in a sorted structure per instrument and range-scan `[min(prev, now), max(prev, now)]` on each tick.
- Alternative: a flat list scanned in full per tick. No structure to maintain on create, delete, or re-arm; no pointer chasing; handles every rule type uniformly, including the windowed ones an index cannot hold anyway.
- Decider: rules on the hottest single instrument. At the 200-per-instrument average a flat scan is ~200 compares, about 0.4µs per tick, which is free. At 500k rules and 200 ticks/s it is 100M compares/s, one saturated core, and at the 1,000 ticks/s an earnings print produces it is five cores on a partition that cannot be split. The crossover is around 10k rules on one instrument.
- Alternative wins when: no instrument accumulates more than a few thousand rules, or the rule mix is dominated by windowed and expression rules that have no fixed point on the price axis to sort by, in which case the index covers a minority of the work and you pay its maintenance for little return.

**At-least-once with idempotent dispatch, or end-to-end exactly-once**
- Choice: at-least-once through the pipeline, with duplicates absorbed at the dispatcher by `{alert_id, arm_epoch}`, where the epoch increments on every re-arm.
- Alternative: transactional exactly-once from ingest through the stream processor to the sink, which removes a whole class of "why did I get two alerts" tickets and simplifies the audit story.
- Decider: the last hop. Push and email providers are plain HTTP with no transaction to enlist in, so the pipeline can be exactly-once and the user still gets two pushes; meanwhile transactional commits push evaluator checkpoint latency from tens of milliseconds into the hundreds, against a 5s end-to-end budget where the 10k/s burst is the real risk. A dedupe key costs one Redis GET per fire, at 17/s average and 10k/s peak.
- Alternative wins when: the fire triggers something that is not idempotent. A conditional order or stop-loss that places a real trade cannot be deduped after the fact, and at that point you are not building a notification system; you route it through the order path with its own transactional guarantees.

**How to read the diagram:** ticks come in at the top, rules and last-known prices live in the evaluator's local state, and fired alerts leave through a delivery pipeline at the bottom. The centre of the system is the stateful evaluator, not the notifier.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** polling every rule against every price is the thing being avoided. Routing prices and rules by the same key means the worker handling an instrument already has the rules it needs in memory when a tick arrives.

**What this layout buys you:** low-latency evaluation at very high tick volume. The tradeoff is that partitioning becomes the defining decision of the design, because the whole approach depends on the right data meeting on the same worker.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Matching a tick to the rules it can fire.** Everything else in this design exists to put the right rules in the same process as the right ticks so that this loop is a local memory operation.

Per instrument the evaluator holds three things: the last price with its timestamp, a threshold index (rules sorted by trigger price, in a skip list or balanced tree), and a flat list of rules whose trigger level is not a fixed number (percent change over a window, volume spikes). A tick runs:

```
on tick(instrument, price, ts):
  prev, prev_ts = state.last_price.get(instrument)
  state.last_price[instrument] = (price, ts)
  if prev is None or ts - prev_ts > GAP: return     # seed only, do not fire
  lo, hi = min(prev, price), max(prev, price)
  for rule in state.threshold_idx[instrument].range(lo, hi):
    if rule.state != ARMED: continue
    if rule.dir == UP   and prev <  rule.value <= price: fire(rule, price, ts)
    if rule.dir == DOWN and prev >  rule.value >= price: fire(rule, price, ts)
  for rule in state.windowed[instrument]:           # no index, full scan
    if rule.state == ARMED and rule.eval(price, ts, state.window_buf): fire(...)
```

Three things in that loop earn their place.

*The range scan.* A flat scan costs one comparison per rule on the instrument per tick. At the 200-rules-per-instrument average that is nothing: 250k ticks/s over 16 shards is ~15k ticks/s per shard, times 200 compares at ~2ns, is about 6ms of CPU per second. The index exists entirely for the tail. On NVDA with 500k rules a flat scan is 100M compares/s at 200 ticks/s, and five times that during the earnings print. With the index, a tick that moves the price 0.01% touches only the rules whose thresholds sit in that sliver, typically single digits, and the 8% earnings jump touches only the rules in that 8% band rather than all rules on the name. Range scan is O(log N + matched). Skip lists and balanced trees have had that bound since the 1970s and 1990 respectively; the choice between them here is about concurrent update cost, not asymptotics, because rules are created and re-armed while ticks are being evaluated.

*The half-open comparison.* `prev < value <= price` fires exactly once, at the moment the boundary is crossed, and still fires when a tick jumps clean over the threshold (199.00 to 201.00 on a gap open, where no tick ever lands on 200). Writing `price >= value` instead is the most common wrong answer in this question: it is a level test, so every subsequent tick above 200 refires the rule, and the user gets an alert on every tick for the rest of the session.

*The gap guard.* After a checkpoint restore, `prev` is whatever the checkpoint held, possibly ten minutes stale. Without the guard, the first tick after restore looks like one enormous price move and fires every rule between the two prices simultaneously. The same guard covers a market-data feed outage: treat the first tick after any gap beyond a few seconds as a reseed rather than a crossing. This is a deliberate choice to miss real crossings that happened during the blind window rather than to invent a crossing that did not happen, which is the right way round for a regulated broker.

**The rule state machine.** Matching is only half of correctness. Each rule is a small state machine, and `ARMED` is the only state in which a tick can fire it. A crossing moves it to `FIRED`. If the user asked for fire-once, that is terminal. If they configured a cooldown, it moves to `COOLDOWN` for the configured window, then through a brief `RE_ARMING` state (which lets the dispatcher confirm any in-flight delivery) back to `ARMED` with `arm_epoch` incremented. `DISABLED` is user-controlled pause. `STALE` is set when the feed has gapped beyond threshold, and fires from that state are tagged and suppressed.
