#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Segment-matcher CPU at weekend peak.** Matching is the only stage whose cost scales with the global segment corpus, and a 10x upload spike is a 10x CPU spike. Autoscale on Kafka consumer lag rather than CPU, because lag leads CPU by minutes; pre-warm capacity on a weekly schedule, since the spike is perfectly predictable; and shed the backfill consumer group before touching the live one. Trade-off: paying for idle capacity midweek.
- **Dense-city cell fan-out.** A level-13 cell in central London or Manhattan holds thousands of segment starts, so the prefilter returns ~80k candidates instead of ~10k and the corridor stage dominates. Adaptively descend to level 15 (~280m across) for cells above a segment-count threshold: more cells to look up, far fewer candidates. Trade-off: a per-cell level map that must stay identical across matchers.
- **Hot segment leaderboard key.** Alpe d'Huez or a popular commuter climb concentrates writes on one Redis ZSET and one `efforts` partition. Reads are absorbed by a short-TTL cache of the top 100, which is what everyone actually looks at; writes are buffered and applied in small batches, since a leaderboard being 5 seconds stale is invisible. Trade-off: the athlete's own new PR must be read-your-writes, so the response merges the buffered effort client-side.
- **Effort write amplification.** 20x the upload rate, ~16k writes/s at peak into the highest-cardinality table in the system. Batch efforts per activity into a single multi-partition write, and keep the effort row narrow (~120B) so the amplification costs rows rather than bytes. Trade-off: a partial batch failure requires the whole activity's efforts to be replayed, which the idempotent effort key makes safe.
- **Backfill floods.** One new segment on a busy road can enqueue millions of stream fetches from the object store and saturate egress. Backfill runs the funnel in reverse off a coarse `s2_cell_level11 -> [activity_id]` inverted index built at processing time (~400B/activity, ~1TB/yr), then re-runs only stages 3 and 4 on the candidates. Bound it hard: separate consumer group, hard rate limit, 24-month cap, recent activities first so the board becomes useful early. Trade-off: a complete historical leaderboard can take days.
- **Feed fan-out for pro athletes.** An athlete with ~1M followers makes fan-out-on-write expensive. The hybrid push/pull split from #8 applies unchanged, with the threshold tuned lower here because activity volume per athlete is low (~1/day, not ~20 posts/day).

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mobile recorder | App killed mid-activity; in-memory samples lost | Client-side gap detection on next launch; server-side elapsed-vs-point-count mismatch | Every sample committed to on-device SQLite in the same transaction as session state; on relaunch the app offers to resume or upload the partial activity |
| Upload | Client retries after a network drop and uploads twice | Duplicate `upload_uuid` on the uploads table | Idempotent key generated at recording start, not upload time; the second commit returns the existing `activity_id` |
| Parser | A firmware update emits a FIT variant the parser mishandles; stats silently wrong | Per-device-model outlier alert on distance and elevation distributions | Raw uploads retained 12 months; fix the parser and replay the affected `(device_model, date_range)` cohort |
| Terrain raster | Elevation tile shard unavailable; activities process with zero climb | Elevation-gain-is-zero rate per region | Fail the stage rather than emit a wrong value: park the activity in a retry topic, publish the feed entry without elevation, backfill on recovery |
| Segment matcher | Matcher node starts with a stale segment index; recent segments never match | Index-version gauge per node against the segments-table watermark | Refuse to consume until the index is within N minutes of the watermark; the version is stamped on every effort so a stale window can be replayed |
| Leaderboard cache | Redis node loss wipes the ZSETs for its slots | Key-count drop; leaderboard read miss rate | ZSETs are a cache, not the source of truth: rebuild any segment's board from a single `efforts` partition read, and serve directly from `efforts` while rebuilding |
| Privacy service | Zone lookup fails and a worker publishes an untruncated polyline | Zero-truncation-rate alarm per region; fail-closed assertion in the publish path | Fail closed: if the privacy service cannot be reached, the activity is published with no map at all and reprocessed later |
| Heatmap job | A bug lowers the effective k below threshold in one render | Pre-publish audit: sample cells and assert distinct-athlete counts | Tiles are versioned and published atomically; roll back to the previous render set via CDN origin swap |

**Unresolved**

**Privacy zones reduce the leak, they do not close it.** The naive design, hiding every point within R metres of home, leaks the home outright: the visible endpoints all lie on a circle of radius R around the house, three points determine a circle, and a dozen published rides fit the centre to within metres. Randomising R per activity does not help, because the endpoints then fill an annulus with the same centre. The working version truncates by distance *along the path* plus a uniform random extra, snaps the cut to a road junction many other athletes also use, and suppresses every correlated channel: the polyline, start and end place names, the heatmap contribution, photo EXIF, the live beacon, and any segment effort whose segment start falls inside the zone. That is a reduction, not a guarantee, and I would not present it as one. Junction snapping still narrows home to the dwellings reachable from that junction, which in a rural setting can be one. Correlation defeats it from outside the zone entirely: a training partner whose own activity starts at the same address, a club ride photo, or simply the fact that the truncated start happens at 07:02 every weekday. And nothing retracts what was published before the zone existed and has already been scraped. The only strong control is hiding whole activities, which most athletes will not use because publishing is the product, so the honest move is to say that in the UI rather than let a zone imply safety.

**We cannot measure our own false-negative rate.** The funnel's contract is that no stage drops a real match, but nothing in production can verify it. False positives surface loudly, because another athlete disputes a KOM. False negatives are silent: nobody reports an effort they never knew they should have had, and there is no ground truth to compare against. Zero-effort-upload rate is the closest proxy and it is weak, since genuinely remote routes produce zero efforts legitimately. What I would do is partial: keep a golden corpus of a few thousand hand-labelled activity and segment pairs replayed on every matcher change, and shadow-run a 0.1% sample at a 40m corridor with the ordering checks relaxed to estimate how many matches the tight settings are throwing away. Both are estimates on a biased sample, because the golden corpus is whatever someone bothered to label and it will over-represent cases that already generated complaints. Recall is a number I would refuse to quote.

**The corpus mutates under the derived data and we only partly follow it.** Backfill is capped at 24 months to protect the live pipeline, so a segment created today never acquires efforts from 2013 rides, which means a board labelled "all-time" is provably not all-time and the athlete holding the genuinely fastest recorded time may simply be absent from it. Segment edits are worse: when a creator moves an endpoint, every existing effort was timed against different geometry and none of them is comparable to a new one, so we version the segment and orphan the old efforts, and a crown changes with no event its holder can see. More compute does not fix either; the backfill cap is a deliberate trade against the live pipeline, and re-timing 400k efforts means re-fetching 400k streams from cold storage. What I would actually do is stop lying in the label (show the effort count and the earliest date a board covers) and make an edit mint a new segment id linked to its predecessor rather than mutate one in place, so the old board stays frozen and honest. That second part is a product decision we have not won.
#### Drill questions
1. A new segment is created on a road a million activities have already ridden. How does its leaderboard get populated?
2. Two efforts on the same segment are processed concurrently and both take the KOM. What happens?
3. An athlete's GPS drops out in a tunnel in the middle of a segment. Do they get an effort?
4. Someone uploads a car journey as a bike ride and takes every KOM on the motorway.
5. Why does hiding everything within 500m of home still reveal the home address?
6. How do you serve age-group and weight-class boards without materialising hundreds of millions of sorted sets?
7. The device reports 3,000m of climb on a flat ride. Why, and what do you use instead?
8. How do you stop one person's private trail appearing on the global heatmap?
9. Why keep the segment corpus in RAM on every matcher rather than behind a spatial database?
10. An athlete rides an out-and-back and covers the same segment twice. What should the matcher produce?
11. Should matching run inside the upload request? What does that cost at Saturday-morning peak?
12. A segment's creator moves its start point 200m up the road. What happens to the 400,000 existing efforts?
13. The athlete stops at a café for nine minutes mid-ride. What does that do to distance and moving time if you do nothing?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. A bounded backfill job driven by an inverted `s2_cell -> [activity_id]` index built at processing time; candidate activities are re-run through the corridor and map-match stages only. *If pushed:* build that index at level 11 rather than 13, because backfill can afford false positives and the coarse version is ~400B/activity instead of ~3.4KB. It must run on a separate low-priority Kafka consumer group with its own rate limit, capped at the last 24 months, with the leaderboard visibly in a "backfilling" state, or one popular new segment starves the live upload pipeline on a Saturday morning.

2. Read-modify-write in the worker races and both send a "you took the KOM" push. Make the sorted set the arbiter: `ZADD` plus `ZRANGE key 0 0` inside one Lua script, so exactly one call observes itself at rank 1. *If pushed:* notifications must also be idempotent on `(segment_id, effort_id)` because Kafka is at-least-once, and the same effort can legitimately be processed twice after a consumer restart.

3. No, if the gap check is doing its job: the ordered match enforces a maximum distance and time gap between consecutive matched vertices, and a 400m hole through the middle of a segment fails it. *If pushed:* this is a genuine trade-off, since tunnels and urban canyons are exactly where real efforts happen. The refinement is to allow a gap when the surrounding points are consistent with continuous travel *and* the implied speed across the gap is plausible for the sport, and to mark such efforts as interpolated so they can be excluded from leaderboards while still counting for the athlete's own history.

4. Sport-specific plausibility gates before the effort reaches a leaderboard: sustained speed above a per-sport ceiling, implied power above a world-record W/kg curve for that duration, acceleration profiles no human produces, and a straight-line teleport through the segment. Flagged efforts are written but excluded from public boards pending review. *If pushed:* add community flagging with a reputation weight, and treat repeated flags on one athlete as a signal rather than acting on any single one. The cost of removing a legitimate KOM is high enough that automated removal should be reserved for the physically impossible, not the merely improbable.

5. Because every visible endpoint then sits on a circle of radius 500m centred on the house, and three points determine a circle. *If pushed:* randomising the radius does not help, since the endpoints just fill an annulus with the same centre. Truncate by distance *along the path* plus a uniform random extra, snap the cut to a shared road junction, and hide every correlated channel including segment efforts starting inside the zone. Even then it is a reduction rather than a guarantee, for the reasons in Unresolved.

6. Materialise only `alltime` and `this_year` for the ~2M recently active segments, and compute every filtered board on demand from a single `efforts` partition read (`partition segment_id`, clustered `elapsed ASC`) with application-side filtering over the top ~10k rows. *If pushed:* for the few hundred genuinely famous segments, materialise the filtered boards too and accept the write amplification. It is a bounded set you can enumerate, and it is where all the leaderboard read traffic actually goes.

7. Summed positive deltas of an altitude signal noisy to about 15m, over thousands of samples. Sample a 30m terrain raster at each cleaned position and accumulate only monotone climbs above a ~3m threshold. *If pushed:* store the raster version on the activity so an upgrade triggers a bounded reprocessing campaign. Silently changing historical elevation totals is a support incident, because athletes compare year-over-year climb figures.

8. k-anonymity at aggregation time: a cell renders only with at least 3 *distinct* athletes, deduplicated, plus exclusion of private activities and anything inside a privacy zone. *If pushed:* the dedup is the whole point. Counting activities rather than athletes lets a single frequent user clear any threshold, which is precisely how an aggregate map becomes a map of one person's routine.

9. Because the corpus is enormous in row count and tiny in bytes: ~35M segments at ~500B is ~18GB, and the cell index alone is ~560MB. Held locally, the join is hash lookups and float comparisons over memory. Behind a database it becomes 80 to 800 proximity queries per second against one shared store, each returning thousands of rows the application must post-filter anyway, so you pay the network and the shared bottleneck and still run stages 3 and 4 yourself. *If pushed:* the price is index freshness. A matcher holds a snapshot, so a segment created 30 seconds ago may not match. Stamp the index version on every effort and refuse to consume when a node falls behind the segments-table watermark, which turns a silent correctness bug into a bounded, replayable window.

10. Two efforts, and the monotone walk produces them without a special case: the cursor only advances, so the return leg is a second walk starting where the first finished. On a directional segment the return leg fails the walk and only one effort is written, which is correct. The bug to avoid is running the walk once and letting it stitch the outbound and return legs into a single effort with an implausible elapsed time. *If pushed:* cap efforts per `(activity, segment)` pair but set the cap high, because a criterium on a 1km circuit legitimately produces 40 efforts and that is a real case rather than an anomaly.

11. Arithmetically it is fine on a median activity: ~55ms of parse, clean and derive plus ~55ms of matching turns a ~150ms ack into ~260ms. The cost shows up at peak and in the tail. 800 uploads/s at a ~100ms mean is ~80 cores that must be warm with the ~18GB index loaded at the moment of the spike rather than absorbed as queue depth, and the dense-metro tail of 300 to 600ms lands in the athlete's request. *If pushed:* the flip is real. At ~50k segments (one city, or a race-timing product) the funnel costs ~1ms, the queue buys nothing, and a synchronous response removes the "still processing" state, the eventual-consistency complaints and the read-your-writes problem at once.

12. Every one of them was timed against different geometry, so none is comparable to a new effort. Current behaviour is to version the segment and orphan the old efforts, which means the crown can change with no event its holder can see. Re-timing is possible but means re-fetching 400,000 streams from cold storage and re-running stages 3 and 4, which is the backfill job pointed at one segment instead of at a corpus. *If pushed:* I would rather remove the choice, and make an edit mint a new segment id linked to its predecessor so the old board stays frozen and honest while the new one starts empty and backfills. That is a product decision rather than an engineering one, and it is unpopular with segment creators.

13. Nothing good. Consumer GPS wanders in roughly a 10m circle at about 0.3 m/s while genuinely still, so nine minutes of standing adds 0.3 × 540 ≈ 160m of fabricated distance, and the whole nine minutes counts as moving time. Detect clusters whose bounding circle stays under ~15m for more than 30s and collapse them to their centroid, then compute moving time as the sum of `dt` where instantaneous speed exceeds a per-sport threshold (~0.5 m/s running, ~1 m/s riding). *If pushed:* that threshold is a published product decision, not an implementation detail, because elapsed minus moving is the number athletes argue about and changing it silently rewrites everyone's average speed.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, frame it.** Lead with the thesis, not the components: "the upload is not the problem. This is a geospatial join, run once per write, against a corpus 35 million times bigger than the request." Then ask the two clarifying questions that actually fork the design: are segments user-created and unbounded, and how fresh must efforts be after upload. State the assumptions you are working from out loud: ~2.5B activities/yr, ~80 uploads/s steady, ~800 at peak, ~35M segments, ~20 efforts per activity. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine.** Six boxes: phone, upload API with the object store beside it, queue, processing workers, matcher with the segment index sitting *next to* the matcher rather than behind it, then efforts, leaderboards and feed. Say the placement rules as you draw each arrow, because they are the answer: bytes go straight to object storage and never through the app tier, the ack happens once bytes are durable and not once they are processed, everything expensive hangs off the event. Then the storage split, early, because it sets both the storage bill and the feed latency: ~2KB summary with a simplified polyline for the feed, ~30KB columnar stream in object storage for the detail view, 15x apart. Say once that everything after parsing is a pure function of `(cleaned stream, index version, raster version)`, because that single sentence is the answer to backfill, reprocessing and DR later.

**15-35, the funnel.** Protect this time; it is the interview. Do the naive arithmetic on the board first: 35M × 2.5B is ~10¹⁷ comparisons a year, ~35s of CPU per upload, ~2,800 cores steady and ~28,000 at peak. Then draw the four stages with cardinalities underneath: 35M, 10k, 1.2k, 50, 22, at ~100ms. State the invariant explicitly, because it is the thing being tested: any stage may pass a candidate that does not match, no stage may drop one that does. Give the correctness argument for the start-point index, since it is short and it is what shows you actually derived the design: a complete traversal passes through the start point, so the start point is inside the dilated cover. Then say the sentence that separates a derived answer from a memorised one: this is map-matching, not intersection. Two polylines crossing at a junction intersect, and so does a ride on the opposite carriageway. Explain how the monotone cursor gives you direction for free. Then take the corridor-width fork on your own terms: 15m against an 11m dual-carriageway separation and a 5m open-sky GPS error. Keep the dense-metro cell descent and the entry/exit interpolation as one-liners you can expand if asked.

**35-45, concede and close.** Volunteer the privacy geometry before anyone asks for it, because it is the part that shows you understand the leak is in the shape of the redaction rather than in the access control: a radius blackout puts every visible endpoint on a circle around the house, three points determine a circle, a dozen rides fit it to metres. Give the fix, then concede that it is a reduction and not a guarantee. Add the other two gaps: we cannot measure our own false-negative rate, and backfill is capped so "all-time" is not all-time. Close with the operational surface in two minutes: zero-effort-upload rate as the canary for a stale index, the ~20x effort-write amplification, autoscaling on consumer lag rather than CPU, and shedding the backfill consumer group before the live one.

Cut first: the on-device recorder detail (ring buffer, chunked resumable upload, sensor resampling), then the heatmap and the live beacon, then the terrain-raster elevation mechanism. All three are real and none changes the architecture. Never cut: the naive arithmetic, the funnel invariant, ordered match rather than intersection, and the privacy geometry.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **activities_summary** (wide-column, partition `athlete_id`, cluster `start_date DESC`): `(activity_id, sport, start_ts, distance, elapsed, moving, elev_gain, encoded_polyline, counters)`, the ~2KB feed representation
- **activity_streams** (object store, key `athlete_id/activity_id/streams.zst`): columnar per-channel arrays, ~30KB, fetched only on activity detail
- **raw_uploads** (object store, cold tier, key `upload_uuid`): original FIT/GPX bytes, 12-month TTL
- **segments** (relational source of truth, sharded by `s2_cell_level8` of start point; full copy mmap'd on every matcher): `(segment_id, name, sport, start_cell, polyline, bbox, direction)`
- **segment_cell_index** (in-RAM hash on matchers, key `s2_cell_level13`): `cell -> [segment_id]`, ~560MB
- **activity_cell_index** (backfill only, key `s2_cell_level11`): `cell -> [activity_id]`, ~400B/activity
- **efforts** (wide-column, partition `segment_id`, cluster `elapsed ASC`), with a secondary view partitioned by `athlete_id` and clustered by `start_date`
- **leaderboards** (Redis ZSET, key `seg:{segment_id}:{board}`, member `athlete_id`, score `elapsed`), see #22
- **follows** and **feed** (relational graph plus a Redis ZSET per athlete, key `feed:{athlete_id}`), see #8
- **privacy_zones** (relational, partition `athlete_id`): encrypted centre and radius; never returned by any read API
- **heatmap_tiles** (object store + CDN, key `{z}/{x}/{y}.png`), **beacon** (Redis, key `beacon:{token}`, TTL 4h)

**API contract**

```
POST /uploads/init          body: { sport, device, upload_uuid }  → { upload_id, put_url }
PUT  <put_url>              body: <FIT|GPX|TCX bytes>             → 200
POST /uploads/{id}/commit                                          → { status: "processing" }
GET  /uploads/{id}                                                 → { status, activity_id?, error? }
GET  /activities/{id}                                              → { summary, polyline, efforts[] }
GET  /activities/{id}/streams?keys=latlng,altitude,heartrate,watts → { streams: { ... } }
POST /segments              body: { activity_id, start_idx, end_idx, name } → { segment_id }
GET  /segments/{id}/leaderboard?board=all_time|this_year&age=35-44 → [{ rank, athlete, elapsed }]
GET  /feed?cursor=…                                                → [{ summary, polyline }]
POST /activities/{id}/kudos                                        → { count }
WS   /beacon/{token}        ← { lat, lng, ts }  every ~30s
```

**Observability**

- **Upload to feed-visible latency** (commit to feed entry written), SLO p95 < 30s. This is the number athletes perceive; it must not be coupled to segment matching, and an alert here should fire before anyone notices efforts are late.
- **Upload to efforts-complete latency** (commit to last effort written), SLO p95 < 90s. Tracked separately precisely so it can be allowed to degrade during a spike without paging.
- **Segment-match funnel cardinality per stage** (median candidates surviving each of the four stages). Alert when stage-2 output exceeds ~30k, which means a cell has become too dense and the adaptive level split is not engaging.
- **Effort-write rate against upload rate** (the amplification ratio), expected ~20x. A sudden rise means a segment-creation storm or a matcher regression producing spurious efforts; a fall means the index is stale and real efforts are being missed.
- **Zero-effort upload rate** (activities that produced no efforts at all). Baseline is a few percent, from genuinely remote routes. A jump is the canary for a stale or corrupt segment index, and it is far more sensitive than matcher error rate, because a broken matcher usually fails silently by matching nothing.
- **Privacy truncation rate** (activities with a zone that were truncated, divided by activities with a zone), SLO 100%, alert on any miss. This is a fail-closed correctness metric, not a performance one.
- **Kafka consumer lag on `activity.uploaded`**, SLO < 60s at p99. It is the leading indicator for both latency SLOs above and the input to matcher autoscaling.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** athletes are homed to a region, and uploads, streams and summaries are written and processed locally. `efforts` and leaderboards replicate asynchronously to a global view because a segment's leaderboard is inherently cross-region: a climb in the Alps is ridden by athletes homed in a dozen regions. The segment corpus is a globally replicated read-mostly dataset pushed to every matcher fleet.
- **RTO:** ~5 minutes for in-region replica promotion of the summary and efforts stores. Full regional failover is 15 to 30 minutes: uploads reroute by DNS immediately since the object store is multi-region, but the matcher fleet in the surviving region must scale up and load the ~18GB segment index before efforts resume.
- **RPO:** ~0 for the activity itself, because bytes are durable in the object store before the client is acked, so a region loss during processing costs a replay rather than data. Seconds for efforts and leaderboards, which are derived and fully rebuildable from the raw uploads; a forced failover may lose the most recent KOM notifications, which are re-emitted idempotently on replay.
- **Failover cadence:** automatic in-region; cross-region game-days quarterly, exercising the segment-index cold-load path specifically, since that is the long pole. Backfill and heatmap jobs are paused during failover.
- **Cross-region cost:** efforts (~18TB/yr at RF=3) and summaries (~15TB/yr) replicate globally; the ~75TB/yr stream store and ~125TB of raw uploads deliberately do **not**, staying region-local with cross-region reads on the rare tap from a distant follower. The segment corpus is ~18GB pushed on change, which is negligible. Photo egress via CDN dominates the actual bill.

### 45. Design Goodreads (Book Catalog, Shelves & Reviews)
#### Problem
Maintain a catalog of every book ever published, let members shelve and rate editions of it, aggregate ratings and reviews per creative work, and recommend what to read next. The catalog is not authored in house: it arrives from publisher feeds, library records and member submissions that disagree with each other in every field, so deciding which records describe the same book is an inference the system makes rather than a key it looks up. Every one of those inferences is visible on a public page within minutes of being made.
#### Core
The catalog is not given to you, it is inferred, and that one fact organises the whole design.

Model three levels. A *work* is the abstract book (Dune, Frank Herbert, 1965). An *edition* is one manifestation: the 2021 paperback, the audiobook, the Polish translation, each with its own page count and cover. An *identifier* is an ISBN or ASIN, and it maps to a list of editions, never one, because publishers reuse and misassign them. Ratings and reviews aggregate at the work; shelving and progress hang off the edition, because that is the object the reader is actually holding. User content stores `edition_id` and never `work_id`.

Records arrive disagreeing on title, author spelling, page count and year. Comparing 300M of them pairwise is 4.5×10¹⁶ comparisons, which no cluster fixes, so block first: only score pairs sharing a cheap normalised key such as the first three title tokens plus a folded author surname plus language. That is ~500M pairs, eight orders of magnitude fewer, and minutes of wall clock. Score each pair on weighted evidence, auto-merge above 0.92, route 0.75 to 0.92 to human moderators, and make everything below a new work.

A merge is a pointer write into a cluster table plus an append to a merge log, never a rewrite of review rows. That is what makes it reversible, and reversibility is the requirement, because over-merging puts a horror novel's 900 reviews on a children's picture book and someone screenshots it.

Serving is easy by comparison. A book page is identical for every viewer, so it is a CDN object at a 92% hit rate, with your shelf status spliced in from a separate 5ms call. Peak writes are about 750/s.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a union catalogue for every library on earth, staffed by one very stubborn cataloguer. Publishers, libraries and members all post index cards through the letterbox, and the cards are a mess. The same novel arrives as "Dune", "Dune (Dune Chronicles, Book 1)", "DUNE: 50th Anniversary Edition" and a Polish translation called "Diuna", each with a different ISBN, three different page counts and the author's name spelled four ways. The cataloguer's job is to decide which cards describe the *same book* and file them in one drawer, while keeping every original card intact. On top of that drawer, members pin their own notes: "want to read", "on page 240", "four stars, and here's why".

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Trust the identifier the industry already prints on the cover.* Group records by ISBN, group ISBNs by whatever work identifier the feed declares, and ship. It costs nothing to build and it is correct for records from a well-behaved source. It fails on everything else: books printed before ISBNs existed, self-published records, translations that carry no link back to the original, and the plain fact that most feeds do not populate a work identifier at all. It wins when you can restrict the catalog to a few clean sources and are content to show duplicates for the rest.

*Group cheaply, then score inside the group.* Compute a coarse key that near-duplicates almost always share, compare records only within a key, and act on a weighted similarity score. This is the only approach that survives hundreds of millions of dirty records, and it gives you two dials to set separately: how confident you must be to act automatically, and how confident is confident enough to bother a human. It costs a real pipeline, a labelled set to calibrate against, and a moderation queue that never empties.

*Refuse to decide, and let readers decide.* Keep every record separate, show likely duplicates on the page as suggestions, and let members merge and split with full history. It never asserts a confident wrong answer, and for the titles anyone cares about the crowd beats any model. It costs an editing interface, vandalism handling, and a permanently unresolved cold tail.

In practice the second and third combine: the pipeline acts where the score is decisive and the people handle the middle.

**The single-request walkthrough, the read path:** a logged-out visitor arrives from a search engine at `/work/12345/dune`. The request hits a CDN edge node. Book pages are the SEO surface and ~90% of views are anonymous or render identically, so the *anonymous page shell* (work metadata, edition list, aggregate rating, histogram and top 10 reviews) is a CDN object with a 5-minute TTL. At a ~92% hit rate that returns in ~20ms and the origin never wakes up. On a miss, the Catalog Service reads the work document (~1ms from Redis), the edition list (~2ms), the `work_aggregates` row holding `(sum_stars, count, histogram[5])` (~1ms), and the top-10 review IDs from a per-work ranked cache (~3ms), hydrating review bodies in one batch read (~6ms). Server-side total ~40ms, p99 ~180ms. If the visitor *is* logged in, the shell is still the cached object; a second tiny call, `GET /me/shelf-state?work_id=12345`, returns `{shelf: "currently-reading", progress_pct: 43, my_rating: null}` in ~5ms and the client splices it in. Splitting personalised state out of the cacheable body is the single biggest lever in the whole design.

**The single-request walkthrough, the write path:** the visitor taps "Want to Read" on the 2021 paperback. `PUT /me/shelves/want-to-read/{edition_id}` writes one ~120B row to the shelvings table (wide-column, partitioned by `user_id`, clustered by `(shelf_id, added_at)`), which is a single-partition append at ~8ms. It also increments the per-edition shelf counter (so the book page can say "1.2M people want to read this"), emits an activity event onto Kafka for the follower feed, and returns. Later they rate it 5 stars: the rating row is written keyed by `user_id`, and an aggregate-update event goes to a stream processor that folds it into `work_aggregates` for the *work*, not the edition. The displayed average changes within ~30s. The page-count they are tracking progress against comes from the *edition* they shelved. Work-level aggregation, edition-level shelving: that split runs through everything.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Works, editions and identifiers.** A document store such as MongoDB or DynamoDB, holding three levels, deliberately. A *work* is the abstract creative thing ("Dune" by Frank Herbert, first published 1965). An *edition* is a physical or digital manifestation: hardback, 2021 reissue, audiobook, Polish translation, each with its own page count, cover and publisher. An *identifier* is an ISBN-10, ISBN-13 or ASIN, and the mapping is many-to-many in both directions: one edition can carry several ISBNs, and publishers do reuse and misassign ISBNs, so the identifier index maps to a *list* of edition IDs, never one.
- **Cluster table.** A key-value union-find structure, and the only thing a merge writes. `edition_id → cluster_id` and `cluster_id → work_id`. Union-find (also called disjoint-set: a structure that tracks which items belong to the same group and merges groups in near-constant time) means merging two works of 200 editions each is a pointer update, not 400 row rewrites.
- **Merge log.** Append-only. Every merge and unmerge, with the similarity score, the evidence fields that fired, the actor (pipeline or human moderator), a timestamp, and the full pre-merge membership of both clusters. This is what makes merges reversible, which is a hard product requirement, not a nicety.
- **Shelvings and ratings.** A wide-column store such as Cassandra: billions of tiny rows, append-mostly, read by `user_id` for "my shelves" and by `edition_id` for the counters. Cassandra because the access pattern is a single-partition read of an ordered list, which is exactly what it is good at.
- **Reviews.** Wide-column, partitioned by `edition_id`: body text, spoiler flag, helpfulness votes. Critically, a review stores the `edition_id` it was written against and *never* a `work_id`. The work is resolved through the cluster table at read time. That one decision is what makes a bad merge recoverable.
- **`work_aggregates`.** Redis with a durable backing store: `(sum_stars, count, histogram[5], last_recompute_ts)` per work. Incrementally updated on every rating; fully recomputed by a batch job after any merge or unmerge.
- **Entity-resolution pipeline.** Spark, batch plus streaming. It normalises incoming records, blocks them into small candidate groups, scores pairs, and either auto-merges, queues for human review, or creates a new work.
- **Search and recommender.** OpenSearch for search, offline batch for recommendations. The search index is over works with edition titles folded in and ISBNs as exact-match keyword fields; typeahead is a separate precomputed structure (see the autocomplete pattern, #10). Recommendations are precomputed offline and read as a list (same shape as the Spotify recommender, #40).

**The thing that makes it hard:** deciding whether two records are the same book. You have ~300M edition records arriving from publisher feeds, library MARC records and user submissions, and they disagree with each other in every field. Naive pairwise comparison is 300M² ÷ 2 ≈ 4.5×10¹⁶ comparisons, which is not a tuning problem but an impossibility. Worse, the failure is asymmetric and highly visible. Fail to merge and you get two "Dune" pages splitting the ratings, which is annoying and generates complaints. *Over*-merge and the reviews for one novel appear under a completely different one: a reader opens the page for a children's picture book and finds 900 reviews discussing a horror novel with the same title. That is the kind of bug that gets screenshotted. And it happens constantly, because "Selected Poems" by a common surname is a genuinely ambiguous record even to a human.

**Why this design and what it costs:** blocking plus scored pairing plus a reversible merge. *Blocking* means you only compare records that share a cheap key: normalised first-three-title-tokens, folded first-author surname, language. That yields ~80M blocks averaging ~4 records; Σ C(n,2) across them is ~500M pairs instead of 4.5×10¹⁶, eight orders of magnitude cheaper, and it runs in minutes. Within a block you score pairs on weighted evidence: shared ISBN-13 (strong but not conclusive), title edit-distance after normalisation, author match after transliteration folding ("Достоевский" / "Dostoevsky" / "Dostoyevsky" fold to the same key), page count within ±10%, publication year within ±1, publisher. Above ~0.92 auto-merge; 0.75–0.92 goes to a human review queue; below that, a new work. The cost is real: blocking guarantees false negatives (a record whose title was typo'd in the first three tokens lands in the wrong block and never gets compared), so you run a second pass with an alternate blocking key, ISBN prefix or last-three-title-tokens, to catch what the first missed. And because *no* threshold is safe, every merge is written as a cluster-pointer change plus a log entry, so unmerge is a replay, not a restore-from-backup.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Document store (DynamoDB / MongoDB) for works and editions. Cassandra for shelvings, ratings and reviews. Redis for `work_aggregates` and hot work documents. Kafka for activity and aggregate-update events. Spark for the nightly full dedup pass, Flink for the streaming pass on newly-ingested records. OpenSearch for catalog search. CDN in front of every anonymous book page.
- Entity resolution:
  ```
  resolve(record):
    key   = block_key(fold(record.title)[:3], fold(record.author_surname), record.lang)
    cands = block_index.get(key) ∪ isbn_index.get(record.isbn13)
    best, s = argmax(cands, sim(record, ·))
    if   s >= 0.92: cluster.union(record.id, best.id)          -- auto-merge
    elif s >= 0.75: review_queue.push(record.id, best.id, s)   -- human decides
    else:           cluster.create(record.id)                  -- new work
    merge_log.append(record.id, best.id, s, evidence, prev_members, actor, ts)
  ```
- Book-page read path:
  ```
  shell = cdn.get(work_id) or render_shell(work_id)   -- anonymous, 5 min TTL
  state = shelf_svc.get(user_id, work_id)             -- ~5ms, never edge-cached
  return splice(shell, state)
  ```
#### What this is really testing
Whether you can tell the difference between an identifier and a judgement. `work_id` looks like a primary key and behaves like a hypothesis: it is the pipeline's current best guess about which records describe the same book, made under uncertainty, revised as evidence arrives, and sometimes wrong in a way a reader notices before you do. Every good decision in this design follows from taking that seriously. User content keys on the thing that never changes, the edition, so the guess lives in one indirection layer instead of being smeared across two billion rows. Merges write pointers and an audit log, so revision costs a few hundred writes rather than a restore. The auto-merge threshold is set by which error you would rather make, not by an F1 score, because the two errors are not commensurable. A candidate who models `books` as a table with an `id` has not noticed there is a question here, and everything downstream, including the recommender and the ratings average, quietly inherits the mistake.

The contrast is with the music streaming question. On the surface they are the same system: a hundred-million-item media catalog, a user library, ratings and plays, an offline recommender, a CDN in front. The catalogs are nothing alike. Music arrives from a few hundred rights holders under contract, with an authoritative identifier already attached to the recording and the release, and when two records disagree you email the label. Identity is given, so that interview is spent downstream: delivering audio bytes cheaply, honouring licensing windows, offline caching, and a recommender fed by users replaying the same track four hundred times. Books have no bytes worth delivering, so the entire interview sits upstream of serving. The signal is thinner too: one rating per book per user, ever, and only ~12% of those carry a word of text, which is why the popularity-skew fix here has to be structural rather than a matter of collecting more data.

Closest question: Q40
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Do we own the catalog, or ingest it from publisher feeds, library records and user submissions?
- Do ratings aggregate at the work level or per edition?
- Are shelves the three defaults only, or arbitrary user-defined shelves?
- Does search cover ISBN and review full-text, or just title and author?
- How social is it: public reviews only, or a following graph with an activity feed?
- Do recommendations ship at launch, and must they cover the long tail?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Catalog is ingested from dirty third-party and user feeds | needs an entity-resolution pipeline with blocking, scored merges and a reversible audit log as a first-class component, not a batch script |
| Ratings aggregate at the work level | reviews and ratings key on `edition_id` and resolve to a work through a cluster table, so a bad merge can be undone without touching review rows |
| Arbitrary user shelves | shelvings are a `(user_id, shelf_id, edition_id)` wide-column row with the shelf as part of the clustering key, not three boolean columns |
| Search includes ISBN and typo tolerance | an inverted index with keyword fields for identifiers plus fuzzy title matching, and a separate precomputed typeahead structure (see #10) |
| Following graph with an activity feed | a fanout service with a celebrity-pull path for high-follower reviewers (see #8) rather than fanout-on-write for everyone |
| Long-tail recommendations required | popularity-discounted collaborative filtering plus a content-based cold-start path (see #40), because pure CF only ever surfaces the head |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** book page (work + editions + aggregate + reviews), shelve an edition to a default or custom shelf, track reading progress, rate and review with spoiler tagging, search by title/author/ISBN, follow users and read a friend activity feed, reading challenges and groups, and merge/unmerge catalog entries with an audit trail.
- **NFR:** book page p99 < 200ms server-side and < 30ms on a CDN hit, at ~9k views/s peak; shelf write p99 < 150ms; a new rating reflected in the work average within 60s; 100% of merges reversible in one operation; duplicate-work rate ≤ 1% among the top 100k works.

**Scale**

- **Members:** assume ~150M registered accounts. Book-social engagement is low-frequency, so assume ~20% monthly active → ~30M MAU, and roughly MAU ÷ 7.5 → ~4M DAU.
- **Catalog:** assume ~300M edition records clustering to ~90M distinct works (~3.3 editions/work; a bestseller has 200+, most of the long tail has exactly 1). Feed ingest ~200k new-or-changed edition records/day ≈ ~2.3/s, a trivial write rate attached to a brutal matching problem.
- **Edition record:** ~2KB (title 120B + subtitle 80B + 4 author refs × 16B + isbn10 10B + isbn13 13B + asin 10B + publisher 60B + pub_date 8B + page_count 4B + language 8B + format 8B + description ~1KB + cover key 64B + source provenance ~300B + padding ~250B). 300M × 2KB = ~600GB; RF=3 → ~1.8TB.
- **Work record:** ~1.5KB × 90M = ~135GB; RF=3 → ~400GB. Small enough that the entire works table fits in a cache tier, which is why book pages are cheap to serve.
- **Shelvings:** assume ~5B rows. ~48B logical (user_id 8B + edition_id 8B + shelf_id 4B + added_at 8B + updated_at 8B + progress 2B + flags 2B + padding 8B) → ~120B on disk once you add the clustering key, column names and wide-column row overhead. 5B × 120B = ~600GB; RF=3 → ~1.8TB. **This asymmetry is the point:** five billion rows and it still fits on a handful of machines. Shelvings are a *partitioning* problem (one user with 30k books, one book with 5M shelvers), not a capacity problem, so partition by `user_id` for the read path you actually serve, and keep the `edition_id` side as counters rather than a full reverse list.
- **Ratings:** ~40% of shelvings sit on the `read` shelf → ~2B; ~90% carry a star → ~1.8B ratings × ~40B (user_id 8B + edition_id 8B + stars 1B + ts 8B + flags 2B + padding 13B) = ~72GB; RF=3 → ~216GB. Rounding error next to the catalog.
- **Reviews with text:** ~12% of ratings → ~220M. ~700B each (body ~560B, since the median review is two sentences and the tail runs to essays, plus ~140B metadata and vote counters). 220M × 700B = ~154GB; RF=3 → ~460GB, plus a full-text index at ~0.4× corpus ≈ ~60GB per replica.
- **Covers:** assume ~60% of editions have artwork → 180M × 3 resolutions (thumb ~8KB + list ~40KB + full ~180KB = ~230KB) = ~41TB; erasure-coded at ~1.4× → ~58TB in object storage, CDN-fronted.
- **Write rate:** 4M DAU × ~4 write actions/day (shelve, progress ping, rate, review) ≈ 16M writes/day ÷ 86400 ≈ ~185/s average; evening peak ~4× → ~750/s; the January reading-challenge spike ~10× → ~2k/s. Genuinely small.
- **Read rate:** book pages are the organic-search surface, so assume ~250M page views/day → ~2.9k/s average, ~9k/s at 3× peak. Read:write ≈ 250M : 16M ≈ **~16:1** at the request level, and closer to ~100:1 once you count per-page fan-out (work + editions + aggregate + 10 reviews + shelf state). At a 92% CDN hit rate the origin sees ~230/s of shell renders, so the cache is doing almost all the work.
- **Dedup compute:** naive pairwise = 300M² ÷ 2 ≈ 4.5×10¹⁶ pairs. Blocking into ~80M blocks averaging ~4 records gives Σ C(n,2) ≈ 80M × 6 ≈ **~500M pairs**. At ~20µs per scored pair that is ~10k CPU-seconds ≈ ~3 CPU-hours, which is minutes of wall-clock on a modest Spark cluster, run nightly.
#### Key decisions
**One auto-merge threshold, or a threshold plus a human band**
- Choice: two cut points. Score above 0.92 auto-merges, 0.75 to 0.92 goes to a moderator queue, below 0.75 becomes a new work. On a full pass that is ~2M auto-merges and ~400k queued pairs out of ~500M scored.
- Alternative: one cut point and no humans. Pick the score that maximises F1 on the labelled set, act on everything above it, leave everything below separate, and accept the resulting duplicate rate as a known cost.
- Decider: the two errors are not the same size, so there is no single point on the curve to pick. Under-merging splits a book's ratings across two pages: users complain, the average is wrong by a bit, and nothing is unrecoverable. Over-merging publishes 900 reviews of a horror novel on a children's picture book. Auto-merge precision therefore has to clear ~99.5%, because at 2M merges per pass even 0.5% is 10k wrong ones, and on our labelled pairs that pins the upper cut at 0.92. Recall at that precision is poor, and the pairs you lose are not junk: the band from 0.75 up holds real duplicates that no feature set separates from real distinct books. Discarding them costs more than staffing a queue.
- Alternative wins when: there is no moderation capacity, or the band is nearly empty. If the ambiguous band is under ~1% of merge candidates, the queue is not worth the tooling, the on-call rota and the SLA; take the conservative single threshold and let the duplicate rate ride. It also wins, in a different form, when the crowd can be the queue: a wiki-style catalog pushes the whole band to contributors, which is a staffing choice rather than an algorithmic one, and it produces better data on popular titles and nothing at all on the tail.

**Two exact blocking keys, or one similarity-preserving key**
- Choice: two independent exact-match blocking passes, unioned. Pass one keys on `(first 3 normalised title tokens, folded author surname, language)`; pass two keys on the ISBN-13 registrant prefix. A record has to be missed by both to escape comparison.
- Alternative: a single locality-sensitive hashing pass, MinHash over title and author shingles banded so that pairs above the target Jaccard similarity collide with a stated probability. One structure, one tuning knob, and a recall guarantee you can write down.
- Decider: blocking's false negatives are silent and permanent, so the question is what guarantee you get about them. Exact keys have a known, ugly hole: one typo inside the first three title tokens and the record lands in a block it will never leave, and nothing in the system will ever tell you. Two independent keys make a miss require two independent failures, and ISBN prefix and title tokens fail for genuinely uncorrelated reasons. The cost is arithmetic: pass one gives ~500M pairs at ~20µs each, ~3 CPU-hours; the ISBN pass adds ~200M more for ~40% more scoring work, which is still about ten minutes of wall clock on the same 200-core cluster. Recall bought for two extra minutes a night is cheap.
- Alternative wins when: there is no second reliable structured field to build an exact key from. Books have ISBNs; a catalog of free-text user submissions with nothing but a title has only the title, and LSH is then the only thing offering a recall bound instead of a hope. Be fair about it: LSH also degrades on the same skew that hurts us, because a band full of "Selected Poems" is a giant bucket either way, and the honest reason to prefer exact keys here is operational rather than mathematical. They are debuggable. When a duplicate is reported you can compute its block key by hand and see why the two records never met, and you cannot do that with a hash band.

**Partition shelvings by user and keep the book side as counters, or maintain a full reverse index**
- Choice: one copy of shelvings, partitioned by `user_id` and clustered by `(shelf_id, added_at)`. The edition side gets per-shelf counters only, no member list.
- Alternative: a second materialised copy partitioned by `edition_id`, so "who shelved this book" is a range read rather than something you have to reconstruct.
- Decider: 5B rows at ~120B is ~600GB, ~1.8TB at RF=3, which fits on a handful of machines, so this was never a capacity question. It is a distribution question, and the two sides are skewed in opposite directions by six orders of magnitude. The user side is well behaved: even a 30k-book power user is a ~3.6MB partition. The edition side is not: the most-shelved book has ~5M shelvings, a ~600MB partition that no wide-column store is happy with and that no product surface actually reads. Every feature that looks like "who shelved this" is really "which of the ~200 people I follow shelved this", which is ~200 single-partition point reads against the copy we already have.
- Alternative wins when: something genuinely needs unfiltered book-side reads. Co-occurrence for the recommender and any bulk export do, and for those the answer is not a serving-path index but a nightly dump of the shelvings table into columnar files partitioned by edition, which the batch jobs read and which nothing pages on. The serving-path inversion becomes right when follow lists get large: at 50k follows the friend intersection is 50k reads and reading the book side once wins, which is why this fork flips for a product whose social graph looks like a follow-anyone feed rather than a reading circle.

**How to read the diagram:** everything above the dashed line is the request path and everything below it is offline. The CDN sits in front of the whole read path because a book page is nearly identical for every viewer; the three services fan out from a cache miss, and each owns one store. The two batch jobs write *into* the stores rather than serving traffic.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** catalog correctness and user state have opposite properties. The catalog changes rarely, is read enormously, and is globally identical, so it is cached hard and rebuilt offline. Shelvings and ratings change per user, cannot be shared between viewers, and are cheap individually, so they are served live from a partition-by-user store and deliberately kept out of the cacheable body.

**What this layout buys you:** a book page that mostly never touches a database, and an entity-resolution pipeline that can take hours without any user noticing. The trade is staleness: a rating posted now shows on the cached page up to 5 minutes late, and a merge takes minutes to propagate to aggregates and search.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The mechanism: deciding that two records are the same book, and being able to take it back.**

One modelling premise, because the rest depends on it. An `edition_id` is minted once when a source record is ingested and never changes and never merges. A `work_id` is the pipeline's output, an inference over editions. Every user-generated row (rating, review, shelving, progress) stores `edition_id`, nothing outside the cluster table stores `work_id`, and the resolution from one to the other happens at read time.

*Normalise.* Fold case, strip punctuation and series suffixes ("(Dune Chronicles, Book 1)"), expand numerals, transliterate non-Latin author names into a Latin key so "Достоевский", "Dostoevsky" and "Dostoyevsky" collapse to the same token, and validate the ISBN check digit. A failed check digit is not a reason to discard the record; it is a feature, because it says a human typed this field by hand.

*Block.* The two exact-key passes described above, unioned. Roughly 80M blocks, about 90% of them with three members or fewer. The tail is where the work is: "Selected Poems", "The Bible", and the bucket of records with no usable title. C(50000, 2) is 1.25B pairs inside a single block, which parks the whole Spark stage on one partition, so block size is hard-capped at 1000 by appending a sub-block key, publisher first and publication decade after that. That deliberately loses recall on exactly the most generic titles, which is also where merging is riskiest, so the error lands in the safe direction.

*Score.* Around eight weighted features per candidate pair: shared ISBN-13 (+0.4, capped, never decisive alone), title Jaro-Winkler after normalisation, author key match, page count within ±10%, publication year within ±1, publisher match, description shingle overlap, and cover perceptual-hash distance. Weights are fitted on a few thousand hand-labelled pairs. The useful artifact is not the weights, it is the precision-recall curve, because that curve is what sets the two cut points and what you re-examine every time someone proposes moving them.

*Decide and record.* Above 0.92, union the two editions' clusters. Between 0.75 and 0.92, enqueue for a moderator. Below, create a new cluster. Every merge appends to the merge log with the score, the per-feature evidence that fired, the actor, a timestamp, and the full pre-merge membership of both clusters.

Stage budget for a nightly full pass: 300M editions in; normalisation is a pure map at ~4 min on 200 cores; blocking produces ~80M blocks; scoring ~500M pairs at ~20µs each is ~3 CPU-hours of compute, but the stage is shuffle-bound rather than CPU-bound and lands at about 8 min of wall clock on the same 200 cores; ~2M auto-merges and ~400k queued pairs come out; cluster writes plus aggregate recompute take ~15 min. Under an hour end to end. Newly ingested records run the same scorer against the standing block index and resolve in ~200ms each, so a book a member adds today lands on the right page immediately rather than tomorrow.
