**Why a merge is a pointer write and nothing else.** The obvious merge rewrites every rating, review and shelving row from `work_A` to `work_B`. On a heavily reviewed work that is millions of updates spread across several stores. It is slow, it is not atomic, it half-applies when the job dies, and it is irreversible: once the original `work_id` is gone from the rows, undoing it means a restore from backup, and every review written since the merge has no correct home in that backup. None of those are tuning problems.

So the merge touches only the cluster table. Point cluster B's editions at cluster A, mark B superseded, append the log entry, and enqueue an aggregate recompute plus a search reindex for the surviving work. Union-find keeps that to a few hundred pointer writes even when both sides carry 200 editions. Unmerge reads the log entry, restores the recorded memberships, and re-runs the same recompute; merge and unmerge are the same code path with the membership list supplied from a different place, which is the property that makes anyone willing to press the button.

Worked example. Someone merges a children's picture book called *The Gift* into a horror novel of the same name. 900 horror reviews appear on the picture book's page. A reader reports it, a moderator hits unmerge, and both pages are correct within ~2 minutes, including the twelve reviews written during the merge window, because each of those recorded the edition its author was actually looking at rather than whatever work the page was showing at the time.

**Where reversibility stops.** "Every merge is reversible" holds for a merge in isolation and not for a merge in history. Merges compose: A folds into B on Monday, B folds into C on Wednesday, and undoing Monday needs the shape of the tree before Wednesday flattened it, which path compression has already discarded. Two things together make it survivable. First, each log entry stores the full pre-merge membership of both clusters rather than a parent pointer, so a snapshot exists even after compression. Second, undo is last-in-first-out per cluster: unmerging Monday requires unmerging Wednesday first. That restriction points the wrong way, because the oldest bad merges are the ones discovered late, and it is the first conceded gap below.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Blocking-key skew.** Blocks like "Selected Poems", "The Bible" or an untitled-record bucket can contain 50k+ members, and C(50000, 2) is 1.25B pairs in a single block, which stalls the whole Spark stage on one partition. Hard-cap block size at 1000 by appending a sub-block key (publisher, or pub-decade); accept the extra false negatives and rely on the second blocking pass to recover them. The trade is a slightly higher duplicate rate on exactly the most generic titles, which is also where merging is riskiest, so leaving them separate is the safer error.
- **Hot work page.** A book club pick or prize winner takes 1000× traffic. The CDN absorbs reads, but the `work_aggregates` row and edition shelf counters become single-key write hotspots. Promote hot works to sharded counters `(work_id, hash(user_id) % N)` summed on read; the cost is N reads instead of one on every page render, so only do it above ~500 writes/s.
- **Merge storm invalidation.** A pipeline change that merges 2M pairs in one pass enqueues 2M aggregate recomputes and search reindexes at once, saturating both. Rate-limit merge application to a fixed budget per hour and prioritise by rating count so the visible works reconcile first. The trade is that low-traffic duplicates linger for a day.
- **Review ranking recompute.** Wilson-bound ranking (the Wilson lower bound on the up-vote proportion, a statistical lower bound on the true helpfulness rate given the votes seen so far) over every review of a work is wasteful when only one vote changed. Recompute the top-50 cache lazily on a vote-count threshold (every 10 votes, or on any vote landing in the current top 100) rather than per vote; ranking is then up to a few minutes stale, which nobody perceives.
- **Fanout for high-follower reviewers.** A reviewer with 800k followers posting five reviews in an evening triggers 4M timeline writes. Use the celebrity-pull path from #8: above ~10k followers, do not fan out; merge their recent activity at read time. The trade is a slower feed render for their followers.
- **Search reindex cost after catalog change.** Every merge changes a work document and its edition list, and full reindexing of 90M works is hours. Index incrementally off the merge log with a nightly full rebuild into a parallel index that is swapped in atomically, so a bad partial index never serves traffic.
- **Human review queue backlog.** The 0.75 to 0.92 confidence band produces ~400k pairs per full pass, far more than moderators can clear. Prioritise the queue by rating count on both sides (merging two heavily-reviewed works is the highest-stakes decision) and auto-expire the low-stakes tail after 30 days as "keep separate", which is the reversible default.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entity resolution | Model change causes a wave of false merges; reviews appear under wrong books | Merge-rate anomaly vs 7-day baseline; spike in user reports per merged work | Cap auto-merges/hour; require human sign-off when both sides have >1000 ratings; bulk unmerge by replaying the merge log for a time range |
| Identifier index | Feed reuses an ISBN, resolver picks the wrong edition | `ambiguous` resolve rate per feed source; ingest validation on ISBN checksum | Map identifiers to a list, treat shared ISBN as capped evidence requiring corroboration; quarantine the offending feed source and re-run its records |
| CDN | Edge purge storm or cold cache after a deploy sends full read volume to origin | Origin request rate vs baseline; CDN hit-rate drop below 85% | Request coalescing per POP, stale-while-revalidate, staggered purges; origin autoscale plus a load-shed that serves the last-good shell without personalisation |
| Aggregate stream | Consumer lag or a lost event leaves work averages wrong | Kafka consumer lag; nightly reconciliation diff count | Idempotent event UUIDs with dedupe; nightly recompute of every work touched in 24h; a manual recompute endpoint per work for support |
| Shelvings store | Hot partition from a power user or a mass CSV import times out writes | Per-partition write p99; partition size histogram | Cursor-only paging, never full-shelf reads; rate-limit bulk imports and collapse them into one activity event |
| Review ranking cache | Ranked-review cache cold or stale after a merge | Cache hit rate; age of the top-50 list per work | Fall back to sort-by-recency (always cheap and always correct) rather than blocking the page; rebuild lazily in the background |
| Abuse pipeline | Brigading detector misses a coordinated wave | Rating-velocity anomaly per work; share of ratings from accounts under 30 days old | Auto-quarantine new ratings on the work into a holding buffer; keep the raw average internal; publish the histogram so the skew is visible |
| Search index | Swap of a partially-built index serves empty or wrong results | Zero-result rate; index document count vs expected | Build into a parallel index and swap atomically only after a document-count and smoke-query gate; instant rollback to the previous index alias |
| Recommender | Batch job fails; recommendation lists go stale or empty | Job success alert; recommendation freshness age | Serve the previous day's list (staleness is invisible for a weekly-cadence product); fall back to a popularity-plus-genre list rather than an empty shelf |

**Unresolved**

**Undo is last-in-first-out, and bad merges are found out of order.** The merge log lets us reverse any single merge, but merges compose, and unmerging one that a later merge has built on top of is not well defined: the later merge's decision was made against a cluster that included the editions we are about to remove, so replaying it is not the same operation. Our rule is to refuse, and to require unwinding the newer merges first. That is exactly backwards from how the problem arrives, because the merges people report are the old ones that quietly sat wrong for a year while three more merges piled on. What we actually do in that case is manual: reconstruct the intended memberships from the log by hand, write them directly, and take the aggregate recompute. It works and it does not scale past a few a week. The clean version is a proper versioned cluster history where each merge records a full immutable snapshot and any state is addressable by version, so an undo becomes "re-derive from version N with this one decision inverted". That is a rewrite of the cluster store, we have not done it, and I would not claim the log alone gives us arbitrary undo.

**Nobody agrees what a work is, and our threshold answers the question by accident.** Is a translation the same work as the original? An abridgement? A graphic novel adaptation? A three-book omnibus? The scoring function has an opinion about each of these, expressed as a number, and it was never a deliberate product decision. The omnibus is the worst case and we handle it badly: one edition record containing three novels, so a rating of the box set lands on whichever work the omnibus clustered into and contaminates that book's average with an opinion about three books. Translations we currently merge, which suits the ratings average and infuriates readers who want to see reviews in their own language separated from 40k English ones. The honest fix is a `contains` and `derived-from` relation between works, so aggregation becomes a small graph traversal with a policy about which edges to follow, and the policy is set per surface rather than by a similarity score. That turns a pointer read into a traversal on the hottest path in the system, which is why it has not been built.

**The duplicate-rate SLO is measured where the pipeline is strongest.** We report duplicates against the top 100k works, where dense metadata, many corroborating sources and moderator attention all point the same way, and we hit ≤1% comfortably. The true rate across all 90M works is unmeasured and much worse, because the cold tail is precisely where blocking loses recall, where the ambiguous band auto-expires as "keep separate" after 30 days, and where nobody reports anything. A queue that clears 400k pairs per pass against moderator capacity of a few thousand a day is not a backlog, it is a permanent structural condition, and the 30-day expiry is the real merge policy for the tail rather than a fallback. Sampling would at least tell us the number: draw a stratified sample by rating count, label it by hand each quarter, and publish that figure next to the headline one. We have not, so any claim we make about catalog quality is a claim about the head.
#### Drill questions
1. You merge two works that were actually different books. What does the user see, and how do you recover?
2. A publisher feed reuses an ISBN-13 that already belongs to a different book. What breaks?
3. A book gets 40k one-star ratings in six hours before it has even been published. What do you do?
4. A celebrity book club picks a title and its page gets 1000× traffic in minutes.
5. Two users rate the same book at the same instant and the average comes out wrong.
6. A user has 30,000 books on their to-read shelf. How do you page it, and does the partition blow up?
7. A debut novel has zero ratings. How does it ever get recommended to anyone?
8. How do you handle an audiobook, where there are no pages?
9. Sorting reviews by helpful votes puts a review with 3 up-votes and 0 down above one with 900 up and 40 down. What sort do you use instead?
10. A user pastes an ISBN into the same box they type "dune" into. What does the query path do?
11. Someone proposes lowering the auto-merge threshold from 0.92 to 0.88 to cut the duplicate rate. How do you decide, and how would you ship it?
12. A merge from a year ago was wrong, but the surviving cluster has been merged twice since. Can you undo the old one?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Reviews for one novel appear under another, which is highly visible and embarrassing. Recovery is one operation because no review row was mutated: reviews key on `edition_id`, the work is resolved through the cluster table, so unmerge rewrites cluster pointers, replays the `merge_log` entry, and triggers an aggregate recompute plus search reindex. Correct within ~2 minutes. *If pushed:* reviews written during the merge window still resolve correctly, because each recorded the edition its author was actually reading. Rate-limit auto-merges per work per day so a bad model deploy cannot cascade, and require human sign-off for any merge where both sides already have >1000 ratings, because those are the ones people notice.

2. Nothing, if the identifier index maps to a *list* of edition IDs rather than one. The resolver treats a shared ISBN as strong-but-capped evidence (+0.4, not decisive) and requires corroboration from title, author or page count before merging. `GET /resolve?isbn=…` returns `ambiguous: true` with candidates rather than guessing. *If pushed:* if you built the index as a unique key, the second record either overwrites the first (silent data loss) or fails ingest (a stuck feed). Both are worse than modelling the real-world many-to-many.

3. Detect it as a velocity anomaly: rating rate versus that work's trailing baseline, distribution skew toward the extremes, and account-quality features: new accounts, no prior shelvings, no reading progress, correlated signup times, shared ASN. Response is graduated: pre-publication rating lock (you cannot rate a book that is not out yet), then per-work rate limiting, then a quarantine where new ratings land in a holding buffer excluded from the displayed average until reviewed. *If pushed:* weight the *displayed* average by account history rather than deleting ratings, and keep the raw average available internally, because silently deleting user content generates a second, louder controversy. Publish the histogram; a brigade is obvious in the shape of the distribution in a way it is not in the mean.

4. The page is a CDN object, so the edge absorbs almost all of it; the origin sees a thundering herd only on the first miss per POP. Use request coalescing at the edge (one origin fetch per key per POP) and stale-while-revalidate so an expired shell keeps serving while the refresh runs. *If pushed:* the write side is the real risk. The `work_aggregates` row and the edition's shelf counter become single-key hotspots at thousands of increments/second. Shard both as `N` sub-counters keyed on `(work_id, hash(user_id) % N)` and sum on read, promoting a work to sharded counters automatically when it crosses ~500 writes/s.

5. Aggregates are not read-modify-write in the application; they are atomic increments (`INCRBY` on Redis, or counter columns) driven off an idempotent event stream, so concurrent writers commute. Rating *edits* apply a delta computed from the previous value stored on the user's own rating row, which is single-writer per user. *If pushed:* events carry a UUID and the stream processor dedupes on it, so at-least-once delivery does not double-count; and the nightly reconciliation pass recomputes every work touched in the last 24h from the ratings table, which is the real safety net against slow drift.

6. Clustering by `(shelf_id, added_at)` means the shelf is an ordered range within one partition and paging is a cursor over the clustering key, with no offset and no sort. At ~120B/row, 30k rows is ~3.6MB, well inside a healthy partition. *If pushed:* the problems appear at sorting by anything other than the clustering key (sort-by-title requires a client-side sort of the page, or a secondary materialised ordering) and at bulk import, where a CSV of 30k books must be rate-limited so it does not emit 30k activity events into every follower's feed. Collapse bulk imports into a single "added 30,000 books" activity item.

7. Content-based cold start: embed the description, subjects, author, publisher and, as soon as any exist, the user-created shelf names it has been added to, then recommend on similarity to neighbours in that space. User-created shelf names ("dark-academia", "cosy-mystery") are a rich free taxonomy that no publisher metadata provides, and they are the single best cold-start feature available here. Reserve an exploration slot, roughly 10% of each recommendation list, for low-rating-count items so the system generates its own training signal. *If pushed:* the reason plain collaborative filtering cannot do this is the skew. Assume the top ~1,000 works hold ~25% of all ratings while ~60% of works have fewer than 10, so co-occurrence counts are dominated by books that co-occur with everything and the model recommends the same fifty bestsellers to everyone forever. Discount item scores by `count^0.5` so a book with 2M ratings does not automatically outrank one with 2k, and measure catalog coverage, the fraction of the catalog recommended to at least one user in a week, alongside click-through. Optimising click-through alone collapses onto the head monotonically, and coverage is the only metric that catches it happening.

8. Progress is stored as a percentage, never a page number, and each edition declares its own progress unit (`pages`, `minutes`, or none). The client converts whatever the user enters into a percent using the shelved edition's metadata. *If pushed:* a user who reads half the hardback and finishes on audio expects one continuous progress bar. Model progress against the *work* with a pointer to the currently-active edition, so switching format carries the percentage across; the page counts of the two editions are irrelevant once you have normalised to percent.

9. The Wilson lower bound on the up-vote proportion, which is a statistical lower bound on the true helpfulness rate given how many votes have actually been seen. It ranks 900/940 above 3/3 because three votes carry almost no evidence, and it needs no hand-tuned minimum-vote threshold. Blend it with a recency decay, since a review of a 2010 book written last week usually beats one from 2011, and a length signal. *If pushed:* the top ~50 review IDs per work are precomputed and cached so the list stays shareable across viewers, and the friend boost for logged-in users is applied to that cached list at request time rather than baked into it. Recompute lazily on a vote-count threshold, every 10 votes or on any vote landing in the current top 100, because per-vote recomputation is pure waste and a few minutes of ranking staleness is imperceptible.

10. Detect the shape before you search. A 10 or 13 digit string with a valid check digit is not a text query; route it to `GET /resolve?isbn=` and, on a unique hit, redirect straight to the book page rather than rendering a result list. In the index itself, ISBNs and ASINs are exact-match keyword fields with no analyzer, because fuzzy-matching an identifier is never what anyone wants. Text queries go to the inverted index over works, with all edition titles and author-name variants folded into one document and edit-distance 1 to 2 on title tokens for typos. *If pushed:* ranking has to blend BM25 with a popularity prior, otherwise "dune" returns a geology textbook that mentions sand dunes forty times ahead of the novel. That prior is also the thing that makes new books invisible, so cap its contribution and let an exact title match beat it outright. Type-ahead is a separate precomputed structure, not a query against this index (see #10).

11. Do not decide it from the duplicate rate; decide it from the labelled precision-recall curve, then confirm in production. Take the current labelled set, look at what precision is at 0.88 rather than at 0.92, and multiply: if precision at 0.88 is 98.5%, the extra ~300k merges in that slice carry ~4,500 wrong ones, against maybe 290k genuine duplicates resolved. Whether that trade is acceptable depends on the visibility of the wrong ones, so weight by rating count: a false merge between two works with 5,000 ratings each is worth several thousand between records nobody has ever opened. *If pushed:* ship it shadow first. Score at 0.88 without acting, sample a few hundred of the newly-eligible pairs for human audit, and only then enable, with a cap on auto-merges per hour and mandatory sign-off when both sides exceed 1,000 ratings. The threshold is also not one number: the right shape is a threshold that varies with stakes, lower for two records with no ratings at all, higher than 0.92 for two established works.

12. Not with one click, and this is the sharpest limitation in the design. The merge log stores the full pre-merge membership of both clusters, so the intended state is recoverable, but the two later merges made their decisions against a cluster that included the editions we are now removing, so replaying them is not the same operation and the tooling refuses. The supported path is last-in-first-out: unwind the two newer merges, unwind the old one, then re-apply the newer two against the corrected clusters and let a moderator confirm each. *If pushed:* in practice a moderator reconstructs the intended memberships from the log by hand, writes them, and takes the aggregate recompute. That is fine at a few a week and nowhere near a general answer. The real fix is a versioned cluster history where every state is addressable and undo means re-deriving from an earlier version with one decision inverted, which is a rewrite of the cluster store rather than a feature on top of it.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, name the three levels and say where the difficulty is.** First sentence: "the hard part is not serving book pages, it is deciding which records are the same book, and being able to unmake that decision." Then say "work, edition, identifier" out loud and define each in one line, because that is the problem stated correctly and most candidates never get there. Ask the two questions that actually change the design: do we own the catalog or ingest it from dirty third-party feeds, and do ratings aggregate at the work or the edition. State your assumptions as numbers: ~300M editions, ~90M works, ~150M members, ~250M page views/day. Draw nothing yet.

**5-15, the spine and the arithmetic.** Draw the request path top to bottom: client, CDN, three services (catalog, shelf and review, social), one store each, and two batch jobs hanging underneath that write into the stores rather than serving traffic. Two numbers as you draw. First, ~16:1 reads to writes at the request level and closer to 100:1 in fan-out, on content that is byte-identical for every viewer, which is why the CDN carries the system and why the only thing that must not be in the cached body is the small personalised shelf fragment. Second, and say this one slowly: 300M² ÷ 2 is 4.5×10¹⁶ pairs, and blocking takes it to ~500M. That arithmetic is the interview.

**15-35, entity resolution and reversibility.** Protect this time; it is the whole question. Walk the five stages and put the cardinality on each: normalise, block into ~80M blocks, score ~500M pairs on about eight weighted features, decide against two thresholds, write clusters and log. Then take the threshold fork on your own terms: 0.92 for auto, 0.75 to 0.92 to humans, and explain that the band exists because the two errors are not the same size, with the picture-book-and-horror-novel example to make it concrete. Then the design decision the interviewer is waiting for: no user-generated row stores a `work_id`, so a merge is a few hundred pointer writes plus a log entry, and unmerge is the same code path. Volunteer the block-skew cap ("Selected Poems" is 50k records) and the second blocking pass, since both show you know what blocking costs you. Keep the shelvings partitioning fork in your pocket as a two-liner: 5B rows is under 2TB, so it is a partitioning problem, one user with 30k books and one book with 5M shelvers, opposite treatments.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the gaps before they are found. Undo is last-in-first-out while bad merges surface oldest-first. Nobody agrees whether a translation or an omnibus is the same work, and the similarity score is currently answering that product question by accident. The duplicate-rate number is measured on the top 100k works, which is where the pipeline is strongest. Then two minutes of operations: auto-merge precision as the metric that governs whether the threshold can move, CDN hit rate as a paging alert because the capacity plan assumes 90%, aggregate freshness under 60s, and the rating-velocity anomaly that catches brigading.

Cut first: the social layer and the feed, which is question 8 and adds nothing here; then the recommender mechanics, which is question 40, keeping only the one sentence about popularity skew being structural; then search ranking and type-ahead. Never cut: the three levels, the blocking arithmetic, and why reviews key on `edition_id`.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **works** (document store, partition by `work_id`): `(work_id, canonical_title, author_ids[], subjects[], first_pub_year, cluster_id)`
- **editions** (document store, partition by `edition_id`): `(edition_id, cluster_id, title, isbn10, isbn13, asin, publisher, pub_date, page_count, format, language, cover_key, source, ingested_at)`
- **identifier_index** (KV, partition by `identifier`): `(isbn13|isbn10|asin) → [edition_id, …]`, always a list, because reused and misassigned ISBNs are real
- **clusters** (KV union-find, partition by `cluster_id`): `edition_id → cluster_id`, `cluster_id → work_id`, the only rows a merge rewrites
- **merge_log** (append-only log, partition by `day`): `(merge_id, from[], to, prev_members[], score, evidence, actor, ts, reverted_by?)` where `prev_members` is the full pre-merge membership of both clusters, which is what survives path compression
- **shelvings** (wide-column, partition by `user_id`, cluster by `(shelf_id, added_at)`): `(user_id, shelf_id, edition_id, added_at, progress_pct, updated_at)`
- **shelf_counters** (KV, partition by `edition_id`): per-shelf counts only, not a member list
- **ratings** (wide-column, partition by `user_id`; second copy partitioned by `edition_id` for backfill): `(user_id, edition_id, stars, ts)`
- **reviews** (wide-column, partition by `edition_id`, cluster by `review_id`): `(review_id, edition_id, user_id, stars, body, spoiler, helpful_up, helpful_down, ts)`, with no `work_id` column
- **work_aggregates** (Redis + durable backing, partition by `work_id`): `(sum_stars, count, histogram[5], last_recompute_ts)`
- **follow graph** and **timeline cache** (Redis sorted set, partition by `user_id`), same shape as #8
- **search index** (OpenSearch, sharded by hash of `work_id`); **covers** (object store + CDN)

**API contract**

```
GET  /work/{work_id}                      → { work_id, title, authors[], editions[], avg_rating, ratings_count, histogram[5] }
GET  /work/{work_id}/reviews?sort=helpful&cursor=…  → { reviews[], next_cursor }
GET  /edition/{edition_id}                → { edition_id, work_id, isbn13, page_count, format, cover_url }
GET  /resolve?isbn=9780441013593          → { edition_id, work_id, confidence, ambiguous: bool }
GET  /me/shelf-state?work_id={id}         → { shelf, progress_pct, my_rating }     (personalised, never edge-cached)
PUT  /me/shelves/{shelf}/{edition_id}     body: { position? }                      → { shelf, added_at }
POST /me/progress                         body: { edition_id, page | percent }     → { progress_pct, updated_at }
POST /edition/{edition_id}/review         body: { rating, body, spoiler }          → { review_id }
POST /review/{review_id}/vote             body: { helpful: bool }                  → { helpful_count }
GET  /search?q=dune+herbert&type=work     → { hits[] }                             (typeahead: see #10)
GET  /me/feed?cursor=…                    → { activity[] }                         (fanout: see #8)
GET  /me/recommendations                  → { works[], reason[] }                  (offline batch: see #40)
POST /admin/merge                         body: { work_ids[], reason }             → { cluster_id, merge_id }
POST /admin/unmerge                       body: { merge_id, reason }               → { restored_work_ids[] }
```

**Observability**

- **Book page latency**, edge and origin measured separately. SLO p99 < 30ms on a CDN hit and < 200ms on origin render; the two are different systems and a single blended number hides an origin regression behind a healthy cache.
- **CDN hit rate on book pages.** SLO ≥ 90%; the whole read-side capacity plan assumes it, so a drop to 80% doubles origin load and is a paging alert, not a dashboard.
- **Auto-merge precision**, from a sampled human audit of merges above the 0.92 threshold. SLO ≥ 99.5%; at ~2M merges per pass, 0.5% is 10k wrong merges, so this is the metric that governs whether the threshold can be lowered.
- **Aggregate freshness**, rating write to work average updated. SLO p99 < 60s; also alert on nightly reconciliation *drift* (number of works whose recomputed average differs from the stored one) exceeding ~0.01% of works touched.
- **Rating-velocity anomaly per work.** Alert when a work's hourly rating rate exceeds 20× its trailing 7-day baseline *and* more than 50% come from accounts under 30 days old; this is the brigading trigger.
- **Human review queue depth and age.** SLO: 95% of high-stakes pairs (both sides >1000 ratings) resolved within 7 days; a growing queue means the thresholds are miscalibrated, not that moderators are slow.
- **Recommendation catalog coverage**, distinct works recommended to ≥1 user per week ÷ catalog size. Watch for monotonic decline, which is the signature of popularity collapse even while click-through looks fine.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** active-active for reads everywhere, because the catalog is globally identical and read-only at request time, so full read replicas per region plus CDN edges are cheap and obvious. Writes (shelvings, ratings, reviews) are home-region per user with async cross-region replication; the entity-resolution and recommender batch jobs run in a single primary region and push their outputs (cluster table, aggregates, recommendation lists, search index) to every region.
- **RTO:** ~5 minutes for in-region replica promotion. Loss of the batch region is not an outage at all: the serving path keeps using the last-published cluster table and recommendation lists, so the only impact is that newly-ingested books stay unresolved until the job region recovers, tolerable for hours.
- **RPO:** ~seconds for shelvings and ratings via async replication; a forced failover may lose the last few writes, mitigated by idempotent client retry keyed on `(user_id, edition_id, action)`. The catalog itself has an RPO of zero in practice, since it is rebuildable from the source feeds plus the merge log.
- **Failover cadence:** automatic in-region; cross-region game-days quarterly, including a deliberate batch-region failure to confirm the serving path degrades to "stale but correct" rather than failing.
- **Cross-region cost:** the catalog snapshot and search index (~2TB) replicate on a nightly cadence rather than continuously. That is the dominant egress line, and the reason to compress and ship deltas off the merge log rather than full dumps. Shelving and rating deltas are ~2GB/day, negligible. Cover images live in a multi-region object store behind the CDN and never cross regions on the request path.

### 46. Design an LLM Inference & Serving Platform
#### Problem
Serve an autoregressive transformer behind a public API with streaming and non-streaming completions, at high throughput, predictable per-token latency and a defensible cost per million tokens.
#### Core
Inference is two workloads sharing one set of weights, and everything follows from that split. Prefill pushes the whole prompt through the model in one pass and runs near the arithmetic roofline. Decode emits one token per sequence per step, and every step re-reads every weight out of HBM, so a lone stream achieves a fraction of a percent of the machine. Throughput comes from batching decode, which makes the batch the thing the system is actually scheduling.

What caps the batch is memory, not arithmetic. Each sequence in flight holds key and value tensors for every token of its context, about 320KB per token on a 70B model with grouped-query attention. A 1,100-token conversation is 350MB, a 32k one is 10.5GB, and concurrency is just a division: KV pool over bytes per sequence. Capacity models built from FLOPs and parameter count will tell you the machine is compute-bound while it sits out of memory at batch 40.

So requests wait in a queue, never on a GPU. A per-replica scheduler owns the KV pool and admits from that queue only when free blocks allow, re-deciding batch membership every step rather than every request. KV lives in fixed 16-token blocks with a per-sequence block table, which is virtual memory for attention, and it makes shared prompt prefixes a refcount rather than a recomputation.

Output length is unknown at admission, so admission is optimistic and preemption is the safety valve: evict the newest low-priority sequence and recompute its prefill when it returns.

Weights are 140GB, an 80GB GPU cannot hold them, so a replica is 8 GPUs tensor-parallel inside one NVLink domain. Scale is replicas, and the number the business watches is dollars per million tokens.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a restaurant kitchen with one enormous, extremely slow oven. Getting the oven up to temperature for a dish (reading the prompt) is fast and parallel, and you can slide fifty trays in at once. But every dish then has to come *out* of the oven one spoonful at a time, and each spoonful requires the entire oven to cycle. The only way to make that economical is to cook fifty dishes simultaneously in the same cycle. The catch: each dish reserves a fixed shelf of oven space that grows as it cooks, nobody tells you how long any dish will take, and the oven has a hard shelf limit. Scheduling that oven *is* the system.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Give each request the machine.* One generation at a time per copy of the model, sized so that copy hits the latency target. It is trivial to reason about and the latency a request sees is the latency it always sees, because no stranger's arrival can change it. It also burns the entire memory bandwidth of the hardware to produce one token, which is roughly a hundredth of what the machine can do. This wins for a single-tenant deployment with a hard latency floor, or for a model small enough that you can afford many copies and route one request to each.

*Fill a batch at the door and run it to completion.* Collect a fixed number of requests, generate for all of them together, then take the next set. Batching is where the throughput is, and a fixed batch shape is easy to optimise for because nothing changes shape mid-run. The cost is that the batch only retires when its longest generation finishes, and output lengths vary by more than an order of magnitude, so most slots spend most of their life producing nothing. It wins for offline bulk work with no per-token deadline, especially when the work is length-homogeneous.

*Put a scheduler in front of the memory and re-form the batch every step.* Requests queue outside the GPU. The scheduler admits one only when it can afford the memory the sequence will hold, drops finished sequences the step they end, and takes work back when it over-committed. Utilisation tracks offered load instead of collapsing to the slowest member, worth several times the throughput of the previous option. The cost is a stateful, latency-critical component in the hot path, and the fact that every sequence admitted slows down every sequence already running. This wins for interactive multi-tenant traffic with variable output lengths, which describes almost every public completions API.

**The single-request walkthrough, prefill:** a client POSTs 800 prompt tokens to `/v1/completions` with `stream=true`. The gateway authenticates, checks the tenant's token bucket (see #1), tokenises the prompt (~3ms) and pushes the request onto a priority queue (see #16). The scheduler for a replica, meaning the 8 GPUs holding one tensor-parallel copy of the model, checks whether it can afford the request: 800 tokens ÷ 16 tokens per KV block = 50 blocks, ~16MB of key/value tensors. It can, so it admits. The prefix cache is consulted: the first 600 tokens are a system prompt this tenant has sent 40,000 times today, so those KV blocks already exist and are simply refcounted in, leaving only 200 tokens to compute. Prefill runs the whole 200-token span through all 80 layers **in parallel**, one dense matmul pass, ~112 TFLOP for a full 800-token prompt, ~8ms for the 200 uncached tokens on a replica doing ~3.6 PFLOP/s. First token emitted. **TTFT ≈ 25ms** on a cache hit, ~70ms cold.

**The single-request walkthrough, decode:** now the request joins the running batch of ~256 sequences and generates one token per scheduler step. Each step reads *every weight in the model* out of HBM, 17.5GB per GPU at ~2.3TB/s achieved for ~7.6ms, plus the KV cache for all 256 sequences (~10.2GB per GPU, ~4.4ms), plus ~2ms of tensor-parallel all-reduce. **One step ≈ 14ms, and it produces one token for all 256 sequences at once.** Per-stream that is ~71 tokens/s; per-replica it is ~18,000 tokens/s. Those 14ms are almost entirely spent *moving bytes* rather than doing arithmetic, which is why the batch is close to free throughput and why running one sequence alone wastes 99% of the machine. 300 output tokens later the sampler hits a stop token, the sequence's KV blocks are freed back to the pool the same step, and a queued request is admitted in its place.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **API gateway.** Authn, per-tenant token-bucket quotas on both requests/min and *tokens*/min (see #1; tokens, not requests, are the real unit of cost), request shaping, SSE connection management. Must propagate client disconnects downstream, because an abandoned SSE stream that keeps generating is pure burned GPU.
- **Priority queue (durable, partitioned by tenant and tier).** See #16. Requests wait here, not on the GPU. Queue depth is the load-shedding signal; admission is a scheduler decision, not a load-balancer one.
- **Scheduler (per replica, in-process).** The heart of the system. Every step it evicts finished sequences, preempts if the KV pool is exhausted, admits from the queue against the free-block budget, and issues one fused forward pass. This is *continuous batching*: batch membership changes every 14ms rather than every request.
- **Paged KV cache.** KV tensors stored in fixed 16-token blocks, allocated non-contiguously, with a per-sequence block table. It is virtual memory for attention. The attention kernel is rewritten to gather from the block table instead of assuming one contiguous buffer.
- **Prefix cache (refcounted KV blocks, LRU).** Blocks keyed by a rolling hash of the token prefix. A shared system prompt is computed once and reused by every request that starts with it, across tenants only when the prefix is byte-identical.
- **Model registry (object store + metadata DB).** Versioned safetensors shards, ~140GB per bf16 version. Replicas pull and mmap on cold start.
- **Usage ledger and telemetry.** Per-request prompt and output token counts, TTFT, inter-token latency histogram, finish reason; feeds billing and the metrics pipeline (see #17).

**The thing that makes it hard:** **the KV cache is the binding constraint, and it is invisible in every FLOP-based capacity model.** Every sequence in flight holds a key and a value tensor for every token, for every layer, permanently, until it finishes, and it *grows by one token every step*. With 80 layers, 8 grouped-query KV heads and head dimension 128 in bf16, one token costs `2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2B = ~320KB`. A 1,100-token conversation is ~350MB of GPU memory. An 8k-token one is ~2.6GB. A 32k-token one is ~10.5GB, a single user occupying an eighth of an 80GB GPU. So the concurrency ceiling is set by memory, not compute, and it moves as prompts get longer. Worse, in the naive allocator each sequence reserves `max_tokens` worth of *contiguous* memory up front, because the attention kernel wants one flat buffer, so a request that declares `max_tokens=8192` and generates 40 tokens holds 2.6GB to use 13MB. Between that internal waste and external fragmentation of the free list, a naive server leaves 60-80% of its KV memory unused and then reports that it is "out of memory" at a batch size of 20.

**Why this design and what it costs:** PagedAttention, published in 2023 and the technique vLLM is built on, borrows the operating-system answer. Split KV into fixed-size blocks of 16 tokens, keep a per-sequence page table mapping logical token positions to physical blocks, and let the attention kernel gather across them. Allocation becomes lazy and per-block: a sequence holds only what it has actually generated, rounded up to 16 tokens. External fragmentation disappears entirely because every block is the same size; internal fragmentation is bounded at 15 tokens, so 15 × 320KB ≈ ~4.8MB against a ~350MB sequence, under 1.5%. Concretely, on our ~452GB per-replica pool: contiguous pre-allocation to an 8k ceiling gives 452GB ÷ 2.6GB = **~173 slots**; paged allocation at true length gives 452GB ÷ 350MB = **~1,290**, roughly a 7× concurrency win from an allocator change alone. Copy-on-write between blocks makes parallel sampling and beam search nearly free (n candidates share the prompt's blocks and fork only where they diverge), and shared prefixes fall out as refcounted blocks. The costs are real: the attention kernel is now a custom gather that runs a few percent slower than a contiguous one, the block table is an extra indirection on the hot path, and you have inherited a memory allocator along with every eviction-policy, thrashing and accounting bug that implies.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- vLLM or TensorRT-LLM as the engine (both ship paged KV, continuous batching, chunked prefill, speculative decoding). Ray or a plain Kubernetes StatefulSet for replica placement, one replica per 8-GPU NVLink node. Envoy at the edge for SSE. Kafka for the request queue (#16), Redis for tenant token buckets (#1), Prometheus + a columnar store for usage (#17).
- Scheduler step, which is the whole design in fifteen lines:
  ```
  BLOCK = 16          tokens of KV per physical block
  RESERVE = 512       blocks held back so running seqs can grow

  def step():
      while queue and kv.free_blocks() > RESERVE:
          req = queue.peek_highest_priority()
          shared = prefix_cache.lookup(req.prompt)     refcount, skip that prefill
          need = ceil((len(req.prompt) - shared) / BLOCK)
          if kv.free_blocks() - need <= RESERVE: break
          running.add(prefill(req, skip=shared, chunk=256))
          queue.pop()

      logits = model.forward(running)                  one token for every running seq
      for seq in running:
          seq.append(sample(logits[seq]))              may need a new block
          if seq.stopped(): emit_done(seq); kv.free(seq)
      while kv.free_blocks() == 0:
          preempt(newest_lowest_priority(running))     swap out or drop and recompute
  ```
#### What this is really testing
Whether you can find the binding constraint by arithmetic rather than by naming components. Almost everyone reaches for parameter count and FLOPs, concludes the problem is compute, and sizes a fleet that runs out of memory at a twentieth of the batch they planned for. The number that governs the design is bytes of key-value state per token, `2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × dtype`, and once you have it the architecture is forced: concurrency is a division, so the serving platform is a memory allocator with a scheduler on top of it, and every subsequent decision is about how that memory is spent. The second half of the same insight is that prefill and decode are different machines, one compute-bound and one bandwidth-bound, which is why a single blended latency SLO describes nothing and why batching helps one phase and is irrelevant to the other. A candidate who says "we'll shard the model and autoscale on GPU utilisation" has named two things that are both wrong here: the sharding is forced by weight size and is not the interesting choice, and GPU utilisation reads 100% on a batch-1 decode achieving 0.2% of peak.

The contrast is with the RAG question. That design treats the model as a black box behind an HTTP call with a fixed latency, and its entire difficulty is upstream of that call: how documents are chunked, which embedding model, how the vector index is built and refreshed, whether a reranker earns its latency, and how you measure whether the retrieved passage was the right one. Its unit of correctness is relevance, and it can be evaluated offline against labelled queries. Nothing in this question is about relevance. Here the model is not a black box, it is the whole problem, and correctness is a memory budget that either balances or does not. The two meet at exactly one place and it is worth saying out loud: RAG generates long prompts with a large shared prefix, since the system prompt and instructions are constant while only the retrieved chunks vary. That is simultaneously the input distribution that stresses KV memory hardest and the one that prefix caching pays off on best, so a RAG workload is the case where the serving platform's cache hit rate is a first-order cost lever. Answer this question with chunk sizes and embedding models and you have answered the other one; answer the other one with block tables and you have optimised the cheap half.

Closest question: Q50
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- One model, or a fleet of models and per-tenant LoRA adapters served from shared base weights?
- What maximum context window must we support: 4k, 32k, or 128k?
- Is streaming required for all traffic, or is some of it batch/offline where latency is irrelevant?
- Multi-tenant with hard isolation and per-customer quotas, or a single internal consumer?
- Interactive-latency-sensitive (chat) or throughput-sensitive (bulk document processing)?
- Can we quantise, or is bit-for-bit output parity with bf16 a hard requirement?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Many models / per-tenant adapters | shared base weights in HBM with LoRA adapters swapped per request; otherwise one model per replica pool and route by model id |
| Long context (32k+) | KV memory dominates everything: concurrency falls ~30×, chunked prefill becomes mandatory, and KV quantisation moves from optional to required |
| Streaming required | SSE end to end, TTFT and inter-token latency as separate SLOs, and disconnect propagation to abort generation |
| Multi-tenant with quotas | token-bucket limits on tokens/min not just requests/min (see #1), per-tenant queues and fair-share admission to stop one tenant monopolising the batch |
| Throughput-sensitive | push batch size past the roofline crossover, disable speculative decoding, and offer a cheaper async tier with a relaxed TTFT |
| Quantisation allowed | fp8 weights halve the decode bandwidth term and free ~70GB/replica for KV; gate it behind an eval suite, not a vibe check |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** streaming and non-streaming completions, per-tenant quotas and usage accounting, multiple model versions with safe rollout, request cancellation, deterministic sampling on request (seed + temperature).
- **NFR:** TTFT p95 < 400ms and inter-token latency p95 < 30ms (≥ 33 tok/s per stream) at 2k req/s peak; 99.9% availability; cost ≤ ~$0.50 per million blended tokens at realistic fleet utilisation.

**Scale**

- **Traffic:** assume ~1k req/s daily average and ~2k req/s peak (2× diurnal, US-daytime concentrated). Representative mix ~800 prompt + ~300 output tokens → peak = 2000 × 1100 = **~2.2M tokens/s**, ~190B tokens/day.
- **Weights:** 70B params × 2B (bf16) = **~140GB**. An 80GB GPU cannot hold it, parallelism is forced on us, not chosen. fp8 → ~70GB, int4 → ~35GB.
- **KV bytes per token:** assume 80 layers, 64 query heads, **8 KV heads (GQA)**, head_dim 128, bf16. `2 (K+V) × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 327,680B` ≈ **~320KB/token**. With plain multi-head attention (64 KV heads) it is 8× that, ~2.5MB/token. GQA is the single largest KV lever, and it is an architecture decision rather than a serving one.
- **KV per request:** 1100 × ~320KB = **~350MB**. At 8k context: 8192 × 320KB = ~2.6GB. At 32k: **~10.5GB for one sequence**.
- **Per-replica memory:** 8 × 80GB = 640GB. Weights TP-sharded: 140 ÷ 8 = 17.5GB/GPU. Reserve ~6GB/GPU (activations for a 256-token prefill chunk, CUDA graphs, NCCL buffers, allocator slack). KV pool = (80 − 17.5 − 6) × 8 = **~452GB per replica**.
- **Concurrency is a memory number:** 452GB ÷ 350MB = **~1,290 sequences** at the 1.1k-token mix; ÷ 2.6GB = ~173 at 8k; ÷ 10.5GB = **~43 at 32k**. Identical hardware, 30× fewer users, purely from context length. The paging win falls straight out: contiguous pre-allocation to an 8k ceiling gives those same ~173 slots at *every* context length, so paging is **~7×** here, for ≤1.5% internal fragmentation (≤15 unused tokens × 320KB ≈ ~4.8MB of ~350MB).
- **Decode step:** per GPU, weight read 17.5GB ÷ (3.3TB/s × ~70% achieved = 2.3TB/s) = ~7.6ms; KV read at B=256 × ~1000 tokens ctx × 320KB ÷ 8 = ~10.2GB → ~4.4ms; all-reduce and launch ~2ms. **ITL ≈ 14ms** (~71 tok/s/stream). Replica decode throughput = 256 ÷ 14ms = **~18k output tokens/s**. Machine balance is ~1 PFLOP/s ÷ 3.3TB/s ≈ **300 FLOP/byte**, so decode stays memory-bound only up to batch ≈ 300; past that each added sequence costs latency roughly linearly, which is the hard ceiling on "just batch harder".
- **Prefill:** ≈ 2 × 70e9 = **~140 GFLOP/token** (the attention n² term adds ~1.5% at 800 tokens; at 32k it is no longer ignorable). 800 tokens = ~112 TFLOP/request. At ~45% MFU → ~3.6 PFLOP/s per replica → **prefill ≈ 31ms**.
- **Fleet:** decode 2000 × 300 = 600k tok/s ÷ 18k = **~33 replicas (264 GPUs)**. Prefill 2000 × 800 = 1.6M tok/s × 140 GFLOP = 224 PFLOP/s ÷ 3.6 = **~62 replicas (~500 GPUs)**. Peak ≈ **~765 GPUs ≈ 96 eight-GPU nodes**; ~half at daily average.
- **Prefix caching pays for a third of the fleet:** if ~600 of the 800 prompt tokens are a shared system prompt at a ~75% hit rate, effective prefill = 800 − (600 × 0.75) = 350 tokens/request → prefill drops to ~220 GPUs, total ~485.
- **Cost per million tokens:** assume **~$2.50/GPU-hour** amortised. Peak 765 GPUs = ~$1.9k/hour serving 7.9B tokens/hour → **~$0.24/M at 100% utilisation**; at a realistic ~50% average fleet utilisation, **~$0.48/M** before margin. An output token costs ~2.7× a prompt token here (264 GPUs for 600k tok/s against ~500 for 1.6M tok/s), which is exactly why providers price them separately.
- **Weight distribution + cold start:** 140GB pulled from object store at ~2GB/s effective = ~70s, plus shard load, CUDA-graph capture and warmup → **~3-5 min to first healthy token**. 12 live versions × 140GB ≈ ~1.7TB stored; a full fleet roll is 96 × 140GB ≈ **~13TB of egress**.
- **Telemetry + usage:** 2k req/s × ~2KB metadata (tenant, model, token counts, TTFT, ITL histogram, finish reason, and no prompt content by default) = ~4MB/s → **~350GB/day**; RF=3 → ~1TB/day, 30 days hot then rolled to columnar (#17).
#### Key decisions
**Tensor parallelism inside a node against pipeline parallelism across nodes**
- Choice: TP=8 within one NVLink domain, one replica per 8-GPU node, no pipeline parallelism. 140GB ÷ 8 = 17.5GB of weights per GPU, leaving ~56GB each for KV.
- Alternative: split the layers into pipeline stages across two or more nodes, so each stage ships only the boundary activation over the network rather than all-reducing every layer.
- Decider: interconnect bandwidth measured against the per-token latency budget. TP all-reduces twice per transformer block, so per decode step it moves `B × d_model × 2B × 2 × layers` = `256 × 8192 × 2 × 2 × 80` ≈ 670MB. On NVLink at ~900GB/s that is ~0.7ms on a 14ms step. On a 400Gb/s fabric at ~50GB/s effective it is ~13ms, which nearly doubles the step and eats the entire margin under a 30ms p95 ITL SLO. So TP is bounded by the NVLink domain, and the domain is 8 GPUs.
- Alternative wins when: the model does not fit in one domain at all. A 400B model in bf16 is ~800GB against 640GB per node, so it is TP=8 inside nodes and PP=2 across them, and there is no choice to make. It also wins on prefill-heavy or offline tiers, where many independent prompts are queued so micro-batches are plentiful. Be honest about what PP costs in decode: the idle fraction is `(p−1)/(m+p−1)`, and decode naturally runs one micro-batch in flight, so p=2 idles 50% of the fleet. Filling the pipe means splitting the batch into m micro-batches, and each micro-batch re-reads the stage's weights, so m=8 reads 140GB eight times per token round instead of once. Filling PP bubbles costs precisely the arithmetic intensity that makes batched decode economical, which is why PP is a consequence of model size and almost never an optimisation.

**Continuous batching against static batching**
- Choice: continuous batching. Batch membership is re-decided every step, finished sequences are evicted the step they stop, and queued requests take the vacated slots immediately.
- Alternative: static batching. Assemble a fixed cohort, run it to completion, take the next cohort, optionally grouping by predicted output length to cut the padding.
- Decider: the occupancy gain against the ITL swing a live stream has to absorb. With output lengths roughly exponential around a mean of 300, the expected maximum of 32 draws is 300 × H₃₂ ≈ 1,220 tokens, so a static batch retires on a member running four times longer than average and the mean slot generates padding for ~75% of its life. Continuous batching takes occupancy past 90% and is worth 2 to 4×. It costs a stream a per-token latency that moves with strangers' arrivals: 9ms at B=64, 14ms at 256, 22ms at 512, so a request can see its own ITL degrade 2.4× mid-response. Under a 30ms p95 SLO that fits behind an interactive batch cap of ~192. Under a 12ms SLO it does not, and the cap needed would give back more throughput than static batching's padding costs.
- Alternative wins when: the work is offline and length-homogeneous. Bulk embedding, classification, and fixed-schema extraction all produce outputs within a narrow band, so the padding loss is small, and a fixed batch shape lets you capture CUDA graphs and delete the scheduler from the hot path entirely. It also wins on any runtime without a paged attention kernel, where variable batch composition means real reallocation rather than a block-table update.

**Speculative decoding on or off**
- Choice: off at production batch sizes, enabled per tier when the running batch drops below ~64, as a load-adaptive switch rather than a deployment-wide setting.
- Alternative: always on with a tuned k, treating the draft model as a permanent part of the serving path.
- Decider: the draft model's measured acceptance rate on your own traffic, against the running batch size. With k=4 the expected accepted tokens per verify is `(1 − α^(k+1))/(1 − α)`. At B ≤ 64 the step is ~9ms and a verify plus 4 draft forwards is ~10.2ms, so break-even is 1.13 accepted tokens, α ≈ 0.12, and a realistic α of 0.7 yields 2.77 tokens for ~3.7ms per token against 9ms, a 2.4× win. At B=256 the verify pass covers 256 × 5 = 1,280 token positions against a machine balance of ~300 FLOP/byte, so it is compute-bound and costs roughly 14ms × 1280/300 ≈ 60ms. Break-even there needs 4.3 accepted tokens per verify, which requires α above ~0.93, and no general-purpose draft model reaches that. Below the threshold you are paying verification cost for tokens you throw away.
- Alternative wins when: the generation is low-entropy enough that a prompt-lookup or n-gram draft hits α > 0.9. Code editing that copies long verbatim spans, structured reformatting, and quote-heavy summarisation all qualify, and there speculation wins even at full batch. It also wins on a fixed on-prem fleet at low QPS, where GPU-hours are sunk and throughput has no marginal value. This fork should be re-measured rather than settled once: trained self-drafting heads published from 2023 onward (Medusa, EAGLE) push α materially higher than a separate small model, and the break-even moves with them.

**How to read the diagram:** requests never wait on a GPU. They wait in the queue, and the per-replica scheduler pulls them in only when the paged KV pool can afford them. Inside the replica, prefill and decode are two different workloads sharing the same weights and the same KV pool, and the scheduler interleaves them every 14ms.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** admission has to be co-located with the memory it is spending. A generic load balancer can see request counts but not free KV blocks, so it will happily route a 32k-token prompt to a replica that has 12MB left. Putting the scheduler next to the allocator is the whole trick.

**What this layout buys you:** GPU utilisation that tracks offered load instead of collapsing to the slowest request in a batch, and a single number, the free-block count, where backpressure, preemption and load-shedding are all decided. The trade-off is that the scheduler is now a stateful, latency-critical component you cannot restart casually.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**One mechanism carries this system: the scheduler and the paged pool it spends.** Everything else is configuration around it.

Start from bytes per token. `2 (K and V) × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 head_dim × 2B` = 327,680B, call it **320KB per token**, held for every token of context, for the entire life of the sequence, growing by one token every step. A 1,100-token conversation is ~350MB, a 32k one is ~10.5GB, and on a replica with a ~452GB pool concurrency is a division and nothing else: 452GB ÷ 350MB ≈ **1,290 sequences**, or ~43 at 32k. Same hardware, thirty times fewer users, purely from context length.

The naive allocator throws most of that away. The attention kernel wants one flat buffer per sequence, so each admitted sequence reserves `max_tokens` of contiguous memory up front. A request declaring 8,192 that stops after 40 tokens holds 2.6GB to use 13MB. Add external fragmentation, where a 2.6GB hole cannot serve a 2.7GB request, and 60 to 80% of the pool sits idle while the server reports out-of-memory at a batch of 20.

**Paging, published as PagedAttention in 2023.** Fixed 16-token blocks, a per-sequence block table mapping logical token positions to physical block ids, and an attention kernel that gathers across that table instead of assuming contiguity. It is virtual memory, and the properties transfer exactly. Allocation is lazy and per-block, so a sequence holds what it has generated rounded up to 16 tokens. External fragmentation is gone because every block is identical in size, and internal fragmentation is bounded at 15 tokens: 15 × 320KB ≈ 4.8MB against a ~350MB sequence, under 1.5%. On our pool, contiguous pre-allocation to an 8k ceiling gives 452GB ÷ 2.6GB ≈ 173 slots at *every* context length, while paged allocation at true length gives ~1,290, about **7× concurrency for an allocator change**. Two more properties fall out. Blocks are refcounted, so copy-on-write makes parallel sampling and beam search nearly free: n candidates share the prompt's blocks and fork only where they diverge. And a shared prefix is just a block run with refcount above one, so a 600-token system prompt costs ~192MB held once rather than per request. Key blocks by a rolling hash at 16-token granularity, pin the top ~50 tenant prompts for ~9.6GB of the 452GB pool, and ~75% of the prefill fleet's work disappears. The cache key must carry the model version, or a rollout serves KV computed by the previous weights.

**Then the hard part: admission without knowing the output length.** The scheduler knows the prompt length exactly and the output length not at all, so it must commit memory for a job whose size it learns only when the job ends. Reserving `max_tokens` is safe and catastrophic, because it is the contiguous mistake in new clothing. Admission is therefore optimistic: charge only for the blocks the prompt actually needs, hold back a `RESERVE` of ~512 blocks so every running sequence can grow by one block on the next step, and let the pool run hot.

Which makes **preemption** a routine control path rather than an error path. When free blocks reach zero mid-step, evict a victim and either swap its KV to host DRAM over PCIe (~350MB at ~16GB/s ≈ 22ms each way, on bandwidth shared with weight loading) or drop it and recompute the prefill on readmission (1,100 tokens × 140 GFLOP ÷ 3.6 PFLOP/s ≈ 43ms, stateless, and contending only for compute). Recompute is the sane default. Victim choice matters more than the mechanism: preempt the **newest, lowest-priority** sequence, because preempting the oldest discards the most accumulated work and produces convoys in which the same nearly-finished requests are evicted repeatedly. Newest-first starves late arrivals under sustained pressure, so age the queue: after two preemptions a request is promoted and becomes ineligible as a victim.

Tune `RESERVE` so preemption stays under ~1% of steps. Above ~5% the pool is thrashing, which is the allocator's classic failure in a new costume: throughput collapses while every instantaneous gauge looks healthy, because the free-block count reads fine immediately after each eviction. Alert on preemptions per thousand steps and on recomputed tokens per second, never on pool occupancy alone.

Output length can be *predicted*, with a small classifier over the prompt at roughly 60% accuracy for a short/medium/long bucketing, and used to order admission so long generations do not all land in the same step. Never use it to reserve. A wrong prediction that reserves is strictly worse than no prediction, because it converts a recoverable over-commitment into memory nobody can use.

**Which constraint actually binds is workload-dependent, and both regimes occur in the same fleet on the same day.** At the 1.1k-token mix, memory permits ~1,290 concurrent sequences while the 30ms p95 ITL budget permits ~256, so latency binds and the pool runs at roughly 20% occupancy. Push the mix to 8k contexts and memory binds first at ~173, well below any latency cap. The scheduler needs both limits live, and an operator reading pool occupancy alone will misdiagnose whichever regime they are not in.

**The scheduler's step loop (visual).** Cardinalities at peak on one replica: ~1.2k requests queued platform-wide, ~256 running, ~50 KV blocks per admitted 800-token prompt, ~17.5k of ~88k blocks allocated (452GB ÷ 5.12MB per block). Latency budget per step: admission and block accounting ~0.3ms, one 256-token prefill chunk ~10ms when present, the fused decode forward ~12ms, all-reduce ~2ms, sampling and detokenisation ~0.5ms, eviction and free-list return ~0.2ms.
