**All three lanes close the same way.** Whichever lane granted it, a reserve produces one artefact: a hold record with a TTL, 15 minutes at checkout entry and 10 on a drop. Nothing about the lane leaks past that point, which is what lets a single checkout saga serve all three. `confirm(hold_id)` turns the hold into an allocation after payment and is the only step that makes a sale final. `release(hold_id)` and TTL expiry both return the quantity, and on a hot SKU that means adding it back to the in-memory counter so the consumer keeps draining, putting an abandoned unit back in front of the queue rather than losing it. Expiry runs on native TTL with keyspace-expiry events rather than a polling scan, because millions of holds expire in the same minute after a sale and a sweeper that falls behind makes real stock invisible.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hot inventory row.** One SKU absorbs ~8k reserve/s and neither optimistic retry nor a row lock keeps up. Route by measured SKU heat: conditional update for cold, 32-way bucketing for warm, single-consumer stream serialisation for hot. Trade-off: the hot lane makes reserve asynchronous (ticket plus SSE) and introduces a single-consumer failure domain that needs sub-second partition reassignment.
- **CDN origin stampede at T=0.** A drop page not yet in cache produces ~90k simultaneous origin misses. Pre-render and pre-push drop pages and images to every POP an hour ahead, and enable request coalescing at the edge so concurrent misses for the same key produce one origin fetch. Trade-off: pre-warming costs egress for pages that may not sell, and a late content edit must re-warm.
- **Search index CDC lag on price changes.** A price edit reaches the search index seconds to minutes later, so a price-sorted results page can be visibly wrong. Keep price out of the cached result card where possible and hydrate it from the edge KV; index a coarse price *band* for filtering rather than the exact value. Trade-off: exact-price sorting is then approximate near band boundaries.
- **Checkout saga orchestrator as a shared dependency.** Every order flows through it, so its outage stops all purchasing while browse continues. Run it as a durable workflow engine with persisted state so a restart resumes mid-order rather than restarting the saga, and shard workflow ownership by `hash(order_id)`. Trade-off: durable workflow state adds ~2 extra persisted writes per order.
- **Hold-expiry sweeper backlog.** After a sale, millions of holds expire at once and a slow sweeper leaves stock invisible for minutes. Prefer native TTL with keyspace-expiry events over a polling scan, and treat the sweeper as a backstop that reconciles, not the primary mechanism. Trade-off: TTL-driven expiry gives weaker ordering guarantees, so the reconciler must be idempotent against holds already released.
- **Payment provider rate limits during a spike.** 800 orders/s can exceed a provider's per-merchant limit and turn into a wall of 429s. Bulkhead the payment step with its own concurrency budget and queue, spread across two providers with health-based routing (see #23). Trade-off: multi-provider adds reconciliation complexity across two settlement reports.
- **Load shedding that sheds the wrong thing.** At 100x load something must give, and the naive answer of shedding by request rate throws away shoppers who already hold stock and a payment authorisation, wasting all three. Grade the ladder explicitly: personalisation and recommendations first because nobody notices, then reviews from a stale snapshot, then search reranking with a fall back to plain relevance ordering, then admission of *new* checkout entries at the waiting room, and never browse or an in-flight checkout. Trade-off: the ladder has to be wired into every service as a tier flag rather than enforced at one choke point, so it is real work that pays off only during an incident.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| CDN | POP-wide eviction or cold cache at drop time causes origin flood | Origin request rate vs. baseline; cache hit ratio drop below 90% | Request coalescing at the edge; pre-warm before scheduled drops; origin shield tier; serve stale-while-revalidate for up to 60s |
| Catalog store | Partition unavailable; PDP misses cannot be rendered | Per-partition error rate; origin 5xx by `sku_id` prefix | Serve stale CDN copy beyond TTL (`stale-if-error` 24h); degrade to a minimal page with title and price from the edge KV |
| Search | Index shard down or reranker timing out | Shard health; search p99 and empty-result-rate alerts | Fail over to replica shards; bypass the reranker and serve BM25 order; cache top-1k head queries for a full-outage fallback |
| Inventory hot lane | Single consumer for a hot SKU dies mid-drop | Consumer heartbeat; partition lag alert at > 2s | Standby consumer takes the partition; replay from the last persisted offset; `hold_id` dedupe makes re-application safe; worst case ~50ms of decrements re-applied |
| Inventory buckets | Skewed hashing empties some buckets while stock remains | Per-bucket remaining distribution; sold-out-with-stock counter | Next-bucket probe then steal-from-fullest; forced merge and promotion to the queue lane when `total_remaining < 2N` |
| Holds | Hold expires while payment is in flight | `PAID_UNRESERVED` order count; hold-extension failure rate | Extend TTL before the charge step; on failure re-reserve immediately, else automatic full refund plus goodwill credit and an alert |
| Checkout saga | Orchestrator crashes between payment success and hold confirmation | Orders stuck in `PENDING` beyond 60s | Durable workflow state resumes from the last completed step; a reconciler queries the provider by idempotency key (see #23) and either confirms or compensates |
| Payment provider | Provider degraded or rate limiting during the spike | 429 rate; auth latency p99; provider health endpoint | Bulkheaded concurrency budget with a bounded queue; failover to secondary provider; if both are down, shed *new* checkouts and keep browse fully up |
| Order store | Order shard primary fails after payment capture | Shard write error rate; replication lag alert | Synchronous replica promotion; the payment step is never acked to the client until the order row is durable, so a lost ack becomes an idempotent retry |

**Unresolved**

**A cart that mixes lanes cannot be reserved as a unit.** A shopper puts the doorbuster and three ordinary items in one cart. The three ordinary lines reserve synchronously in about 3ms each; the doorbuster line returns a ticket and an answer that may take 250ms or, behind a deep queue, several seconds. There is no transaction across those. What we do is reserve the cold lines first and hold them while the hot line is queued, which means ordinary stock is held hostage to a queue for as long as the ticket takes, and if the hot line comes back sold out the shopper either buys a partial cart or we release everything they had. Neither is good and neither is hidden from them. The only clean fix is to make the hot line synchronous, which is exactly the property we removed to survive the spike. We cap the cold-line hold at the hot lane's p99 and bias toward partial fulfilment, shipping what we can and telling the shopper plainly that the doorbuster missed, because a partial order recovers most of the basket value and a full release recovers none. It is a policy choice papering over a missing guarantee.

**We cannot promise the price a shopper saw.** Promotions depend on the rest of the cart and tax depends on an address, so a product page can never hold the authoritative number, and a re-quote at checkout is structural rather than a bug. Everything we do about it is presentation: `quoted_total` with a `changes[]` array explaining each delta, `accepted_total` echoed back on `POST /orders` so nobody is charged a number they did not see, and a configurable threshold that absorbs small increases, say under 2% or £1, rather than hard-coding a policy that varies by jurisdiction. None of that changes the experience of being shown £40 and asked for £43. The alternative, a genuine price lock for the duration of a session, means a promotions-engine write per browsing session at 2.8k page views a second and re-opens the arbitrage of stacking locks taken before a promotion expired. We have not built it and I would not claim the explained delta is equivalent.

**The heat classifier is reactive, so the first seconds of an unannounced spike run in the wrong lane.** A 10-second rolling window means a viral post or an unplanned restock hits the cold lane for its first few seconds, during which one row absorbs thousands of conditional updates. It fails safely, because a conditional update that loses simply affects zero rows and rejects the buyer, so this is degraded latency and lost sales rather than an oversell. But it is lost sales during the only seconds that mattered. Shortening the window makes the classifier flap on ordinary noise, and flapping during a bucket merge is the one transition that can actually lose count, so the window is not free to tune down. Scheduled sales are pre-classified and that covers most real traffic, but "most" is the concession: the unannounced case is the one this design handles worst, and the honest mitigation is a fast path that promotes on a burst detector at the load balancer rather than on a rate window, which we have specified and not built.
#### Drill questions
1. Why not just use optimistic concurrency on the inventory row?
2. Then why not a pessimistic row lock, which is correct and simple?
3. Where do you reserve, at add-to-cart or at checkout?
4. A buyer hashes to an empty bucket while 4 units sit in other buckets. What happens?
5. Would you ever deliberately oversell?
6. A shopper double-taps Buy on a flaky connection. Two orders?
7. The hold expires while the payment is still in flight. Now what?
8. A SKU goes viral with no warning. What happens in the first three seconds?
9. Why not put every SKU on the queue lane and delete the classifier?
10. A cart holds one doorbuster and three ordinary items. What do you reserve, and in what order?
11. Why can't you charge the price cached on the product page?
12. A guest with two of a SKU in their cart signs in, and the account cart already has two of the same SKU. How many do they end up with?
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Because under high contention the retry loop is the problem. One writer per round succeeds and the rest retry, and retries stack on top of new arrivals, so goodput falls as offered load rises, which is a livelock rather than a slowdown. *If pushed:* optimistic control is correct and cheap when contention is *rare*, which is true for 99.99% of SKUs, so we do use a conditional update in the cold lane. The mistake is applying one concurrency strategy uniformly; the fix is to detect the hot minority and route them somewhere that does not retry.

2. It is correct, and it does not keep up. A ~3ms critical section gives one row ~330 decrements/s against ~8,000 arrivals/s, so the wait queue grows by ~7,670 per second and never drains within the event. *If pushed:* the second-order damage is worse than the latency, because waiters pin database connections, the pool exhausts, and unrelated SKUs start timing out. A hot row should never be able to take down cold ones; isolate it in its own lane with its own capacity.

3. Checkout entry by default. Reserving at add-to-cart with ~2.5% conversion means ~97.5% of holds expire unused, so you show "sold out" with full warehouses. *If pushed:* limited drops invert this, because stock is fixed, the queue is the product, and losing the item at the payment step is unacceptable, so drops reserve at add-to-cart with a 10-minute TTL and a visible countdown. Make it a per-SKU-class policy flag, not a global constant.

4. Untreated, they are told "sold out" when stock exists, which is underselling, the expensive failure. Mitigate in two layers: probe the next bucket and then steal from the fullest before giving up, and set a merge threshold so that when `total_remaining < 2N` a coordinator collapses all buckets into one row and promotes the SKU to the queue lane. *If pushed:* the merge needs a brief exclusive window across all `N` rows, which is a real if short stall. Do it under a distributed lock (see #35) with a hard timeout, and if the merge fails, fail *closed* to the queue lane using the last consistent total rather than leaving buckets half-merged.

5. Yes, on replenishable stock. An oversell costs a cancellation, a goodwill credit, and some brand damage; an undersell costs the whole margin on a unit that existed plus the acquisition spend on that session plus the customer who buys it elsewhere. A ~0.1–0.5% oversell rate on the long tail is a rational trade. *If pushed:* never on limited drops, where no unit can be conjured and each cancellation is a public incident. Track oversell rate as a first-class SLO with an automatic tightening of the buffer when it breaches, and make the cancellation path generous and automatic rather than a support ticket.

6. No. The `Idempotency-Key` is written under a unique index in the same transaction as the order row, so the second insert violates the constraint and we return the original order. *If pushed:* the key must be generated once per checkout session and stored with the cart, not per click, because a fresh UUID per submit makes the scheme decorative. If the duplicate arrives while the first is still `PENDING`, return `409` with `Retry-After` and the `order_id` and let the client poll, rather than blocking a thread on the payment provider.

7. The saga extends the hold before calling payment. The TTL is refreshed to `now + payment_timeout + margin` as the charge step begins, so a hold cannot expire under a live authorisation. If it expires anyway (a sweeper race, or a payment that outran its timeout), the order lands in `PAID_UNRESERVED`: the money is real, the stock is not. *If pushed:* re-attempt the reserve immediately; if it fails, this is an oversell and the compensation is a full automatic refund plus a goodwill credit, alerted as an SLO breach. Never leave a paid order without either stock or a refund, because that state is a support incident by default.

8. It runs in the cold lane for its first few seconds, because the classifier needs a 10-second window to see the rate. One row absorbs the burst as conditional updates, most of which affect zero rows and reject the buyer. It fails safely rather than overselling, but those are exactly the seconds you wanted to sell in. *If pushed:* do not fix it by shortening the window, because the classifier then flaps on ordinary noise and a lane change during a bucket merge is the transition that can lose count. Fix it with a separate burst detector on request rate at the load balancer that can promote a SKU straight to hot within about a second, leaving the rate window to handle demotion. Scheduled sales are pre-classified hours ahead and never touch this path.

9. Because a partition per SKU means 200M partitions and no broker runs that. Multiplex 1,000 SKUs into one partition and you have reintroduced head-of-line blocking between SKUs that have nothing to do with each other, which is the exact thing the lane exists to prevent. *If pushed:* the second reason is latency. The queue lane turns a 3ms synchronous reserve into a ticket plus a push with a p99 near 250ms, and 99.99% of reserves have no contention to resolve. It is the right default only for a small catalog, roughly under 10,000 active SKUs, or for a drops-only business where an asynchronous reserve is the normal experience.

10. Cold lines first, synchronously, then queue the hot line and hold the cold ones while the ticket is outstanding. Ordinary stock is then held hostage to the queue, so cap that hold at the hot lane's p99 rather than at the full 15-minute TTL. *If pushed:* there is no transaction across the lanes and I would not pretend otherwise. If the hot line comes back sold out, bias toward partial fulfilment: ship what we can and say plainly that the doorbuster missed, because a partial order recovers most of the basket and a full release recovers none. Making it atomic requires a synchronous hot reserve, which is the property we deliberately gave up.

11. Because the product page cannot know the answer. A "buy 3 get 1 free" promotion depends on the rest of the cart and tax depends on an address, so the displayed number is a cached opinion and the checkout evaluation is the fact. *If pushed:* the design obligation is transparency, not equality. Return `quoted_total` with a `changes[]` array explaining each delta, carry `accepted_total` on `POST /orders`, and reject with `price_changed` if the two disagree so nobody is charged a number they did not see. Whether to absorb a small increase is business policy that varies by jurisdiction, so make it a threshold, for example under 2% or £1. The rule underneath all of it: never build a design where cache invalidation has to be correct for money to be correct.

12. Two, not four. Merge is a union by SKU taking `max(qty)` rather than `sum(qty)`, because a shopper who added the same item on a phone and a laptop meant to buy one lot of two, and silently making it four is a real and common complaint. *If pushed:* `max` occasionally under-counts someone who genuinely wanted four, and that is the cheaper error because it is one click to fix in the UI whereas the other direction is a wrong charge and a return. Lines that conflict, a delisted SKU or a saved price that moved past a threshold, come back in a `conflicts[]` array for the UI to surface rather than being mutated silently.
#### Whiteboard script
**0-5, split the problem before you draw anything.** Open with the ratio, not the components: "there are about 1,600 page views per order, so browse is a caching problem and buying is a contention problem, and I am going to design them separately." Then ask the three questions that actually change the answer: is stock replenishable or are these limited drops, do we ever accept overselling, and are flash sales scheduled or can they start unannounced. State the numbers you are working from out loud: 200M SKUs, ~11k page views/s at normal peak, ~8k reserve attempts/s against one SKU row at T+0 of a drop.

**5-15, the two columns.** Draw the read path down the left: client, CDN, catalog and search on origin miss. Say the one thing that makes it work, which is splitting the page where volatility changes, a shell cached for minutes and a price and stock fragment cached for seconds. Say immediately that none of it is authoritative, because the checkout re-prices, and give the rule: never build a design where cache invalidation has to be correct for money to be correct. Then the write path down the right: gateway, cart, checkout saga, inventory, payment as someone else's problem (#23), fulfilment. The two columns share only the gateway, and that is deliberate: a saturated inventory row must not be able to slow down browsing.

**15-35, the hot SKU, which is the whole interview.** Protect this time. Start with why both textbook answers fail and put numbers on it: optimistic retry livelocks because retries stack on new arrivals, and a row lock at a 3ms critical section gives 330 decrements/s against 8,000 arrivals/s, so the queue grows by 7,670 a second and pins connections until unrelated SKUs start timing out. Then introduce the classifier before any lane, because the classifier is the design. Draw the three lanes: conditional update, 32 bucket rows, single-consumer log. Name the property that justifies the third one, which is that a lock queue must be walked and a log can be truncated once the counter hits zero. Then volunteer the bucket endgame and the merge at `2N` before it is found, because underselling is the expensive error. Finish the band on the business layer: state the oversell against undersell arithmetic in money, then commit to a per-SKU-class policy rather than one global rule, and say you would carry the oversell rate as an SLO so the deliberate trade cannot quietly become an accident.

**35-45, concede and close.** Give the gaps first: a cart mixing a hot line and cold lines has no atomicity, the displayed price cannot be guaranteed, and the classifier is reactive so an unannounced spike runs in the wrong lane for a few seconds. Then the operational surface in two minutes: pre-warm and a waiting room for scheduled drops, the graded shedding ladder with browse and in-flight checkouts protected absolutely, and the four metrics you would page on, which are oversell rate, sold-out-with-stock count, hot-lane drain time after zero, and checkout success by stage.

Cut first: the search and ranking pipeline, then the guest-cart merge rules, then the multi-region and DR detail. All three are real and none of them changes the shape of the answer. Never cut: the read-to-write ratio that justifies two systems, why a row lock queues faster than it drains, and the oversell decision stated in money.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **products** (partitioned document store, e.g. DynamoDB), partition key `sku_id`; ~4KB/doc, 200M docs
- **catalog_index** (OpenSearch), routing key `hash(sku_id)`; fed by CDC from `products`
- **inventory** (in-memory counters with durable backing, Redis Cluster + Postgres), partition key `(sku_id, location_id)`; warm SKUs additionally keyed `(sku_id, bucket_no)` for `bucket_no ∈ [0, N)`
- **holds** (Redis with native TTL), key `hold:{sku_id}:{hold_id}`, value `(cart_id, qty, expires_at, state)`
- **carts** (KV store), partition key `cart_id`; a `user_id` secondary index resolves the signed-in cart on merge
- **orders** (Postgres, sharded by `hash(order_id)`), partition key `order_id`, secondary index on `(user_id, created_at)`
- **idempotency** (same order shard, unique index on `idempotency_key`): never a separate service, so the dedupe and the order commit share one transaction
- **order_events** (append-only Kafka topic), key `order_id`; the audit trail and the fulfilment feed
- **prices_promos** (rules store + edge KV projection), key `(sku_id, market)`; the projection is display-only, the rules store is authoritative
- **media** (object store + CDN), key `{sku_id}/{rendition}`

**API contract**

```
GET  /search?q=&facets=&page=   → { results:[{sku,title,price,rating,thumb}], facets, total }
GET  /p/{sku}                   → { sku, title, media[], attrs, description }   (CDN, 5m TTL)
GET  /p/{sku}/live              → { price, stock_band, promos[] }               (edge KV, 15s TTL)

POST /cart/items                body: { cart_id?, sku, qty }
                                → { cart_id, lines[], subtotal }
POST /cart/merge                body: { guest_cart_id }
                                → { cart_id, lines[], conflicts[] }

POST /checkout/session          body: { cart_id }
                                → { checkout_id, holds[], expires_at, quoted_total, changes[] }
POST /orders                    headers: Idempotency-Key
                                body: { checkout_id, address, payment_token, accepted_total }
                                → { order_id, status: confirmed|price_changed|sold_out|queued }
GET  /orders/{id}               → { status, lines[], timeline[] }
WS   /checkout/{id}/events      ← { granted|sold_out|expired }   (hot-SKU queue result)
```

**Observability**

- **Product page latency** (edge hit and origin miss, tracked separately). SLO p99 < 200ms at the edge, < 400ms on origin miss; the edge number is the one shoppers feel at scale, and separating them stops a good hit ratio from hiding a rotting origin.
- **CDN cache hit ratio** (per surrogate-key class). SLO ≥ 95% for product shells, ≥ 80% for the live fragment; a hit-ratio dip is the leading indicator of an origin overload, minutes before latency moves.
- **Oversell rate** (units sold beyond on-hand ÷ units sold). SLO ≤ 0.1% on replenishable stock and 0 on limited drops; breach auto-tightens the oversell buffer and pages, because this is the metric where a deliberate trade-off becomes an accidental one.
- **Sold-out-with-stock counter** (reserve rejections where total remaining across buckets > 0). SLO ≈ 0; every occurrence is lost revenue and it is the only direct signal that the bucket endgame is misbehaving.
- **Hot-lane queue depth and drain time** (per hot SKU). Alert when depth exceeds 100k or drain time after zero-stock exceeds 2s; a rising drain time means the consumer is not short-circuiting and is walking the backlog instead.
- **Checkout success rate by stage** (session → reserve → payment → confirm). SLO ≥ 98% reserve-to-confirm; a stage-attributed drop distinguishes an inventory problem from a payment problem within one dashboard glance.
- **Price-change divergence rate** (orders returning `price_changed`). SLO < 0.5%; a spike means edge KV TTLs or promo propagation are out of step and shoppers are being repeatedly re-quoted.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** catalog, search, media and carts are active-active, because they are read-dominated and tolerant of seconds of staleness. Inventory and orders are **single-writer per key**: each SKU is homed to one region, each order to one shard's region. This is the one place where active-active is wrong; a multi-master counter resolves conflicts by merging, and merged decrements oversell by construction.
- **RTO:** ~30s for in-region replica promotion (catalog, cart, search). ~5 minutes for inventory home-region failover, because the new home must replay the durable hold log before accepting reserves, and accepting them early is exactly how you oversell.
- **RPO:** ~0 for orders and payments (synchronous quorum before ack; nothing is confirmed to a shopper until it is durable). ~seconds for carts and catalog (async replication; a lost cart edit is recoverable by the shopper). Holds: ~50ms, bounded by the counter persistence interval, which is why a re-applied decrement must be idempotent on `hold_id`.
- **Failover cadence:** in-region promotion is automatic; cross-region inventory failover is a deliberate operator action with a runbook, because the replay step is not safely automatic. Game-days quarterly, and one mandatory rehearsal in the four weeks before a known peak event.
- **Cross-region cost:** the catalog is the bulk, at ~800GB of documents plus ~520TB of media, replicated once and then served from CDN, so steady-state egress is dominated by cache fill, not by replication. Orders and the event log are ~0.5GB/day, negligible. Inventory replicates a change log of ~64B records at ~2k/s peak ≈ ~130KB/s, which is trivially cheap and worth doing synchronously within a region.

### 49. Design Ticketmaster (High-Demand Ticket Booking)
#### Problem
Sell specific numbered seats for a live event to more than a million people who all press "buy" at the same publicly announced second. No seat may ever be sold twice, and the funded, organised operations whose business is beating real users to the good seats must not take the allocation.
#### Core
The write race everyone reaches for is the easy part. One conditional set on a seat key settles two buyers in a microsecond. The load is on the read side, and the whole design is an inversion: make everything the crowd looks at a single shared object, and meter everything else.

At the announced instant about 1.5M people arrive in ten seconds against 60,000 named seats, 25 buyers per seat. Each arrival gets a queue token carrying a random 64-bit sort key, written to a sharded in-memory set: 150k writes/s with no counter and therefore no hotspot. From then the client touches no origin. It polls two cacheable objects: a global now-serving watermark of about 20 bytes on a 2s TTL, and a 2-bit-per-seat status bitmap, 5KB gzipped, republished once a second. Position is subtraction on the client. A per-user position endpoint would be 300k QPS of pure overhead; one shared object collapses it to 50 origin requests per second.

An admission controller releases users into the purchase flow at a rate from Little's law: cap in-flow buyers at 25,000 so the worst case is one venue's worth of seats held, mean session 240s, so about 100 admissions/s. Refill from completions, not a clock. Inside the gate a hold is a lease: conditional set with a 600s expiry, seats acquired in ascending id order, release compares before it deletes.

The random sort key is the fairness decision. First-come-first-served sells the show to whoever has the lowest latency, which is the bots.

Then be honest about the terminal state. 60,000 seats go in seven minutes, so 97% of the queue must be told "sold out" inside a minute rather than left watching a countdown.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a stadium box office with exactly 60,000 numbered seats, and a queue outside that goes from empty to a million people in ten seconds because the on-sale time was printed on a poster. Everyone wants row 5 centre. A security guard at the door lets people in at a rate the tills can actually serve, hands everyone else a numbered slip, and tells the people at the back the truth as soon as it is known: the seats will be gone long before you reach the front. This is deliberately *not* the hotel problem (see #19). Hotel demand arrives as a smooth Poisson-ish trickle against interchangeable room-type counters, and a hot room-night is a rare pathology. Here the demand curve is a spike, the inventory is individually identified seats that buyers contend for *by name*, and there is an organised, funded adversary whose entire business is beating your real users to row 5.

**The approaches people actually take:**

*Meter the crowd before it reaches the application.* Hand every arrival a cheap token, publish one shared number saying how far the sale has got, and let a gate release buyers at a rate you chose. Buys a purchase path that never sees more than a few hundred concurrent buyers however many are outside. Costs a visible waiting room and an obligation to be honest about scarcity. Wins when arrival rate exceeds serviceable rate by more than an order of magnitude, which here it does by three.

*Sell from one shared picture, refreshed on a fixed tick.* Rather than every client asking the inventory store what is free, publish one compact snapshot of every seat's status to the edge each second, identical bytes for everyone. Buys read load independent of audience size. Costs up to a tick of staleness, so some clicks land on seats already taken and must be refused in the response rather than prevented. Wins when the shared object is small enough to republish often: fine for 60,000 seats in a few kilobytes, hopeless for anything per-user.

*Decide who gets served by drawing lots rather than by arrival order.* Buys two things at once: the latency advantage money can buy becomes worthless, and the ordering shards with no coordination because there is no counter to increment. Costs a direct contradiction of what users believe fairness is, and it does not stop an attacker buying more entries. Wins when inventory is exhausted inside the window where network position, not human reaction, decides the order.

**The single-request walkthrough (the read path, the one that kills you):** at 09:59:50 a user loads the event page. They get a static HTML shell and a JavaScript client from the CDN, with no origin request at all. The client calls `GET /event/42/queue` and receives a queue token: a 16-byte opaque id plus a random 64-bit `sort_key` drawn at issue time. That is one origin write, about 150k of them per second across the arriving crowd, absorbed by a sharded counter-free token service (random keys mean no single INCR hotspot). From then on the client is entirely CDN-fed. It polls `GET /q/42/serving` every 5s, a ~20B JSON object holding a single `now_serving` watermark cached at every POP with a 2s TTL, and it polls the seat bitmap every 1s so the waiting room can show a live map rather than a spinner. 1.5M clients at 1 poll / 5s is ~300k req/s for the watermark, but the origin sees ~100 POPs ÷ 2s ≈ ~50 req/s. Position is computed *on the client* by comparing its own `sort_key` rank against the watermark. The waiting room costs essentially nothing in origin capacity; what it costs is edge egress, which is a bill rather than an outage.

**The single-request walkthrough (the write path):** the watermark passes the user's key at 10:03:12. The client exchanges its token for a session at `POST /event/42/admit`; the Admission Controller checks a risk score, then grants a 15-minute purchase session. The client fetches the venue geometry if it has not already (~2.4MB of section/row/seat coordinates, immutable per venue configuration, cached at the CDN forever behind a versioned URL). The user clicks seats 118-C-7 and 118-C-8. `POST /event/42/hold` sorts the seat ids ascending (deadlock avoidance), then issues `SET seat:42:118-C-7 <session> NX EX 600` against Redis, a compare-and-set that succeeds only if the key is absent. Both succeed in ~1.5ms; a hold record is written behind to the durable store. The user has 10 minutes. Checkout runs the payment saga (see #23), flips both seats from `held` to `sold`, and emits two ticket records with rotating-barcode seeds. If the user does nothing, the Redis key TTL returns the seats to `available` and the next bitmap publish shows them green again.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **CDN with short-TTL micro-objects (Fastly/CloudFront).** Serves the waiting page, the `now_serving` watermark and the seat-status bitmap. This is the single most load-bearing component. Every one of those objects is *shared* across all viewers, so a 150,000:1 request-collapsing ratio is available for free; you only get it if you make the object global rather than per-user.
- **Queue token service (Redis Cluster, random sort keys).** Issues a token per arriving user. Deliberately *not* a monotonic counter: a single `INCR` tops out around 150k ops/s and, worse, makes arrival order the thing being competed for. A random 64-bit key is a lottery draw, shardable across 16 nodes with zero coordination.
- **Admission Controller (token bucket, see #1).** Releases users from the queue into the purchase flow at a rate derived from Little's law rather than from a guess. Same primitive as a rate limiter, sized by inventory rather than by capacity.
- **Seat state store (Redis with `SET NX EX`, plus write-behind to Postgres).** The authoritative *hot* copy of every seat's status. An in-memory store with atomic conditional-set primitives and native key TTLs gives hold acquisition, hold expiry and hold release in one operation each, at about 100µs. See #35 for the general lock semantics; a seat hold is a lease with a TTL, which is a distributed lock wearing a business name.
- **Risk Engine.** Scores every token at issue and again at admission: device fingerprint, TLS/JA3 signature, residential-proxy ASN reputation, account age, payment-instrument reuse. Its output is *challenge / allow / shadow-deny*, never a hard block, because a hard block is a free A/B signal for the attacker.
- **Order and ticket store (Postgres, partitioned by event).** The durable record, and small: about 60k tickets per event. The difficulty here is arrival shape, not volume.

**The thing that makes it hard:** the demand curve is a spike, and *the read side is bigger than the write side*. Everyone fixates on "two people want the same seat". That race is real but it is one `SET NX` and it is over in a microsecond. The actual failure is that 1.5M browsers each want a live picture of 60,000 seats, refreshed as other people take them. Naively that is 1.5M × 60k seat states/s of read amplification. Every naive fix fails in a different way. Querying the seat table per client melts the database on *reads* before a single hold is attempted. Holding a WebSocket per client for push updates means 1.5M connections opened inside ten seconds, a connection-establishment stampede your load balancers will not survive. Optimistic retry on the seat rows produces livelock: 500 clients all CAS on row 5 centre, one wins, 499 retry, they collide again, and the retry traffic grows faster than the inventory shrinks. And the queue itself, if you implement it as "everyone polls an application server for their position", is a 300k QPS service that exists purely to tell people to wait.

**Why this design and what it costs:** you invert the problem. Make the hot state a *single shared immutable object* rather than a per-user query, and put a rate-limiting gate in front of everything that is not. The seat bitmap is one ~5KB artefact republished once per second; 1.5M viewers of one object is a CDN's happiest possible day, and one second of staleness costs a user an occasional "that seat just went", the same acceptable friction #19 accepts between its search index and its inventory rows. The virtual waiting room converts an unbounded spike into a controlled trickle: admit about 100 users/s, and the purchase path never sees more than a few hundred concurrent buyers no matter how many are outside. What it costs is honesty about scarcity. With 60k seats and 1.5M buyers, roughly 97% of the queue will never be admitted, and the queue's most important job is telling them that quickly rather than fairly ordering people who cannot be served.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Fastly or CloudFront for the waiting page, watermark and seat bitmap. Redis Cluster for queue tokens and seat state (`SET NX EX` plus keyspace-expiry events). A small Go admission service. Postgres partitioned by `event_id` for orders and tickets. Kafka for the write-behind and the audit log. Stripe behind the saga of #23.
- Admission and hold hot path:
  ```
  issue_token(event, req):                    -- ~150k/s at the spike
    tok = { id: uuid4(), sort_key: rand64(),
            risk: risk.score(req.fingerprint, req.asn) }
    redis.zadd("q:{event}", tok.sort_key, tok.id)   -- sharded 16 ways
    return tok                                -- client polls CDN from here on

  admit_loop(event):                          -- one leader per event
    while inflight(event) < CONCURRENCY_CAP:  -- 25,000
      tok = queue.pop_lowest_sort_key()
      if tok.risk > THRESH: challenge(tok); continue
      grant_session(tok, ttl=15min)
      publish_watermark(event, tok.sort_key)  -- CDN object, 2s TTL

  hold(session, seat_ids):                    -- all-or-nothing
    for s in sorted(seat_ids):                -- ascending: no deadlock
      if not redis.set("seat:{e}:{s}", session, nx=True, ex=600):
        release(acquired); return 409 CONFLICT
      acquired.append(s)
    kafka.emit(HoldTaken(session, acquired))  -- write-behind durability
    return { hold_id, expires_at: now+600 }
  ```
#### What this is really testing
Whether you put the defence in front of the transaction or inside it. At 25 buyers per seat the seat lock is the trivial part: one conditional set, one winner, microseconds, no retry loop. The system is the read fan-out and the gate. A candidate who spends the hour on isolation levels and row locks has answered a reservations question and missed that the database in this design is never allowed to see contention it was not admitted for. The second half of the insight is that fairness here is not a UX detail but a security control: whichever ordering rule you pick is the rule the adversary optimises against, and arrival-time ordering is an auction on network latency that you would be running on the scalpers' behalf.

The contrast is with the e-commerce flash sale. That question shares almost everything: an announced instant, a spike two or three orders of magnitude above baseline, and bots. It differs on exactly one axis, and that axis changes every answer. Flash-sale inventory is a *count of interchangeable units*. A count can be split across N shards holding stock/N each, so contention divides by N and effectively disappears; it can be deliberately oversold by a fraction and reconciled afterwards with a refund and an apology; and a buyer who wanted the third unit does not care which one they get, so the server can pick, batch, and shed load at will. None of that exists for seat 118-C-7. It is one object, so there is nothing to shard it into. It has no substitute, because a buyer who wants row 5 centre will not take row 40 and will say so publicly. And it cannot be oversold and settled with money, because two people holding tickets for the same seat both physically walk to it. So Q48 can spend its budget on write-path sharding and can afford to be approximate at the margin, while Q49 has to spend its budget keeping the crowd away from the write path entirely and has a correctness bar with no acceptable error rate.

Q55 is the other neighbour and is further away than it looks. It is also contention at a deadline, but the deadline is the *end* of the sale rather than the start, there is one item with no substitute rather than 60,000, and the contention is price discovery over days rather than a rush at an instant. The central move here, throttling arrivals so the write path never sees the crowd, is unavailable there: you cannot make a bidder wait past the close.

Closest question: Q48
#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Reserved seating with a seat map, or general admission by quantity?
- Is the on-sale time publicly announced, or a rolling/staggered release?
- Fairness model, strict first-come-first-served or a randomised draw at the on-sale instant?
- Are we in the resale market too, or primary sales only?
- What is the purchase limit, and enforced against what identity: account, payment instrument, or delivery address?
- Is pricing fixed at announcement, or does it move during the on-sale?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Reserved seating with a seat map | seat-level state with atomic per-seat holds, plus a shared CDN-published status bitmap for reads; general admission instead collapses to a sharded counter, closer to #19 |
| Publicly announced on-sale time | a virtual waiting room is mandatory, not optional; the spike becomes the primary design driver |
| Staggered / rolling release | admission control can be gentler, and the queue becomes a smoothing buffer rather than a dam |
| Randomised draw fairness | tokens carry a random sort key, killing the latency advantage bots buy; strict FCFS instead needs a monotonic sequencer that is both a hotspot and a bot subsidy |
| Resale in scope | tickets need transferable identity and rotating barcodes, plus a price-cap policy engine |
| Purchase limits per payment instrument | identity resolution across accounts becomes a first-class service, not a validation rule |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** browse events, view a live seat map, join the queue, be admitted, hold specific seats, check out, receive transferable tickets; enforce purchase limits; release expired holds.
- **NFR:** zero double-sold seats (hard, every incident is a postmortem); seat map staleness ≤ 1s; queue-position update ≤ 5s; hold acquisition p99 < 100ms; the system must absorb ~150k arrivals/s for ~10s with no origin saturation; ≥ 90% of primary inventory sold to non-automated buyers.

**Scale**

- **Platform baseline:** Ticketmaster reports on the order of ~600M fee-bearing tickets/yr across Live Nation platforms (earnings disclosures, approximate). 600M ÷ 365 ≈ ~1.6M tickets/day average. The average is a lie for this system: essentially all of the engineering difficulty lives in a few hundred on-sale minutes per year.
- **The on-sale spike:** assume a ~60k-seat stadium show and ~1.5M users arriving within the first ~10s. Arrival rate = 1.5M ÷ 10 = ~150k new sessions/s. Buyer-to-seat ratio = 1.5M ÷ 60k = **25:1**. At an average order of ~2.4 seats, tickets wanted = 1.5M × 2.4 = ~3.6M against 60k, so **~60:1 by ticket**. Roughly 1 in 60 arrivals leaves with anything.
- **Concurrent on-sales:** ~10k events are live in the catalogue at any moment, but only ~200 are inside an active on-sale window on a busy Friday morning. The 10k figure sizes resident seat state; the 200 figure sizes bitmap publishing and hot-path capacity. Keep them apart or every downstream number comes out 50× wrong.
- **Seat-map reads (the load nobody budgets for):** static geometry = 60k seats × ~40B (seat_id 4B + section 2B + row 2B + number 2B + x/y 8B + tier 1B + label ~12B + padding ~9B) ≈ ~2.4MB, immutable per venue configuration. Dynamic status = 2 bits/seat, so 60k × 2 bits = ~15KB raw, ~5KB gzipped. Queued users see the live map too (a waiting room with no visible reason is worse than one with), so assume all 1.5M poll status every 1s. From origin that is 1.5M × 5KB = ~7.5GB/s ≈ ~60 Gbps sustained. CDN-served with a 1s TTL, the origin serves one object per POP per second: ~100 POPs, so ~100 req/s. A **~150,000:1** collapse, and the whole reason the read path is survivable. Edge egress stays at ~7.5GB/s, which for a ~10-minute on-sale is ~4.5TB and a two-figure dollar bill.
- **Queue-position reads:** 1.5M clients × 1 poll / 5s = ~300k req/s. Published as one global `now_serving` watermark (~20B) with a 2s CDN TTL, so origin = ~100 POPs ÷ 2s ≈ **~50 req/s**. Position is computed client-side.
- **Admission rate (derived, not guessed):** Little's law. Cap concurrent in-flow buyers at C = 25,000. Each may hold ~2.4 seats, so worst case 25,000 × 2.4 = 60k seats held, exactly one venue's worth and no more. Average in-flow session ≈ 4 min = 240s (most users abandon or finish well inside the 10-min hold TTL). Admission rate = 25,000 ÷ 240 ≈ ~104 users/s, round to **~100/s**.
- **Time to sell out:** 60k seats ÷ 2.4 seats/order = ~25k orders needed; at a ~60% checkout completion rate that requires 25k ÷ 0.6 ≈ ~42k admissions. 42k ÷ 100/s ≈ ~420s ≈ **~7 minutes**.
- **Queue drain vs inventory (the honest number):** draining all 1.5M at 100/s would take 1.5M ÷ 100 = 15,000s ≈ **~4.2 hours**, but inventory is gone in ~7 minutes. So ~1.46M users (~97%) must be told "sold out" without ever being admitted. Design the terminal state first.
- **Seat state per event:** ~80B/seat (seat_id 8B + status 1B + holder_token 16B + hold_expiry 8B + order_id 16B + price_tier 2B + version 4B + padding ~25B). 60k × 80B = **~5MB per event**, so an entire stadium on-sale's hot working set fits in one Redis shard. ~10k live events × 5MB = ~50GB cluster-wide; RF=2 in memory gives ~100GB.
- **Hold write rate:** ~100 admissions/s × ~2.5 hold attempts each (users retry after losing a race) × ~2.4 seats ≈ **~600 CAS ops/s per event**. Trivial in absolute throughput. The difficulty is contention on the *same* keys, not ops/s, which is exactly why gating admission is the right lever.
- **Durable records:** order ≈ ~400B (order_id 16B + user_id 16B + event_id 8B + seats array ~6×8B + price 8B + payment_ref 32B + status 4B + timestamps 24B + delivery ~200B + padding ~44B). Ticket ≈ ~200B (ticket_id 16B + order_id 16B + seat_id 8B + event_id 8B + barcode_seed 32B + rotation_epoch 8B + status 1B + transfer_ptr 8B + audit ~80B + padding ~23B). 600M tickets/yr × 200B = ~120GB/yr; RF=3 gives **~360GB/yr**. The dataset is small; the arrival shape is the problem.
- **Venue geometry assets:** ~10k distinct venue configurations × ~2.4MB ≈ ~24GB of immutable CDN objects. Never invalidated: a new configuration is a new URL.
- **Queue tokens:** 1.5M × ~64B (id 16B + issued_at 8B + sort_key 8B + risk 2B + fingerprint_hash 16B + padding ~14B) ≈ **~100MB per on-sale**, TTL'd 24h after the on-sale opens.
- **Hot vs cold:** seat state is hot for the ~2 hours around on-sale and read-mostly forever after. Evict settled events from Redis within 24h; only live and upcoming on-sales stay resident, which is what keeps the ~50GB figure flat rather than growing with the catalogue.
#### Key decisions
**Randomised draw at the on-sale instant, or strict first-come-first-served**
- Choice: a random 64-bit `sort_key` assigned at token issue, served in ascending key order. Everyone arriving in the first 60s goes into one randomised pool; arrivals after that are appended FCFS behind the pool, because by then the fairness question is moot.
- Alternative: strict FCFS by arrival timestamp. This is genuinely defensible and it is what most users assume they are getting. It is legible without explanation, it does not require you to tell someone who clicked at exactly 10:00:00.000 that a die was rolled, and it is what several promoters put in the contract. A randomised draw also has a real failure mode FCFS does not: it makes "I was first" meaningless, which for a small, loyal, non-adversarial audience destroys something people valued.
- Decider: how much of the arrival stream the inventory spans, compared with the latency advantage that money can buy. Inventory here is nominally exhausted by 60k ÷ 150k/s = the first 0.4s of arrivals. A bot on a cloud instance 3ms from the edge beats a home-broadband user by 30 to 50ms, which at 150k arrivals/s is 4,500 to 7,500 positions, so the entire allocation is decided inside a window where only network position varies and human click time does not enter. Second half of the decider: a monotonic sequencer to produce FCFS order tops out around 150k ops/s, which is exactly peak, with zero headroom and a livelock risk on retry.
- Alternative wins when: inventory spans more than about a second of arrivals, so human reaction spread (a few hundred milliseconds across a real crowd) dominates the purchasable network advantage. Concretely, at 5k arrivals/s a 60k allocation spans 12s, and FCFS then really is ordering people rather than ordering their ISPs. It also wins outright when the on-sale time is not publicly announced (no instant to race to), or when the promoter contractually requires it, in which case the honest engineering answer is to build FCFS and spend the saved fairness budget on identity-bound caps instead.

**Seat truth in an in-memory lease store, or in the transactional store alone**
- Choice: Redis as the authoritative hot copy, `SET NX EX 600` for holds, key TTL as the expiry mechanism, write-behind to Postgres via Kafka, and `held → sold` as a synchronous Postgres transaction.
- Alternative: hold state in Postgres only, with a unique partial index on `(event_id, seat_id) WHERE status <> 'available'` doing the mutual exclusion and an `expires_at` predicate doing the lease. One store, one truth, no reconciliation protocol, no class of incident that begins "Redis lost 300ms of holds". At ~600 CAS/s per event, throughput is not the reason to reject it.
- Decider: bitmap publishing cost across concurrent on-sales, plus who owns expiry. One publish is a 60k-row status snapshot. For a single event at 1 Hz that is 60k rows/s, which Postgres serves from shared buffers without noticing. At the ~200 concurrently active on-sales assumed above it is 200 × 60k = 12M rows/s of scanning that exists purely to feed a read cache, plus a reaper sweeping expired holds across all of them and competing with the same tables. Above roughly 20 simultaneous on-sales, or if you want the map fresher than 1 Hz, the in-memory copy stops being an optimisation and becomes the only shape that works.
- Alternative wins when: you run a handful of large on-sales at a time, which describes a single-venue or single-promoter operator rather than a marketplace, or when you cannot staff the runbook the split demands. Be clear about what the split costs: two stores means a window in which Redis holds state Postgres has not seen, so failover is a freeze, rebuild from Postgres `sold` rows plus the ordered Kafka log, and reopen, roughly 30 to 60s of downtime that you must have rehearsed. A single store has no such protocol because it has no such window.

**Bot defence: detect at the gate, or remove the resale margin**
- Choice: both, but weight the spend towards removing the margin. Layer cheap controls at the token gate (a ~200ms proof-of-work, TLS/JA3 and device fingerprinting, residential-proxy ASN reputation, identity-graph caps, shadow-denial for high-confidence bots), and make the ticket a registered instrument: rotating `HMAC` barcode, transfer only through the platform, price cap on resale.
- Alternative: detection only, leaving the ticket a transferable bearer instrument. This is the honest choice when the promoter wants a liquid resale market, when group organisers and gift-givers are a large share of buyers, or where consumer law protects a purchaser's right to resell freely, which is the case in a growing list of jurisdictions.
- Decider: the attacker's margin per ticket against your cost per blocked attempt. A $150 face ticket that resells at $600 leaves $450 of margin, so 1,000 tickets on one show is ~$450k. Against that, residential proxy bandwidth is a few dollars per GB and CAPTCHA-solving farms charge on the order of $1 to $2 per 1,000 solves, putting the attacker's cost per attempt in the single-digit cents: a ratio around 10,000:1, at which no detection control clears its own false-positive cost. A 10% resale price cap collapses $450 of margin to ~$15 and the attack stops funding itself. State the target as a number, because "stop the bots" is not one: ≥ 90% of primary inventory to non-automated buyers.
- Alternative wins when: transfer restriction is unlawful or contractually barred in the market, or the product genuinely is a tradeable asset (season tickets, corporate boxes, secondary-market inventory you list yourself). Then detection is all you have, and you should budget it as continuous adversarial operations staffing rather than as a feature you ship once. It is worth conceding that detection-only is not hopeless, just expensive and permanently ongoing: layered signals do measurably move the humans-to-bots ratio, they simply never converge.

**How to read the diagram:** the left column is the read path and it never touches the origin. The waiting page, the position watermark and the seat bitmap are all shared CDN objects. The centre column is a funnel: a token service that absorbs the spike, an admission controller that meters it, and a purchase API that only ever sees a few hundred concurrent buyers. The right column is state and adjudication.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** the arrival rate and the service rate differ by three orders of magnitude, so something has to buffer. Putting the buffer in front of the application (a queue of tokens) rather than inside it (threads, connections, database locks) means the expensive tier is sized for the sustainable rate, not the peak. The Risk Engine sits at the *token gate* rather than at checkout because rejecting a bot after it holds a seat has already cost you the seat for ten minutes.

**What this layout buys you:** an origin that is nearly flat through the spike, and a database that never sees contention it was not admitted for. The trade is a user-visible waiting room and up to one second of seat-map staleness, the same bargain #19 makes between its search index and its inventory rows, taken further because the mismatch here is far larger.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**The waiting room and the admission gate.** This is the mechanism that distinguishes the question, and it is where the hour goes. The seat lock gets sixty seconds; this gets twenty minutes.

**Invert the position query.** The naive waiting room is an endpoint that returns "you are number 843,201". At 1.5M clients polling every 5s that is ~300k QPS of per-user state lookup, an entire service tier whose only output is the word "wait". Invert it. The server publishes one global watermark, `now_serving_rank`, about 20 bytes, as a cacheable object with a 2s TTL. The client already knows its own rank, because the token carried the `sort_key`, so it subtracts. Origin load falls to ~100 POPs ÷ 2s ≈ 50 req/s, and, importantly, that number is independent of audience size: three million arrivals produce the same 50 req/s as one and a half. The estimated wait is `(my_rank − now_serving) ÷ observed_admission_rate`, computed locally and smoothed over the last three polls so it does not jitter every time the admission rate wobbles. The client cannot cheat by claiming a better rank, because the rank is signed into the token and re-verified at the gate.

**The same trick on state that actually changes.** The seat map is the harder version of the same idea, because unlike a rank it mutates constantly. Encode every seat's status in 2 bits (available, held, sold, blocked): 60,000 seats is 15KB raw and about 5KB gzipped, and you republish that one object every second. Every viewer receives identical bytes, so 1.5M clients polling at 1 Hz reach the origin as roughly 100 requests per second and cost ~7.5GB/s of edge egress. Keep the per-tick object tiny by splitting immutable from mutable: the ~2.4MB of seat coordinates is geometry, immutable per venue configuration, cached forever behind a versioned URL, and it never appears in the tick. The price of the tick is that every client acts on state up to a second old, which is why `hold` returns `409 CONFLICT` carrying the seat's current status inline. The client greys the seat immediately rather than waiting for the next publish. Conflict is handled in the response, not prevented in the read.

**Do not reach for WebSockets outside the gate.** Push looks like the right answer for a live map and it is the wrong one here. 1.5M TLS handshakes inside ten seconds is a connection-establishment stampede that exhausts load-balancer accept queues before a single seat is sold, and each surviving connection then pins memory in exactly the tier you are trying to keep empty. Push becomes correct *after* admission, where there are ~25,000 concurrent sessions rather than 1.5M, and where you genuinely want it for hold countdowns and seat-taken invalidation. Cheap polling outside the gate, expensive push inside it.

**Size the gate with Little's law, not with a guess.** Pick the concurrency cap from inventory first. At most C buyers in flow, each able to hold up to `max_order` seats, so `C × max_order ≤ total_seats` keeps the worst case at "every seat held, nothing oversold". A 6-seat limit against 60k seats gives C ≈ 10,000; at the realistic 2.4-seat average order, C = 25,000 and 25,000 × 2.4 = 60,000, exactly one venue. Then Little's law gives the rate: 25,000 ÷ 240s mean session ≈ 104/s, rounded to 100/s. Both inputs are things you already established (the seat count and the hold TTL) rather than numbers you asserted, which is the point of deriving it out loud.

**Refill the bucket from completions, never from a clock.** The controller is a token bucket (see #1) whose tokens are returned by checkouts, abandonments and TTL expiries. This matters more than it looks. If admission runs on a fixed schedule while sessions run long, say because the payment provider's p99 doubled, in-flow count drifts past C, every remaining seat ends up held by someone, and admitted users arrive at a fully grey map. That is the worst state the system can produce, because it spends the scarcest resource in the design, an admission slot, on a user who cannot buy anything. Completion-driven refill self-tunes the rate downward when the funnel slows. The cost is an admission rate that varies, which you must surface in the wait estimate rather than hide behind a fixed countdown.

**The queue's most important output is a rejection.** 60,000 seats need about 42,000 admissions to clear (25,000 orders at ~60% checkout completion), and at 100/s that is roughly seven minutes. Draining the whole queue would take 15,000 seconds. So about 97% of the crowd will never be admitted, and the only real design decision left is how fast you say so. Compute a projected exhaustion rank continuously from observed sell-through, and terminate everyone beyond a safety multiple of it with "sold out" plus a waitlist opt-in, targeting inside 90 seconds of on-sale. Keep the multiple at 2× rather than 1×, because roughly 40% of holds do not convert and those seats come back needing buyers who are still present. A countdown that quietly stalls generates more support load and worse press than an early, honest no.

Latency budget for one admitted buyer: token issue ~15ms (one sharded Redis write), watermark polling amortised to ~0, admission handshake ~40ms including the risk lookup, geometry fetch ~80ms from a warm POP, bitmap fetch ~8ms, seat hold p99 under 100ms (dominated by a single `SET NX` at ~1.5ms plus network), checkout 2 to 6s with the payment provider dominating (see #23). The funnel below gives the stage-by-stage cardinalities.
